HOLLYWOOD-MAXINE WELDON (From page 32) 
that, whenever a new talent is born all of a sudden everyone turns out to be an 
agent or a manager or wants to be one. So for the next couple of years she ran 
the garnit of managers and the passels of promises they offered. 
Nothing of any major consequence really happened for the Singing Nurse until 
comedy writer Tony Webster caught her act at the Etc. in Hollywood and asked 
her if he could manage her. From that evening on the destiny has changed con- 
siderably for both parties. Tony was able to get Clive Davis to come into the club, 
which resulted in her being signed to Columbia Records. Next it seems Maxine 
was recording a tune that Tony had written only a few weeks earlier, something 
that sounds like a contemporary standard, called "Looking For the Answer." It's 
Maxine's first single for Columbia, and if program directors want to know just 
what "well-done" really is, they'll take a listen. It's a fantastic record. 
Maxine has been looking for answers all of her life, contending, "One has to 
keep plowing ahead. The sun might be awfully hot, and you want to rest, but 
you've got to go on and try just a little harder.." For Maxine it's definitely harvest 
time. Her manager was happy that CASH BOX was the first magazine to do a 
story on her, but he pointed out, "The life story is fine, but the record is the 
thing that can change the life story." She is currently at work recording her first 
album for Columbia and will be appearing on most of the major network TV 
shows this fall. The next time you are fortunate enough to hear Maxine sing 
"Love Is Beautiful" you'll hear truth and you'll see a star being born. 
Ron Baron 
NEW YORK-IRA BLACKER: THE BRITISH ARE COMING 
American Talent International's executive vice-president Ira Blacker, was one 
of the first booking agents in the States to realize the importance and potential 
of the new British bands which were developing during the late Sixties. 
"Many other agents at the time concentrated on pop and r 'n' b attractions, 
but 
I felt a great affinity with British bands like Ten Years After, Jethro Tull, 
Savoy Brown and Faces," comments Blacker. 
"It was probably a matter of taste, but during that time the only rock bands 
happening came from San Francisco or England." 
During his first three years in the music business Blacker was with Asociated 
Booking, where he began his involvement with contemporary British bands. 
Today, three years after the formation of ATI, Blacker handles tours by Faces, 
Wizzard, Atomic Rooster, Uriah Heep, Fleetwood Mac, The Hollies, Badfinger, 
John Baldry, Deep Purple, Osibisa, Status Quo, Savoy Brown, Rory Gallagher 
and the Electric Light Orchestra. "I liked handling British acts because 
I found 
they were anxious for a break here. When Rod Stewart joined Faces, everyone had 
virtually written off the group in preference for Steve Marriott and Humble Pie. 
But 
I took Faces on their first American tour and the impact was such that 
I 
felt sure that at least they were a good second rate attraction." 
"Rod Stewart made a solo album which crept into the bottom of the charts, 
and then came Faces with an album that went into the Top 60-and gradually 
the band made it through several tours here." 
"To make it here a band must be prepared to tour. In Britain the press can 
virtually create interest in a band, but the U.S. is different. A band must have a 
record company behind it all the way, a certain amount of hype and a will to work. 
That's the only way it can happen," says Blacker. 
"A band from Britain must work the key centers. If they come to The States 
on a six -week tour, they must be prepared to work for six days a week. In the 
beginning it was comparatively easy to create interest in a British band. There 
was still a mystique about them. but now that feeling has almost disappeared 
and it requires hard work to establish a band." 
"Rory Gallagher, for example, is going to be an important artist in America, 
but it's taken a long time. He's now completing his third tour, and a fourth is 
arranged for later this year with Rory as headliner for the first time. It needs 
that kind of commitment from the artist." 
Blacker, during the first 18 months of ATI, concentrated on British artists 
through what he terms the "open market." 
"The fastest way to break an artist is through the open market-local pro- 
moters in halls-rather than the college circuit. It's ten times easier to sell 
an act to a local promoter because the colleges always have to refer to commit- 
tees and so forth." 
On the open market, however, Blacker has a simple philosophy: "Sell out the 
theaters. Even if you have to turn away people, 
I always believe those who can't 
get in to see the show will probably become bigger fans of the band than those 
in the theater." 
"That's what happened in Boston with Faces recently when the fans tried every 
possible way of getting inside the hall. It's always a mistake to have less than 
full houses-it creates an aura of failure for a band." Blacker's next project 
is Family's tour of the U.S. in June.

TOM SAWYER-Original Motion Picture Sound- 
track -United Artists NA-LA057-F 
The Sherman brothers, reknowned for their 
expertise at creating scores for youth oriented 
films have come up with yet another gem for 
the fine award -winning Tom Sawyer musical 
adaption film. Musically and lyrically, the Sher - 
mans have perfectly captured the mood and, 
feel of the Twain character and period. An 
extra added attraction is Charley Pride's al- 
ways smooth presence, on the theme from the 
movie, "River Song." Performances by Cleste 
Holm, Johnny Whittaker, Jeff East and Warren 
Oates are all fully entertaining and make this 
soundtrack one of the most entertaining to 
come down river in a good long time.

THE CONVENTION-By the time you're reading this, the 1973 weekend con- 
vention of MONY, the Westchester Guild and the New York State Operators Guild 
will be a pleasant memory for the hundreds of coin and record tradesters who 
treked out to the Poconos' Mt. Airy Lodge for two days of sun, fun and a bit of 
biz. On the latter, a symposium dealing with gripes on singles was to take place 
Friday night at 8:00 PM. Agenda was to cover problems passed (lack of com- 
munication between the two trades and over -long singles) with problems present 
(badly pressed records and the center hole controversey). We'll report the minutes 
next issue 
. 
. 
Speaking of records, Nashboro Record's president Bud Howell is 
proud to announce by some of the people at Tac Amusement in New Orleans, 
one of that town's largest juke and games routes. Buddy says the single originally 
came out on the Play label and will now be marketed on Excello #2335. Hear it's 
already sold 20,000 pieces in the deep south so it sounds like a budding hit. 
Also on records, Mike Douglas (the TV cat) has a juke natural with his current 
'High Hopes'. Johnny Bilotta, into Fun City last week for soccer game and trip 
to Tenth Ave., loves the single but says the label behind it just hasn't pushed it 
hard enough to create national attention. "I don't think it's asking too much 
that a little promotional push be extended to this record," says John. "All they 
really need to do is expose it to operators and route record buyers at the one - 
stop level and 
I think they'll buy it, and 
I think the folks at the locations will play 
the heck out of it." By the way, John's team, the Miami Toros, tied with the New 
York Cosmos last Wed. nite out at Hofstra University. 
Summer Camp, the two most dreadful words any army reservist or guardsman 
can think of, is the ticket for two of our tradesters these two weeks: National 
Shuffleboard's sales manager Joe Veluzzi and DePerri Advertising Al Guizdak. Both 
are attached to the 50th Armored. Have fun, guys! 
We've got a peck of MOA members in this area and we wonder if they're taking 
advantage of MOA's insurance services. If any member needs insurance of any 
kind, we urge you to look into MOA's excellent range of group insurance plans. 
Here they are: 1) MOA Group Life Insurance, 2) MOA Hospital Money Plan, 3) 
MOA Catastrophe Health Insurance and, 4) MOA Income Replacement Plan. 
Brochures and applications are free for the asking from MOA. Queries about 
claims and details of policies, however, should be directed to: John R. Ruddy, 
International Adminstrators, 330 S. Wells Street, Suite 1110, Chicago, Illinois 
60606. Telephone (312) 922-5253. 
Also on MOA, Fred Granger reports that the 1973 Exposition may be the biggest 
in the 25 years history of the association. "Never before has MOA received so 
many advance requests for exhibit space," Fred stated last week. "Right now, it 
appears that all of last year's exhibitors will be back plus many new ones. We've 
already contracted for additional space in the Conrad Hilton Hotel, where the 
Exposition will be held next Nov. 9-10-11." 
THE JERSEY BOUNCE-Bruce Lipkin and Carolyn Fernacola tied the matri- 
monial knot Sat. May 12th and celebrated with a lavish reception at the fabled 
Manor in West Orange. Party went far into the night and saw quite a number of 
coin people in attendance, including the groom's parents Sol and Marge Lipkin 
(American Shuffleboard), brother Gene (Allied Leisure), American president Mrs. 
Mary Cusano, general manager Nick Melone and sales execs Mike Bozza and Dick 
Delfine. Also in from Chicago for the affair was Mr. and Mrs. Herb Perkins (Purvey- 
or Supply).

Productions,

Blue Note's 
All -Time LP; 
`Black Byrd' 
HOLLYWOOD - "Black Byrd," re- 
cently -released 
album 
by 
Donald 
Byrd, has achieved the milestone of 
becoming the biggest selling LP in 
the history of Blue Note Records, the 
jazz arm of United Artists Records, 
according to Eddie Levine, Blue Note's 
national sales and promo manager. 
The collection was issued last Feb. 
It has achieved best seller status, Le- 
vine says, in such key markets as 
New York, Baltimore, Washington, 
Philadelphia, Detroit, and Chicago, 
and is spreading broadly throughout 
the nation. Another plus factor in the 
sales pattern of "Black Byrd" is the 
growing MOR airplay from such ar- 
eas as Philadelphia, St. Louis, Kan- 
sas City and San Francisco. 
Levine reports Blue Note sales at 
an all-time peak with Lou Donald - 
son's "Sophisticated Lou," Alphonze 
Mouzon's "The Essence of Mystery" 
and Horace Silver's "In Pursuit Of 
The 27th Man," all joining "Black 
Byrd" as top movers in LP retail 
outlets from coast -to -coast.

Tony Orlando 
'Look-Alikes' 
NEW YORK - Bell Records has 
launched 
a 
major, 
promotional 
"Look -Alive" 
contest 
backed 
by 
heavy multi -media advertising, public- 
ity and promo in conjunction with 
Dawn's starring engagement at New 
York's Copacabana. Recently number 
1 
with their million -selling single, 
"Tie A Yellow Ribbon Round The Ole 
Oak Tree," the group will headline at 
the famed nightery from June 7-16. 
The contest to find six look-alikes 
for Tony Orlando, lead singer of the 
group, 
is 
open 
to 
all 
students 
presently enrolled in high schools, 
junior colleges and colleges 
in the 
greater 
New 
York 
Metropolitan 
Area. It culminates on Friday, June 
15, when six winners and their dates 
will be Tony's guests at the Copa. 
Already moving into high gear, 
Bell launched its Tony Orlando look - 
alike contest in mid -May with the 
mass 
mailing of the contest an- 
nouncement and rules, photos and bio 
material to every high school, junior 
college and college in the New York 
Metropolitan area including Long Is- 
land, Connecticut and New Jersey. 
Immediate follow-up includes ad- 
vertising in selected school papers 
and radio spots on both school and 
local radio stations. Bell has printed 
5,000 specially designed contest flyers 
which are now being distributed on 
school campuses and through retail 
record outlets throughout the Metro- 
politan area. 
Dawn's Copa 
opening will gain 
further impetus from a "Rockin The 
Palace" segment taped on the Coast 
in mid -May which will be aired on 
ABC-TV on June 6 and a taped ap- 
pearance 
on 
the 
CBS -TV 
Mike 
Douglas Show, set for June 7.

Tiger Tail 
Kiddie Line 
Mkt Expansion 
NEW YORK - The catalog of Tiger 
Tail Jigsaw Puzzle children's records, 
which now numbers over 25 titles 
encompassing a wide range of en- 
tertainment and instruction material 
for three to nine years old, is expand- 
ing its marketing base. 
Distributed by Audio Fidelity Rec- 
ords, Tiger Tail has been marketed 
up till now in traditional record out- 
lets, but is moving toward expanded 
representation 
in 
the toy depart- 
ments of chain store, supermarket 
and discount toy outlets. 
Audio Fidelity exec vice president 
Harold Drayson states that catalogs 
and display material are available 
and he is interested in inquiries from 
sales reps covering potential Tiger 
Tail outlets. Drayson also notes that 
many of the Tiger Tail titles are 
"ideally" suited to premiums and he 
is considering expanded activity in 
that area. 
Tiger Tail's recorded songs and 
stories are packaged in covers pre- 
cut as jigsaw puzzles thereby com- 
bining a record album and a game 
for the suggested list price of $1.98. 
Titles range from Fairy Tales and 
Mother Goose to early childhod fa- 
vorites such as Goldilocks, Three Lit- 
tle Pigs, Pinocchio and others, to ad - 
Cite Gains In

surprisingly well in the rock format.

television 
has

em-

Farrell Jingle 
Div. On Coast 
In Full Swing 
HOLLYWOOD - The Commercial 
Division of the Wes Farrell Organi- 
zation, which has been successfully 
producing 
music 
for 
commercials 
from its headquarters in New York, 
is now also in full-scale operation on 
the west coast under Tony Asher, 
head of the commercial division's 
west coast office. 
The Los Angeles office, in its first 
month of operation, has produced 
music for commercials for such prod- 
ucts 
as 
Instant 
Maxwell 
House 
Coffee, Mattel Toys and San Diego 
Trust. 
"The reaction so far is terrific," 
says 33 -year -old Asher, the former 
creative supervisor for Ogilvy/Ma- 
ther, Inc. "We are offering something 
unique-a single source of advertis- 
ing music in many different styles by 
our many different writers." 
The Wes Farrell Organization of 
companies encompasses 
music pro- 
duction and 
publishing 
companies 
housing 
a 
stable 
of young 
com- 
posers. These songwriters, who are 
writing hit records, are the same 
ones writing the commercial music, 
according to Asher. 
Asher 
is 
currently preparing a 
mailing to 
local 
area advertising 
agencies and potential users of music 
in commercials of a demo tape of 
spots that have been produced by the 
new west coast division. "Our attrac- 
tion to the advertising community," 
says Asher, "is the Wes Farrell Or- 
ganization's total involvement in all 
areas of the music business. This en- 
ables us the flexibility to produce demo 
jingles considerably faster and more 
economically." 
The west coast office of WFO's 
commercial division has been oper- 
ating since the beginning of April in 
new offices at 9200 Sunset Blvd. in 
Los Angeles.

CashBox Radio-TV News Report 
WNEW-FM `Deserted Island' Poll 
Shows Diversified Music Appeal 
NEW 
YORK - Dave 
Herman, 
WNEW-FM air personality, marked 
his first anniversary on the air for 
the outlet by asking his listeners to 
imagine they would be able to spend 
one year in seclusion on a deserted 
island with a super -powered, battery 
operated sound system. The one catch 
was 
. each person would be al- 
lowed to take only three LP's along 
with him. They could be single or 
multiple record sets, but must be 
packaged as one ablum. He asked his 
listeners to send their replies to him; 
and he programmed all his shows the 
week of May 21, around those re- 
sponses. 
There was a response from 3,870 
people; and 933 separate album titles 
were named in the survey. A list of 
the most requested albums and artists

Ms. Van Dyke 
To Co -Host 
'Miss America' 
HOLLYWOOD - Vonda Van Dyke 
has been 
signed as 
the first 
co - 
hostess and featured performer on 
the Sept. 8 national telecast of the 
Miss America Pageant on NBC-TV 
from Atlantic City. 
The former Miss America, who re- 
cords for Myrrh, recently established 
her own music publishing company, 
Miss A (ASCAP), with an initial re- 
lease of six songs, all with music and 
lyrics by Vonda Van Dyke. 
On June 5 she tapes the syndicated 
Mike Douglas Show from Sea World, 
near Cleveland, on which she'll both 
sing and water ski. 
She opens July 2 for an extended 
engagement at Top of the World in 
the 
Contemporary 
Hotel, 
Disney 
World, Orlando, Fla., the July 
4 
weekend beginning the summer sea- 
son.

KRBE 6-10 AM Air Personality. The pig became a prize in the "KRBE Swine 
Off" -a contest promoting "Charlotte's Web" and the soundtrack album.

Design Seminar 
Offered In July 
NEW YORK - The Institute of Au- 
dio Research, Inc. has announced that 
their five-day Audio Systems Design 
Seminar will take place July 25-29. 
The seminar concentrates on the ap- 
plication 
of modern 
audio design 
techniques and is intended for de- 
sign, studio, maintenance and sound 
system engineers. 
Audio System Design has been suc- 
cessful 
as 
a 
three-week, 
70 -hour 
course. "The condensed course was 
created to meet the needs of engi- 
neers who were unable to attend the 
full course," said 
Iry Diehl, 
co- 
founder of the Institute. 
The seminar is an intensive study 
of practical systems engineering. It 
covers practical theory and applica- 
tion of modern 
design techniques 
which employ the "gain block" and 
constant voltage approach, as well as 
traditional 
methods 
of 
inpedance 
matching, thermal noise evaluation 
and grounding practice. 
Total 
fee 
for 
the 
seminar 
is 
$295.00. This covers cost of texts and 
all other printed materials. Student 
comprehension is aided by texts, a 
complete book of lecture notes and 
extensive reference materials. 
For information and registration, 
contact Iry Diehl at the Institute of 
Audio Research, Inc., 64 University 
Place, New York, 10003, 212/677-7580. 
Deadline for registration in the sem- 
inar is July 11, 1973.

Grosses $56G's 
ATLANTA -A benefit concert held

Industry Execs 
Join Board 
Of Blind Org. 
NEW YORK - Josephine Whitford, 
Dean of Students, Manhattan School 
of Music and president of the Louis 
Braille Foundation for Blind Musi- 
cians, announces the appointment to 
the board of directors of Bruce G. 
Lundvall, vice president, Columbia 
Records, Jerry Greenberg, general 
manager, 
Atlantic 
Records), 
Kal 
Rudman (publisher of The Friday 
Morning Quarterback and contribut- 
ing editor of Record World) and Leon- 
ard Zissu, music and theatrical at- 
torney. 
The Foundation is a national, non- 
profit organization working to pro- 
mote the interests of the blind in the 
field of music. The Foundation exists 
to 
help 
talented, 
blind 
muscians 
achieve professional status as per- 
formers and educators, in order to 
function on a par with their sighted 
colleagues. 
The services of the Foundation are 
available to any blind person. 
Atlantic Picks 
Jilmore Single 
For Release 
PHILADELPHIA - Jilmor Produc- 
tions Inc. has been formed by Gilda 
Woods and Cathy Morrell with head- 
quarters located at 
1 
Maplewood 
Mall, Philadelphia. They have been 
associated together in various fields 
for the past several years. 
Gilda and Cathy recently produced 
their first record for Jilmor at Sigma 
Sound Studios in Philly. The plug 
side is "There's An Island" backed 
with "A Little Bit Of Soap." The rec- 
ord features the voice of newly dis- 
covered "Bobby Newton." 
Jilmor has placed artist and master 
with Atlantic Record's Jerry Green- 
berg. Atlantic has already released 
the record in the U. S. A. and are 
presently planning release in England 
and other foreign markets. "There's 
An Island" has a reggae rhythm and 
sound. Its lyric is appropriate for this 
time of the year and the summer sea- 
son. 
Jerome Joins 
Opal Studios 
NEW 
YORK - Opal Recording 
Studios, 254 West 54th St., New York 
City, announces the signing of Steve 
Jerome as chief engineer. Jerome, a 
veteran of 10 years engineering ex- 
perience has most recently been asso- 
ciated with 
Groove Sound Studios 
where he held posts as chief engineer 
and head of maintenance. He is also 
known in the industry as a producer 
and will work in that area with the 
studio's production arm, Opal Produc- 
tions, Inc. 
Most recently, Jerome was a co- 
producer of the international hit 
"Popcorn" which he also engineered. 
Other chart makers that can be found 
in his list of credits are: "Walk Away 
Renee," "Ving Dong The Witch Is 
Dead," and "Pretty Ballerina."

Polydor Inks Weston 
NEW YORK - Jerry Schoenbaum, 
president of Polydor Incorporated, 
has announced the signing of Randy 
Weston to an exclusive 
recording 
contract. 
The 
progressive 
pianist - 
composer has just completed work at 
New York's Record Plant on his Poly- 
dor debut album, set for a June re- 
lease. 
"Tanjah," the new LP, features a 
19 -piece orchestra in a varied pro- 
gram of Weston's music, as arranged 
and conducted by Melba Liston and 
produced by Weston. Title of the al- 
bum is an Arab -Berber rendering of 
Tangier, the Moroccan city where 
Weston has made his home for the 
past five years. 
ASCAP Mgrs. Retire 
NEW YORK - Harry G. Ferguson, 
vet manager of the Denver office of 
ASCAP, and William H. Vincent, head 
of the society's Philadelphia office for 
many years, will retire at the begin- 
ning of June, ASCAP national sales 
manager Clarence C. Rubin has an- 
nounced. 
Ferguson has been employed by 
ASCAP in Denver since 1940, and 
Vincent has been working in ASCAP 
sales since Jan. of 1939. The Denver 
office was recently closed, and ap- 
pointment of a new district manager 
for Philadelphia will be announced 
shortly. 
Talent Search 
Picks L.A. Group 
LOS ANGELES - Champion has 
been named as the winning rock com- 
bo in the Los Angeles regional semi- 
finals of the national talent search 
sponsored by the Newport Jazz Fes- 
tival and the Tea Council of the 
U.S.A. The seven -piece rock group is 
one of 21 semi-finalists in the rock 
combo category selected from 
21 
regions and thousands of artists from 
all parts of the country who entered 
the "Young Discoveries in Tea and 
Jazz" talent search. 
Champion was awarded $100 and is 
now preparing a new 5 -minute tape 
of their latest original work to be 
entered in the Tea Talent Search 
finals in which three winners will be 
selected from the Jazz group, Rock 
combo and pop vocalist categories. 
The three winners will be awarded an 
all -expenses -paid trip to the Newport 
Jazz Festival -New York and will per- 
form at the special 6 and 10 p.m. "Tea 
Concerts" at Philharmonic Hall July 5.

Schaefer Fete 
Set To Open 
In Central Park 
NEW YORK - June 20th is the 
opening date of the annual Schaefer 
Music Festival, underwritten for the 
past six years by the F&M Schaefer 
Brewing Company for the purpose of 
making available to the public the 
best popular entertainment at prices 
it can afford. The series is produced 
in cooperation with the Department 
of Parks by Ron Delsener who initi- 
ated the event eight years ago. The 
Festival has become one of the Me- 
tropolitan area's most popular sum- 
mer attractions drawing an audience 
of some 300,000 each season. 
Bill Cosby and Little Anthony & 
The Imperials co -headline the first of 
44 concerts which will be presented 
this summer in the Festival's perma- 
nent home, Wollman Memorial Skat- 
ing Rink Theater. Showtime 
is 
7 
p.m. on the 20th. In case of rain the 
show will be postponed until 5:30 on 
Thursday the 21st. Admission prices 
are the same as last year: $2 in the 
orchestra; $1.50 for balcony seats. 
Among the more than 
100 pop 
rock, soul, jazz/folk and comedy star 
attractions who will appear during 
the 1973 season, which runs through 
Sept. 7, are Blood Sweat and Tears; 
Blues Project Reunion; John Sebas- 
tian; Deodato; Richie Havens; Rod 
McKuen; Erroll Garner; Buddy Rich 
and 
his orchestra; 
Judy 
Collins; 
Frankie Valli & The Four Seasons; 
Canned Heat; Machito; Sergio Men- 
des Brasil '77: Robert Klein: Cheech 
& Chong; B. B. King; Jose Feliciano; 
Helen Reddy; Mahavishnu Orchestra; 
Buffy Sainte-Marie; Mary Travers 
and Sha Na Na. 
Tickets will be available beginning 
June 1st, at Korvette's in Manhattan. 
Brooklyn and Paramus, N.J. as well 
as Music Inn (W. 4th Street), Chevy's 
Men's Shop (Brooklyn), and Changes 
(Forest Hills). Any remaining tickets 
will 
be 
sold 
two 
hours 
before 
showfime on the day of the concert at 
the Wollman box office. Most conve- 
nient entrance to the theatre is 59th 
Street at 5th Avenue. A special phone 
(212) 249-8870 has been provided for 
all 
information 
regarding 
tickets, 
weather and raindates.

Phonogram 
Consolidates 
Distribution 
CHICAGO -A major step has been 
taken by Phonogram Inc. to consoli- 
date its distribution in certain mar- 
kets. Malverne Distributing of Long 
Island now will distribute the Phono- 
gram label in northern New Jersey in 
addition to its New York territory. 
Malverne formerly split the areas 
with Apex -Martin of New Jersey. 
"This is another step in Phono - 
gram's drive to consolidate distribu- 
tion where exceptionally strong mar- 
keting exists," stated Lou Simon, 
Senior 
Vice 
President/Director 
of 
Marketing. 
Added Jules Abramson, Sales Man- 
ager: "We are evaluating other mar- 
kets where two distributors exist 
where one would do. One distributor 
provides us with a chance for deeper 
penetration into the market place and 
diminishes distributors stock and the 
number of warehouses with product.

Angel Culls 
Single From 
Scott Joplin LP 
HOLLYWOOD - Angel Records has 
rushed onto the market a single re- 
lease of two tracks from its "The Red 
Back Book" album of compositions 
by Scott Joplin. Nation-wide requests 
from pop radio stations and jukebox 
operators inspired the release, accord- 
ing to Brown Meggs, Capitol's mar- 
keting vice president. The single, in a 
full -color sleeve, will be distributed 
and promoted through Capitol's full 
singles marketing organization. 
The "Red Back Book" album was 
recorded in Boston by the New Eng- 
land Conservatory Ragtime Ensem- 
ble led by composer -conductor and 
jazz scholar Gunther Schuller. Re- 
sponse on both dealer and consumer 
levels, says Meggs, has been "tremen- 
dous." "This proves again the artifi- 
ciality of the old categories, because 
Joplin's music appeals to all kinds of 
people. Ragtime can't be categorized, 
because it's classical pop music and 
popular classical music.

EYES ON ALBUMS-Get ready for one of the heaviest album releases ever. Be- 
tween now and mid July album product will be released by Carole King, Cat 
Stevens, George Harrison, and The Allman Brothers. Also anxiously awaiting new 
LP product from Jethro Tull and Emitt Rhodes. 
New Jose Feliciano album, "Compartments" is by far the most impressive he's 
released to date. It's gonna take some time before it catches on, but it promises 
to be a giant top 40 seller. 
Deep Purple currently have 3 albums on the Cash Box charts: "Made In Japan," 
"Machine Head" and 'Who Do We Think We Are." The answer: a super -group! ! 
First album by Art Garfunkel due to arrive next week. Lots of people are going to 
be surprised when they hear it. Album should be charted almost immediately. 
That'll mean chart albums by Simon and Garfunkel and The Beatles greatest hits 
sets. Who said they broke up? 
Would really love to see an edited version of Yes' "Siberian Khatru" released 
as a single from their "Close To The Edge" album. It's one of those absolutely 
magnificent songs that just has to be a huge hit based on group's talents and 
successes with "Your Move," and "Roundabout". 
As promised -here's the results of your top 10 all-time favorite albums: (1) 
Abbey Road -The Beatles; (2) The Beatles White album; (3) Sticky Fingers -Rolling 
Stones; (4) Sergeant Pepper -The Beatles; (5) Deja Vu -C, S, N & Y; (6) Led Zep- 
pelin -first album; (7) Days Of Future Past -Moody Blues; (8) Eat A Peach -Allman 
Brothers; (9) Bridge Over Troubled Water -Simon & Garfunkel and (10) All Things 
Must Pass- George Harrison. Once again, thanks to all those who took the time to 
list their favorite albums and send them in. 
SIGHTS 
ON SINGLES-Two singles on Columbia have the potential and the 
sound to easily go top 10. They are "Silver Train" by Johnny Winter, and 
"Avenging Annie" by Andy Pratt. It would really be a shame if they were lost. 
Other giant -singles -to -be are: "Goin' Home," -The Osmonds; "Over The Hills & Far 
Away," -Led Zeppelin; "Brothers Gonna Work It Out," -Willie Hutch (potential top 
10'er); 'There's No Me Without You," -Manhattans; "All Over The World," -The 
Heywoods; "Over & Over," -The James Boys; "Brother Louie," -Stories; "Free Elec- 
tric Band," -Albert Hammond; and "Giving It All Away," -Roger Daltry. Watch out 
for the new single by a group called Tribe on ABC. Single is called "Koke, Part 
1" -and it's a winner. Concentrated airplay could break it wide open nationally. 
Congratulations to Deep Purple on their first big single since the group's 
"Hush" days. "Smoke On The Water" looks to be a top 20 record for sure. Isn't 
it interesting that three supergroups who never before had singles success -are 
having hit singles now? Groups are Jethro Tull ("Living In The Past," "A Passion 
Play"); Deep Purple ("Smoke On The Water"); and Pink Floyd with "Money." 
It just goes to show you that a hit act is worth more than a hit record because 
hit acts will always have hit records!

CHICAGO CHATTER 
From the local newspapers comes word of a proposal, currently under consider- 
ation, to build an amusement park -fun center in the vicinity of the Northwest 
Tollway, about 45 miles from the Chicago downtown area. If plans materialize the 
complex would be built on 800 acres of land and would serve northern Illinois, 
southern Wisconsin and northwest Indiana. 
J. F. FRANTZ MFG. CO. prexy John Frantz items that his "U. S. Marshall" gun 
has been doing big business of late, not only domestically but, most especially, in 
the foreign markets! Since late last year the Frantz line has been handled by 
Nova of Germany. The gun's been selling beautifully in Europe, according to 
John, "and we couldn't be more pleased about it," he said, adding that "Canada 
is also a very good market for us." 
ROCK -OLA MFG. CORP.'S executive veepee Ed Doris just got back from a 
business trip to Venezuela ... Ad manager George Hincker returned to his office 
last week after attending the Virginia -Carolinas vending convention in Myrtle 
Beach, So. Carolina ... Earlier this month the Rock -Ola people entertained a very 
distinguished visitor, and friend, Mr. Adickes who was in from Germany to spend 
some time at the factory. 
BOB SHERWOOD, EXPORT MANAGER AT Chicago Dynamic Ind., received a 
cable from the Master of the Soviet ship Mikhail Lermontov, inquiring about the 
possibility of securing a Chi Coin "Holiday" ball bowler for placement in the 
ship's recreation area. Arrangements have not been confirmed, as yet. The ship is 
on its maiden voyage to the U. S., in the hopes of wooing the tourist trade, and 
is expected to dock in New York around June 11 ...ChiCoin's Avron Gensburg 
departed for Europe last week on a routine visit to the factory's distribs, reps, et 
al. 
UNDERSTAND FROM UNITED ARTISTS RECORDS' local representative Walter 
Paas that operators in the area have been showing a great deal of interest in the 
new single by Lou Donaldson called "Black Byrd." 
"MONTE CARLO" AND "ODDS & EVENS" continue to be the biggest sellers of 
the day at Bally Mfg. Co.-and there's no let-up in sight, according to Herb Jones! 
WITH THE COMPLETION, LAST WEEK, of sample shipments of the new single 
player "Gulfstream" by Williams Electronics Inc., factory distribs are now display- 
ing (and selling) the new piece-in a big way, according to Bill DeSelm! Bill also 
mentioned that "Paddle Ball," the video ping pong game, and "Golden Triangle," 
the new shuffle, are presently being shipped-in quantity! 
ON THE SINGLES SCENE: Gus Tartol of Singers One Stop notes that the 
following are among current releases being programmed by area operators: "Hey 
Mama" by Al Martino (Capitol), "Hurt" by Bobby Vinton (Epic), "Satin Sheets" 
by Jeanne Pruett (MCA), "Monster Mash" by Bobby Boris Pickett (Parrot) and 
"Kodachrome" by Paul Simon (Columbia). 
MILWAUKEE MENTIONS 
Jack Hastings of Hastings Dist. Inc. will be scheduling a Rock -Ola service 
school just as soon as a date can be confirmed with Rock -Ola engineer Bill 
Findlay. Meanwhile, the Rock -Ola phono models are selling like crazy out there! 
Jack's also enjoying steady sales activity on the Valley pool tables line. Although 
the Frigidaire ice machine is an all year around seller at Hastings, the expected 
surge at this time of the year is already being felt. 
HOPE ALL IS TIP TOP WITH Marie Pierce of Pierce Music in Broadhead. She's 
had some problems with a leg ailment and was scheduled to undergo corrective 
surgery-but not before all of her work was completed! 
CHATTED WITH STU GLASSMAN of Radio Doctors on one of his favorite 
subjects, that of how to better serve operators! "The importance of the operator 
must be recognized," he said, "considering the fact that operator purchases 
account for about one half of the total 45 record sales! We feel very strongly 
about this at Radio Doctors and frequently institute additional service tech- 
niques, geared specifically to our operator customers, to provide speedy and 
efficient handling of their orders" . 
. 
. As for some of the current items being 
programmed by area ops, John Jankowski, the expert in that department, 
noticed that more and more ops are putting rock and soft rock singles into their 
easy listening programming formats. This past week John has sold a lot of the 
new Deep Purple single "Smoke On The Water". Also, "Last Tango In Paris" by 
101 Strings w/Bebe Bardon, "Send Me No Roses" by Tommy Overstreet and - 
"Daisy May And Daisy May Not" by Terri Lane. Also selling steadily are the 
oldies of '55 thru '65 vintage.

Zeppelin Tour: A Merry May; 
Attendance Mark In Frisco 
NEW YORK -- Led Zeppelin would 
up the first half of their current 
American tour by playing to more 
than 100,000 paying customers in Cal- 
ifornia in less than one week, includ- 
ing the largest single concert crowd 
in the State's history. 
On June 2, the superstars drew 49,- 
304 paying fans at Kezar Stadium in 
San Francisco breaking the atten- 
dance record for California set two 
years ago by Grand Funk Railroad 
(45,000). 
Led Zeppelin sold out the Los An- 
geles Forum (18,000 seats) twice on 
May 31 and on June 3. 
With their fifth album, "Houses of 
Holy," simultaneously No. 1 on the 
national music sharts of both the 
U.S. and England just three weeks 
after its release, the quartet opened 
on May 4, to an official record crowd 
of 49,236 at Atlanta Braves' Stadium 
in Georgia. The figure shattered a 71/ 
year old attendance record set by the 
Beatles for Atlanta's biggest concert 
audience, and set a new record for the 
largest concert crowd ever assembled 
in the State of Georgia. 
The Beatles' Atlanta attendance 
record had been 33,000. The Led Zep- 
pelin concert marked the first time in 
the baseball stadium's history that 
seating had 
been allowed 
on the 
grass, in response to the huge demand 
for tickets. 
The following night, May 5, Led 
Zeppelin pulled off an even bigger 
feat in Tampa, Florida, where they 
broke another Beatles' record, this 
time for the largest concert atten- 
dance and gross in the history of the 
United States. A capacity crowd of 
56,800 paid 
$309,000 to see them 
break the Beatles' record of 55,000 
and $301,000 set at New York's Shea 
Stadium in 1965. Tampa has a popu- 
lation of less than half a million, 
which means that by projection, Led 
Zeppelin could conceivably draw a 
million people to concerts in the New 
York or London areas. 
Led Zeppelin travelled from city to 
city on a nine -passenger private Fal- 
con jet. An entourage of 30 including 
lighting men from England, sound 
crew, security men, and road manag- 
ers accompanied them on tour. A 
stereo system of four channels of 
3000 watts each, larger than that used 
at Woodstock, and claimed to be "the 
biggest in the world," was used to 
transmit the Led Zeppelin sound. 
All together, Led Zeppslin's con- 
certs ran an average of 2'/2 hours of 
uninterrupted music, a physical per- 
formance which far exceeds that of 
those given by any groups of com- 
parable popularity. 
Led Zeppelin set another record in 
Texas when they sold out two succes- 
sive nights at the Dallas Memorial 
Auditorium (May 18 10,000 people) 
and the Fort Worth Tarrant County 
Convention Center (May 19 13,500 
people). No other artists in history 
have sold out both venues back to 
back, drawing essentially from the 
same audience from two cities within 
a 30 minute drive of each other. 
Cities in the first half of the tour 
included Atlanta, Tampa, Jackson- 
ville, Tuscaloosa, St. Louis, Mobile, 
New Orleans, Houston, Dallas, Ft. 
Worth, San Antonio, Albuquerque, 
Denver, Salt Lake City, San Diego, 
Los Angeles, and San Francisco. Dur- 
ing the second half of the tour begin- 
ning on July 6, Led Zeppelin will 
appear in Chicago 6-7), St. Paul (9), 
Milwaukee 
(10), 
Detroit 
(12-13), 
Buffalo (15), Boston (20), Providence 
(21), 
Baltimore 
(23), 
Pittsburgh 
(23), and New York (27-28).

DUAL ROLE-Mark Meyerson, A&R coordinator for Atlantic Records has an- 
nounced the signing of Billy Cobham, drummer for the Mahavishnu Orchestra. 
Shown above are Cobham's manager Nat Weiss, Mark Meyerson, Billy Cob- 
ham, and Atlantic president Ahmet Ertegun. Cobham will continue to play 
and record with the Mahavishnu Orchestra, but will record as leader with his

Aspen Sets 2 
New Projects 
NEW YORK - William E. McEuen, 
head of Aspen Recording Society, the 
initiator, architect, producer and proj- 
ect engineer for the "Will the Circle 
Be Unbroken" album by the Nitty 
Gritty Dirt Band, has moved into two 
new production projects and will also 
shortly launch a new album produc- 
tion by the Dirt Band as well. 
First of the new campaigns is 
aimed at the disk launching of come- 
dian, parodyist 
and 
banjo 
picker 
Steve Martin. Martin has already be- 
come a "Tonight" show vet, having 
appeared on that vehicle nine times, 
and has also appeared twice on "Mid- 
night Special" on NBC-TV. 
Matin has completed recording his 
first album, which contains a gener- 
ous amount of live material, cut at 
different venues during a recent tour. 
It also contains some choice selec- 
tions of banjo picking. McEuen ex- 
pects to announce a disc deal on this 
shortly. 
McEuen has also developed and 
produced 
a new group, known as 
Manseau, Saxon and Buell. Initial 
product was etched at Jim Guercio's 
Caribou Ranch studios near Denver. 
A distribution arrangement for this 
album 
is 
also 
in 
the negotiation 
stage. Manseau, who will be in the 
spotlight with the group, formerly 
was lead singer and guitarist with the 
Sunshine Company. 
Also 
immediately 
upcoming 
on 
McEuen's agenda is a live Dirt Band 
recording to be cut at Stan Plesser's 
Cowtown Ballroom in Kansas City. 
Tentative dates for this are June 
22-23. 
McHugh Award 
HOLLYWOOD -- Donald Crockett, a 
junior at The University of Southern 
Calif., School of Music majoring in 
Composition, is this year's winner of 
the $600 Jimmy McHugh Award for 
the outstanding composition of 1973. 
He composed several pieces of music- 
f or chamber singers, for soprano, for 
large choral group, and also for or- 
chestra. 
Crockett is a resident of Pasadena, 
Calif. He has won The Bank of Amer- 
ica Fine Arts Prize, The Town and 
Country 
Award, the Arion Prize 
which is a National Award, and is a 
performer with the University of 
Southern California Singers.

Greene Plans Session Men % Deal 
NEW YORK - Charlie Greene, pres- 
ident of G_eene Bottle and Greene 
Mountain Records, has announced he 
is planning to form a stable of com- 
pany musicians to work his labels, 
and establishing a "musicians' al- 
liance fund" which will hold one per 
cent of all sales to be dispersed 
among musicians on a semi-annual 
basis. 
Greene said his primary concern is 
the establishment of a strong rapport 
with his artists. So far as the alliance 
fund is concerned, he said: "The mon- 
ey will not come out of the artists' 
take, but from the record company. 
Musicians will be certain of a better 
reward than a mere $37 session fee." 
Musicians will be drawn from the 
U.S., Britain and Europe. His plan is 
to have six or seven artists from each 
country on call for session work. 
They will be able to do outside jobs 
as well, but Greene asks that his la- 
bels have first option on anything 
they do on their own. 
While in London recently where he 
is setting up headquarters, Greene 
signed as first musician 
on "the 
Greene plan" Chris Mercer, who is 
also recording an LP for Greene 
Mountain. 
Greene Says 
Royalties To 
Tornado Victims 
HOLLYWOOD - Charles Greene, the 
record producer, has wired Governors 
of 13 states with an offer of financial 
assistance to victims of the recent 
tornados which ravaged the southern 
part of the nation. 
Greene indicated that he had in- 
structed his 
lawyer, 
Alfred 
Sch- 
lesinger, 
to 
draft 
an 
agreement 
whereby all profits due his recording 
company, Greene Mountain Records, 
from its current release of the Little 
Richard record "In The Middle Of The 
Night"-all artist royalties due Little 
Richard himself and mechanical re- 
cording profits due the publisher, 
United Artists 
Music Corporation, 
would be donated to tornado victims. 
Greene's wire was directed to the 
Governors 
of Alabama, 
Arkansas, 
Florida, Georgia, Virginia, Kansas, 
Tennessee, 
Mississippi, 
Michigan, 
North Carolina, Oklahoma and Tex- 
as. In his message he noted that he 
would make monies payable to a pub- 
lic service agency aiding tornado vic- 
tims in each state or the Red Cross.

Form Rap Label 
HOLLYWOOD - Record and Artist 
Marketing (RAM), has been formed 
announced by Bill Valenziano and 
Caroline Dees, both recently affiliated 
with M.M.I. and Capitol Records. 
With offices are located in Los An- 
geles, RAM will function as an inde- 
pendent service organization to the 
record industry in the areas of record 
promo, sales, merchandising and ad- 
vertising. Additionally, a publicity di- 
vision known as Record and Artist 
Publicity (RAP), will be headed by 
Jeannie Schoel, a previous associate 
of Valenziano and Dees. 
RAM will specialize in devising and 
instituting comprehensive marketing 
plans for a select number of records 
and artists, tailoring each campaign 
to meet the particular needs of the 
client. 
The publicity division will special- 
ize in providing complete services to 
recording artists, producers and pub- 
lishers, offering these individuals a 
priority publicity service uniquely 
suited to their needs. 
The new offices of RAM and RAP 
are located at 5325 Sunset Blvd. in 
Los 
Angeles. Telephone is: 
(213) 
466-2227.

MADISON SQUARE GARDEN, NYC 
-At the end of the concert with the 
audience pleasantly exhausted, mildly 
hysterical, 
and 
completely 
enter- 
tained, there wasn't much doubt left 
in anyone's mind as to which group 
takes the prize for sheer showmanship 
in America's rock pantheon. 
It was Alice Cooper all the way, 
from their flashing excited entrance, 
through 
the 
perfectly 
contrived 
stunts and tableaus and string of hits 
they sung, to the not -to -be -believed, 
flag waving, 
sentimental, 
stirring, 
sophisticated 
finale-which 
if 
you 
don't know by now, consists of the 
band and cast of characters parading 
under the Stars and Stripes, saluting 
it, and then pummelling Nixon -look - 
alike Richard M. Dixon, a California 
actor, when he attempts to do the 
same. 
The professionalism, musicianship, 
and total dedication the group displays 
earned them rave reviews on every 
stop of their incredible tour, and they 
deserve every compliment, and more. 
The Garden show was one of their 
best, Alice agreed later, and it was a 
traditional and fitting venue to cul- 
minate their successful tour. 
One thing: comparisons were made 
at the party following the concert by 
people who hadn't seen Alice Cooper 
in a while, or hadn't seen them per- 
form at all, and they were in agree- 
ment that the group has outranked the 
Stones in terms of total performance. 
As one spectator, a man in his 40s, 
said: "With the Stones, it's Jagger, 
Jagger, Jagger. The energy rises and 
falls according to his performance. 
But it's not Alice alone, here. It's the 
Van Morrison 
Jackie DeShannon 
TROUBADOUR, L. A. - Jackie De - 
Shannon has done quite a bit more 
than just follow her golden advice of 
"Put a Little Love in Your Heart." 
She has also put a lot of strength 
into her voice and a lot of soul into 
her song interpretations. She was 
backed up by one vivacious black go- 
spel singer called Tessie Caldren, who 
possessed the voice of at least three 
singers. 
DeShannon 
herself 
now 
sings as if she's been trained by gos- 
pel singers and one easily pictures 
the Atlantic recording artist spending 
her Sunday's singing in a Baptist 
church. Her blue-eyed soul act works 
well for the most part however at 
times her minstrelsy tends to get a 
bit too ministerial. DeShannon de- 
lighted with her new single, "Sweet 
Sixteen," written and produced by 
Van Morrison. A tune she penned 
with Van called "Santa Fe" only took 
a few bars to score as a definite 
smash. 
Morrison came on with an ensem- 
ble large enough to fill a van. Every 
time Morrison plays Los Angeles his 
back-up musicians, the tightest any- 
where around, seem to grow in num- 
bers. For his Troubadour engage- 
ment he had added a whole section of 
strings. 
This 
pleasant 
addition 
provided perfect sweetening to his 
exciting 
array 
of jazz/rock/blues 
compositions. Van sounded especially 
good on "Saint Dominic Preview," 
and "Listen to the Lion." Truly fan- 
tastic was "Lovers Do," which sounds 
like an easy top -ten chart contender. 
Highlights to the act were the sax- 
ophone and trumpet solos by Schroer 
and Atwood. Van has an inclination 
to chew gum while he performs, but 
one thing his audience can be certain 
of-he's anything but a bubblegum- 
mer. His peppy uptempo rhythmic 
numbers would make one guess it 
was piquant peppermint.

graphed, calculated group effort." 
The Alice Cooper Show is ultimate 
spectacle. The staging is top-notch. 
The music comes in great symphonic 
chords, set against flashing strobes 
and whirling bodies, never stopping 
until the audience is completely satis- 
fied. The theme of the show, in fact 
of each and every song, is an accurate 
statement on where things are at- 
from the audience's point of view. 
Congratulations, again, to Alice, 
Neal Smith, Dennis Dunaway, Mike 
Bruce, Glen Buxton, the rest of the 
cast and crew. Truly a dynamic eve- 
ning.

Merl Saunders 
ASH GROVE, L.A. - One often 
heard objection to the for -the -night 
only coalition of talent is that the 
arrangements 
invariably 
lead 
to 
strategems of one upsmanship. It's 
true. Guitarist Jerry Garcia (Warner 
Bros.) and organist Merl Saunders 
(Fantasy), both rarae avi as individ- 
uals and in their respective arenas, 
seemed as a duo in a quartet of musi- 
cians to have some trouble avoiding 
collisions 
with 
one 
another. 
Too 
much tailgating on the bridges, ap- 
parently. Limp pun that that is, their 
occasional 
gluttony 
during 
these 
transitions made things sound down 
right sloppy if not unrehearsed. But 
in between, the soloing was exact, 
tight and clean. 
It was a relatively short, primarily 
instrumental set whose apex came 
with "After Midnight," 
a number 
that had everybody jamming, but ex- 
celling, including Bill Vitt on drums 
and John Kahn on bass. If you would 
have to fault -find, it would be in the 
length of the number, which free- 
wheeled around in some jazz varia- 
tion for ten or so minutes and abso- 
lutely refused to expire. In fact, a 
couple of others threatened a similar 
circumstance but were 
brought -in 
with a nice peaking of enjoyment for 
us all. 
b.m. 
Diana Trask 
PALOMINO CLUB, NORTH HOLLY- 
WOOD - Diana Trask transfixed her 
audience at this country and western 
club last week. The Dot recording art- 
ist is billed as "Miss Country Soul," 
though in actuality she is mostly 
country. The "soul" label is a bit 
misleading. Even so, Diana continues 
to be a leading female exponent in 
the country field breaking all attend- 
ance records in Vegas and every- 
where else she performs. 
The repertoire offered by this Aus- 
tralian -born singer consists mainly of 
c&w standards like "Your Cheating 
Heart," "Release Me," "Stand 
By 
Your Man," and Joe South's "Games 
People Play"-each song was pre- 
ceded by insouciant slap -happy re- 
marks a la Hee Haw, a style much 
appreciated by her Palomino patrons. 
Diana proved to her crowd that she 
was a seasoned professional and that 
all she need do is build up a catalog 
of her own hits. Her new single "Say 
When" should be the first among 
them. 
Other 
impressive 
offerings 
were" I Wish I Was a Teddy Bear" 
and "Help Me Make It Through the 
Night." Miss Trask was backed ex- 
pertly by the Tony Booth band. 
r.b. 
Paul Simon 
CARNEGIE HALL, NYC - Paul 
Simon, "the only living boy in New 
York", staged three SRO shows here 
at New York's world-famous hall. 
Resplendent in white because as he 
said, "it's what you wear when you 
play your home -town" Simon plainly 
gave a lesson to anyone who will ever 
give a solo concert. He performed 
a little over two hours and kept his 
audience mystified, probably for as 
long as they can hold the memories 
of that evening in mind. 
He appeared on stage and ran 
through a number of songs by him- 
self and then he brought out Uru- 
bamba, who backed him up on "El 
Condor Pasa." He then humbly gave 
them the limelight for two songs of 
their own. A short break followed 
but he returned solo again 
and 
treated the crowd to his fast climb- 
ing single, "Kodachrome". A few 
songs later he introduced The Jesse 
Dixon Singers who backed him up for, 
"Mother And Child Reunion" and 
"Bridge Over Troubled Waters", and 
he again gave up the stage allowing 
them to perform themselves. 
Paul Simon had finished what he 
had come to New York to do. He is 
back again where he belongs and he 
is greatly loved. He did one encore, 
"America". Paul Simon, at Carnegie 
Hall, did indeed break the "Sounds 
Of Silence."

Rock And Roll 
Revival Vol. XIII 
NYC - MADISON SQUARE GAR- 
DEN-Chuck Berry was the head- 
line act at Vol. 13 of the Rock & 
Roll 
Spectacular 
co -produced 
by 
Richard Nader. Always flashy and a 
great crowd pleaser, Chuck duck - 
walked across the stage, sang, played 
guitar, until Nader told him time was 
up (about half an hour after he be- 
gan). The crowd of about 14,000 was 
on it's feet throughout the show, 
clapping and singing along to "Reel- 
ing and Rocking", "Johnnie B. Goode", 
"Roll Over Beethoven" and a medley 
of other hits. 
Bo Diddley, who received a gold 
record for his achievements from the 
president of Chase Records, has been 
recording for 18 years now and one 
still can distinguish his material. His 
first record, both sides of which he 
performed was part of his short set. 
"Bo Diddley" and "I'm A Man" were 
the titles. Bo as well as Chuck ap- 
peared alone and were backed up by 
Bobby Comstock and his band. 
Chubby Checker stole the show and 
in a short 15 minutes had the garden 
on its feet and exhausted from watch- 
ing him dance the twist and the pony. 
It was quite an exhibition and he was 
called back for several encores. I 
though he was going to collapse! 
The Shirelles followed Chubby and 
slowed the pace down somewhat but, 
as did the Five Satins, the group still 
showed that their voices are good and 
that they have a lot of fans. They 
sang many songs such as "Soldier 
Boy," and "Will You Still Love Me 
Tomorrow". 
Brenda Lee, whom to my recollec- 
tion has not appeared in N.Y. in 
many years was very fine. Her voice 
is still excellent as she sang "All 
Alone Am I" and "I Sorry" only two 
of the many oldies she performed. 
A 
Kris 
Krisstoferson 
composition 
"It's Over", her latest record for MCA 
was also presented. Brenda was on 
for about half an hour and she sang 
to everyone constantly moving around 
the stage located in the center of the 
arena. In a very attractive pink gown 
with white lace trim, she gave this 
listener a really enjoyable show. I 
Jonathan Edwards 
Melissa Manchester 
It was a pleasure to once again 
have Jon Edwards in town. The folk 
singer's songs are refreshing and al- 
ways performed well. Opening the 
Thursday early set with "Athens 
County", the Atco recording artist 
had the audience with him through- 
out the show. It also seemed as if 
several hard core fans were there. 
Songs from both of his albums were 
presented such as "Sunshine", "Stop 
And Start It All Again" and "Train 
To Glory". As an encore, Edwards 
and his sidemen Stuart Schulman and 
Bill Keith treated us to "Everybody 
Knows Her" ala Chi -Lites complete 
with Choreography. A very enjoyable 
set. 
Back on the scene after a long 
absence 
was 
Melissa 
Manchester. 
About two years ago she was ap- 
pearing unaccompanied at Folk City 
singing well but too low-keyed. Now 
equipped with an excellent album on 
Bell "Home to Myself" and a fine 
back up band, the 
former Bette 
Midler Harlet, performed very well. 
Full of energy yet seemingly relaxed, 
Melissa talked to the crowd and made 
everyone feel at home with her. With 
a nice clear voice, "Funny That 
Way" which goes out to Joni Mitchell 
and Laura Nyro, "Jenny" is a beauti- 
ful ballad, and "If it Feels Good (Let 
it Ride)" is an untempo rock and roll 
endeavor. All the songs were very 
nice. Melissa Manchester is definitely 
an up and coming artist to keep a 
close eye on. She has the potential of 
becoming a big star. 
p.s. 
Dawn 
Holly Sherwood 
COPACABANA, NY-After 14 years 
in the industry, first as singer, then 
music publishing exec and back to 
singer, Tony Orlando, featured voice 
for the two gals and a guy hitsters, 
has, by his own admission, made the 
big time by opening at the Copa. 
Dawn, of course, has already made 
the bigtime on Bell Records, having 
had a series of big hits, including 
their latest. "Tie a Yellow Ribbon 
Round the Ole Oak Tree," which Tony 
and the gals used to excellent sing - 
along advantage opening night. 
Orlando, 29, is a solidly -built, gen- 
ial and "loose" performer whose voice 
is big, yet capable of subtle, soul -like 
emotion when the occasion calls for 
it, as, indeed, it was when he sang 
such numbers as "Drift Away" and 
"Freedom for the Stallion." As for 
the gals Joyce Vincent and Telma 
Hopkins they fully reflect the fact 
that prior to their Down association, 
they helped make many hits as back- 
ground voices. They have an excellent 
solo spot doing hits by Bacharach & 
David. Dawn provides a most enjoy- 
able night of honest -to -goodness sing- 
ing and general geniality. 
Opening the bill is Rocky Road 
artist Holly Sherwood, a compact, 
onetime member of the original cast 
of "Godspell." There's lots of vocal 
impact from a small -frame, yet she 
should minimize a broad theatrical 
quality when singing in a night club. 
Her best number was a persuasively 
commanding "Day by Day" from 
"Godspell." 
hope she comes back soon. 
Danny & the Juniors who naturally 
sang "At the Hop" opened the festivi- 
ties with a resoundingly excellent set.

R I3 B INGREDIENTS-Bremar Services, Inc., (headed by Barry Gib- 
son, Don Sainte-Johnn and Wil Johnsen), based in Chicago, have one of the 
first and only nationally synicated three-hour weekly soul music count down 
shows, "Black 40". The show has been in production since the beginning of 
the year, and the acceptance is broadening. KALO of Little Rock and KOWH in 
Omaha, have recently bought the show and listener response has been excel- 
lent. "B-40" is also adaptable to top -40 radio according to Sainte-Johnn, WGRT- 
Chicago morning air personality, who hosts "Black 40". Weekly interviews are 
featured with artists who have current records on national charts. ("B-40" 
plays from the charts of a national publication). The show runs 45 -minutes, 
leaving 15 -minutes for station time (CA's, etc.). The show is offered on an 
exclusive market basis, according to company spokesmen ... Curtis Mayfield's 
new album release. "Back To The World", has a cut entitled, "Keep On Trip - 
pin' ", and the tune came through purely by accident. While guitarist -producer 
Phil Upchurch; bassist Lucky Scott and drummer Quentin Joseph were foolin' 
around during a studio session, Curtis overhead the impromptu session. He 
taped it, penned some lyrics and dubbed it, "Keep On Trippin' " and it is a 
standout track on the LP ... Also, from Curtom, a major publicity campaign, 
which may include a 10 -city tour, is being mapped out for Curtom artist LeRoy 
Hutson in conjunction with the release of his current album "Love Oh Love"

cent Saturday morning in New York. He fought of his attackers and he is now 
at Montifiore Hospital recuperating from a fractured nose and multiple frac- 
tures. But, come what may Colon will be back with his fans shortly 
. Half 
Note patrons, throughout the years, will be saddened to learn that William 
Alberg, better known as "Al the Waiter" died of a heart attack on May 7th in 
his apartment in NYC. Sonny and Mike Canterino, owners of the West 54th 
Street Jazz Club, found the body in his apartment late that night when the 
reliable longtime employee did not show up for work. Alberg, 58, was known 
throughout the jazz community for his warm sense of humour and for his

NEW YORK: RICHARD NADER: PROMOTER WITH A TWIST 
While his first feature film, "Let The Good Times Roll," was debuting around 
town, racking up raves from critics, Richard Nader was padding around his Upper 
East Side offices in his stocking feet listening to taped radio spots announcing 
his next project-"The 1960s British Rock Invasion Revisited." The spots fol- 
lowed the format set by his other rock revivals-quick bursts of old, familiar 
melodies with a voice-over listing the time and place of concerts and artists to 
appear. The formula has been phenomenally successful. 
"Young people lead their lives much faster today, and thus are quicker to be 
nostalgic. 
I feel the 'invasion' will have strong appeal to the 21-25 age group 
who were labeled teeny-boppers when this music came around for the first 
time," he feels. 
The British revival package will be produced by Nader's Music Production Con- 
sultants and sold to local promoters. William Morris is booking the tour. 
"My approach is that 
I don't consider myself a promoter," Nader told Cash 
Box. "I consider myself a 'conceptual producer.' " 
"I go to an audience first and see what they want," he explained. "I design 
my presentations with a specific market in mind." 
This is not only different, he believes, from the standard approach taken by 
most promoters or producers who buy an act and then arrange tours or appear- 
ances, but it is also the "secret" of his success. 
Nader, 32 -years -old, has been in the business of reviving rock and r & b acts 
since he first began producing sock -hops as a high school freshman in Mason- 
town, Pa., (5,000 pop.) 60 miles south of Philly. That was in 1954. 
He was barely out of high school when he approached WMBS, a local CBS - 
affiliated radio station, with the concept of an all -request show. "Seventy per- 
cent of the requests were for oldies," he recalled. "So 
I started playing oldies." 
Rock and roll was still regarded in some markets as "race records" in those 
days, and the programming apparently wasn't greeted too warmly by station 
HOLLYWOOD-THE ASSOCIATION: AN EXCEPTIONAL SIGNATURE 
For several years, The Association has considered making super hits a perfectly 
natural act. And for good reason, too. Since the band's formation, they have 
basked in the glow of three gold albums and four gold singles while continuing to 
cultivate their own originality and at the same time becoming a sort of musical 
paradigm for other groups to follow. But as the first, the forerunner, their 
appearance on the scene couldn't have been more opportune. The spawning 
season of the mid -sixties, adhering to the usual ten-year cycle, had the acid -rock 
exiting and a softer, more moderate type of music entering. The original sextet- 
members would later leave, return, be added and even die-were part of this 
sound in that they, more than any other group, surpassed other product in terms 
of lyrics, music and arrangement. Their distinction, though, lay in their heavy use 
of harmonics in pop rock, expressing a style definitely uncommon to the drum - 
dented ears of that era. They caught on. "Along Came Mary," "Cherish," 
"Windy" and "Never My Love" all went to the top, and the group had made it. 
"Let's face it; it's difficult now. We haven't had a hit in a while, the college 
market has changed radically and we've even changed. Who is to say?" 
Guitarists Jim Yester (rhythm) and Jules Alexander (lead) and both members 
form the Association's inception reflected upon the status of the group and 
possible routes for their overdue ascension in a tete-a-tete with Cash Box. 
"Bad to us would be a lack of college dates because that is where our market 
is at. We'll survive, but we would be less than honest if we said that we didn't 
rely on college dates, at the present time. For example, there was just a 
convention of western colleges that put out 
a directive suggesting that the 
schools not spend over $1,500 for an act. And so with colleges, where there used 
to be 
a couple of hundred that bought our act, the number. has dropped 
significantly. They have found that they can bring -in a lesser known act for that 
RICHARD NADER 
THE ASSOCIATION 
execs. "Mail and sponsors were coming in good," Nader said. "But they wanted 
to return to Top 40 at the station." 
Undaunted, he took his format to WANB in Waynesburg, Pa., where it was 
accepted. By this time he was enrolled in Wheeling College, West Va., and added 
another station, WHMC, Gaithersburg, Md., to his roster. He hopped back and 
forth between college and the two stations for nearly five years. 
In 1964 he was drafted into the Army, sent to Korea, and soon named program 
director of Radio Cavalier, part of the Armed Forces network there. The show was 
beamed to troops of the 1st Cavalry Division. 
Korea was where Nader's future career started coming together. During in- 
formal Saturday afternoon bull sessions devoted mainly to soldiers' reminiscences 
about things back in the States, Nader became the center of conversation when- 
ever the subject turned to music-discographies, group line-ups and histories, 
and past and present hits. 
One man, Pfc. Jim Pewter, began stumping Nader with questions about oldies. 
The two became friends. Pewter, a Mid -Westerner, knew groups who worked that 
.area, like Del Shannon and Johnny and the Hurricanes. 
"I guess that's where I first got the idea for revival shows," Nader said. "We 
used to sit there for hours, magining, make-up shows, arguing over who got 
top billing." 
Another soldier joined the discussion group. Specialist Pete Johnson was his 
name. He went on to program "Rock and Roll Revisited," an oldies format now 
featured in 32 countries around the world on the Armed Forces Network. That 
project evolved into a career for Johnson, too. He left the Army to later write 
and edit the syndicated 48 -hour radio special, "The History of Rock and Roll," 
and work with Warner Brothers publicity department. 
Nader's returned to civilian life and joined Premier Talent in 1966 as a book- 
ing agent during the years of the British invasion. He was booking "oldie" acts 
from time to time and yearning to start his revivals but Frank Barcelona warned 
against it. "Don't buck a trend" was his advice. 
Nader bided his time and struck up an acquaintence with another oldies' 
freak, Ray Ranieri, former road manager for Mitch Ryder and one-time associate 
of Dick Clark, Murray the K and Alan Freed. 
By the summer of 1968 Nader was tired of waiting. "We tried to get some- 
thing going with other promoters, record companies, get them interested in back- 
(Cont'd on page 43) 
price and do a half -way decent business, so their economics shuts the door to us. 
As a result, we are having to look for other markets." 
A couple of those "other" markets involve a five-year Las Vegas deal and a 
new record deal with one of the TOP producers in the country. Almost as curious 
is that the members have retained such a healthy philosophy about themselves 
and their music despite a professional nadir in late 1971 that would have meant 
the demise of any other group less talented and tenacious. This low -point also 
claimed the life of Brian Cole, another original member. 
"It's like starting over again, in a lot of ways. Sure everybody knows us and so 
we have a certain advantage of reputation and certainly of exprience. But also, 
we're really a brand new group. We have a new member, a new rhythm section, 
and most important, a new attitude. That attitude is one of openess; we're now 
amenable to alternative directions whereas before any tampering would have been 
vetoed either by the group from within or by the record company. A case in 
point: A few years back if we had come -out with a funky blues record, it probably 
wouldn't have been accepted whether it was any good or not. Your reputation can 
work for you and against you. But now we know a heavy jazz player who is 
getting ready to cut an album and we're thinking of doing the vocals behind him. 
We wouldn't have dared to do that before. Now it would be a lark!" 
If you think about it, that makes sense. The band was not formed for dancing; 
it was formed to play for an audience who appreciated a sensory treat in their 
heads as opposed to their feet. They have matured, addressing themselves to the 
examination of other modes of expression. The current coalition (Ted Bluechel, 
Jr./guitar & bass, Larry Ramos/lead guitar & bass, Richard Thompson/piano, 
Maurice Miller/drums and David Vaught/bass) is as adept in the soundcrafting of 
a string of successive hits as was the group a couple of years back. In fact, last 
year's business is about half of what this year's has been. And there will be a 
return to the college circuit-they're booked solid through November-with a 
smattering of clubs thrown -in. 
"Look at it this way. You've got to lead or you've got to follow. We can only do 
what we know. We can't imitate anybody else." 
No you can't. And vice versa.

NEW YORK: RICHARD NADER (from page 38) 
ing a revival, but we just couldn't swing it. Finally 
I said 'the hell with it' and, 
without a dime, 
I called the Garden and told them to hold Oct. 18 for a rock 
revival." 
The rest, as they say, is history. 
Armed with a dog-eared copy of his original proposal and "the sixth carbon 
of a working budget," Nader approached 69 -year -old James E. Ashman, president 
of Grey Mfg. Co., makers of dictation systems and teaching aids, whom Nader 
heard was interested in diverse investments. 
Ashman bought the idea, impressed with nothing else, Nader recalls, if only 
the zeal and conviction the latter delivered with the proposal. The show sold out. 
It featured Chuck Berry, The Platters, Bill Haley and others. 
Nader knew that the ball had to kept rolling. The Felt Forum management was 
happy with the packed house. The men who comprise Madison Square Garden 
Attractions were happy, too, They wanted to become Nader's partners. 
The next show was held a month later, featuring Jackie Wilson, Bill Haley 
again, The Five Satins and the Mello -Kings, among others. 
The following year the Richard Nader revivals moved into the Garden's 18,000 - 
seat main arena. 
"We sold out three days in advance," Nader said. "And we've been in the main 
arena ever since." 
The most recent (1) revival was the 13th "volume" of the Nader oldies pack- 
age to hit the Garden. Now the show also goes on the road, with Nader's Music 
Production Consultants co -promoting with Madison Square Garden Productions.. 
Three national tours have been planned. And there's the film. And the British 
revivals. 
"The spin-offs on this thing have been incredible," Nader said. "We've put 60 
different artists into major gigs they may never have gotten otherwise. We spent 
two -and -half million dollars on talent. Nationally, we grossed over $5 -million. In 
the Garden alone we grossed over $1 -million." 
"I feel we've turned the industry around. On radio they've gone from a half - 
dozen stations programming oldies on any regular schedule to where you now 
have a choice of one or two major stations per market." 
He noted the increased demand for oldies product, the familiar TV com- 
mercials featuring oldie stars, and the oldies' series put out by several major 
labels since the whole thing started. 
His latest coup was reuniting Latin stars Tito Puente and La Lupe for Nader's 
Latin Music Festival Ill last week (2) at the Garden. Nader also was named Pro- 
moter of the Year at the first annual Latin Achievement Awards night (May 20) 
at the Cheetah. 
The Latin shows reflect Nader's approach to producing and promoting. "I saw 
the audiences' needs," he said.. 
He worries about promotion. "A bad promo campaign can destroy talent," he 
believes. "I try to judge an audience, build their community spirit, or their national 
feeling, and make them feel welcome when they're sitting out front." 
So far, he feels he's achieved the objectives he set out to reach when he 
launched the revival format. He wanted major productions for the talent, a tour 
package, a movie or TV spectacular, and a European tour. He got them all. 
"The film is the culmination of our objectives to date," he said. "And the 
Rock and Roll Revival European tour is all set for the fall." 
The British Invasion Revisited kicks off the end of this month (26) at Saratoga, 
N.Y. Busy times ahead for the promoter, excuse us

Free Sunday Jazz At Museum 
Gets Start From Business 
NEW YORK -A 40 -week series of 
free live jazz concerts featuring name 
performers will be offered at the New 
York Jazz Museum, 125 West 55th 
Street, starting Sunday, June 10th, it 
was announced Monday, June 5, at a 
press luncheon at the museum. Known 
as the Calvert Extra Sunday Concerts 
at the Jazz Museum, it's believed that 
this represents the first time that 
business has supported a continuing 
series of jazz events over a period of 
a year in one city. 
The first of the series will headline 
the renowned Roy Eldridge and his 
quartet. Each 
Sunday 
concert 
is 
scheduled from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. 
Guest of honor at the announce- 
ment 
luncheon 
was 
Mrs. 
Lucille 
Armstrong, wife of late jazz great 
Louis Armstrong, and a member of 
the museum's board of trustees. It 
was revealed that his birthday in ear- 
ly July will be celebrated by dedicat- 
ing the fourth concert on Sunday, 
July 1, to his memory. A special pro- 
gram for that event will be an- 
nounced shortly. 
Howard E. Fischer, executive direc- 
tor of the museum, hailed Calvert Ex - 
Top Polydor Acts 
At Jazz Festivals 
NEW YORK - Polydor Incorporat- 
ed will be represented by seven acts 
at this year's Newport Jazz Festival, 
Newport Jazz Festival -West and Bay 
Area Jazz Festival. Set to appear are 
Chick Corea, Roy Buchanan, Man- 
drill, John Mayall, Randy Weston, 
Tony Williams and 
Roy Ayers- 
virtually the entire roster of jazz - 
and jazz -related artists on the Poly- 
dor label. 
Keyboard wizard Chick Corea and 
his group Return to Forever, whose 
Polydor LP "Light As A Feather" 
has enjoyed both jazz and pop chart 
action, will perform at the Santa Mo- 
nica Civic Auditorium, June 19 and 
Berkeley Community Theater, June 
20 as part of the Newport -West and 
Bay Area festivals. Then on July 6, 
they make a Newport Festival ap- 
pearance at Philharmonic Hall in 
New York. Polydor has just released 
a dynamic debut album by group 
member Stan Clarke, "Children of 
Forever." 
Guitar virtuoso Roy Buchanan is 
also scheduled for all three festivals, 
appearing June 18 at the Berkeley 
Community Theater, June 23 at the 
Hollywood Bowl and June 30 at New 
York's Wollman Amphitheatre. Just 
off 
a highly successful 
European 
tour, Buchanan has garnered wide- 
spread acclaim with two Polydor al- 
bums and "Sweet Dreams," a just 
released single. 
On July 1, Mandrill will have the 
honor of sharing the bill with Duke 
Ellington 
at 
Philharmonic 
Hall. 
"Composite Truth", their third LP re- 
mains high on the charts five months 
after release, along with "Fence - 
walk," their recent single. The groqp 
heads 
into the studios later this 
month for work on a new album. 
Blues legend John Mayall is set for 
two New York Festival appearances: 
July 4 at the Singer Bowl, as part of 
a tribute to Louis Armstrong, and 
the following night at Philharmonic 
Hall. The Philharmonic date offers a 
stimulating 
musical 
venture 
that 
shares the title of Mayall's most re- 
cent Polydor LP, "Jazz -Blues Fu- 
sion." 
Pianist Randy Weston, drummer 
Tony Williams and vibist Roy Ayers 
will all be appearing July 7 in New 
York. The presentation of Rany Wes - 
ton's African Rhythms at the Woll- 
man Amphitheatre reflects the key- 
board veteran's five-year tenure in 
Morocco, where he has been deeply 
involved in the African sources of 
Western musical forms. Newly signed 
to Polydor, Weston has just com- 
pleted recording "Tanjah," his debut 
tra's sponsorship of the concert series 
as an important breakthrough 
in 
gaining business community support 
for America's sole original art form. 
A non-profit organization, the muse- 
um is the only one of its kind in the 
world devoted to the entire jazz 
scene. 
"It's our hope," stated Alvin Fle- 
ischman, president of Calvert Distil- 
lers Company, "to help expose the 
performance of jazz music on a con- 
cert basis to all segments of society. 
This is being done in the tradition of 
the museum for the benefit of young 
and old, of all economic, social and 
cultural backgrounds. Through the 
museum jazz has reached a cultural 
level not possible before and Calvert 
is most pleased to be part of it." 
Fischer declared that subsequent 
Calvert Extra Sunday Concerts would 
feature leading performers from the 
U.S. and abroad. He added that as 
future performers are scheduled their 
names and appearance dates would be 
publicly announced. The June 17th 
concert, he said, will star Barry 
"Kid" Martyn, England's top jazz 
drummer, whose six -piece group plays 
New Orleans -style jazz. 
"The missionary effect of the Cal- 
vert Extra concert series," Mr. Fisch- 
er stated, "is not only expected to 
promote wider appreciation of jazz 
among the public, but also to encour- 
age participation by more leading ar- 
tists than ever before, many of them 
legendary figures in the jazz world." 
Among the museum's board of 
trustees are Clark Terry, Billy Tay- 
lor, Nesuhi and Ahmet Ertegun, Ben- 
ny Goodman, Marian McPartland, Nat 
Hentoff, Artie Shaw, Sy Oliver, John 
Hammond, 
Milt 
Hinton, 
Harvey 
Sampson, Jr., Goddard Lieberson and 
George Avakian. Opened in mid -1972 
in a converted carriage house, the 
museum provides a unique setting for 
live and recorded jazz performances, 
as well as a variety of educational 
and related activities. Included are 
jazz exhibits, films and audio-visual 
programs. 
Recent exhibits of photos, paint- 
ings, posters, instruments and other 
memorabilia have 
featured 
Louis 
Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Billie 
Holliday. The screening room shows 
films featuring such personalities as 
Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, 
Roy Eldridge, Lester Young, Artie 
Shaw and Count Basie. 
The museum presents Jazz Pan- 
orama, its audio-visual outline of jazz 
history for special groups. It also 
provides at moderate cost a touring 
'program for colleges, schools and 
community organizations. 
This 
in- 
cludes jazz commentary, films, live 
jazz, the Jazz Panorama, jazz tap 
dance and rap sessions with musi- 
cians. 
'Further information about the pro- 
gram 
is 
available 
from 
Howard 
Fischer, the New York Jazz Museum 
(765-2150).

this month. 
Tony Williams is also scheduled at 
the Wollman Amphitheatre, as part 
of the 
whimsically 
titled 
"Drum 
Stick." Williams' four Polydor al- 
bums 
(most 
recently, 
"The 
Old 
Bum's Rush") have solidified his rep- 
utation as one of the top drummers 
in the world. 
Finally, the Roy Ayers Ubiquity 
takes the stage at Philharmonic Hall. 
Ayers' fourth Polydor album, just 
out, is his motion picture soundtrack 
for "Coffy," the American Interna- 
tional action -drama now in the first - 
run release throughout the country. 
The as -yet unspecified personnel of 
the Newport Festival's fabled Jam 
Sessions should also include many of 
the above. In any case, the massive ar- 
ray of talent at the three upcoming 
festivals, including seven of Polydor's 
most vital 
and entertaining acts, 
should dispel all doubts that jazz mu- 
sic is alive and well.
