Open Door Agency 
Wins Graphics Prize 
NASHVILLE - The 
Open Door 
Agency, a Nashville pr/promo oper- 
ation geared towards entertainment 
clientele, has been named a winner 
among 1,500 competing entries at this 
year's Southern Creativity Show in 
Ashland, Ky. Honors resulted from an 
entry made on the firm's letterhead. 
The artwork on the stationery was 
developed in Nashville by Design 
Graphics. Formed in May, 1972, the 
agency currently represents Danny 
Davis & The Nashville Brass, Welton 
Lane, Dot Records, Enterprise (Stax) 
Records, 
Shorty 
Lavender 
Talent 
Agency, and the Oak Ridge Boys. 
Sheriff Pusser 
Endorses Disk 
NASHVILLE - "A speech for me is 
like a woman having a baby. Easy to 
conceive but difficult to deliver." So 
said Tennessee crimefighter Buford 
Pusser at a press conference in RCA's 
studio A in Nashville as he endorsed 
a new record titled "The Ballad of 
Buford Pusser." The record, written 
and recorded by RCA's newest artist, 
Dave Hall of Tupelo, Miss., follows 
the plot of the film "Walking Tall" 
which stars Pusser. 
Hall, who operates Dave Hall Pro- 
ductions in Tupelo, Mississippi, a cus- 
tom recording company, wrote "The 
Ballad," came to Nashville two weeks 
ago pushing another song, and hap- 
pened to mention his "Ballad" to Roy 
Dea at RCA. 
Tillis Named 
To Dean Martin's 
Regular Line -Up 
NASHVILLE - MGM recording art- 
ist Mel Tillis has been selected for 
the regular fall series on the Dean 
Martin Show. Taping is set for Sept. 
12-13-14 and additional tapings will 
take place in November and December. 
Tillis is currently appearing on the 
summer replacement 
show 
"Dean 
Martin Presents Music Country." Til- 
lis was formerly a semi -regular on 
the Glenn Campbell Goodtime Hour. 
One of the busiest groups in the 
industry, the Mel Tillis Show, 1973 
edition, 
is 
booked 
for 
36 
per- 
formances during the months of Au- 
gust & September. Plans for his 1974 
show have just been completed and 
the show will be expanded and has a 
completely 
different 
format. 
WPLO Readies 
Appreciation Week 
ATLANTA - Beginning 
August 
13th, Atlanta country music fans will 
be treated to one of the biggest weeks 
in memory as Radio Atlanta, WPLO, 
presents another Appreciation Week. 
This year, as in years past, the line- 
up is dotted with stars such as Char- 
lie 
McCoy, Don Williams, Jeanne 
Preutt, Bobby G. Rice, Donna Fargo, 
Freddie Hart, Skeeter Davis, Bobby 
Bare, Freddie Weller, Mel Tillis, Bar- 
bara 
Fairchild 
and 
many 
more. 
WPLO's four -night extravaganza is 
the highlight of the summer for At- 
lanta fans and those who travel from 
miles around to follow the caravan 
show as it makes stops at four major 
shopping centers around the city.

CashBox Country Roundup 
(Cont'd from p. 41) 
... Kay Adams has just signed a long-term recording contract with Capitol 
Records. Miss Adams was previously signed to Tower Records, a subsidiary of 
Capitol, and had many big hits such as "Little Pink Mac", and "Step Aside 
Girl". Cliffie Stone, Kay's personal manager, will be producing her up -coming 
record dates this year, which include several singles and albums. 
Bob Young (KRMD Shreveport) will be the new program director of WMC 
Memphis starting August 13 ... Effective September 1, KFOX Long Beach, 
Los Angeles will be Jon Fricke's new home. He will be operations manager 
there, and will remain with WMC as a consultant, working directly with Bob 
Young. 
Jon says, "It's nice to know that the Queen Mary is docked outside KFOX 
studios, especially if California falls into the ocean". 
Bobby Fisher has started a new operation called American Country Promo- 
tions. He will retain his current position as national promo man for MGB 
Productions and continue to operate out of his present office ... Josie Brown 
recently signed a personal management contract with Owens -Fair and Asso- 
ciates of Nashville.

Cash Box/R(IB News Report 
Atlantic `Gold' 
From NATRA 
(Thom Bell Top Producer) 
NEW ORLEANS - Atlantic Rec- 
ords' superstars came away from the 
1973 National Association of Televi- 
sion and Radio Artists 
(NATRA) 
Golden Mike Awards Show in New 
Orleans last week toting a respecta- 
ble share of the gold bullion under 
their arms. 
Winning four Gold Mike Awards 
out of the seventeen categories, At- 
lantic took the Best Duo of the Year- 
Roberta Flack and Donny Hathaway; 
Best Female Vocalist of the Year- 
Aretha Franklin; Best Male Vocal 
Group of the Year-Spinners; and 
the Best Producer of the Year- 
Thom Bell. 
Thom Bell is the highly talented, 
independent producer who Atlantic 
contracted to produce the Spinners 
album titled, "The Spinners." The re- 
sults were three gold singles and a 
gold album (all RIAA certified) for 
the group. 
The eloquent Paul Johnson, Atlan- 
tic's national promotion director or 
R&B who accepted the Golden Mike 
Awards for the "heavies", described 
the momentous occasion as the "phan- 
tasmagorical mind -mesmerizer of the 
year!" 
(L To R) Paul Johnson and Thom 
Bell 
Baccus & Vogelhut 
Form R&B Pdtn's 
NEW YORK - Barbara Baccus and 
Reid Vogelhut announce the opening 
of the New York office of R & B 
Productions, a multi -service concert 
promotion, management and adver- 
tising venture. Nationally, the pair 
will 
produce 
their 
own 
concerts, 
coordinate the acquisition of major 
acts for colleges and universities and 
develop new talent. 
Prior to the organization of R & B 
Productions, Ms. Baccus served as di- 
rector of the concert division of Mu- 
sic Fair Enterprises, Inc., in charge 
of booking and producing contem- 
porary and variety attractions for 
the chain of East Coast theatres -in - 
the -round. Ms. Baccus was also re- 
sponsible for the management of Sly 
& The Family Stone, Genya Ravan, 
Peaches and Herb for a number of 
years. 
Vogelhut, who has produced many 
concerts 
throughout 
the 
country, 
will remain as president of Nazz 
Advertising, located 
in 
Baltimore, 
Md., handling advertising and promo- 
tion campaigns for R & B projects. 
Previously, he was with Tract Adver- 
tising in Philadelphia, heading up 
their concert advertising accounts. 
R & B Productions is located at 
527 Madison Avenue, Room 700-16, 
New York, New York 10022. Tele- 
phone (212) 753-6108. 
'Lady A', 
Founded Stax 
Back In Biz 
MEMPHIS - Mrs. Estelle Axton, 
long recognized as one of the leaders 
in Memphis Music for many years, 
re-entered the music business after a 
five year absence. 
"Lady A" as she is fondly referred 
to, founded Stax Records with her 
brother, Jim Stewart, in 1958. From a 
humble beginning on East McLemore 
in a renovated theatre, Estelle Axton 
and Jim Stewart created the giant 
rhythm and blues studio known all 
over the world. Such recording art- 
ists as Isaac Hayes, Rufus and Carla 
Thomas, The Mar -Keyes, Otis Red- 
ding, Staple Singers and many others 
began their record careers under the 
watchful eyes of this brother/sister 
duo. 
Now Estelle Axton is beginning a 
new music career. Long a strong be- 
liever in new talent, Mrs. Axton has 
established a company dedicated to 
discovering 
and 
developing 
new 
promising talent. Songwriters will 
form a strong nucleus of new talent 
but it will not be limited to songwrit- 
ers. 
A subsidiary of Fretone Music is 
being formed entitled Discovery Un- 
limited. "We believe that Discovery 
will fill a basic need in our communi- 
ty" said Mrs. Axton. "Many of our 
talented people have no one to see or 
hear their work and this is what we 
will endeavor to do. In addition to 
songwriters, we intend to see and 
hear singers, musicians, actors, an- 
nouncers, and models for films. We 
have an "open 
door" 
and "Open 
Mind" policy to anyone that has tal- 
ent in the recording, film, TV, or 
related industries. We do not promise 
you stardom, only a chance to be 
heard. If you have what it takes, we 
will do what we can to develop that 
talent," stated Mrs. Axton. 
Ted Cunningham, former general 
manager of the Memphis Symphony 
Orchestra for many years and a staff 
member of Trans Visual Productions, 
will co-ordinate Discovery Unlimited.

R f3 B INGREDIENTS-Before getting into the NATRA segment of 
this particular column, it's necessary to say that the current NYC Lincoln Cen- 
ter, 'Soul At The Center' Series, is a well run and beautifully organized program. 
The producers, Ellis Haizlip and Gerry Bledsoe deserve a lot of credit. The 
shows start on time. The acts begin on time and intermissions are exact. What 
more can one ask? And, of course the talent has been superb. Check out the 
CB Talent On Stage section in this issue for preview, of some these shows .. . 
The new Duke Ellington release, "Yale Concert" (Fantasy #9433), was errone- 
ously described as a reissue in an earlier press release. Actually, "Yale Con- 
cert" is one of five albums of unreleased Ellington material acquired by Fantasy 
Records

AT NATRA - NATRA held its annual event at the Marriott Hotel in New 
Orleans, August 8 thru the 12th.. Of course, the highlight of the event is the 
Golden Mike Awards Show. It was held Saturday (11th) evening. The Ballroom 
capacity crowd was treated to an enjoyable evening as the ceremonies un- 
folded. The event was hosted by E. Rodney Jones who puts plenty of zip into 
the works. He is together! D. J.'s, record execs and industry personnel from 
throughout the country gathered at the Marriott for this event and most every- 
one will agree it was a swinging affair, without incident or trouble, and despite 
elevator delays the affair went smoothly. The hospitality suites kept things 
hummin' with plenty of music including the new product to be released shortly. 
And, you can believe it, Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes will be filling the air- 
waves very shortly. Judging from the reaction when hearing the cut in the 
Columbia suite, it can't miss. 
I, also, wish to take this opportunity to express my sincerest thank you to 
all of you for the fine reception accorded me at my first NATRA event. By the 
way, New Orleans is a gem of a city. 
don drossell

rector for the label. Brown will be 
situated at the UA offices in New

of

Baltimore 
and

ATI Expands 
To TV Music 
NEW YORK - American Talent In- 
ternational is expanding its involve- 
ment in the area of television by 
signing an agreement with Hanna - 
Barbera Productions to produce the 
music for their new animated televi- 
sion series, "Butch Cassidy." The an- 
nouncement was made by Buddy Ep- 
stein, executive head of ATI's west 
coast office, who completed the nego- 
tiations with Hanna -Barbera. 
ATI will furnish the music for the 
new series which will be performed 
by a four -member group to be known 
as 
The 
Sundance 
Kids featuring 
Butch Cassidy. Buddy Buie, writer 
and producer of such hits for the 
Classics 
IV 
as 
"Stormy" 
and 
"Traces," will produce the music for 
the show as well as producing the 
group for MGM Records. 
The "Butch Cassidy" series will air 
on Saturday mornings at 10 on NBC 
starting in the fall.

KQV Air -Staff 
To M.D. Telethon 
PITTSBURGH - The annual Jerry 
Lewis Telethon, benefitting the Mus- 
cular Dystrophy Foundation, and tel- 
evised Sunday and Monday, Septem- 
ber 2-3, Labor Day weekend, will in- 
corporate the talents of the KQV Ra- 
dio personalities. 
The Telethon will be broadcast on 
WIIC-TV, Channel 11. Beginning at 
6:00 p.m. Sunday, September 2, and 
continuing until 6:00 p.m. Monday, 
September 3, each of the KQV on -air 
personalities' shows will 
be aired 
from the Channel 11 studios, while 
they are simultaneously being seeen 
on television. 
Last year, through the cooperation 
of the KQV personalities, the local 
chapter of the Muscular Dystrophy 
Foundation raised over $70,000 on 
the Jerry Lewis Telethon. 
Much of the program will emanate 
from the Sahara Hotel in Las Vegas 
with "pick-ups" from New York, 
Nashville and Hollywood.

Dick Clark Presents 
'Rock & Roll Years' 
NEW YORK - Chuck Berry, Fabi- 
an, The Drifters, Marty Robbins, 
Lesley Gore, Chubby Checker, James 
Brown, and Donovan will be part of 
a new ABC Television Network spe- 
cial, "Dick Clark Presents the Rock & 
Roll Years," 
airing 
on Thursday, 
Sept. 27 (8:00-9:00 p.m., EDT). The 
musical special was announced by 
Edwin T. Vane, vice president and 
national program director for ABC 
Entertainment. 
Dick Clark hosts a history of the 
rock & roll years live, on film, and on 
tape, with stars who represent the 
many elements which combined to 
create this musical phenomenon. 
It all began with the music of peo- 
ple 
like 
Chuck 
Berry 
and 
The 
Drifters, and went 
on 
to include 
country -western 
influences 
from 
Brenda Lee and Carl Perkins. The 
rock & roll "Idols" like Fabian and 
Bobby Vee led to dance crazes like 
Chubby Checker doing the Twist. 
James Brown and The Supremes rep- 
resent the soul side of rock & roll, 
while Gerry & the Pacemakers, and 
Chad 
& Jeremy, were among the 
stars in the important British rock 
invasion. Finally, the music reached a 
calmer stage with the lyrical love and 
peace themes of Three Dog Night 
and Donovan. 
Presented before a live audience at 
the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium, 
"Dick Clark Presents the Rock 
& 
Roll Years" will recreate the feeling 
and the atmosphere which produced 
the music that spanned two decades. 
The special is produced by Bill 
Lee, with Mark Warren as director, 
for Dick Clark Teleshows, with Dick 
Clark as executive producer.

W. Houdini, 
Calypso Star, 
Dies in NYC 
NEW YORK - Wilmoth Houdini, a 
native of Trinidad who was one of 
the key figures in the introduction of 
calypso music into the United States 
in the 1930s, died Aug. 6 at his home 
in Harlem. He was 77 years old. 
Mr. Houdini followed the fashion 
of calypso singers in adopting anoth- 
er name. He was born Frederick Hen- 
dricks. 
A singer/songwriter, he is 
best remembered as the author of 
"Stone Cold Dead In The Market," 
which was a keystone of his act and 
a hit for Ella Fitzgerald. He and the 
Duke of Iron were two of the most 
popular black entertainers of their 
day. 
His early recordings were cut in 
Trinidad by Decca. His work is still 
available 
on the Decca 
collectors 
series. 
Burial was Friday, Aug. 10, in 
Woodlawn Cemetery. 
Dick Friedenberg 
To Dynamic House 
NEW YORK - Larry Crane, pres- 
ident of Dynamic House, Inc./Tele 
House, Inc., has announced the ap- 
pointment of Dick Friedenberg to the 
position of vice-president. In this ca- 
pacity, he will work closely with 
Crane in all aspects of the Company. 
Prior to his appointment, Frieden - 
berg served for two years as Pres- 
ident of the Canadian wings of the 
Capitol Record Club and the Lon - 
gines Symphonette Society. He held 
various marketing and A&R posi- 
tions at Longines (U.S.) including 
Product Manager of Broadcast Sales. 
Friedenberg was previously associ- 
ated with the CBS Direct Marketing 
Division-Columbia House. He is a 
graduate of New York University, 
School of Business.

NEW YORK - Bob Regehr, director

S. C. Studio 
Catering To 
Gospel Music 
ATLANTA - The midpoint has been 
reached in the construction of an ad- 
ditional 
sixteen -track 
studio 
in 
Greenville (S.C.). Project supervisor 
Harold Huffman has indicated that 
the facility will be completed no later 
than September 1st. 
Located adjacent to the present 
Mark Five building, the studio will 
utilize only the very latest equip- 
ment, and a new acoustical design in 
the recording area. This will be the 
first operation devoted to Gospel Mu- 
sic, requiring two complete 16 track 
studios. The present production has 
been working beyond its capacity, 
and the additional space will make it 
much easier to book studio time and 
allow for faster service on orchestra- 
tions and re -mix sessions. 
Ex-Conducter 
D. Savino Dies; 
Was Also Publisher 
NEW YORK - Maestro Domenico 
Savino, 
composer -member 
of 
the 
American Society of Composers, Au- 
thors and Publishers since 1924, and 
music director for the CBS Sympho- 
ny Orchestra and 
Bell Telephone 
Hour in the 1930's died last week (8) 
at Doctors Hospital in New York 
City after a short illness. He was 91 
years old, and lived at 320 West End 
Avenue. 
Savino 
was a prolific composer 
who had more than 1,500 classical 
and semi -classical works published. 
He was also chief editor of the "Big 
3" music companies, and had been a 
partner in Robbins Music, as well as 
music director for the Paramount 
Hour. 
He was born in Taranto, Italy in 
1882, educated at the Royal Conser- 
vatory of Naples and came to the 
United States in 1905. Savino was 
actively composing until a week ago, 
and his latest composition was re- 
corded in May of this year. 
He is survived by two sisters in 
Taranto. His wife died in 1972. Ser- 
vices were held at Riverside Chapel, 
Aug. 9.

MASTERPIECE-The oil portrait of singer Tom Jones that adorns his latest 
album, "The Body and Soul Of Tom Jones," is to accompany the Parrot/London 
artist on the second half of his current coast -to -coast U.S. tour. The painting 
is the work of Los Angeles artist Shel Starkman. Shel had intended it as a 
gift for his wife, but Jones' manager, Gordon Mills, saw it, liked it, bought it. 
and used it on the new album. A slew of offers to buy the portrait followed its 
appearance on "Body and Soul," but instead of selling it, Mills turned it over 
to Tom's U.S. record company, London Records, on a 3 -month loan. Because 
of the interest, excitement, and demand that the painting had already gen- 
erated, London's director of promotion, Sy Warner, recommended that the 
portrait travel with Jones to all the key cities included on the remainder of 
his current U.S. tour. 
Mobile Amp 
On Market 
NEW YORK - James William Guer- 
cio has partnered with Wayne Kim- 
bell and Richard Edlund and the mu- 
sic group Chicago in the production 
and distribution of a new amplifier 
with the name Pignose. 
Forming Pignose Industries, the 
group are marketing what has been 
certified to be the first low-cost, pro- 
fessional quality, completely portable 
lightweight 
amplifier. Invented by 
Kimbell and Edlund, the amplifier re- 
tails for $89.50, approximately half 
the cost of amplifiers of similar qual- 
ity already on the market, weighs a 
slight five pounds, is powered by six 
11 
volt, size AA batteries or by an 
A/C volt converted. The Pignose can 
handle 
keyboards, 
horns, 
synthe- 
sizers, steel guitar, harmonicas, bass, 
electric fiddles or can be used as a 
portable p.a. system for small busi- 
ness meetings.

AFM Members OK Label Pact 
NEW YORK, NEW YORK - Ameri- 
can Federation of Musicians Pres- 
ident Hal Davis today announced ap- 
proval by affected members of the 
AFM of a 27 -month contract between 
the 320,000 -member union and the 
phonograph record industry. Tenta- 
tive agreement between negotiators 
for the industry and the Federation 
was announced on July 23, after 
which 
those AFM 
members 
who 
earned $1,000 or more from recording 
during the calendar year 1972 were 
polled by secret -ballot. The result of 
the mail ballot was 907 in favor of 
acceptance, 156 opposed. Union nego- 
tiators had recommended acceptance 
of the pact, which is retroactive to 
Aug. 1, 1973. 
Davis noted that "In the symphonic 
field, an area where during the past 
several years we have been experi- 
encing sharp decreases in employment 
opportunities, agreement was reached 
on not only a substantial wage in- 
crease, but also on the availability of 
a four hour session and on a reduc- 
tion in the amount of product that 
can be taken from a session. It is our 
firm hope," he said, "and this is 
shared by symphonic players and by 
management representatives attend- 
ing 
the 
negotiations, 
that these 
changes will result in increased re- 
cording activity for U.S. and Canadian 
symphonic players." 
Davis noted that in the area of 
non -symphonic recordings, "we suc- 
cessfully 
obtained 
scale 
increases 
which in our judgement will not only 
benefit our players financially but 
will not dilute the number of job op- 
portunities currently available to mu- 
sicians working in this industry." 
He said that a most significant 
agreement was reached to clarify the 
language of the Special Payments and 
Music 
Performance 
Trust 
Funds, 
dealing with employer contributions 
to those funds. "This will eliminate 
many disputes and expedite the flow 
of money to the funds," he said. 
Contract highlights include: 
Scale wages: 
Non -symphonic: For a three-hour 
session, $95, going to $100 effective 
September 15, 1974. (The old rate was 
$90.) Special Session 
(11 
hours): 
$63; rising to $66 on September 15, 
1974. 
(Old rate was $60..) 
Special 
Canadian rate: $79; $83 in September 
of 1974. (Old rate, $75.) 
Symphonic: For three hour session, 
$101; going to $106 on September 15, 
1974. (Old rate was $95.) Entirely 
new is provision for a four hour ses- 
sion, which will pay $134.67, and 
which will be increased to $141.33 
effective September 15, 1974. This will

due 
in 
no small part," 
explains 
Sachs, "to their total involvement in 
concentrating on each project and art- 
ist. Our point of volume and growth 
has necessitated that sort of detailed 
concern in the merchandising, mar- 
keting, supervision and eventual dis- 
tribution of our. project."

In addition, there will be two major 
New York events in mid -Sept. A 
George & Ira Gershwin exhibit will at 
the Hallmark Gallery Sept. 19 for six 
weeks, featuring Gershwin memora- 
bilia and live entertainment daily. 
Also, the first George Gershwin film 
festival, an idea created by Chappell, 
will open at a major museum in Sept. 
This will include a sheet music and 
film still exhibit. 
Other Events 
Extensive radio, TV and press cov- 
erage is anticipated. Symphony or- 
chestras across the U.S. are already 
planning special Gershwin tributes. 
One of these, featuring the Mormon 
Tabernacle Youth Chorus & Sympho- 
ny was televised last week on WNET. 
In addition, there will be numerous 
store displays in the metropolitan 
area. 
Currently, there is a Gershwin show 
that is touring the Northeast area. 
Entitled "The Gershwin Years," it 
features all Gershwin material cel- 
ebrating the 75th birthday with such 
stars as Helen Gallagher and Barbara 
Cook. 
The U.S. Postal Service has already 
saluted Gershwin with its Gershwin 
commemorative stamp issued earlier 
this year featuring the head of Gersh- 
win against a montage of figures 
from "Porgy and Bess." 
Internationally, many events are in 
the works. Chappell -London has is- 
sued a biographical brochure for dis- 
tribution abroad and are coordinating 
radio/TV and press events. The BBC 
is planning a Gershwin special. Chap- 
pell -Germany has arranged for every 
German broadcasting station to do a 
special Gershwin program in Sept. 
For instance the RIAS in Berlin is 
preparing a 90 minute program. Oth- 
er branches such as those in Holland 
and Paris are also deeply involved in 
the worldwide celebration. 
Weiser Comment 
Norm Weiser, president of Chap- 
pell, noted that with the assistance of 
the worldwide Polygram Group "we 
are certain that people in every civi- 
lized country in the world will be 
re -exposed to the wonderful music 
created by the Gershwins." 
Abroad, Meyerstein-Maigret, pres- 
ident of Polygram S.A., is coordinat- 
ing 
worldwide 
publishing 
efforts 
from his headquarters in Paris. 
In the U.S., Ed Silvers, president of 
Warner Bros. Music, Sol Reimer and 
Henry Marks are working with Chap- 
pell on the 75th anniversary cam- 
paign.

Motown's Big 
Campaign On 
Gaye's New LP 
HOLLYWOOD - Motown Records is 
preparing a big marketing campaign 
to launch the new Marvin Gaye album 
"Let's Get It On," according to Phil 
Jones, director of sales, Motown Rec- 
ords. 
Except for the soundtrack album 
"Trouble Man," this is Gaye's first 
album since the release of "What's 
Going On" in 
1971. Motown sales 
execs feel that "Let's Get It On," a 
concept album dealing with the emo- 
tions of a love affair, has a broader 
range of appeal than anything pre- 
viouly recorded by the artist. There- 
fore, the company's public relations/ 
advertising/merchandising thrust has 
been aimed at reaching a much greater 
range of consumers. 
The album is scheduled to ship this 
week as the single preceding it is 
number one on the charts. One of 
the largest -selling singles in Motown 
history, "Let's Get It On" went gold 
within six weeks of release. 
National Consumer Advertising 
In addition to radio spots adver- 
tising the album, Motown will place 
its first wave of advertising in na- 
tional publications such as the Na- 
tional Lampoon, Time (college edi- 
tion), Essence, Jet, and Rolling Stone, 
and in important local publications 
such as the Los Angeles Times Sun- 
day Calendar. 
For further local advertising, the 
company has created a series of ad 
mats in various sizes. A large bill- 
board on Sunset Boulevard will go up 
shortly after the album is released. 
A public relations campaign for re- 
views of the album will begin with the 
release of the record. Nearly 4,000 
entertainers, sports figures and other 
celebrities will receive copies of it. 
Two posters-one 4 x 6 feet and 
another 22 x 33 inches will be supplied 
to stores and radio stations, as will 
"Let's Get It On" lapel buttons. 
Late in Sept. "The Master: The 
Magic of Marvin Gaye," a 90 -minute 
radio special documenting the record- 
ing career of the artist through the 
new album, will be made available to 
radio stations. The program will be 
co -produced by Motown and Water- 
mark, Inc., producers of American Top 
40 and the Elvis Special. 
Planning for the campaign was 
handled by Mike Lushka, album sales 
manager; and Herb Wood, director of 
advertising. Dave Swaney's Company 
was retained by Motown to develop 
merchandising and public relations 
elements for the campaign. 
spots have been running on Radio 
Veronica to promote the groups' ar- 
rival. 
The groups' stay in Holland cli- 
maxes with their appearance at the 
Sportshalle 
in 
Rotterdam 
where 
they'll perform for 8,000 spectators 
and be televised on "Top Pops," Hol- 
land's most important scheduled TV 
special this fall. 
Previous CBS International coordi- 
nated European tours have resulted in 
the shaping of these artists' European 
careers. Albert Hammond's first tour 
produced sales of half a million co- 
pies of "It Never Rains In Southern 
California," and is considered an im- 
portant factor in the success of his 
current single, "Free Electric Band," 
now on the charts throughout Eu- 
rope. Hammond will introduce his 
third single, "Peacemaker" in Europe 
shortly. Redbone's prior European 
trip resulted in their current "Wound- 
ed Knee" smash there. Dr. Hook is 
making their first visit to Europe, 
following up on their earlier Europe- 
an success with "Sylvia's Mother" and 
their record currently rising on the 
Dutch charts, "Roland The Roadie." 
All tours have been closely coordi- 
nated between 
CB.S International's 
New York and European operations 
offices.

Wallichs Shows 
1st Profits 
In Four Years 
HOLLYWOOD - Wallichs Music & 
Entertainment Company, Inc., has re- 
ported a sales increase of 4.5% and its 
first profit from operations in four 
years for fiscal 1973, ended May 31. 
Net income, before extraordinary 
item, was $26,507, or 
2 cents per 
share, on revenues of $8,168,085. This 
compares to a net loss, before ex- 
traordinary item, of $18,857, or a loss 
of 1% per share on revenues of $7,- 
840,489 for the previous fiscal year. 
The extraordinary item for fiscal 
1973 of $17,000 or 1 cent per share, 
resulted from a tax benefit operating 
loss carryover. In fiscal 1972, the 
company had an extraordinary item 
of $67,875, or 5 cents per share, from 
insurance benefits paid upon the death 
of Glenn Wallichs, a founder of the 
company. 
In announcing results, Clyde 
O. 
Wallichs, president, said sales in all 
departments increased with gains of 
5.1% in records; 5.4% in pianos and 
organs and 3.4% in television and 
stereo. 
He said the gain in record sales 
was achieved in the second half when 
a switch from reliance on jobbers to 
direct buying improved selection. 
Among other factors cited for con- 
tributing to the company's up swing 
in sales and return to profit were 
overhead reductions, reorganization 
of the stores and a better balanced 
advertising program.

selves unjustly at plaintiff's expense. 
The 
appropriating 
of 
the 
per- 
formances recorded by plaintiff and 
selling 
them in 
competition with 
plaintiff constitutes unfair competi- 
tion in North Carolina. Such unfair 
competition entitles plaintiff to recov- 
er damages and it is subject to in- 
junctive restraint," the Court de- 
clared. 
The Court also cited the U. S. Su- 
preme Court decision in Goldstein v. 
California which, it noted, found that 
a statute "which bars unauthorized 
copying of sound recordings (is) a 
valid exercise of the powers of the 
state." 
Rejecting 
the 
claim 
that 
the 
plaintiff record companies were as- 
serting a monopoly in violation of the 
State constitution, the Court observed 
that "plaintiff is simply trying to pre- 
vent defendants from stealing its 
property. Defendants are not restrict- 
ed from securing their own per- 
formers, 
recording 
these 
per- 
formances, and selling their own rec- 
ords or tapes in fair competition with 
the plaintiff." 
As to the defendants' claim that the 
sale by a record company of an album 
with a number of different composi- 
tions constitutes a tie-in sale, the 
Court declared: "Upon the basis of 
the undisputed facts, the conduct of 
plaintiff in marketing its products has 
not been shown to be improper or 
contrary to public policy." 
Finally, on the question of the re- 
fusal by legitimate record companies 
to license their material to pirates, 
the Court held that "the evidence 
shows that this action on the part of 
plaintiff was unilateral and not pur- 
suant to any agreement 
. not to 
deal with the defendants. In the ab- 
sence of conspiracy or monopoly, one 
may deal with whom he pleases."

ASCAP Annual 
War, John Cage 
NEW YORK - The American Soci- 
ety of Composers, Authors and Pub- 
lishers, has announced the completion 
of the 13th annual meetings of the 
Special Awards Panels. Society pres- 
ident, Stanley Adams, advised that 
$629,000 in cash awards, in addition 
to the normal royalty distributions, 
will be distributed this year to the 
Society's writers to offer financial en- 
couragement and in recognition of 
their important role in American mu- 
sic. 
Since the inception of this pro- 
gram, in 1960, the Society has dis- 
tributed some 6 million dollars in 
awards to its composer and author 
members. The program was devised 
and sums set aside to encourage and 
foster the contribution of ASCAP 
members to American music. Its pur- 
pose is to give recognition to those 
writers 
whose unique 
contribution 
may not 
be 
sufficiently rewarded 
through normal earned royalties. In 
volunteering to allocate a share of 
their earnings in this way, the mem- 
bers of the Society give tangible evi- 
dence of their continuing support of 
contemporary music. 
The awards recipients represent the 
complete spectrum in contemporary 
composition. Among them are such 
writers of international renown as 
Gian -Carlo 
Menotti 
whose 
Spoleto 
festival draws thousands of music 
lovers every year, Broadway figures 
Warren Casey and Jim Jacobs with 
the longest running musical "Grease" 
and the "Purlie" team, Gary Geld and 
Peter Udell, who have a new show 
coming up this season "All The Com- 
forts Of Home"; John Gage, a semi- 
nal figure in American music; Nash- 
ville country writer Buzz Cason; Joe 
Raposo, the chief writer for Sesame 
Street; rock groups such as "War," 
"Steeley Dan" and the "J. Geils 
Band"; and Richard Feliciano, pioneer 
in new religious liturgies. 
Young ASCAP writers are carry- 
ing on the tradition of such early 
members as Jerome Kern and Victor 
Herbert with contributions to the On 
and Off Broadway Theatre. Steven 
Schwartz

Groove Merchant 
Tape Via Ampex 
ELK GROVE, CALIF. - Ampex Mu- 
sic and Groove Merchant Internation- 
al, Inc., have agreed on a long-term 
tape licensing contract for the United 
States, it was announced today by 
William L. Slover, Ampex vice pres- 
ident and general manager of AMD. 
Ampex will market Groove Mer- 
chant's existing catalog of 18 albums 
as well as new titles as they become 
available. 
"The addition of the Groove Mer- 
chant label will give us solid jazz 
artists 
such 
as 
Dakota 
Staton, 
Reuben Wilson, Jimmy McGriff, Car- 
men McRae, Groove Holmes, O'Donel 
Levy, and many others," Slover said. 
The contract was negotiated by 
Slover and by Ery Bagley, Groove 
Merchant vice president.

Cash Box/R4B News Report 
Wayne Tucker 
Eastern Reg. 
Fantasy Promo. 
BERKELEY - Wayne Tucker has 
joined 
Fantasy/Prestige/Milestone 
and will be doing Eastern Regional 
Promotion for the family of labels. 
Tucker will assume his duties on Au- 
gust 13th. 
Tucker's 
interesting and 
varied 
jazz background will no doubt be of 
great help to him in his new job. He 
has played an active role in commu- 
nity organizations 
concerned with 
keeping jazz in Washington, D.C., 
and has hosted shows on WHFS-FM 
in Bethesda, Md., and the "Jazz Un- 
derground" program at WETA-FM. 
Tucker worked for a year at Wash- 
ington's largest record store, The 
Soul Shack, and also spent much time 
on the air at WGTB-FM and WHUR- 
FM. 
Wayne Tucker will be based at the 
Fantasy/Prestige/Milestone office at 
15 Columbus Circle, New York City 
10022.

Roger Durham, 
of Bloodstone, 
Dies at 27 
NEW YORK - Roger Lee Durham, 
member of London Records' group 
Bloodstone, died recently in Kansas 
City at the age of 27 after a lengthy 
illness. 
Durham, born in Charlotte, N.C., 
grew up in Kansas City, Kansas where 
he and four friends formed a group 
called 
The Sinceres, later 
to 
be 
known as Bloodstone. He was vocal- 
ist, percussionist as well as writer for 
the group which has recently begun 
to gain world-wide recognition both 
because of their current hit single 
and album, "Natural High," and ex- 
tensive concert and club appearances. 
Durham toured with Bloodstone until 
February when his illness forced him 
to return to Kansas City. 
Durham is survived by his parents 
and a half brother who live in Kansas 
City and a sister who lives in Los 
Angeles.

. Paul Moore, Anglican Bishop of New York, re- 
cently announced that a press conference to be given by Ossie Davis, Jeoffry 
Holder and Dick Kennard is to be held, Sept. 5th at 11 a.m. in the Afro -Asian 
Chapel in the Cathedral Church of St. John The Divine at Amsterdam Ave. & 
112th St., Manhattan. Plans will be announced for an emergency benefit for 
the people of the Saheel (Mauritania, Senegal, Mali, Upper Volta, Niger, Chad) 
who have- been victims of a devastating five-year drought. The benefit to be 
held in late September will call upon the services of major black talent in 
the US and the event will be entitled, "Balmaya" (a West African word mean- 
ing brotherhood)

Tom T. Hall 
Gets `Boot(ed)' 
Out Of Texas 
NASHVILLE - Shading their eyes 
from the sun, Tom. T. Hall and his 
Storytellers were waiting this week 
as a private Lear jet swooped down 
on a Missouri runway. Furnished by 
El Paso's Tony Lama Company Inc., 
the plane was there to whisk Hall and 
the entire group off to El Paso for a 
"Boot In." 
Partaking of the on -board luxuries, 
including a "flying saloon," the group 
disembarked in El Paso and were 
promptly escorted to the boot compa- 
ny where Lama personally outfitted 
all of the group with several pairs of 
custom boots. 
Privately jetted back to Nashville, 
Hall was asked his opinion of his new 
footwear. Flexing his leather clad 
feet while eyeing his additional as- 
sortment of reptile and multi -colored 
footwear, Hall smiled and endorsed 
his new pediwear by quipping, "Well, 
you can bet your boots we got a boot 
out it." 
Lubbock's KDAV 
To Celebrate 
20 Country Years 
LUBBOCK - The world's first full- 
time country music station, KDAV in 
Lubbock, Texas, will celebrate its 20th 
Anniversary with an all -day party at 
the Villa Inn, Sept. 19th. 
On hand to join the festivities will 
be 
KDAV 
owner 
"Pappy" 
Dave 
Stone, general manager of the Dave 
Stone Stations; Bonnie Paris, and 
KDAV's general manager Bob Clark. 
Also expected are some of the former 
KDAV 
dee -jays and 
personalities 
from the country music industry. Two 
former KDAV air personalities are 
Waylon Jennings and Bill Mack. 
The No. 
1 country record when 
KDAV hit the airwaves on September 
19, 1953 was Jean Shepard and Ferlin 
Husky's "Dear John Letter." 
Another interesting side -note is the 
fact that the Dave Stone Stations to- 
tal 80 years of continuous country 
music broadcasting: 
20 
years for 
KDAV; 19 years for KPEP-San An- 
gelo, Texas; 
18 years for KZIP- 
Amarillo, Texas; 16 years for KPIK- 
AM, and 7 years for KPIK FM, Colo- 
rado Springs, Colorado. (KPIK has 
also just added stereo.) 
Po' Boys Trounce Twittybirds 21-9 
HOLLYWOOD - Country 
music 
stars 
Bill 
Anderson and 
Conway 
Twitty and their bands got together 
on Aug. 7 to play a baseball game for 
charity at Nashville's Madison Park. 
The two artists have always had an 
active interest in baseball. Conway, at 
one time, nearly signed a professional 
contract with the Philadelphia Phil - 
lies. Proceeds went to the Nashville 
Camp Fund for the Blind Children. 
WSM Radio's Ralph Emery was the 
announcer and Bud Wendell, manager 
of the Grand Ole Opry, was the base 
umpire. Other personalities who con- 
tributed their time and talents were 
MCA Record's John Brown and re- 
cording artist L. E. White, who played 
on Conway's team, and singer Mary 
Lou Turner, who was pinch hitter for 
Bill Anderson. 
The final score was 21-9, Bill And- 
erson's favor.

Tulsa Show

tion KTOW, Sand Springs, Oklaho- 
ma, covering the Tulsa area, will hold 
its 
fourth 
semi-annual 
sponsored 
country 
show at the Tulsa Fair- 
grounds Exposition Building Friday, 
Sept. 14, at 8:00 p.m. It will bring 
together two Dot recording artists 
for their single appearances in Tulsa 
this year. 
Hank Thompson, who is celebrating 
his 27th year in the music business, 
and his Brazos Valley Boys; will 
share honors with beautiful Diana 
Trask. 
the 
Australian -Nashville 
transplant who has been riding high 
on the charts with "Say When" and 
"It's A Man's World." Mac Sanders 
will emcee and Hank Penny will head- 
line the comedy section. The Proud 
Country Singers will add choral back- 
ground along with David Ingles.

Town Honors 
Jimmy Gateley 
NASHVILLE-Country music artist 
Jimmy Gateley returned to his home- 
town, Pleasant Hope, Mo., to be hon- 
ored by "Jimmy Gateley Day" on Fri- 
day, Sept. 7, and appeared at a spe- 
cial benefit show at the Pleasant 
Hope High School to raise money for 
new uniforms for the high school 
band. 
Bill Anderson, the country music 
singer and composer, brought his 
whole show to Pleasant Hope to per- 
form at the benefit performance. Jim- 
my Gateley has been a featured per- 
former with the Bill Anderson Show 
for nine years. 
Gateley, who is a talented singer, 
guitarist and country "fiddler" has 
appeared in concert with the Ander- 
son Show all over the United States. 
He is seen each week on the Bill 
Anderson Show which is carried by 
more than 100 television stations.

MGM's 'Top Week' Splurge
Is Across -The -Board Affair
HOLLYWOOD - MGM Records reg-
istered what it calls "the label's most
successful week of 1973" during the
Aug. 27-31 period, according to Tony
Scotti, senior vice president -product.
He credited this acceleration on or-
ders and sales to a coordinated prod-
uct release and marketing effort that
"came together at every turn, without
exception."
According
to
Scotti.
this
record
week was paced by the Osmonds' "Let
Me In" single from their "The Plan"
LP; Donny Osmond's two-sided hit,
"Young Love"/"A Million To One,"
and sister Marie Osmond's debut sin-
gle, "Paper Roses"; and MGM's new-
ly -released series of motion picture
soundtracks, six albums marketed as
"Those Glorious MGM Musicals."
Soundtracks Score
"The six double -packages of MGM
musical motion picture soundtracks
just released have proved to be a very
profitable
repackaging
venture,"
Scotti commented. ".
.
. dealer re-
sponse has been tremendous. We find
that this is a commodity the public
has been hungry for as a part of the
nostalgic trend."
He continued, "We are now enjoy -
FRONT COVER:
,s..,5.
Gilbert O'Sullivan first hit Amer-
ican shores with his smash hit "Alone
Again (Naturally)." The young Brit-
ish singer -songwriter then wasted no
time in coming forth with his second
consecutive hit, "Clair," a bit of a
departure from his first. His latest,
"Get Down" a Top Ten staple for
some time decisively proves that the
artist is here to stay.
The MAM recording artist also has
to
his credit the best selling LP,
"Alone Again (Naturally)" and his
latest charted collection, "Back To
Front," both of which contain the art-
ists compositions and more than amply
demonstrate his talents as songwriter.
The future certainly looks bright for
Gilbert O'Sullivan. He is produced by
Gordon Mills.

FBI Pirate Raids:
St. Louis, Atlanta
ST. LOUIS - FBI agents raided a
converted bowling alley in which pi-
rated tapes were being manufactured
and seized more than 2,000 bogus
tapes, winding equipment and more
than a dozen "pancakes," large reels
of pre-recorded tape, each containing
recorded material to fill up to 35 tape
albums. The seized evidence, it was
said, will be presented shortly to a
Federal Grand Jury.
The premises, located in the town of
Imperial, about 20
miles
south
of
here, were occupied by Record Wide
Distributors, alleged
to have been
making and selling under the "Quala-
Sonic" label copyrighted recordings
produced by a number of legitimate
recording companies. FBI agents, who
had conducted their own surveillance
after being alerted to the operation
by the Recording Industry Associa-
tion of America, were armed with a
search warrant signed by U.S. Magis-
trate William Rund.
Among the seized tapes were pirat-
ed
versions
of such
recordings
as
"Joplin in Concert"; "Blood, Sweat
and Tears' Greatest Hits"; "Fifth Di-
mensions' Greatest Hits"; "Big Bam-
boo,"
by
Cheech
and Chong, and
"Bedtime Story," by Tammy Wynette.

the home of a suspected tape pirate,

19 Stars At
PUSH Expo In
Chi; Sept. 19-23
CHICAGO -A 5 -night sellout audi-
ence of 60,000 will see 19 star black
acts at the PUSH Expo at the Interna-
tional Amphitheatre in Chicago, Sept.
19-23.
The 5th annual Black Business &
Cultural
Expo,
sponsored
by Rev.
Jesse
Jackson's
operation
PUSH
(People United to Save Humanity) is
basing this year's theme on "Save the
Black Colleges." More than 1 million
are expected to see exhibits and at-
tend workshops.
Set for the talent nights at the
12,000 -seat
Amphitheatre
are
Al
Green, the 5th Dimension, the Inde-
pendents,
Roberta
Flack,
Barry
White, Quincy Jones,
4 Tops, Su-
premes, Temptations, Smokey Robin-
son, the Jackson 5 Revue, Nancy Wil-
son, Ahmad Jamal, James Cleveland,
Donny Hathaway, Issac Hayes, B. B.
King, the Dells and Zulema.
In addition, leading black comics
are expected to be on hand as emcees,
including Bill Cosby, Flip Wilson, and
Redd Foxx. Tickets for each night are
scaled at $4.50, $5.50 and $6.50. Part
of this year's income will go to the
African Relief Fund, setup to aid Af-
rican countries in draught conditions.
A full-length documentary of last
year's event, featuring many of the
acts appearing this year, opens in
New York on Sept. 19. Released by
Paramount Pictures,
it
carries the
title
of last
year's PUSH Expo
theme, "Save the Children." It's un-
derstood that negotiations are under-
way for a soundtrack album to be
marketed by a leading label.

Pickwick Gains
In Fiscal Qtr
NEW YORK - Amos
Heilicher,
president of Pickwick International,
Inc., stated at the company's annual
meet here last week that fiscal 1974
first quarter operations ended July
31, achieved new record results. This
marks the 81st consecutive compara-
tive quarter in which sales and earn-
ings
exceeded
the
previous
year's
quarter.
During the first quarter, sales rose
25% to $33,630,912 from $27,019,180
and net income rose 19% to $1,235,-
804 from $1,041,873
in fiscal
1973.
Earnings per share for the quarter
ended July 31, rose
to $0.29 from
$0.25, an increase of 16% from the
previous fiscal quarter ended July 31,
1972. A 4% stock dividend was de-
clared for shareholders of record on
Oct. 1, payable Oct. 31.
In commenting on these figures,
Heilicher stated "We are
gratified
with the results despite the increased
cost of borrowed funds and the fact
that this period is traditionally the
smallest of the year. It remains our
determination to decrease the effect
of increasing costs by trimming in-
ventories and other operations which
can be streamlined.
"Our strategy in adding retail out-
lets and strategic regional warehous-
ing units, we believe,
continue
to
contribute sales and profit growth to
our
operations.
Our
international
participation
via
our
English
and
Canadian companies are also great
sources of satisfaction in terms of
current contributions and future po-
tential.
"The new product of our Proprie-
tary Records Division and its innova-
tive record packages and ideas should
continue to add its strength to our
operations for the year.
"On June 25, 1973, Pickwick con-
cluded its acquisition of Keel Manu-
facturing Corp., a record
pressing
plant in Hauppauge, Long Island and
on July 2, 1973, we acquired certain
record
pressing
facilities
of
True
Sound Manufacturing Corp., a divi-
sion of A.B.C. Records. Both of these
were reported to you previously. It is
our expectation that after the current
short integration period, these facili-
ties will make their contribution to
sales and profit.
UA's DeMann: 'Ringmaster'
For Label's 'Super Circus'
HOLLYWOOD - The
undisputed
highlight of the recently concluded
United Artists/UDC confab was the
multi -media extravaganza
billed
as
the UA Super Sales Circus, presented
under the aegis of the label's creative
merchandising director, Freddy De -
Mann, during one of the morning ses-
sions. If, in his own words, DeMann
set out to remake the usual product
presentation into "something different
and exciting," the consensus was that
he certainly achieved his goal.
2 Months Planning
DeMann's "circus" was over two
months in the planning and called for
a cast of 50 with the support of a
crew of up to 60 people. The creative
team for the project was the staff of
Chiaramonte
Films
of
Hollywood,
headed by Andy Chiaramonte. Said
DeMann, "I knew what I wanted basi-
cally and was interviewing a number
of firms, as well as media agencies,
and Chiaramonte emerged as the most
unique and innovative
in their ap-
proach. They also impressed me with
their feel for music."
As for the budget, DeMann pointed
out that it came within the amount
annually set aside for such projects,
but pressed for figures, he would say
no more than that "while it
cost
something like $600,000 to produce
'Mame' on Broadway, we didn't spend
anything like that."

include LP's by Sun Re, Dexter Gor-

Black Lion product will retail at the

be available in tape configurations.

Lion catalog have been recorded by
top names in jazz at jazz symposiums

important

throughout the world. In the near

is
re-

Initial List
Over 1000 For
NARAS 'Hall'
NEW YORK - Well over one thou-
sand initial nominations to the new-
ly-organiz&I NARAS Hall of Fame
have poured into the national offices
of the record academy in response to
recent requests issued to members for
their recommendations of outstand-
ing recordings released before
the
1958
inception
of
the
Grammy
Awards.
The list covers as broad a musical
spectrum as that of some of the
NARAS members who have
sub-
mitted
their
lits, such as Leopold
Stokowski, Guy Lombardo, Johnny
Mathis, Nelson Riddle, Laurindo Al-
meida, George Beverly Shea, Percy
Faith, Pee Wee King, Teddi King,
Meredith Wilson, John Scott Trot-
ter, Cy Coleman, David Rose, John
Green,
Sam Donahue
and
Cliffie
Stone.
Included
among
the
suggestions
are recordings by such legendery mu-
sical figures as Enrico Caruso, Ar-
turo
Toscanini,
Paul
Whiteman,
Louis Armstrong, Glenn Miller, Tom-
my Dorsey,
Billie
Holiday,
John
Charles Thomas, Gene Austin, Nat -
"King" Cole, Judy Garland, Hank
Williams, Al Jolson, Mario Lanza,
Bessie Smith, Bix Beiderbecke, Jelly
Roll Morton, the Original Dixieland
Jazz Band, plus many more who are
still
active
on
today's
recording
scene.
The widely varied list of Initial
Nominations
extends
all
the
way
back to the year 1903 when Caruso
recorded his famous version of "Ves
ti La Giubba," to 1905 when Byron G.
Harlan introduced "School Days," and
to 1907 when Billy Murray waxed
"Harrigan." Ben Selvin, one of the
founders and first secretary of the
New York Chapter of NARAS, was
cited
for
his
1919
recording
of
"Dardanella," described as the first
pop million seller. Perhaps the most
concentrated and dedicated of all lists
came from one member who cited 43
separate
selections,
every
one
of
them sung by Bing Crosby.
Weston Comment
The
abundance
of
ballots
and
breadth of initial nominations drew
this
response
from
arranger -
conductor Paul Weston, co-chairman
with Frank Jones of the NARAS
Hall of Fame: "I'm tremendously en-
thused with the response, both as re-
gards the number of members who
have sent in their suggestions as well
as the reaction of the industry in
general to this move by NARAS-to
finally
bring
long -overdue
recogni-
tion
to
those great recordings re-
leased before there ever were any
Grammy Awards."
A Final
Nominating
committee,
comprised of 30 NARAS members,
elected by the Academy's National
Trustees, will soon be announced, and
will
then
select
the
twenty-five
NARAS Hall of Fame nominations.
Following this, the voting procedure
will be turned over to a larger, nine-
ty -man board, consisting of many of
the industry's most knowledgable cit-
izens, who will then select the five
recordings that will become the initi-
al entrants into the NARAS Hall of
Fame.

Howard Stein 
Expanding In 
Concert Dates 
NEW YORK - Howard Stein, rock 
concert producer is expanding his in- 
terests. 
In addition to rock, the future will 
see more diversification for the 30 
year 
old 
impressario. 
Stein will 
present in concert houses in New 
York and throughout the country 
semi -classical, pop and rhythm and 
blue artists. He'll be producing such 
Josephine Baker at both Carnegie 
Hall 
(Nov. 29) 
and Philharmonic 
Hall (Dec. 3) and at the John F. 
Kennedy Concert Hall in Washing- 
ton, D.C. (Nov. 20) and the American 
Premiere performance of Greek com- 
poser, Mikis Theodorakis who wrote 
the musical scores for the films "Z" 
and "Zorha, the Greek" at Philharmo- 
nic Hall (Oct. 1). Entitled "Theo- 
dorakis Conducts Theodorakis," the 
program will feature an ensemble of 
Greek musicians and vocal soloists. 
Another first will be the appearance 
of a rock group on Broadway when 
Stein presents Sha Na Na, at Broad- 
way's Longacre Theatre late Feb. 
Other projects include his appoint- 
ment as producer of entertainment 
for the new 3500 seat Westchester 
Premier Theatre. Personal appear- 
ances by established artists, musical 
and dramatic events, symphony and 
ballet as well as pop, rock 
and 
rhythm and blues concerts will be 
featured. In addition, he will be re- 
sponsible for all pre -production activ- 
ities. 
Stein is also exploring other enter- 
tainment possibilities in 
television 
and Broadway. 
Stein will continue as independent 
producer of rock concerts at the 
Academy of Music and other concerts 
at Philharmonic and Carnegie Halls, 
Madison Square 
Garden and Felt 
Forum. 
Chris Kearney 
In Pascal Deal 
TORONTO - The signing of con- 
tracts 
between Editions 
Musicales 
Claude Pascal, of Paris, France, and 
Mattawa Music Limited, of Toronto, 
Canada, was announced effective Aug 
1. The French Company will publish 
the material 
of Canadian singer - 
songwriter Christopher Kearney in 
France and the Benelux countries. 
Kearney has proved successful in 
Canada with his two Capitol LPs, and 
has received international attention 
for his recordings and his appearance 
at last year's Maple Music Junket 
concert in Toronto. He will be em- 
barking on his first major U.S. con- 
cert tour in October of this year, and 
plans are being formulated for a Eu- 
ropean visit at the beginning of 1974. 
A new LP will be recorded this fall, 
and "Sarah's Stopover," a cut from 
his 
most 
recent 
LP 
"Pemmican 
Stash" is being readied for single re- 
lease in September. 
Negotiations were started on a vis- 
it by Claude Pascal to Canada this 
summer, and were completed by M. 
Pascal and Dennis R. Murphy, rep- 
resenting Mattawa Music Limited. 
Smith, Rapp Merge 
NEW YORK - Frank Smith, pres- 
ident of Edgemont Productions, an- 
nounces he has formed a merger with 
Joseph Rapp and John 
Gomez of 
Joseph Rapp Enterprises 
in New 
York. Smith is a director and pro- 
ducer of night club shows. Rapp is 
the personal manager of Nipsey Rus- 
sell, Kaye Stevens, and Marty Brill, 
and with Gomez, who also heads up 
JoGo Enterprises, Inc., handles Joey 
Dee and Beverly Bremers. 
Edgemont 
Productions 
currently 
has about 20 acts on its roster. One 
act, the Rainy Days, has just been 
signed to Sunburst Records. A second 
act, J. D. Mann, has also been signed 
with the label and will have its first 
single produced by Richard Landis 
and Charlie Calello. 
DAVE MASON, who recently signed an exclusive recording contract with 
Columbia Records, was in New York recently to perform at the Schaefer 
Festival in Central Park and to discuss his first album for the label, "It's Like 
You Never Left," which has just been released. Shown in the photo (left to 
right) are: Charles Koppelman, vice president of national A&R for Columbia 
Records, Mason, and Irwin Segelstein, president of Columbia Records. 
ASCAP Burkan Winner 
NEW YORK - John Harvith of Ann 
Arbor, Michigan has won the $250 
First Prize in the 1973 Nathan Bur - 
kan Memorial Competition at The 
University of Michigan Law School, 
reports Stanley Adams, president of 
ASCAP. The competition at The Uni- 
versity of Michigan was under the 
supervision of Dean Theodore J. St. 
Antoine, and the title of the winning 
essay was "The Legal Protection of 
Sound Recordings." 
The Nathan Burkan Memorial Com- 
petition is sponsored annually by AS - 
CAP, in memory of ASCAP's first 
general counsel who died in 1936. It is 
designed to stimulate interest in the 
field of copyright law. First and sec- 
ond prizes of $250 and $100 are 
offered in each of the leading law 
schools throughout the nation. 
A 
panel of judges then considers all the 
prize-winnisg papers which are re- 
ceived 
from 
participating 
law 
Gladys Shelley 
Wedding Song 
NEW YORK - Gladys Shelley has 
written a new wedding song with a 
contemporary concept. It's called "As 
Long As We Both Shall Love." It's 
been cut by Jane Meryll on the Grand 
label, a subsidiary of GSF Records. 
The singer is appearing nightly at the 
Golden Eage Lounge of the Holiday 
Inn here on 57th St. 
schools, and selects the outstanding 
essays for National Awards of $1500, 
$1000, $750, $500 and $250.

'Most Valuable'

the establishment of annual 
Most

ing the contribution of studio musi- 
cians and background singers to a 
recording, the L.A. Chapter Board Of 
Governors 
believes 
these 
people 
should be recognized by their peers in 
the industry.

Bahler, Harold Battiste, Jules Chaik- 
in, and Marilyn Jackson (a winning 
background 
singer in 
a 
simarily- 
staged New York event last year) set 
the systems and procedures for what 
will be an annual recognition. Awards 
will be given to cover all orchestral 
sections: brass, woodwinds, strings, 
rhythm, miscellaneous, male backup 
vocalist, and female backup vocalist. 
Active Academy members who work 
with these individuals in studio re- 
cording conditions 
are eligible to 
vote. 
Ballots are being sent to qualifying 
Los Angeles NARAS members this 
week. The awards presentation 
is 
scheduled as a mid -November musical 
afternoon with presenters selected 
from leading industry notables.

Frank Music 
Bessie Smith, 
'Broadway' Folios 
NEW YORK - Neil Baudhuin, gen. 
mgr. of publications at Frank Music 
Corp., has announced the release of a 
music folio "Great Musical Moments 
From Broadway," and he and Bert 
Haber, professional mgr. of publica- 
tions for the firm, announced a joint 
venture with Empress Music Inc. to 
produce a new song book, "Bessie 
Smith: Empress Of The Blues." 
"Great 
Musical 
Moments 
From 
Broadway" contains 
30 
standards 
from shows such as "Damn Yankees," 
"Guys And Dolls," "Hans Christian 
Andersen," 
"Kismet," 
"The 
Most 
Happy Fella," "The Music Man," "The 
Pajama Game," and "The Unsinkable 
Molly Brown." 
"We've never published such a com- 
plete collection of music from our 
shows," said Baudhuin, "and we felt 
it was time to offer the music buying 
public 
an 
extensive collection 
of 
hits." 
Frank Music was founded by the 
late songwriter Frank Loesser, and 
owns copyrights several popular mu- 
sical productions. "Great Musical Mo- 
ments From Broadway folios will be 
distributed through music jobbers and 
retail music stores. 
On the Bessie Smith project Haber 
said, "We've signed Chris Albertson, 
author of "Bessie" to write bio mate- 
rial, select music and photos, and 
serve as consultant on this major 
work. Albertson is considered the 
Bessie Smith authority, and his work 
on the bio and the Grammy Award 
winning Columbia Record series on 
the 
blues 
artist 
are 
excellent." 
Baudhuin added. "Bessie ... was the 
greatest classic blues singer who ever 
lived." 
"Bessie Smith: Empress Of The 
Blues" will include 30 of her major 
songs, supplemented by photos, dis- 
cography, material on blues as an art 
form, and Albertson's bio material. 
Frank Music plans to distribute the 
soft cover edition through regular 
music stores and is working on a 
book trade deal with a major publish- 
er. 
The firm owns a number of stan- 
dard copyrights including music from 
Broadway, blues, and contemporary 
music, including the Roberta Flack 
single, "Jesse" written by Janis Ian. 
"The Bessie Smith project is one of 
many new efforts at Frank Music 
Corp. and it is part of a revitalized, 
aggressive 
print 
program," 
said 
Baudhuin. 
Release First 
Bassey Folio 
NEW YORK - Peer -Southern Publi- 
cations has announced the release of 
a new Shirley Bassey folio, entitled 
"Never, Never, Never." The folio, 
Bassey's first release in the U.S., in- 
cludes hits from her UA LP of the 
same name. The "Never, Never, Nev- 
er" single, published by Peer Interna- 
tional (BMI), has had international 
success and is highlighted in Bassey's 
current North American concert tour. 
Axelrod Signs 
With Junat 
HOLLYWOOD - Producer -composer 
David Axelrod has signed a non- 
exclusive production contract with 
Junat Productions, calling in part for 
an album for which he will write and 
arrange the music. The album will be 
produced for Junat by Cannonball 
Adderley. 
Axelrod has also just completed 
production 
on an album for Funk, 
Inc., on Fantasy Records and has co - 
produced, with Nat Adderley, an al- 
bum for Joe Williams. The just - 
released "Inside Straight" by Cannon- 
ball Adderley (Fantasy) is likewise a 
co -production between Axelrod and 
the artist.

Charley Pride 
TersPresenta 
71PRIDESMEN 
ARMS FULL OF EMPTY-Buck Owens-Capitol 
ST -11222 
The linear notes on the back of this album 
state that this is an unforgettable collection of 
love songs by a country superstar. The past 
statement is true but to go one step further it 
is magnificent. All the compositions were writ- 
ten by Buck and if there ever was any doubt to 
his writing ability this album will quickly lay 
them to rest. The album is entitled after his 
chart busting single. Buck stands out on the 
whole album but these are my preferred cuts: 
Arms Full Of Empty, 
I Won't Be Needing You, 
Songwriters Lament and Love Makes The World 
Go Around. The country music market won't be 
able to "buck" this one. 
MOTHER MAYBELLE CARTER-Mother May - 
belle Carter-Columbia KG 32436 
A much eagerly awaited album that has 
been long in coming, will immediately gain 
instant success. Most of us know Maybelle's 
legend but for those who don't she is a mem- 
ber of the country music hall of fame, sang on 
the first country record ever released, a mem- 
ber of the legendery Carter family and mother- 
in-law of Johnny Cash. She is a top country 
artist and this album will definitely enhance 
her image even more. A two -record set con- 
taining 19 songs, some of the enjoyable cuts 
are: Tennessee Waltz, The Bells Of St. Mary 
and Good Old Mtn. Dew. This album will bring 
many happy hours of listener enjoyment. 
BEST OF GEORGE JONES: VOL. 2-George 
Jones-RCA APL1-0316 
It's been awhile since George left RCA for 
Epic records and being a top artist anything he 
releases will sell automatically. The album 
features both ballads and up -tempo country 
songs. George's fan will enjoy & listen to this 
album many times over. Some of the preferred 
cuts are: Take 
Me, Things 
Have Gone to 
Pieces, Life Turned Her That Way. The seven 
other cuts are enjoyable too. A definite must 
for his many, many followers. 
CHARLEY PRIDE PRESENTS THE PRIDESMEN 
The Pridesmen-RCA APL1-0315 
At the beginning of this album Charley Pride 
explains that when he's playing he doesn't get 
a chance to really enjoy his band. So as you 
might have assumed that is what he is giving 
us the opportunity to do now. The Pridesmen 
come off as very excellent musicians and they 
have the potential to strike out on their own 
and really make it big. The album is delightful 
and it will have a strong appeal to the record 
buyer. Some preferred cuts are: Kiss An Angel 
Good Morning, I'll Come Running, The Battle 
Of New Orleans. The seven other cuts are all 
enjoyable too. 
Country Gents 
Set Fall Tour; 
NYC Included 
After a summer spent performing 
at Bluegrass Festivals throughout the 
nation, Vanguard recording artists, 
The Country Gentlemen, start their 
fall concert tour with an appear- 
ance at Queens College in Flushing, 
New York (Sept. 22). Immediately 
following their New York date, the 
Gentlemen will take part in Balti- 
more's City Fair (Sept. 23). Addition- 
al dates include performances at the 
Up and Away Dude Ranch in Rich- 
mond, 
Va. (Sept. 29); Arni's 
in 
Lafayette, Indiana (Oct. 1-13); and at 
Nashville's Grand 
Old 
Opry (Oct. 
17). 
The 
personnel 
of The 
Country 
Gentlemen includes Charles Waller, 
lead 
singer 
and 
guitarist; 
Doyle 
Lawson, tenor and mandolin player; 
Bill Yates, bass singer and bass play- 
er; and two new additions to 
the 
group, Rick Skaggs, fiddle and Mike 
Lilly, Five -string banjo. 
The first album for Vanguard was 
"The Country Gentlemen." The per- 
sonnel on that record included Charlie 
Wallers, Bill Yates, Doyle Lawson 
and Bill Emerson. 
Buddy Lee 
Inks Imperials 
NASHVILLE - Buddy Lee Attrac- 
tions, Inc. has acquired an outstand- 
ing group for bookings with the addi- 
tion of the Imperials, on Impact Rec- 
ords. Previously on tour and in movie 
production with Elvis Presley, the 
Imperials are currently regular with 
Jimmy Dean on appearances and on 
his syndicated TV series. 
The group is completing four weeks 
this year in the Desert Inn, and al- 
ready have 
a minimum of twelve 
weeks in Las Vegas for 1974. In addi- 
tion to over one hundred colleges 
from coast to coast, the Imperials 
have a record of outstanding engage- 
ments including the Hemisfair, Hur- 
rah's, Sahara Hotel, Astrodome, the 
Inaugural Ball, and network TV ap- 
pearances with Mike Douglas, David 
Frost, Mery Griffin and Joey Bish- 
op. 
Buddy Lee Attractions looks for- 
ward to supplementing the Imperials' 
1974 Las Vegas schedule with nation- 
wide bookings in fairs, concerts and 
other special events.

advertising and promotional campaign for
Philadelphia International Records. With such
outstanding artists as Billy Paul,.. The O'Jays,
Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes, and The
Three Degrees, an all-inclusive media and
store dealer campaign has been devised.
The in-store kit includes a four-color mobile,
a counter display unit, free catalogs, and divider

O'Jays, and Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes.
There will be a complete schedule of R&B
and Top -40 radio spots. And one of the most
pervasive print campaigns ever conceived.
Finally, there'll soon be a special album
called "The Sound of Philadelphia'737

Cash Box/R&B News Report
Keeping Up With The Joneses
Phonogram artists the Joneses visited the New York offices of Phonogram,
Inc. recently to discuss the release of the group's first Mercury single, "Baby,
Don't Do It." Sales of the single have been bolstered by the group's extensive
touring activity. Pictured are (from left): Glenn Dorsey, business manager,
non -performing member of the Joneses, and writer of the single; Bobby Noble;
Charles Fach, vice president/A&R at Phonogram; Reggie Noble; and Sam
White. Group member Sy Brooks was not present.
`A Decade of Jazz'
From Blue Note
HOLLYWOOD - Blue Note Records
is currently shipping three "A Decade
of Jazz" double LP sets encompass-
ing the years 1939 through 1969. The
reissue, prompted by innumerable re-
quests from jazz devotees and histo-
rians, contains in three albums a sig-
nificant
cross-section of the
great
recordings released by the blue Note
label during this period.
Volume I of "A Decade of Jazz,"
covering
1939-49,
runs
from
the
"boogie woogie" of Albert Ammons
and Meade "Lux" Lewis to legendary
greats like Sidney Bechet and Bunk
Johnson and experimentalists of that
period like Thelonious Monk.
Volume II (1949-59) contains ma-
jor
performances
by Bud
Powell,
Thelonious Monk, Milt Jackson, Jay
Jay Johnson, Clifford Brown, Miles
Davis, Horace Silver, Jimmy Smith,
Sonny Clark, John Coltrane, Sonny
Rollins, Art Blakey and Lou Donald-
son.Volume III (1959-69) offers tracks
by Jimmy Smith, Ike Quebec, Kenny
Burrell, Donald Byrd, Lee Morgan,
Eric Dolphy, Horace Silver, Stanley
Turrentine,
Ornette
Coleman,
and
Lon Donaldson.
Blue Note, the
jazz
division
of
United Artists Records,
is offering
complete backing to the three pack-
ages via advertising, display material
and
an
all-out
promotional
cam-
paign.

appointed
r&b
southern

has
already
proven himself extremely valuable to

Getz & Jamal
Open Jimmy's
Jazz Season
NEW YORK - Stan Getz and Ah-
mad Jamal and their groups kick off
the fall jazz season at Jimmy's down-
stairs 52nd Street Room, from Sep-
tember 27th to October 6th, it is an-
nounced by Jimmy's owners Sid Da-
vidoff and Dick Aurelio and impre-
sario
Willard Alexander. Getz,
ac-
claimed as one of the jazz world's
premier tenor sax men since the for-
ties when he was a teenage prodigy
playing with the great bands of Stan
Kenton, Jimmy Dorsey and Benny
Goodman, went on to win more crit-
ics' and readers' polls than any other
saxophone player. He has won the
Playboy Jazz and Pop Poll 16 times
and the Down Beat Poll 17 times.
Benny Goodman has praised him as
the finest tenor saxophonist of all
time.
Getz
records
for
Columbia.

. . Grambling College and Morgan State held their 3rd annual football
duel at Yankee Stadium which was again won by Grambling. Over 60,000
blacks were in attendance. The Grambling Band did their thing during half time.

rousing version of "Respect" during the half intermission with the Grambling

the field

and industry personnel were on hand to learn of the forthcoming Roberta Afro
tour which will include Stevie Wonder and the Jackson Five. The concert tour
will be filmed. Plans are in the making to release the filmed concert in this
country.. The proceeds to be used to help black thru Africare. Roberta feels
that blacks should reach out to help blacks regardless what nation they are
living in.

October 'Phila. Intl Sound' Month
NEW YORK - October has been
designated "Philadelphia Internation-
al Month" to herald new album re-
leases by such Superstars as Billy
Paul, The O'Jays, Harold Melvin &
The Blue Notes, and The Three De-
grees.
During
October,
Philadelphia
In-
ternational,
the
Columbia
Custom
Label headed by Kenny Gamble and
Leon Huff, will release the following
Lp's: "War Of The Gods," by Billy
Paul of "Me And Mrs. Jones" fame;
"Ship Ahoy," by the O'Jays, whose
singles,
"Love
Train"
and
"Back
Stabbers" have each sold more than
two million copies; the newest album
release by the Three Degrees, which
is entitled "The Three Degrees"; and
"Black & Blue Featuring 'The Love I
Lost,'" by Harold Melvin & The Blue
Notes.
In addition, the label will be cel-
ebrating its success and saluting its
artists with an album entitled "The
Sound of Philadelphia, '73." Specially
priced at $4.98, this Lp features some
of the past year's
biggest
selling
Philadelphia
International
singles,
including Billy Paul's "Me and Mrs.
Jones;" The O'Jays' "Love Train;"
"If You Don't Know Me By Now" by
Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes;
"It's Forever," by The Ebonys; and
"Family Affair" by MFSB.
In addition, two recently released
albums will be spotlighted-the debut
Lp by the group Spiritual Concept,
and the album "Yellow Sunshine" on
the Gamble label.
"Philadelphia International Month"
will
be
supported
by
massive
promotion and marketing drives de-
signed to call maximum attention to
the new product, as well as the la-
bel's
catalog
items.
Ads
will
be
featured in many prominent Black
periodicals including Soul, Jet, Soul
Sounds and Essence. There will also
be a heavy emphasis on outdoor bill-
board advertising in Black communi-
ties, and multi -product time buys are
being scheduled for bath Black and
Top 40 radio stations.
Jim Tyrrell, Director of National
Sales, Epic & Columbia Custom La-
bels, said, "We are happy to be able
to launch a program which will en-
tail a major involvement of our com-
pany with the entire retail structure,
in the United States, both black and
white. An incentive program is being
offered that will be equitable to both
large and small retail dealers, with
all receiving their share of merchan-
dising
materials.
Billy
Paul,
the
O'Jays and Harold Melvin & The
Blue Notes
took
the
country
by
storm earlier this year, and we are
confident
that
their
second
Lp's
featured in 'The Sound Of Philadel-
phia' Month
will
consolidate
their
position as major recording stars."
The label has assembled a "Sound
Of Philadelphia Kit" for in-store dis-
play. It features a mobile display
unit depicting eleven albums in four
colors; a counter take -one bin which
includes free folders containing pho-
tos and information about the Phila-
delphia International catalog; and di-
vider
cards
to facilitate
customer
findng of the label's product.
Ron Alexenburg, Vice
President,
Epic & Columbia Custom
Labels,
said: "In the past two years one of
the most exciting things that we have
been involved in has been the emer-
gence of the Gamble and Huff labels-
Philadelphia International and Gam-
ble. During these two years, Gamble
and Huff have built a strong artist
roster and upon completion of the
new albums we wanted to emphasize
to everyone that this product has re-
ceived the acceptance of not only the
blacks, but whites as well and are
giving
special
attention
to
their
sound during the month of October.
We are proud to be able to distribute
the Gamble and Huff artistry, as well
as the artists they produce."
Commenting
on
the
upcoming
month
of
activity,
Kenny Gamble
said: "Our thanks and appreciation
we give
to Columbia/Epic Records
for helping us expose 'The Sound Of
Philadelphia' .
. . a Message Of Love
To The People."

Philly Civic Ctr.
To Go After Rock
PHILADELPHIA — The Philadelphia
Civic
Center
is
offering
Convention
Hall
Auditorium
to
promoters
for
rock concerts, according to John Pier-
ron,
exec.
dir.
of the Center. The
de-
cision reverses
a recent
city
decision
forbidding use of the Center for hard
rock.
The
Convention
Hall
Auditorium,
with
11,000
seats
with
unobstructed
view
of
stage
events,
is
totally
air-
conditioned, and has up-to-date acous-
tical
and
lighting
systems. Some
of
the
nation’s
top
soloists, groups and
bands have appeared there.
Inquiries about available dates and
rates
should
be
directed
to
James
Amadie,
Conventions
mgr.
of
the
Philadelphia Civic Center, phone 215-
561-5100,
ext.
21-231.

R&B INGREDIENTS—Things are
really beginning to cook again
in
the R&B musical scene. Labels and
artists are coming with
material that
is
in the groove and Black stations have some smokin’ material to select in con-
tinuing
to
serve
a
black community
(basically
single
buyers)
that
is
and
continues to be enriching to the record
industry. Black producers and writers,
of later (from new releases that have been coming acros my desk) seem to be
returning more and more to basic roots. These basic roots have and continue
to be the
vital
creative force
in the musical spectrum
of today.
But,
this can
so easily be lost. With few exceptions, most of the black artists and producers
have duly paid
their dues, but they, nevertheless, have been able to continue
in the business because
of black
radio. Yes,
it
is true that black music
is
a
big element on what
is
referred
to as the pop scene,
but most
will
have to
agree that
it
is also because of black radio and
black programming that they
now enjoy top 40 success. How many of these performers would now be stand-
ing where they are without the assistance of black radio? Harold
Melvin (The
Blue Notes) popped
into the
Big Apple Thursday (4th)
for
a
small luncheon
with trade and
black press personnel.
Harold, among many topics discussed,
also said that he felt the need and necessity for returning to the roots. Harold
& The
Blue Notes are smokin’ with "The Love
I
Lost".
Harold
is also on the
verge
of announcing some dramatic new ventures.
But, you can
rest assured
that these new ventures
will
retain
the
Harold
Melvin
roots and
identity
.
.
.
Eddie
Floyd
(Stax) “Baby
Lay Your Head Down"
is another
artist who
also
recently
mentioned
that
he
is
returning to
his
roots
in
musical
expression.
Maybe musical
styles and
cycles are synonomous with
our musical
heritage,
but to those
of you who understand where black music
is coming from, there
is just no way to put down the music that
is coming from the soul—white or
black
.
.
. GRC Records hosted and introduced their hot recording act ‘Ripple’
at the Martinque
in Manhattan, Wednesday (3rd) and a goodly number of press
and
industry personnel dropped
in.
Ripple
is
a
solid
performing group and
it
was
a
swingin’ good time for everyone.
Of course,
"I
Don’t Know What
It
Is,
But
It Sure
Is Funky”
is a cooker and the
live performance comes
off as well
as
it does on record.

MGM Splurge
In Country Sales
Ovens Details
Label’s Success
HOLLYWOOD — MGM
Records
re-
ports
gigantic
gains
in
the
country-
field,
and the man
doing
the
report-
ing—one
of
the
label
execs who can
take
credit
for
putting
the company
in
this boom
period—is
Don
Ovens,
director
of
the
label’s
country music
division.
According
to Ovens, MGM occupies
the #3 spot
so far this year
in
total
number
of
records making
the coun-
try music
charts. Last
year, he
said,
the label finished at #8. This rating is
born
out
in
part
by
a
tally
of
the
number
of
acts
on MGM
and
affili-
ated
labels making the
charts during
the same period,
i.e., 24 acts this year
to date as opposed
to only 9
in
all of
1972.
A good
deal
of
this heavy upward
movement, Ovens
said, can
be
traced
to
the company’s
recent
signings,
of
artists
like Eddie Arnold, Jud Strunk
and
Patty
Tierney,
as
well
as
the
crossover to country of an
artist
like
Eydie
Gorme,
with
her
hit
single
“Take One
Step,” and the emergence
of Marie Osmond
(of that family
of
Osmonds)
as
a country
artist
in her
own right.
Boone Scores
Another
recent
pop-to-country
crossover
is Pat Boone, who
cut
his
first
country
record,
“Tying
the
Pieces
Together,”
with Sonny James
producing and
Ovens
serving
as
ex-
ecutive
producer.
“After
all,”
Ovens
said,
“Pat
was bom
and
raised
in
Nashville,
and
it
just
seemed
the
natural
thing
to
do.
So
I
took him
there
in
March.”
Boone’s
latest
is
a
tune written and produced by country
great
Noro
Wilson,
“Candy
Lips.”
As
for
young
Ms.
Osmond’s
per-
sonal
success, Ovens was
directly
re-
sponsible
for
taking
her
to
Nash-
ville,
as
well,
and
for
signing
up
Sonny James once again
as
her
pro-
ducer.
The
result:
her run-away
hit
“Paper
Roses.”
The
news
here,
of
course,
is the single’s rapid crossover
to
the
industry’s pop
charts
and
its
equally rapid
climb. With
sales
well
over
the
500,000
mark,
“Paper
Roses”
is rushing toward gold
status
and clearly guarantees a go-ahead on
another round
of Marie Osmond/Son-
ny James sessions in December.
The
crossover
factor
thus
looms
large
in Ovens’ strategy and accounts
for
the good
deal
of MGM’s growth
as a country
label. The country
divi-
sion’s
share
of
the
company’s
busi-
ness
is now
up
to
about
20%,
ac-
cording
to
Ovens, and
still
growing.
Sales
within
the
division
itself have
doubled.
The
over-all MGM
country
chart
and
sales
record
has
also
been
con-
spicuously enhanced with the recently
concluded
distributiion
deal
with
Wesley
Rose’s
Hickory
label.
Don
Gibson,
Sue
Thompson,
Roy
Acuff,
Glen Barber, Leona Williams—all are
Hickory
artists who have contributed
mightily
to MGM’s
strength
in
the
country
market.
The same
holds
for
artists like Doyle Holly and Ray
Ste-
vens on
the MGM-distributed
Barna-
by
label, with Connie Van Dyke
con-
sidered a sure comer.
Asked
about
his
preference
for
working out
of Hollywood, Ovens
re-
plied that he figured
it was
the only
way.
“After
a
short
time
with
our
Nashville
office,
I
realized
that my
best bet was
to make the home
office
here my
base,
and
to
sit
in
all
the
meetings
I had
to
see that we got a
fair shake
in
the
planning and mar-
keting
of country
product. And
all
I
can
say,
given
the way
things
are
going,
it’s
working
like
a
charm.”
GMA ‘Dove’ Award
Winners Announced
NASHVILLE — More than 1500 gos-
pel music fans, performers and execu-
tives were present
at
the Grand
Ole
Opry
House
in
Nashville
when
the

Association
held
it’s
1973 Dove Award presentation.
Wendy Bagwell served as the mas-
ter of ceremonies.
Bagwell,
leader of
the “Sunliters Quartet”
is well known
for
his
humor,
his
“Rattlesnake
Song”
and many
other
accomplish-
ments such
as being the
first
to
ap-
pear
at
Carnegie
Hall. He
has
also
been
nominated
twice,
in
the
past
three years, for Grammy Awards.
In the category of “Male Vocalist”
the
1973 Dove award went
to James
Blackwood
Sr.,
leader of
the famous
Blackwood
Brothers
Quartet.
James,
also won this category
in
1972.
The “Songwriter of the Year” went
to
Bill
Ga’ther.
He
has
composed
more than 100 gospel songs and
is a
three-time
winner
of
the
GMA’s
“songwriter of the year” award.
The
album
“Street
Gospel”
gar-
nered a
total
of three awards
at
this
year’s ceremonies. The album,
as re-
corded by The Oak Ridge Boys, won
the “Album
of the Year” award and
also
earned
the
“Graphic
Layout &
Design”
for Bob McConnell and took
the honors
in the “Album Cover Pho-
to or Cover Art” for
Bill
Grine. The
album
is on
the Heartwarming
label.
In
the
category
of
“Top
Male
Group” the honors
this year went
to

COUNTRY
MUSIC
