Country
Artist
of the Week:
The Oak Ridge Boys
THE OAKS—Although The Oaks roots remain firmly in their founding fathers
foundation of gospel music, they are
also comfortable
in country, polished at
pop music and
need
not
take
any back
seats
in
soul
music.
Their
current
conglomeration
of talent
is tremendously vast and varied. Their backgrounds
range
all the way from former rock drummer and college music teacher, to a
gospel bom piano player, and genuinely great guitarist
of every
sort.
As a result, The Oaks can deliver virtually any
style
of music that might
be demanded
of them. William
Golden, Richard
Sterband, Duanne Allen and
Willie Wynn make up the
individual
talent components
of today’s
collective
group known as The Oak Ridge Boys. They are backed by band members Mark
Ellerbee, John
Rich, Tony Brown, and Don Breland.
Besides appearing on the Johnny Cash show and the grammy awards pro-
gram, they have hosted their own syndicated television show, “It’s Happening
With The Oak Ridge Boys”, toured Sweden and Norway, given performances
in Hawaii and captured college crowds throughout the country.
Winners of most of the top awards given by the Gospel Music Association,
the group
also took a grammy award
in
1971 on the song, “Talk About The
Good Times”. 1973 has continued as a banner year
in
all
fields
of music for
The Oaks, who last week won three Gospel Music Associations coveted “Dove”
awards, have won
one
of
the
heaviest
schedule
of
appearances
set
so
far.
and are set to appear on two different network specials. They will be part of
NBC’s, “Country Music
Special” which
will
be
televised November
24. The
show will be hosted by pop country artist Mac Davis.
CBS has planned a country music
special
called “Country Comers”,
to be
filmed
in Los Angeles. The Oak Ridge Boys
will appear along with Loretta
Lynn, Tom
T.
Hall
and
Goober
Lindsay
and
it
will
be
televised
around
Christmas.
The Oaks have also filmed a spot on Hee-Haw and
will go
to Philadelphia
for the Mike Douglas Show October 22nd.
The Oak Ridge Boys’ average annual album
sales are
in excess of 300,000.
They record exclusively
for Columbia
Records. Independent producer George
Richey
directs
all
production. Booking
is handled by The Don
Light
Talent
Agency.

Nader 'Revival’ Set
For Oct 12 at MSG
NEW YORK — Richard Nader’s Rock
and Roll Revival, which began in the
Felt Forum in 1969, will celebrate
its
fourth anniversary at Madison Square
Garden
Fri.,
Oct.
12 with a big
line-
up of 50’s performers.
Artists who will appear include Lit-
tle Richard, The Five
Satins, Johnny
Maestro
of
the
Crests
and
Brooklyn
Bridge,
The
Cleftones,
The
Harp-
tones,
The
Penquins,
The
Chiffons,
The Capris, The
Drifters, The Moon-
glows,
and
Bobby
Comstock’s
Rock
and Roll Band. Ten of the eleven acts
represent
each
of
Nader’s
previous
tours. The
Oct.
12
show
will
be
an
hour longer than the usual 3Vi hours
because of the longer line-up.
Wolfman
Jack
of
WNBC,
who
hosts
The
Midnight
Specials,
will
preside as me of the show in his
first
N.Y. personal appearance. Nader has
hosted the shows in the past.
The
first
revival
show,
featuring
Chuck Berry, The Platters, Bill Haley
and the Comets, The Shirelles, Jimmy
Clanton, and Sha Na Na, sold out the
Felt Forum
Oct.
18,
1969. After two
more sell-outs at the Forum the show
moved
to
the
Garden where
it has
played ever
since. The box
office
suc-
cess
of the shows prompted Madison
Square
Garden
Productions
to
join
Nader
in a co-producing partnership,
enabling him
to expand
his
national
Revival tours.
More
than
60
artists
of
the
_50’s
have
appeared
on
the
shows
since
1969 sparking a return
to fashion
of
the cosmetics and clothing of the
de-
cade.
Nader’s
film
“Let
The
Good
Times
Roll,”
released
this
summer,
was one of the top grossing films na-
tionally
in
the
first week
of
its
re-
lease.

Audio Devices
Building Lacquer
Disk Plant
In Va.
GLENBROOK, CONN. — Audio De-
vices,
Inc.,
pioneer
in
the
develop-
ment
and
manufacture
of
lacquer
disks for record production,
will
con-
struct a new 26.000 square-foot plant
at Winchester,
Virginia,
for
its
disk
production.
Said
to
be
the
“most
modem”
facility
of
its
kind
in
the
world,
the new
plant
eventually
will
replace the company’s existing
site in
Glenbrook.
Audio
Devices,
a
subsid
of Capitol
Industries,
Inc., was
the
first Ameri-
can
licensee
of
Pyral,
a French
firm
which
developed
the
manufacturing
process.
It began
production
at
the
Glenbrook site in 1937.
A.
P.
Cunha,
president
of
Audio
Devices,
said
that
the
new
facility
cannot come
too
soon because
of the
increasing demands
for
four-channel
disks for highest
fidelity and
quality
and, in the near future, video disks.
“The trend of disk recording
in the
past 35 years has been
to pack more
and more
information
into
narrower
and
shallower
grooves.”
Cunha
con-
tinued,
“making
manufacturing
tolerances in flatness, smoothness and
cleanliness tighter and
tighter.”
“The new Winchester plant will
in-
corporate
‘clean
room’
coating
and
inspection
facilities,
fully
automated
handling
equipment
and
a new
pro-
prietary process for insuring absolute
flatness
and
smoothness
both
of
the
aluminum
disc
and
the
lacquer
coating which
will make
it
the most
modern
facility
of
its
kind
in
the
world.”
Cunha
said
that
Audio
Devices
is
continually
doing
research
in
the
manufacture of lacquer disks and the
results
of
this
research
will
be
de-
signed into the new facility.
Audio
Devices, which, according to
Cunha, already has more than half of
the market, both domestic and
inter-
national,
looks
forward
to
increased
production
to
meet
increasing
de-
mand. Ground
will
be
broken
within
the next few weeks, and
the plant
is
expected
to
be
ready
for
production
trials within a year.

N.Y. Gets
New Label
NEW YORK — A
new
recording
company, Fenoragh Records, has been
established in New York City. Headed
by S. L. Scher, the new label will con-
centrate
on
the
production
and
dis-
tribution
of contemporary music.
Fenoragh’s
production
division,
Lorenzo Productions, directed by pro-
ducer/arranger
Morty
Jay,
is
cur-
rently completing the
label’s
first
al-
bum,
“Masters
Gone
Modern
(Now
and Then).” The album offers modern-
istic interpretations of classical pieces
by
composers
Tchaikovsky,
Dvorak,
Leoncavallo and
di
Capua.
The
pro-
duction is performed by Larry O’Neill,
a
classically
trained
vocalist
with
a
list of appearances on both opera and
supper club
stages.
Fenoragh
Records
is
seeking new
artists & material for future releases.
The company
is located at 227 River-
side
Drive, New York, N.Y.

Impulse Tour Coordinates
Fall Release Program
HOLLYWOOD
—
On
Oct.
21
ABC/Impulse will kick
off its fall na-
tional
tour
at
Carnegie
Hall with
a
concert
featuring
Gato
Barbieri,
Keith Jarrett, and Alice Coltrane. The
event
is syncronized with the compa-
ny’s
release
of
14
new
LPs
show-
caseing
Barbieri
and
Jarrett
along
with other major innovators
such
as
John Coltrane, Pharoah Sanders, Sam
Rivers, and John Klemmer.
The concert tour will feature
eight
of
the
Impulse
artists
in
a
major
hall /major market
itinerary
that
in-
cludes New York,
Los
Angeles,
San
Francisco,
Detroit,
Boston,
and
Washington,
D.C.
Gato
Barbieri
will
be
the
headliner
at
all
the
concerts,
being backed up with Keith Jarrett on
the East Coast and Alice Coltrane on
the West Coast.
Barbieri, who has gained a
sizable
following
since
his
scoring
of
Ber-
tolucci’s
‘‘Last Tango
in
Paris,”
will
be
working
in
an
entirely
new
format.
The
Argentine
saxophonist
will
be
playing with
muscians from
his native South America, performing
a
style
radically
different from
his
style
on the New York jazz
scene.
Impulse feels that the time
is riedit
for
their
artists’
progressive
music,
and the tour may reach a great por-
tion of the rock concert audience and
introduce them to this “new music.”

Blue Note Culls
Pacific Jazz
HOLLYWOOD — Blue Note Records
is
culling
the
archives
of
its
now-
defunct
affiliated
label
Pacific
Jazz
and
is
releasing
highly-in-demand
vintage
recordings
of a
pair
of
to-
day’s
hottest
acts,
Les McCann
and
the Jazz Crusaders.
“Fish This Week,” the
title
of the
Les McCann double-LP
set,
contains
the
initial
successful
disk
per-
formances by the highly-acclaimed pi-
anist, dating back
to the early 1960’s.
The Jazz Crusaders’ two-record pack-
age, “Tough Talk,” also contains ma-
jor
recordings from
the
early
six-
ties.
Both McCann and the Jazz Crusad-
ers
are
currently
top-selling
artists,
with
the
Atlantic
and
Blue Thumb
labels,
respectively. The
majority
of
their Pacific Jazz
platters have been
unavailable to the public for nearly a
decade.
With Blue Note long established as
a dominant figure in East Coast jazz
circles, and Pacific Jazz a major fac-
tor
on
the West Coast until
its
de-
mise, Blue Note
is planning a reissue
program that will encompass the best
of vintage product.
R&B INGREDIENTS—Shelly’s Manne-Hole,
which became one
of
the best known jazz clubs
in the world during
its nearly twelve years
of oper-
ation,
reopened
at
a new western
Los Angeles
location, 6420 Wilshire
Blvd.,
Tuesday,
Oct.
16, with Carmen McRae and the Julian “Cannonball” Adderley
Quintet. The new Manne-Hole
is downstairs
at the Century Bank
Plaza, where
Tetou’s Restaurant operates during daytime hours. At 9 p.m. the cafe becomes
Shelly’s,
presenting
the
top names
in
jazz
nightly
except Mondays.
Tetou’s
food
will be served
at the Manne-Hole. Jackie and Roy will share the
bill with
Ms. McRae beginning Oct. 23 for one week. Drummer Shelly Manne started the
original
ground-level
Manne-Hole
in the heart of Hollywood,
Nov.
2,
1960.
In
1972 the
club's neighbor and
landlord, Wally Heider Recording, expanded
its
studios and found
that the bandstand amplifiers fed
directly onto their tapes.
Neither
the
Manne-Hole’s
attempt to
book
"quiet”
attractions
nor
Heider’s
soundproofing solved the problem. Shelly shopped
in vain for a place to move,
and
at 2 a.m. on
Labor
Day,
Sept.
4, 1972,
reluctantly
closed.
Eor the past
year, while composing scores for films, television and legitimate theater,
tour-
ing with
his group—Manne-Kind—and
recording
his own albums and sound-
tracks, Shelly has constantly sought the
right spot to
reativate
his club. With
Tetou’s invitation
to
share their spacious new establishment, Shelly’s Manne-
Hole has an
easily
accessible,
centrally
located new home.

HOLLYWOOD — COHN OF THE COSMOS
Motown’s “new white hope”
is composer/performer Stephen
Cohn, who told
Cash Box that his signing with that label was due to a series of "fortunate cosmic
events.” Of course Cohn has
also experienced some unfortunate cosmic events
too, which may be par for the course of Life. His just-released album
is dedicated
to
his father, who negotiated
his contracts but passed away before playback. So
for young Cohn
his emergence as an artist has been an almost pyrrhic victory.
Cohn's
Motown
publicity
pictures show
him
fashioned
after
a
triumphant-
looking Mark Spitz with, instead of medals around his neck, a
lavaliere of bagles.
Which
is actually
far more
practical
since what can one
really do with medals
anyway? The
sensational
tag
line
is
"eleven new world's
records,”
listing
the
songs on his debut LP and their respective times. Caryle’s
definition of a genius
(in
his
Life
of
Frederick the
Great)
is “someone
with
the
infinite
capacity
for
taking pains,” and Cohn’s own genius
is measured by his own share of enduring
pain.
Stephen
began
his
singing
career
in
Washington
with
a
college
folk
group
called The
Coraliers. This
lasted as
long as most
college
folk groups
last. Cohn
next
studied
classical
guitar with
the renown
Romeros.
Five years
of
classical
framing enabled him
to become the
first graduate student given
permission
to
play guitar for his senior recital at Valley State College in California. Hence his first
gold
bagel. He explained how up
until
this
point the guitar
in
college graduate
work was looked on as a bastard instrument.
On campus Cohn met Rob Royer
(this was before Royer was
into Bread) and
was asked to join a group Rob was forming called Rainy Day People. Everyone
in
the group was writing songs, and
it’s here that Cohn
starts composing.
His
first
hit of songwriting was to bossa nova rhythms. While he rehearsed with Rainy Day
People, he also performed with Elizabeth Waldo for modest recompense. Stephen
STEPHEN COHN
HOLLYWOOD — MICHAEL LLOYD:
A VERY ATYPICAL
SCIENTIFIC
FRIENDLY
INTERVIEW
Just prior to interviewing Michael Lloyd, former a & r chieftain at MGM Records
and now
a member
of the new MGM
group
Friends, we
had
read
an
ad
for
Scientific American Magazine. The ad showed two contrasting couples. One was
tagged the average American, displaying an
unaffected,
innocent, immunity from
greed. We were told that the average American
is around 28, didn’t go to college,
watches
television
nearly
four
hours
a
day,
reads
two
books
a
year,
owns
a
five-year-old
car, and earns about $9,500 a year. Next, a
look to the right side of
the
ad, and there was the suave “we’ve made
it”
pair, approximately 33—he
a
college graduate who watches two hours of TV a day, peruses 46 books per year,
owns two cars and
is said to earn considerably more than the average American.
After
deciding
that
the
“scientific”
American
looked
too
sophisticated
and
definitely not as appealing as the
plebian,
Michael
Lloyd entered the Cash Box
offices. He was there
to
tell about
his new group
Friends, made up
of himself,
Darryl Cotton
(formerly with Zoot) and
Steve
Kipner (once
of Tin
Tin).
Michael
looked
like
the
veritable
average
endemic
though
his
biography,
filled
with
accomplishments, told us “not to judge a book by
it’s cover.” Of course this time
we are talking about determining whether he covered 46 books
per year or just
two.
It was obvious
that as
a
recipient
of
12 Gold
Records
that
he would
be
making
more
than
the
average
American
and
even
more
than
the
scientific
American. There were some questions to ask.
Michael
sat down and no doubt anticipated those routine questions pertaining
to
his musical background.
Instead,
his
first question, “How much
television do
you watch
a day?” was followed with “Did you graduate from
college?” He was
startled, looked around to make sure he was indeed
in the right place. Well, as
it
MICHAEL LLOYD
remembers
(how
can
he
forget)
how
Elizabeth
was
fascinated
with
Peruvian
music. He says that she played
Inca music the way she imagined
it might have
been
played.
During one
Incan
incantantion, while
Ms. Waldo was
directing
her
group, Stephen had nobler thoughts than the most noblest of
Inca’s and started
playing
and
composing
a
bossa
nova
tune.
Waldo
promptly
dismissed
him.
Dismissal was
better than
being sacrificed. The song he had written, which had
cost him his gig, was called “In a Blue Room.”
Cohn was able to place his tune with the Baja Marimba Band. He tells us
later
that one
of the
reasons
he
is
able
to
place the tune
is
because
his cousin
is
Julius Wechter. A fortunate cosmic
events. He
quickly adds
that the song was
good besides. This earned him a second gold bagel.
Next he returns to concentrate on
his group with Rob Royer. They rehearse a
lot up at Snuff Garrett’s studio
in Leon Russel’s canyon home. Cohn commented
how Snuff use to have a
lot of musicians hanging around and recording them.
If
anything good came out of
it,
it would belong to Snuff. The something good that
Rainy Day came up with was
called
"Jr.
Executive,” which Stephen thinks was
released on the Hanna Barbera
label. Cohn claims he got a copy of
it, and just
maybe someone else did too.
Rainy Day
People became
the
Pleasure
Faire and
signed
with
Uni
Records.
David Gates produced them. The group featured
a
girl,
Rob,
Stephen, and Tim
Allen. The song Morning Glory Days was a mild
hit. This
led to a writers contract
with Koppleman and Rubin. The only thing his fifty-dollar-a-week salary could buy
a
lot of was bagles. He put out another single on
Uni called "Going to Have To
Let You Go,” and that’s precisely what Uni later told the group.
Stephen recalled how everything seemed to come to an end. He says the only
consolation was that he could
write.
His
lyrics from
a song on the album
called
"Not Enough People Care” epitomizes
his desolation. He penned, “The language
of the
city of angels, leaves you hungry for the silence of your mind,
if you care,
for
L.A. ticks along on bad timing with too many cars, not enough
Air
.
.
.” He
found his solace
in Venice. There he lived and loved
in a house a block away from
the
beach.
Venice was
the
kind
of
artist’s
retreat
he
had
always
sought.
He
discreetly confessed how
a
lot of
lovers,
friends, and enemies passed
thru the
house on Brook Avenue. He says, “it was both the heart and the pit.”
After his days at the beach he met Tom
Driscoll, who signed him to Watermark
Productions.
At Watermark
he worked
with
Ron Jacobs and completed 80
per
cent of an album. The only sensible thing to do was to find a
label. Stephen took
his tapes to Motown. They liked him.
In Cohn they saw cosmopolitan appeal. With
his manager and
executive
producer,
Karl
Bornstein,
and
with
help from
Ste-
phen’s
dad,
they
completed
the
LP
(adding
four
tunes)
and
negotiated
the
contract.
Coincidentiaily Cohn’s
piece de
resistance
in the
LP
(a
strong
single
contender), called “So Many Things," begins with the
line, "So many things have
fallen into place since we got together.”
Although
this wasn't
initally written about
Karl
or Motown
it
certainly seems
appropriate to them now. Whether you fancy bagles or
not,
a
listen
to Stephen
Cohn’s new Motown album
is guaranteed
to
proselytize you. Stephen
begins
a
15-city promotional tour this week. Cohn of the cosmos has been thru “so many
things” that he has practically become ultramundane, ron baron
turned
out, Michael Lloyd
is not
in either classification. He watches as much TV
as the average American and
reads as much
as the
scientific American.
Lloyd
could
hardly be considered average.
After
all, what average person do you know
who’ll go marketing and
ring up a
receipt for $500? And
it’s not the average guy
who has a
fully equipped
16-track studio
in
his home (where
Friends have been
rehearsing and recording since March). Lloyd, who studied classical piano at four,
declared, "My
direction was always
music.
I
never wanted
to
be anything
else
other than
a musician. You might say
I put
all my eggs
into one basket.” Today
he can afford to put $500 worth
of eggs
into one basket and
not worry much
if
some
get
broken.
He's come
a
long way
since
his involvement
with The West
Coast
Pop
Art
Experimental
Band,
followed
by
a
stint
producing Cream
and
Hendrix Songbooks for Transcontinental.
In
1969
Mike
Curb,
from whom
Lloyd
says
he
learned
most
everything
he
knows about
the
music
business, became
president
of MGM
Records.
Shortly
thereafter Lloyd was appointed
a &
r director, not the average position for a man
of
19,
but
his
association
as
the
Osmonds’
producer gave
him
exposure
in
various teenage
fan
magazines.
This and
his work
producing the New Seekers
helped Seekers manager David Joseph to devise the idea of forming a tight group
made
up
of
top
music
people who
had
been
“behind
the
scenes.”
Joseph
considered people
like Mickey Dolenz and Ron
Dante. Both were
unavailable, so
Lloyd,
Kipner, and Cotton were assembled
literally to become “Friends.”
The group's premiere
single
is “Gonna
Have
a Good Time,”
actually an
old
Easybeats
tune
(“Good
Times”)
slightly
renovated—Michael
and
his
Friends
wrote new
riffs and new
lyrics. Their first album has also just been released, and
the
plan on touring to promote
it.
Friends
is the farthest thing from average.
If
the formula
of assembling three great musicians
for
hit
product can
be
called
scientific, then Friends
is scientific as well. Truth
of the matter
is that you can’t
judge the average or scientific by a “cover.” Only the
vinyl contents
will provide
you with some friendly persuasion, ron baron
NEW YORK — SHELLEY FINKEL & JIMMY KOPLIK: PRESENTING
COUNTRY CONCERTS
The two above mentioned gentlemen are the ones who gave us,
(all 600,000 of
us)
the summer
spectacular
at Watkins
Glen
in
upstate
N.Y.
The
anticipated
crowd was 15C>,000 but as usual the unexpected occurred. All the people involved,
promoters; groups and
security, were honestly amazed
at the excellent behavior
of the audience.
The final figures from the concert are not yet
in but
it
is expected that these
two young men
will gross over $1,500,000.00., We must not forget however that
their expenses grew to greater expansions than they expected
(i.e.—The clean-up
bill was supposed to be $6,000 but enlarged to over $50,000).
Shelley and Jimmy deserve
a
very
large round
of applause
for
creating
this
spectacular and
for having
it
run
so smoothly. They have more
exciting
plans
in the works. So, watch for them
in the future, beau eurell
Cash
Box — October
20,
1973

R&B INGREDIENTS—Fans and
blues
afficionados, who
did man-
j
age
to
catch
Willie
Dixon
during
a
limited engagement
recently
at
Kenny’s
Castaways
in Manhattan, certainly did not go away disappointed
in having had
the opportunity to catch
this legendary bluesman. The
artists who have
per-
formed
his material reads not unlike that of a who's who. “Spoonful,” “Back
Door Man,”
“Bring
It On Home” and
“I
Can't Quit You Baby”
are some
of
the scores of tunes from this master storyteller.
Willie,
a
native of Vicksburg,
took up permanent residence
in Chicago when he was 17. His first big selling
tune was, “Signfying Monkey” and then
in the early 50’s Muddy Waters brought
home “I’m Your Hooche Cooche Man." Willie Dixon was
in on the early Chuck
Berry and Bo Diddley sessions. The
Rolling Stones recorded “The
Little Red
Rooster” which was
originally written
for bluesman
Howlin’
Wolf.
Willie
still
handles the standup
bass
with
perfection. Whether
it’s down home
shuffle,
slow
walkin’
or
struttin’,
Willie and
his
back up band
put
it together.
"Soul
Wrinkles”
a new tune
is outstanding.
"Willie Dixon—Catalyst”
is available on
Ovation Records.

.
. Pop jazz organist Seleno Clarke goes into Buddy’s Supper
Club at 1812 Rhode
Island
Ave.,
N.E.
in Wash., D.C.,
Friday the 26th of Oct.
James Stemley
is owner host of the popular spot. Seleno
is now completing
new LP product.

. “In order to be a
real blues singer—speaking from my
own
experience—you
have
to go through some
of the
things that you
sing
about,” says Bobby ‘Blue’ Bland. The ABC-Dunhill Records veteran, who plays
Nov. 7-11
at the Whisky a Go Go
in Hollywood with the
Dixie Hummingbirds,
has had over 30 single records on the music magazine charts, and more than
that on the Harlem,
race, r&b and soul charts.
His current single, “This Time
I’m Gone For Good”
is #32 bulleted on CB R&B chart. His name
is a legend,
even to those who have never heard him sing, and he
is considered one of the
greatest pop-blues singers of our times.
"It’s not what you say,” Bland says,
“but how you say
it.
I
try to do songs
in
a ballad-type way, where
it won’t be
strictly blues. Now what
I have basically to
rely on
is the blues, but
I educate
myself through a spectrum of records, and people that
I think have something
to
offer me. “For instance,”
he admits,
“I’ve always admired Tony
Bennett,
Perry Como and Andy Williams. This
is the thing that
I based my blues on, and
I have quite a few of their records that
I listen to, and learn from.”

Groove Merchant Host ‘Rich’ Bash
ROAR OF ’74 (Seen above, Buddy’s Band in Action)—Groove Merchant Records
hosted a cocktail party and luncheon at Jimmy’s Restaurant on Tuesday, Octo-
ber
9
to introduce
its newly pacted Buddy Rich Band
to
the press,
radio and
New York distributors and dealers. The “Roar of ’74,” the
title of Rich’s debut
album for
the
label, served
as
the theme
of the party which was introduced
via six souped up racing cars roaring thru West 52nd
Street to
a screeching
halt at the front door of Jimmy’s where the Rich band is appearing. Buddy Rich,
a racing car enthusiast
himself, then took the wheel of one of the souped up
racers, much
to the delight of the large lunch time crowd
that had gathered
in front of the restaurant.
Half Note Celebrates Uptown Anni
NEW YORK —
For
fifteen
years
jazz
afficionados
beat
their
way
downtown
to
Spring
and
Hudson
Streets to the Half Note to groove to
the music
of Dizzy and Mingus and
Zoot and Carmen and Anita and
oth-
er
jazz
giants
presented
nightly by
the Half Note proprietors, the Cante-
rino
family. Came
the
rock
revolu-
tion
and
jazz
and
jazz
emporiums
virtually
disappeared
into
the
never
land
of
other
declasse
art
forms
except for diehard
faithfuls,
like the
Half
Note,
which
kept
going
even
though
customers
now
trickled
in-
stead of streamed in.
By
the
late
1960’s
the
neighbor-
hood around Spring and Hudson
fell
into
decline,
but
it
wasn’t
until
last
October 19 that the Canterinos finally
packed
their
reservations
book,
moved
uptown
to
149
West
54th
Street
(the
building was
once Texas
Guinan’s
carriage
house).
Not
only
did
the
regulars
find
the new
Half
Note
but
so
did
a new and younger
crop
of
fans. And
it
looks
like
the
beat will go on. Coincidental with the
Half Note’s move uptown, jazz began
its big comeback
all over town
(even
Horn &
Hardardth’s
doing
it)
and
people are once again coming out
to
dig the sounds of Dizzy and Zoot not
to mention the Modern Jazz Quartet,
another
jazz
establishment
celebra-
ting some 21 years of togetherness —
which
is
currently
playing’
a
two
week
engagement
at
he H
Note
through October 27.

Monument
Inks Hirt
NASHVILLE —
Fred
Foster,
pres-
ident
of
Monument
Records,
an-
nounced
the
signing
of
Al
Hirt
to
world-wide
recording
deal.
Foster
will
produce
the
trumpet
player,
whose
hits
include
“Java,”
“Cotton
Candy” and many more.
Currently recording
for Monument
are such
artists as saxophonist Boots
Randolph,
Nashville
studio
veteran
Lloyd Green and award-winning
har-
monica player Charlie McCoy.
Hirt,
who
will
remain
based
in
New
Orleans,
is
scheduled
for
at
least
two
albums
and two
singles
a
year on Monument.
“We
have
always
been
selective
about the artists signed to Monument
Records, and with Al Hirt
there’s no
doubt
that we now have
one
of
the
all-time
greatest. Both as a musician
and as an entertainer, Al Hirt
is tops
in
his
field.
I
look
forward
to
our
association,” said Foster.
Dolls To Make
Waldorf Date
CHICAGO — To
spotlight
the New
York
Dolls’ appearance
Oct.
31, Hal-
lowe’en Night, at the Grand Ballroom
of the Waldorf Astoria
in New York,
Phonogram,
Inc. has launched a cam-
paign
promoting
the
appearance.
Special
print and radio advertising
is
already
running
to
promote
the
date,
with two
hundred
special
pos-
ters
being
distributed
to New
York
retail
stores
in
conjunction
with
a
giveaway
contest
for

One

of
tickets
will be given away
to
each
of
ten
contest
winners.
There
will
also
be
a
similar
contest
on
WNEW-FM. A
six-foot square of the
album
cover
has
been
made
as
a
backdrop
for
the
stage
and
will
be
used while the Dolls perform.
At
this
point,
the New York
Dolls
will
be the only act appearing
at the

will mark
the
end
of a
three month
cross
country
tour
the
Dolls
have
completed.

RINGO—Ringo Starr—Apple—SWAL 3413
Ringo continues to develop
his own
identity
in
this fascinating Richard
Perry produced
LP
which features the sensational
hit single "Pho-
tograph.”
The
artistry
on
this album
is
the
most unique
in the history of pop music.
All of
the
ex-Beatles, The
Band,
Marc
Bolan,
David
Bromberg, Nicky Hopkins,
Billy Preston, Steve
Cropper, and a host of the finest studio men
in
the world combine to make each track a mas-
terpiece. John Lennon’s “I’m The Greatest”
is
a gem
as
is Randy Newman’s “Hold
On.”
In
fact,
every
cut on
the
LP
is distinguished
by
the
individual genius
of Ringo and the
collec-
tive talents
of
his friends.
FULL SAIL—Loggins & Messina—Columbia KC
32540
Kenny and
Jim’s new LP
is,
as
the
cover
indicates,
a
step
into
paradise.
Led
by
their
current
hit, ‘‘My Music,” the album
is an exer-
cise
in
the
brilliant
collaboration
of two men
with the four musicians who work with them.
Jim’s “You Need A Man”
is one of the
finest
songs
the group has
ever
done,
featuring
a
funky
backbeat
and
Jim’s
distinctive
guitar
highlights.
“Lahaina”
sets
the
stage
for
the
show which
is
full,
rich, and
atmospheric
as
only the duo can render
it. “Coming To You,”
“Sailin’ The Wind,” and "Pathway To
Glory”
are splendid and give notice that the long wait
for this record was worth
it.
BOWIE
PINUPS—David
Bowie—RCA
APL1-
0291
A
collection
of some
of the
finest
esoteric
and
popular
songs
from
Britain’s
mid-1960
period
are the substance
of David’s explosive
new LP which reaches out and grabs you from
the power of "Rosalyn”
(Pretty Things) and
“I
Can’t
Explain”
(The
Who),
to
Bert
Berns’
la-
ment,
“Here Comes
The
Night.”
Bowie
has
always been
a master
stylist, and this LP rein-
forces
his
reputation. With
powerful drummer
Aynsley
Dunbar
lending thumping support
to
Mick
Ronson’s
ethereal
guitar,
Dave
has
a
strong band with which to render this excellent
selection
of
old
hits.
“See
Emily
Play” and
"Friday on My Mind” are our favorites.

of

tongue-in-check poem dedicated to Ms.
Minelli
and
“I Am The Way”
is an
irreverent spoof on
the Jesus
craze.
“Clockwork Chartreuse” and
“Dilated
To
Meet
You”
put
the
finishing
touches to this funny LP.
THE PARTRIDGE FAMILY BULLETIN BOARD—
Partridge Family—Bell Bell 1137
Televisions
have
long
been tuned
into
this
delightful
musical
family
and
record
players
around the world have played their
joyful mu-
sic for years, and this new LP promises to keep
those
machines
running
for
a
long
time
to
come.
“Money Money”
is
a
strong uptempo
rocker
and
“Roller
Coaster’’
is
surprisingly
funky and moves steadily with David Cassidy’s
lead
vocals
superbly
accented
by
Shirley
Jones’ multitracked harmonies. "Lookin’ For A
Good Time”
is a great pop tune with
a catchy
melody and
Cassidy
does
a
beautiful
job on
The
Goffin-King
60’s
hit
"Oh,
No,
Not
My
Baby.”
BLACK & BLUE—Harold
Melvin & The
Blue
Notes—Philadelphia
International
KZ 32407
The
fabulous quartet
has
everything to
be
proud of on
their
latest LP featuring the
soul-
ful single “The Love
I
Lest.”
interestingly, the
group opens this Gamble-Huff produced album
with
the
atypical
"Cabaret,”
but manages to
give
a
very
creditable
performance.
In* fact,
performance
may
be
the
key word
for
this
versatile vocal group because each tune owes
its
brilliance
to the
dedicated
hard work
of
every member of the team.
“It Ail Depends On
You”
is a sweet and sexy ballad complimenting
the powerful rhythms of “Is There A Place For
Me”
and
"Satisfaction
Guaranteed
(Or
Take
Your Love Back),” perfectly.
TATTOO—Rory
Gallagher—Polydor
PD
5539
Rockin’
Rory has
never been any
better as
you’ll
quickly discover from
a
single
listen
to
his new
LP.
Every cut
is on
fire from the heat
Rory makes when he brushes those steel picks
against
his
guitar
strings. “Who's That
Corn-
in' ”
has
to
be one
of the
finest
slide
guitar
rockers
we’ve
ever
heard
and
"Sleep
On A
Clothes-Line”
is a
rock'n’roll beauty
in a
class
by
itself.
Rory's
incredible
slide
technique
is
also featured on “20:20 Vision” and his vocals
cut through the avalanche
of sound
like a hot
knife through
butter. Putting as much
into this
LP as he does
in
live
concert,
Rory has cap-
tured the tiger by the tail.
Cash
Box — November
3,

. The NY chapter of FORE held
a
special seminar at the City Squire, Manhattan, Oct. 31st. Key speakers at the
FORE meeting included Bo Frazier, vp
at Perception-Today Record
Co., Jan S.
Mirsky, treasurer of GSF Productions
Inc., and Ron LeGalt, controller of Polydor
Inc. The major topics, of course, were on the subjects of financing and operating
independent labels and the methods of obtaining financing for starting a
label.
FORE members were
on
hand
including
several
key
personnel
from
many
areas
of the
record
industry.
It was also brought out by the
panel members
that there
is definitely a vinyl shortage that will effect the manufacturing costs
of
records.
It appears that the
costs
will have to be absorbed
or passed on
to the consumer.
It was
also brought out that computerized systems
are
in
vogue for the major operations. One would tend to think that
it
is impossible
to run
a company without a computer. On the other hand, companys such as
Perception manage reasonally well. Money management, corporate accounting
and management accounting were the topics
discussed.
It was
also brought
out that the day of the single may
have had
its day,
but one need
look only
at the impact of a Marvin Gaye, who did well over 2 million
in single
sales, so
there
is much that has to be considered
before that single can be written
off.
It
is true that an LP has a powerful influence on the profit side of things.
But,
it
is
still the single
in combination with
a forthcoming LP that can
make an
act profitable;
it will enable an independent label to continue to be an influence
on the musical scene. Shut
off this single
activity and you may have
snuffed
out the
creative
artist; and
possibly some
of you may have forgotten that
it
is
still
this creative artist, writer, or producer who contributes to the livelihood
of any company.
It
is therefore possible, that many blacks have been washed
into the computer age. When
it comes
right down
to
basics,
it
is
still
roots!
The roots are where
it’s
at, and
I
still don't see where that
is going to change.
It
is
far too easy
to walk
in
the
gray.
Black
is
black and
white
is
certainly
tuned
to black
radio. There are those who say that music
is
universal,
but
I
defy anyone to
tell me that a Rolls Royce
is of the same structure as a Chev-
rolet. Right now
I’ll take the grey, many blacks are thinking, so
it seems.
Black
radio has been
instrumental
in
promulgating and
promoting new
artists
as
well
as
maintaining established
black
artists
for many years. The
time has
come
for re-establishing those goals.
Lets face
it,
black radio with 90%
less
wattage
power
can
outsell
many
of
the
so-called
top 40
stations.
So,
the
company that chooses
it’s goals and aims carefully
will
survive!!! Consult any
Mama and Papa Store or the Laundromat and the Grocery store
in any Ghetto
area.
don drossell

BUCK OWENS (Capitol, P-3769)
Big Game Hunter (2:09) (Blue Book, BMI—Buck Owens)
A great country
novelty number this new track by Buck has an up-tempo
catchy beat. The fast paced
lyric and rocking guitar work
is sure to have Buck
hit the target with this one.
Flip: That Loving Feeling (2:26) (Blue Book, BMI
Buck Owens)
GEORGE JONES (Epic 5-11053)
Once You’ve Had The Best (2:36) (Copper Band, BMI—J. Paycheck)
This gently paced
ballad
is
a tour de force of country
talent. With George
Jones singing the sensitive vocal, Johnny Paycheck writing the
lyric, and
Be'-
gan White arranging the lush string accompaniment there
is
positively no way
this record won’t be a smash.
Flip: No info, availble.

Their vocal harmonies displayed rank them among the best country duos
ex-

to

BRUSH ARBOR (Capitol, P-3774)
Trucker And The U.F.O. (2:57) (House of Hits, BMI— Ken Munds)
From the “Brush Arbor” LP this novelty cut as the
title may suggest offers
a
lot of fun listening. An up-tempo ballad the story line
is about a trucker find-
ing a
U.F.O. There
is excellent guitar and banjo work and this record
will

Larry Lee Rejoins
‘House Of Cash’
NASHVILLE —
Reba
Hancock
an-
nounced
that Larry Lee has rejoined
the
House
Of
Cash,
after
a
three
month leave of absence, where he will
share
the
responsibility
for
The
House Of Cash Publishing firms with
Harland
Sanders. Larry
will
be
con-
centrating
on
the
Gospel
side
and
working
with
some
country,
while
Harlan
will
be working mainly
with
the country product.
Larry
Lee
has
a
most
impressive
background that started
in 1963 when
he
first
started
writing
for
Screen
Gems and later became the director of
their Nashville
office. After
a
period
of almost three years with
that firm
he
resigned
to
head
the
House
of
Cash Publishing firms. After taking a
leave
of absence
he
is now
back
on
the
job
again
and
is
going
on
his
fourth year with the House Of Cash.
As
co-writer with Don and Harold
Reid of the Statler Brothers, on their
song “Do You Remember These”
he
won a BMI award. To date Larry has
had
over
150
songs
recorded
in
his
catalog.
He was featured as “John The Bap-
tist”
in Johnny Cash’s movie “Gospel
Road,” which has enjoyed much
suc-
cess
across
the
country. Among
his
many other
talents, he works
as
tal-
ent
co-ordinator and
director for the
popular Grand
Ole
Gospel show that
originates from the Ryman Auditori-
um every Saturday night and features
some
of
the
best
gospel
acts
in
the
nation.
The
program
is
broadcast
over WSM
and
taped
for
overseas
listening.
Statler Inks
With Chappell
NASHVILLE
-— Henry Hurt, head of
Chappell
Music-Nashville
office,
an-
nounced
that
writer
Darrell
Statler
has been signed to the growing Chap-
pell roster of artists.
Well-known
in
the
country
music
field,
Statler
has
been
in
the
music
business
for
ten
years,
earning
ten
awards during that time. In 1967, dur-
ing
its
first
year
of
existence,
the
Nashville
Songwriters
Association
gave
him
their award
for
“I
Can’t
Keep Away From
You”
which
was
also a SESAC winner.
This was
fol-
lowed by a second SESAC award for
“It’s Another World,” a top-10 hit by
the Wilburn
Brothers, and
one from
ASCAP for “Blue
Collar Job” which
Darrell won
as
producer,
writer and
artist.
Statler’s
popular
“Honky
Tonk
Stardust
Cowboy”
was
a
crossover
success
recorded
by
such
artists
as
Jonathan Edwards, Lefty Frizzell and
Bill
Rice.
In
addition,
his music
has
been recorded by many other country
artists
including
the
Osborne
Broth-
ers, Ernest Tubb, Loretta Lynn, Jim
Ed
Brown,
Tommy
Overstreet
and
Peggy Little.

NEW YORK —
Vittorio
Benedetto
and Jimmy Ienner of C.A.M. have an-
nounced
that
the
musical
score com-
posed by Jacques
Brel- for the
soon-
to-be
released feature
film “L’Emme-
deur,”
(The
Pain
In The
Neck)
has
been
produced
and
published
by
C.A.M.
The
music
was
produced
in
France.
In addition, C.A.M. feature film ac-
tivity
includes
a
number
of
scores
produced
and
published
for
motion
pictures which
will
be
released
here
soon.
George
DeLerue
composed
the
music for “How To Destroy The Rep-
utation of The Most Celebrated Secret
Agent In The World” for C.A.M.; Ar-
mando
Trovajoli
has
composed
the
score
for
“Paolo
II
Caldo”;
Peguri
has written the music for “The Seven
Nuns
of Kansas
City” and
for
“Silk
Worm” starring George
Hilton;
Stel-
vio
Cipriani, composer
of
the
music
for
“The Anonymous
Venetian”
has
turned
his
talents
to
the
film
“The
Last
Trip.”
The
C.A.M.
score
for
“Teenager”
was
composed
by
G.
Ardison,
and
the
C.A.M.
score
for
“Free My Love” was written by Mor-
ricone.
Imhoff Named
AMF
Int’l. Rep.
NEW YORK — Hal
Davis, president
of the American Federation
of Musi-
cians (AFL-CIO, CLC) has appointed
Harold
“Hal”
Imhoff
as
an
interna-
tional representative to
fill the vacan-
cy created by the recent death
of Al-
bert Aan.
Imhoff’s
territory
will be the same
as
that
of
the
late
Aan;
the
Southeastern
and
Atlantic
seaboard
states.
Imhoff, who
will
work
out
of
Ft.
Myers,
Florida, has
had many
years
of union
experience. He has
been an
AFM delegate to the union’s national
convention
since
1968. He
first joined
the Federation in 1943.
Imhoff began studying piano at age
seven, and later studied bass viol, the-
ory,
harmony
and
composition
dur-
ing
his
college
days. He
has
played
with many orchestras, including those
under
the
direction
of Ray
Herrara
and Pee Wee Hunt.

THE 20s REVISITED—Bell Records has been promoting the new Dawn LP,
“New Ragtime
Follies”,
especially
last week
in
St.
Louis where
the
record
company enlisted the staffers at Musical
Isle of America’s mound city branch
as
special good
will ambassadors.
Using
special
ragtime
period
get-ups
including
vests,
arm
garters
and
straw hats, provided by
Bell, MIA’s own kids and senior
citizens formed the
Musical
Isle “Dawn” Patrol and fanned out around
the
city,
telling
stations
and
retail
location customers
all about
Dawn’s new
LP. The MIA
crew
is
shown above, with its captain, vice president of the company, Norm Wienstroer
(kneeling, front right), after making their rounds.

Albums Deal

NEW YORK — Ampex Music
Divi-
sion and Just Sunshine Records have
agreed
on
a
contract
giving Ampex
exclusive

duplicating
and
mar-
keting
rights
for

of

albums, according to William L. Slov-
er, Ampex vice president and general
manager of AMD.
The
five

are
Betty
Davis,
The
Voices
of
East
Harlem,
Ducks,

Holmes
the

Crooner,
and Mississippi Fred McDowell.
“We feel Just Sunshine
is a strong
addition
to our catalog,”
Slover
said.
“Michael Lang’s experience in the rec-
ord
business
is
shown
in
the
first
artists signed by Just Sunshine and in
his
progressive
management
of
the
label. We’re confident we have a win-
ner
in Just Sunshine,” he
said.

NEWCOMER PICKS——
TUBULAR SELLS
TUBULAR
BELLS—Mike
Oldfield—Virgin
VR
13-105
An
incredible solo debut LP for Mr.
Oldfield
who
spent
so many
years
helping
other acts
get off the ground. There are no song titles on
the album, just a
list of the many instruments
Mike plays and explores. Glokenspeil, flageolet,
and
concert
tympani
are
three
of
the
more
exotic devices he
plays from
a combined total
of
twentv-eight,
though
we
wonder
exactly
which sound he got from the Piltdown Man. A
mood LP, the entire effort should be taken as a
highly skilled and diverse attempt to communi-
cate a lifetime of feeling in 48 V2 minutes. Thor-
oughly
enjoyable,
we
reccommend
you
take
your time and
listen.
ASK ME WHAT
I AM—Burt Reynolds—Mercury
SRM-1-693
Burt’s
first venture
into recording looks
like
a
winning
one.
The
LP,
produced
by
Bobby
Goldsboro and Buddy
Killen features Burt
in a
surprisingly tender collection of songs and talk-
ing musical pieces that’s far removed from
his
rough and ready motion picture and TV image.
Highlighted by the
title track the single “Room
For
A
Boy
Never
Used,”
and
“Childhood
1949,"
the
album
is
a
very
moving
effort
showing
a
side
of Burt
heretofore
never seen
before.
“Slow John
Fairburn,”
“Till
I
Get
It
Right,”
"You
Can’t
Always
Sing
A
Happy
Song,” and “There's A Slight Misunderstanding
Between God And Man” are
all very well done.
An interesting package.
ONE MORE TIME—Andy &
David
Williams
MCA MCA-346
The duo's debut LP
is a commercial dream,
loaded with charm and highlighted by the
title
track and good cover versions of "Sweets
For
My Sweet” and the Roy Orbison #1
hit of the
60’s,
“Oh,
Pretty Woman.”
Whether
singing
sweet
ballads
like
“Born
Too
Late”
and
“I
Found
It”
or moving uptempo numbers such
as “Just Like
In The Movies” and “27 Scream-
ing Young
Girls,”
the Williams
brothers seem
to
have
hit upon
that magic
combination
of
sounds
so
essential
to
a
successful
product.
Several arrangers and producers including Wes
Farrell,
Danny
Janssen,
Bobby
Hart,
Jimmie
Haskell, and John Bahler did great jobs on the
LP.
SUSAN PILLSBURY—Susan Pillsbury—Sweet
Fortune SFS-804
Susan’s
fine debut LP on Sweet Fortune
is
like a refreshing breath of sweetly scented sum-
mer air. “Brown Eyes,” the opening cut on side
one,
is
a catchy tune which immediately high-
lights
Susan’s
sexy
voice
as does
“It’s
Hard
To Be
Easy.” Susan wrote
all
but one
of the
ten
compositions
and
it’s
very
evident
that
she’s not only musically adept, but also lyrically
adroit with
her tunes
"I Thought
I Knew The
Answers,” “Never Said
Goodbye,” and
“Love
Never Dies.” Mike Berniker produced the album
which
holds
a
great
deal
of
promise
for the
charming and talented Ms.
Pillsbury.

NEW YORK — Buddy Morris, found-
er and president of Edwin H. Morris
Music Company,
is involved in a vari-
ety
of up-coming
theatrical
projects
with
both
established composers and
several promising new writers assur-
ing an
active
’73-’74
season
for
the
veteran music firm.
The range of Morris projects
is
in-
ternational with shows currently run-
ning or in preparation here and over-
seas. Sylvia Herscher, who directs the
company’s
theatre
department,
de-
tailed these activities.
“Grease,”
the
long-running
rock
musical
by Warren
Casey
and
Jim
Jacobs, has companies performing
in
Mexico, London and France as well as
on Broadway and touring throughout
this country. Also in Paris
is
“Hello
Dolly” where the Jerry Herman score
is
a
success. The
Strouse & Adams
show, “Applause,” recently concluded
a
successful run
in London and join-
ing the activity there is the John Bar-
ry-Don Black version of “Billy Liar,”
which
is in preparation and scheduled
to begin rehearsals in Jan.
Several musicals are in preparation
in New York. They include: “He Who
Gets
Slapped,” produced by Barbara
Schwei and Les Schecter with a score
by
Clint Ballard and Barbara Damo-
shek;
“Gallery” with
an Ed
Kleban
score;
“Hunky
Dory” with
book
by
Ann
Marie
Barlow
and
score
by
Strouse and Adams; “Sextet” by Lee
Goldsmith
and
Larry
Hurwit;
and
“Annie”
whose
score
is
by
Charles
RCA Classics
(Cont’d from
p. 7)
ca,
the
Classic Movies
of Humphrey
Bogart” and “Gone with the Wind,” a
full LP
on Max
Steiner’s
score
for
the classic film.
Traditional
Classics
In
a
more
traditional
classical
vein, Munves
cites the success
of the
company’s
$1.49
“Guess That Tune!”
sampler
in
promoting
a
series
of
LP’s tagged “100 Melodies the World
Loves
Best,”
which
list
in LP form
(they
are
available
on
8-track,
too)
at
$5.98.
Munves’
first
project
for
RCA was
a “Greatest Hits” classical
concept with
total sales
of 250,000.
RCA’s
vaunted
vaults
of
classical
repertoire
is another strong
point
in
RCA’s favor. Munves notes they con-
tain performances by “one
of a kind
performers.” “There are a lot of great
artists
around,
but
only
one
of
the
type
represented
in
our
vault
cata-
log.” Recently, the vaults have uncov-
ered a five volume, 3-LP series of all
Rachmaninoff recordings made by the
pianist-composer
at RCA
from" 1919
until his death in 1942; a new Caruso
set features nine recordings never re-
leased before,
as well as a Lawrence
Melchoir package
containing
40
per-
formances, about %
of which are also
getting exposure
to the public for the
first time.
Coming up
is an
interesting
“con-
trast”
idea
that
will
couple
a
new
recording
of
Dvorak’s “New World”
symphony by Leopold Stokowski and
a
46-year-old
version
by
Stokowski
and
the
Philadelphia
Orchestra,
the
maestro’s
first
electrical
recording.
Strouse and Martin Chamin.
“R.J.”
(Rainbow
Jones)
with
a
score
by
Jill
Williams, produced and
:ted by Gene Persson and starring
Persson, follows
its recent run
in Washington, D.C. with an engage-
ment
in Boston
beginning
Dec.
8. A
New
York
opening
will
follow
the
Boston stand.
Beginning
in
Jan.
with
initial
showings
in
Texas,
the
Carolyn
Leigh,
Moose
Charlap,
Jule
Styne,
Betty Comden, Adolph Green “Peter
Pan”
is
anticipating
a new lease
on
theatrical
life. NBC
Entertainment
Industries
is re-vamping the show for
arena
productions
and following
the
Texas
introduction
will
be
playing
arena
theatres
in
multiple
locations.
Other musicals in various stages of
development at Morris Music are “Ol-
ympian
Games”
by
Barbara Damo-
shek
and
Kenneth
Cavender
(“Alice
In
Wonderland”),
“Valentines
Day”
by
Ron
Cowen
(“Summer
Tree”),
Seth Glassman and Saul Naishtat and
a musical based on “Come Back Little
Sheba”
by
Clint
Ballard
and
Lee
Goldsmith.
Film
Projects
In the film area Morris
is currently
represented
by
the
new
Ingrid
Bergman
film, “From the Mixed Up
Files
of
Mrs.
Basil
E. Frankweiler”
from
which
“Claudia’s
Theme”
is
being recorded. Warner Brothers pro-
duction of “Marne” scheduled for ear-
ly Spring will have a new Jerry Her-
man song
titled
“Lovin’ You”
added
to
the
score. Robert Preston
sings
it
in the film.
Another facet
of the
Morris
firm’s
involvement with
dramatic
music
is
an
oratorio written by Gary William
F riedman
called
“Celebration,”
Friedman, composer
of “The Me No-
body
Knows”
unveiled
his
recent
work at a performance at New York’s
Temple
Israel
on the Jewish
holiday
Simchas Torah which marks
the end
of the year-long reading of the sacred
writings
and
serves
as
“Celebra-
tion’s” theme.
In line with her continuing effort to
involve
writers from
other
media
in
the musical
theatre, Ms. Herscher
is
working
with
“Love
Story”
author
Erich Segal on a new musical project.
Mempro New Execs:
Davis And Duncan
MEMPHIS
-—
Marty
Lacker,
presi-
dent
of Mempro,
Inc., has announced
the appointment of Richard Davis
as
vice
president
of Mempro,
Inc.
and
Diane Duncan as exec assistant to the
president. Mempro
specializes
in
rec-
ord
promo,
in
addition
to
promotion
for
publishers,
public
relations,
pub-
licity, production, and artists manage-
ment. Lacker
is also chairman
of the
Memphis
and
Shelby
County
Music
Commission
and
exec
director
of
Memphis

R&B News Report
AL GREEN CONQUERS NEW YORK—A1 Green came
to New York
City
and conquered
all. Green spent a
full week headlining at Harlem’s prestigious
Apollo Theatre and every show drew SRO houses.
In
fact, Robert Schiffman,
the owner-General Manager
of
the
Apollo,
said, “A1 Green
set
the
all-time
Apollo box
office record during his appearance here during November
2
to
8.”
During
this week, A1 performed an
incredible 17 shows
at the Apollo—all of
which included debut live performances of his new single,
“Livin’ For You”
and on
the
last night he was surprised onstage by
a presentation of a plaque
and
photos awarded
to him
for
his
service
to Harlem community
youth.
It
seems
the Hi/London Records
artist had on past
visits
to New York slipped
away
to
counsel underprivileged
youth of
the
area,
without even
letting
his
management know. AI considers
the Apollo
his home and
the fans welcomed
him.
For that matter, during the hectic week at the Apollo which included
visits
to
all
local
radio
stations with
London
promoiotn
people,
Al
found
time
to
continue
his humanitarian ventures with a
full-blown
concert
at
the dockside
Federal House of Detention
in lower Manhattan before an enraptured, boogy-
ing-in-their-seats audience
of 250 inmates
(see
photo). And
for
this
concert,
no expense or effort was spared, as Al brought along his entire band and per-
formed
a
complete,
specially programmed
set
for
the
institution’s
inmates.
The
delighted
and
appreciative
audience
presented
Al
with
a
hand-painted
card that promised “Peace in the star, Love in the grass” and a book of poems.
Green humbly thanked
the inmates and afterwards noted
that the reason
for
the concert was simply, “They’re locked up and can’t get out, but
I can get in.”

Ashford & Simpson On Concert Swing
NEW YORK — Composing,
produc-
ing
and
performing
team
Nickolas
Ashford & Valerie Simpson have just
begun
a
cross-country
mini-tour
of
the major market
cities
to
introduce
themselves to the concert audience as
a duo, and to meet radio and press
in
each
city
to
discuss “Gimme
Some-
thing Real,” their debut LP for War-
ner Bros.
Records, and
their just
re-
leased
single
“(I’d Know You)
Any-
where.”
Already well-known for their
writ-
ing and production of such r&b hits as
“Ain’t No
Mountain
High
Enough,”
“Let’s Go Get
Stoned,” “You’re
all
I
Need
to Get By” and “Ain’t Nothing
Like
the
Real
Thing,”
Ashford
&
Simpson are making their performing
debut with this tour. Responses
to the
first stop, the Troubadour in Los An-
geles, are indicated by a review in the
Hollywood Reporter saying “Ashford
&
Simpson
brought down
the
house
when they opened Tuesday. The Trou-
badour was trembling with vibrations
of
life, moans and
cries
of apprecia-
tion.”
Other
stops
on
the
Ashford
&
Simpson tour include Alice Tully Hall
in New
York
(November
11th)
the
Ford
Auditorium
in
Detroit
on
November
16th
the
Cellar
Door
in
the
Bijou Theatre
in
Philadelphia on
November 26 & 27, the Saunders The-
Washington,
D.C. on November
19th,
atre
in
Boston
on
December
1,
and
the Happy Medium
in Chicago on De-
cember 3rd and 4th.
Gospel Acts Need Showbiz Help
NEW YORK CITY — The
majority
of gospel
singers
will never graduate
into
the
big money
unless
they
get
organized and
let others handle their
business
affairs,
predicted
one
of
Broadway’s top booking agents.
Herb Moon, who handles the gospel
department
of Queen Booking
Corp.,
said
that
these
groups
will
have
to
stop
booking
themselves
in
whistle
stop
engagements
that
sometimes
don’t gross $200.00.
He
credited
the
success
of James
Cleveland,
rated
the
foremost
male
gospel
singer
in
the
nation,
to
his
professionalism.
His one
night
tours
start
at
$2500
and
often
he
walks
awav from a concert with as much as
$7500.
“There are a few such as Cleveland,
Inez Andrews, Mighty Clouds
of Joy,
Soul
Stirrers
and
Shirley
Caesar,
“said
Moon,” who
have
signed
con-
tracts with our agency. And they are
amazed at the profitable engagements
we
secure for them
in comparison
to
what they once earned.”
While most groups and
singers
in
the gospel
field have restricted them-
selves
to dates
in small churches and
lodge halls that seat 200 and 300 per-
sons, Moon books QBC’s
clients
into
large
concert
halls,
auditoriums
and
on
college campuses. With crowds
of
as
much
as
8000
that
can
be
ac-
comodated
in
these
places, he
points
out
that
the
artist
can
walk
away
with a larger share of the boxoffice.
He
laments
the
fact
that
these
groups
are
poorly
educated
into
the
methods of show business by not hav-
ing
personal
managers,
accountants
and
business
advisers
as
do
bigtime
pop
artists
such
as
Sammy
Davis,
Aretha
Franklin,
Curtis
Mayfield
or
Gladys Knight and the Pips.
“It’s
a
proven
fact,”
said
Moon,
“that performers can’t work
all night
and
then
arise
at
daybreak
to
talk
facts
and
figures
with
shrewd
and
sharp
business men. They need
such
advisers to advance their interests.”
To
bolster
his
arguments
he
said
that the late Clara Ward and Mahalia
Jackson
struggled
for
pennies
until
they
retained
professionals
to
guide
their careers which brought them
lu-
crative
TV,
record
and
theatre
ap-
pearances. The
late Sam
Cooke
and
Aretha
Franklin,
said
Moon,
both
were
products
of
the
gospel
world
and
amassed
a
fortune
when
they
placed
their
business
affairs
in
the
hands of competent persons.

divisions and

joined

of
the

of

re-
sponsibilities in A&R.”
Merenstein,

and

traveled
the

in

at the
crucial period when
rack
jobbers
and new forms
of
dis-

were

into

vettes and Sears.

am Makeba, Mama
Cass, John

droff.
It was during the production of

to join the company.

3 Groups In Shifts
HOLLYWOOD—Three major
record-
ing acts have altered their status quo

Splitting
up
as
of
last
week
were
Capitol’s
Skylark.
Member’s BJ
and

Foster own
the
rights
to
the

will probably con-
tinue
singing

to

a
solo
career.
The
group,
which
steadily
climbed
the
charts
this past year, was due to re-
lease
a new LP
in January.
Also terminated is Soverign’s Flash,
a group with three previous LPs. Ac-
cording
to
a
label
spokesman,
“per-
sonal
accidents”
influenced
their
de-
cision
to
break
up.
Their
latest LP
was
called
“Flash,
featuring
Peter
Banks.”
Banks, who
is
presently
in
the
LLS., has already had
a
solo LP
and may
again
embark
on
his own
career.
Finally
Motown’s

are
again undergoing some changes. Jean
Terrel has departed and
is being
re-
placed
by
Sherry
Payne
(Freda
Payne’s sister, recently with the Glass
House).
Jean
has
left
the
group
to
devote more time
to her private
life,
which includes her new husband, Jay
Thompson. Also, the Supremes’ Lynda
Laurence, has
left due
to pregnancy.
She
is being temporarily replaced by
former
Supreme
Cindy
Birdsong.

dling
of RCA’s

had won him wide respect.

of
a continuing flow
of
materials
to
the
petrochemical
com-
panies
should enable
our
industry
to
get from those companies a fair share
of the petrochemicals we need to pro-
duce recordings,” he said.
“There
is
no
real
possibility,
officials
tell
us, that
the Government
will
allocate
such
products
as
poly-
vinyl
chloride
(PVC)
to
recording
companies or other end users of such
materials,” he
said. “PVC
is
too
far
removed from the barrel of crude
oil,
and
the
number
of
petrochemical
users
is vast.”
Gortikov
explained
that
officials
and representatives
of the RIAA are
working directly with the Petrochemi-
cal Energy
Group,
a
coalition
of
22
leading
petrochemical
producers,
in
Washington
efforts
to secure
priority
treatment
for
petrochemical
produc-
tion.
“The key need now
is to get priori-
ty allocation of the scarce petrochemi-
cal
feedstocks
to
the
petrochemical
companies,” he said.
This action
is
called for
in the
re-
cently-passed
Emergency
Petroleum
Allocation Act, he said. While the Ad-
ministration has not yet acted, “there
are some
encouraging
signs,”
Gorti-
kov
said.
The
administrator
of
the
new
Federal
Energy
Office,
William
E. Simon, has said that refinery
out-
put
will
be
shifted
to
increase
sup-
plies of fuel
oil and “vital petrochem-
ical feedstocks.”

NAIRD Urges Tare Share’ Of
Vinyl For Indie Membership
CHICAGO — NAIRD,
the
National
Association
of
Independent
Record
Distributors
is
calling
for
a
“fair
share” of vinylite for indie labels and
their
distributors. NAIRD
feels
that
independent
firms
should
be
able
to
manufacture quantities relative to
its
participation
in
the free market pro-
ceeding the petroleum
crisis. Alarmed
by
“recent
decisions
of
some
major
record
companies
to
discontinue
pressing for smaller labels
at
a time
when
it
is
virtually
impossible
to
move
to
other
facilities,”
NAIRD
chairman George Hocutt stated:
“Some
of our member
labels were
shocked when RCA
cancelled custom
operations
early
this
year. One
label
had been with them since 78 rpm days
and
we
understand
is
contemplating
legal
action. Capitol stopped pressing
for other firms in early Fall, crippling
Fall
business
for
some
small
labels
who
had
difficulty making
other
ar-
rangements on such short
notice. The
situation
is getting worse and we un-
derstand
that some very
large
firms
that do not have their own plants are
going
to
be
shopping
around
for
pressing
facilities before
long. Those
of
us who
already
press
in
modest
plants may be crowded out. The short-
age of vinylite and pressing facilities
is
certain
to be
inflationary.
It
quite
possibly
is a combination
in restraint
of trade and the problem will worsen
if
proper
government
action
is
not
taken
to
see
that materials
are
allo-
cated
fairly—not only between
press-
ing plant and client, but also between
the
vinylite
supplier and
the
record
industry.
“Vinylite
is
derived from
resin,
a
by-product
of the petroleum-cracking

20% Cut In Japan
TOKYO—An “inevitable” cut of 20%
in
Japanese
record
production
next
year
is being forecast
in view of the
vinyl shortage.
The shortage, which has been great-
ly aggravated by the explosion at the
Naoestu factory of Shinetsu Chemical
Industries,
which
holds
the
largest
supply of PVC resin, has been greet-
ed with
shock
and
profound
uneasi-
ness
in Japan’s music
industry.

and board chairman Mo Ostin hold two
of four platinum LPs

re-
cently to Mary Travers, who
sits between the two execs holding the remain-
ing two
RIAA-certified
million
unit
sellers. The four platinum awards were
for
Peter,

and
Mary’s
“In
Concert’’,
“In

“Moving”,
and
“Album 1700” LPs. All members of the

Detroit Gets
‘Power House’
DETROIT — The
Power
House,
a
new record company, has been estab-
lished
in
Detroit. Headed by
Patrick
Meehan and Johnny Powers, the new
firm
will
concentrate
on
production,
manufacturing,
leasing
and
publish-
ing
of
pop, r&b,
and country
music.
The
production
division
of
the
company
has
developed
a
roster
in-
cluding King Diamond,
Jackie
Ervin,
Carl James, Deacon Jones, and Cana-
dian
acts Ronnie Fray and Joe.
The
Power
House
has
three
staff
writer/producers, Roger Bass, who
is
also head
of a&r, Fiery Bursey, and
Don
Boileau.
Other
writers
are
Joe
Konas, Tommy
Ingram,
and
David
Easley.
The Power House
is seeking
addi-
tional
artists, writers, and
producers.
The company
is located at 19804 Van
Dyke,
Detroit,
Mich.
48234.

Among

Kay, who

at
New York’s Lehman College. Dr. Kay
exchanged impressions
with
the two

of

to
Russia
in
1958. At
that time he was one
of
a
group
of BMI composers who
toured
Russia under
State Department
aus-
pices as part of international cultural
exchange,
the
first
American
com-
posers to do so.

emeritus,

and

of
the
Lenox
Art

Ms.
Grace
Belt and Ms.
Elaine
Hei-
fetz of the U.S. Department of State.

Stars
For
Israel
At
Friars Conf.
NEW YORK —
The
United
States
Stars
for
Israel,
a
morale
building
airlift of entertainers to Israel, begun
on
a
crisis
basis
immediately
after
the
outbreak
of
the
Yom
Kippur
War,
will become
a permanent
pro-
gram,
because
of
the
unrest
in
the
Middle-East. The
announcement was
made at a press conference Fri., Nov.
30, 1973
at the Friars
Club.
Mayor John
V.
Lindsay,
honorary
chairman
of the program, accepted a
check from
realtor
George Mehlman
who
represents
a
group
of
personal
friends
who
have
raised
a
special
fund
for
this
project. The
following
stars
who
have
already
returned
from
entertaining
the
troops
and
veterans
in
Israel
were
introduced
and honored:
Aliza Kashi, The Barry
Sisters,
Allan
Jones
and
Geula
Gill.
Alan
King,
Roberta
Peters and
Elly
Stone, also present at the conference,
are among
a
group
of
entertainers
including
Hazel
Scott
who
will
be
going
to
Israel
in
Dec./Jan.
David Rivlin, Consul General of Is-
rael, expressed his thanks to the U.S.
stars
who
have
gone
to
Israel
to
entertain the troops. Alan King, hon-
orary
co-chairman
of
the
project,
spoke
about
the
great
number
of
stars who have volunteered their
tal-
ents to entertain the disabled in Isra-
el.
In
addition, Azaria Rapoport,
Cul-
tural and Press attache of the Israeli
Consulate
in New
York,
leaders
of
the United Jewish Appeal
of Greater
New York, and members of the advi-
sory
committee
for
the
project
in-
cluding Phil
Schapiro,
Jackie
Bright,
and Joey Adams, were
on hand
for
the presentation.

MILWAUKEE MENTIONS
The new Seeburg “Matador” phonograph
is indeed the center of excitement at
S.
L.
London
Music
these
days!
Nate
Victor
said
the
model’s
been
selling
beautifully
since
its
release
but
he
noted
a
decided
increase
in
activity which
began just after MOA Expo and
is
still
prevailing! There’s also been much repeat
business on the "Regency”
console
.
.
.
Nate
is
very
enthusiastic
about the
Seeburg
audio
visual
training
tape,
which
is
proving
to
be
of
very
valuable
assistance to operators. He was telling us that servicemen come over to London
Music, sometimes
in groups
of three or four,
to
sit and watch the “audio
visual
service school”,
as he
calls
it. The taped
sessions cover Seeburg phonographs
and vending equipment.
Since the
instructions
are
on
tape,
a
serviceman
can
very
easily
replay
the
tape
over
a
particular
portion
of
the
session
he may
not have understood the
first time around. As simple as “asking questions” you
might
say.
Seeburg
has
supplied
its
distributors
with
the
aud;o
visual
installa-
tions as well as the various required tapes.

Electronic Table Game
FORT LAUDERDALE
FLA. — A
brand new electronic game in a brand
new cabinet concept has been released
by Performance Enterprises, Inc. The
game
is
called
(and
is
played
like)
Jai
Alai,
often
dubbed
the
world’s
fastest game. And, the factory
is also
calling
it
a
“table
game,”
actually
hoping players
set
their
drinks
onto
the table top while playing the piece
(see photo).
The two-player item
(set for
2-25(1
pricing)
is a challenging game of jai
alai
where
the
soeed
actually
in-
creases
as
the
volley
continues
(as
with
several video
pieces). The
first
player to score six points
(thru quick
reflex
depression
of
the
control
but-
tons) wins.
The
factory
advises
that
the
mechanism
is
all
solid
state
circuitry
and comes with a twelve month war-
ranty.
PEI
president Bob
Soitler advised:
“We
call these units table games and
we know many crowded locations will
welcome the addition of this beautiful
cocktail
table
to
their
establishment.

Columbia Purchases
Gloria Taylor Master
NEW YORK —
Columbia
Records
has purchased
the master by
Gloria
Taylor
of
“Deep
Inside
Of
You,”
originally
released
on
the
Selector
Sound label out of Toledo, Ohio.
Bill
Craig,
regional
manager
of
promotion
for
the Columbia Records
Branch
in
Detroit,
heard
the
song,
noted
it was breaking wide
open
in
the
Detroit
area, and brought
it
to
the
attention
of
the
National R&B
Promotion
Department
at
Columbia
in New York
Miss Taylor,
24,
is no stranger
to
hit records, having had her
first mil-
lion
seller, “You’ve Got To Pay The
Price,”
on
the
Silver Fox
label,
in
1970. She
also had two
chart records
on Mercury,
“Don’t Want To
Be A
Girl That Cries,” which made the na-
tional
Pop
Charts,
and
“Grounded,”
which
did well on
the
national R&B
charts.
Columbia
will
be
releasing
“Deep
Inside Of You” immediately.
UA Appoints Abbott
Nat’l R&B Director
HOLLYWOOD —
United
Artists
Records
has
appointed
Mike
Abbott
to
the newly-created
position
of
na-
tional
director of r&b promotion. He
will
be
situated
at
the UA
Records
offices in New York.
Abbott
is
a
veteran
of
the
enter-
tainment
business. Most recently
his
Abbott Records
label was
distributed
by United Artists. He also headed the
record
department
of
the
agency,
General Artists Corp., and supervised
the
r&b
promotional
activities
of
MGM Records and Capitol Records.

B.B. King Forms
Blues Society
NEW YORK—B.
B. King
this week
announced the formation
of an
inter-
national
society
for
the
appreciation
of the blues with himself as chairman
of the advisory board.
The new
organization
has
among
its
goals
and
purposes
to
place
the
blues in
its proper historical perspec-
tive, to give recognition and appreci-
ation
to blues artists,
to develop new
blues
audiences,
to promote
a
series
of blues concerts, to research and
col-
lect blues
data,
to maintain
continu-
ous
communication with
blues
musi-
cians
and
persons
interested
in
the
blues, to share materials and informa-
tion
with
individuals
and
organiza-
tions and
to
establish
a
blues muse-
um.

cash box 8L talent on stage
Semesis
ROXY L.A. — A
slide projector cast
the
multi-colored image
of a
pair
of
eyeballs
on
the
rear
wall
as
black-
lights illuminated the entire
stage.
It
was a scene from the psychedelic six-
ties and
in the midst of
it
all was a
vaguely
human
form,
outlandishly
garbed
in
Vincent
Price-Roger
Gor-
man drag. The band sent some open-
ing
chords from
out
of
the
shadows
and the humanoid in the center began
to sing; Genesis launched into Rock n
Roll’s
most
audacious
audio-visual
presentation.
The ground they were treading was
shaky, and
lesser talents might have
allowed the whole show to sink into a
campy
supernatural
exhibition.
But
Peter Gabriel’s performance, with his
costume changes, Rod
Sterling intros
to each
song, and
exercises
in mime
was more droll than
it was
shrill, and
served
to
augment,
rather
than
de-
tract
from
the
excellent
music
that
the band played beside him. Keyboard
man
Tony
Banks made
perhaps
the
best use
of
electronic
effects
to
be
found
in
rock, and
his work
on
the
Mellotron provided a textured quality
that added a tremendous depth to the
group’s music.
As
a
whole,
the
group’s
per-
formance
is
as
musical
as
it
is
the-
atrical, blending the two elements
to-
gether
into
a
dazzling show.
Genesis
records
on
Charisma
Records;
their
LP, “Selling England By the Pound”
was the source of much of the materi-
al they performed at the Roxy.
Dave Mason
Livingston Taylor
James Montgomery
Band
ACADEMY OF MUSIC, NYC—Dave
Mason has come a long way since his
days
with
Traffic,
probably
further
than
most
peonle
suspect,
but
the
Columbia
recording
artist
is now
in
his prime, both as a writer and a per-
former, and
his recent Academy per-
formance
fulfilled
all the promise
he
has been building towards for several
years.
Throughout
the
show Dave
main-
tained
control
allowing
the
music
from
his
latest
LP,
“It’s
Like You
Never
Left”
to
nenetrate. With Bob
Fletcher and Rick Jaeger on bass and
drums,
respectively,
the rhythm
sec-
tion became an innovative force, often
spurring keyboard player Mike Finni-
gan
to
flashy
riffs.
Particularly well
received
were
Dave’s
new
single,
“Baby
.
.
.
Please”,
“Headkeeper”,
and
“Misty Morning
Stranger”.
Capricorn artist Liv Taylor showed
no
signs
of
being
overwhelmed
by
older
brother James
as
he charmed
his w
ray through
to
the
crowd.
His
set was very well received, especially
on “Loving Be My New Horizon”, “I
Can Dream
of You”, and
his
recent
single, a version of the classic, “Over
The Rainbow”. At this stage
it seems
that
Liv’s
prospects
are
endless,
es-
pecially when you consider that he
is
entering the most prolific writing and
performing periods
of
his
career.
An
unexpected
delight
on
the
bill
was another Capricorn group, the ex-
citing James Montgomery Band, who
turned the audience on with a rousing
set. With Montgomery supplying vo-
vals and
sharp harp
riffs,
the group
tore the house apart in the short time
allotted
to
them.
“Train”, an
incred-
ible
piece
of funky
rock from
their
recent album, “First Time Out”, was a
show-stonper as was “Don’t Do That”.
The
entire
band
paid
careful
atten-
tion to dynamics and this resulted
in
a
clean, yet powerful sound.
It looks
to me
like
this band
is going
all the
wa y-
d.fe.
The
Average White Band
WHISKY
L.A. —
The
whimsy
of
their name can be misleading because
the
Average
White
Band
doesn’t
sound
much
like
one.
On
the
con-
trary,
.their, music
is
straight-ahead
R&B, jazz-tinged and
highly
dancea-
ble.
The
set
they
delivered
was
marked by a feverish pace, a driving
rhythm that went on and
on, and the
audience
at
the Whisky
loved
every
minute of it.
A
sextet, the Average White Band
features two guitars, bass, keyboards,
drums
and
a
brilliant
saxophonist,
Molly Duncan who
at
times
sounded
like an entire brass
section. Guitarist
Onnie McIntyre
proved
to
be
an
ex-
cellent
vocalist
and
manipulated
sounds
from
his
guitar
that
resem-
bled,
alternately,
the
styles
of
Steve
Cropper and Wes Montgomery. Pieces
like “Show Your Hand”
and “TLC”
were
made
highly
effective
by
the
groups
extraordinary
tightness
and
consistently inventive treatments. The
Average
White
Band
is
from
Scot-
land. They record on MCA and much
of
their
material
was
drawn
from
their recent LP, “Show Your Hand.”
Opening
the
show,
The
Richard
Greene
Group
presented
some
origi-
nal, very ambitious
material. Greene,
formerly
featured
violinist
with
Seatrain,
composed
most
of
the
group’s
songs and
liberally
sprinkled
them
with
literary
references
to
the
likes of Kafka and Freud.
It was an
interesting
set, but
distinctly lacking
the polish and professionalism needed
to
pull
it
off.
Given
time, work
and
perhaps
a
recording
contract,
the
grouD might
develop
into
something
worth watching.

Glen Campbell
THEATER- GO - ROUND
- NANUET,
NY—An
evening
with
Glen
Camp-
bell proved
to be
a
totally
delightful
experience,
as
the
smooth
voiced
troubadour
spun
out
his
songs from
the
Nanuet
Theater-Go-Round’s
re-
volving
stage.
Beginning
the
show
with
“I
Be-
lieve In Music,” the uptempo song set
the
fast
paced
entertainment
which
lie ahead
for
all. The
easy
listening
sounds
of Glen were
finely displayed
on such
songs as “I Knew Jesus,”
a
considerably
softer
re-arrangement
than
the
original,
Helen
Reddy’s
smash “Delta Dawn,” and the Charlie
Rich
classic
“Behind
Closed
Doors”.
A 11 the
selections
hit beautifully, and
Glen’s
transitions
were
well
timed.
Building the excitement, Glen went
into a spoof
of “Proud Mary” which
was
followed
by
a
great
impression
of Elvis, complete with “Teddy Bear”,
gyrations, and opened
shirt.
Glen then settled into “Mansion On
The
Hill”, a moving ballad from
his
most recent Capitol album “I Remem-
ber
Hank
Williams”.
You
. wouldn’t
believe that
the same emotion Hank
used
to
have
could
be
heard
right
down
in
Glen’s
throat.
Another change
and
Glen brought
the
talents
of Carl Jackson on banjo
for
an
electric
trip
of
blue
grass
smokers.
Kicking
it
off was “Foggy
Mt.
Breakdown,”
with
a
blue
grass
version
of
“Proud
Mary”
and
the
now-classic “Dueling Banjos”
follow-
ing
close
at hand. The answering
se-
quences
and
the
rhythms
were
exe-
cuted
with
technical
brilliance.
A medley followed which displayed
Campbell’s
versatility and segues par
excellence. “By The Time
I
Get To
Phoenix” blended
into “Try A
Little
Kindness” which blossomed
into “Wi-
chita
Lineman”.
“Galveston” meshed
into
“Gentle
On My
Mind”.
Dennis
McCarthy, Glen’s conductor, aptly led
a
tight
group
of accompanying mu-
sicians.
An
auditory
and
visual
gem
was
ours
to
behold
as
Glen
picked
the
“Lone Ranger” theme
while
old
film
clips
of
the Lone Ranger were
pro-
jected
onto
the
floor
of
the
stage.
The
last
trio
of
songs
included
a
forecful rendition of Nilsson’s “With-
out
You”,
a
moving
adaptation
of
“The Impossible Dream”, and conclud-
ing
the show was “Amazing Grace”,
where Glen’s diversity had him play-
ing
the
bagpipes. This
evening with
Glen Campbell was truly a most
en-
tertaining one.
m.d.
Woody Herman
SHELLEY’s MANNE-HOLE-L.A. —
There was
a
lot
of
nostalgia
in the
air but Woody Herman’s
latest herd
was
playing
a
lot
more
than
just
memories. The legendary bandleader,
whose various ensembles through the
years
have
served
as
a
proving
ground for many jazz greats, showed
that even now he
is
capable
of
put-
ting together a dynamic group of mu-
sicians.
The
repertoire
ranged
from
old
Herman
standards
to
more
contem-
porary
compositions
such
as
Col-
trane’s “Giant Steps,” also the title of
Herman’s newest Fantasy
LP.
Other
outstanding numbers included
a Her-
man version
of “Blues
in
the Night”
and Chick Corea’s “La Fiesta.”
Playing
with
Herman’s
current
group was an outstanding young sax-
ophonist, Gregory Herbert, whose nu-
merous
solos,
especially on “Summer
of 42” were marked by
a smoothness
and
dexterity
that
may
place
him
alongside some of the other illustrious
sax
players
that
have
graced
the
Herds of earlier times.
But
the most dazzling part
of the
show was the versatility displayed by
Herman
himself,
a
flexible
quality
that enables him
to maintain his own
musical character while absorbing the
twists and turns of the contemporary
scene.

Cash Box/R&B News Report
E & B INGREDIENTS—"That's The Sound
That
Lonely Makes”
is
the new single from the Tavares LP on Capitol. But, for an LP cut that
is really
sayin’ something, check out, “Hello
Little Girl”
.
.
. Also, the correct title of the
Kool & The Gang LP cut that is getting lotsa play action
is, "Hollywood Swinging”
.
.
. Concerning Kool & The Gang, Henry Nash at Queens Booking Corp. says that
the Gang,
Millie Jackson and RCA’s New Birth are getting
priority attention for
'74. Nash says these three acts are heading
in new directions as far as book-
ings,
etc.
.
.
. Now that the Holiday season
is over, and many among us are
slowly recovering from being a
little tore up,
it’s again time to get down to the
business at hand.
‘Tis true that '73 was one heluva
year.
Despite
all the
'73
problems,
black artists continued
to make headway
in many areas,
including
album and single sales. And, proper credit has to be given to those dedicated
cats male and female
in
black
radio who have
struggled and
survived thus
far
in
serving
blacks
in
their respective communities.
Planting the seed that
serves the need
is what black radio
is about.
It is the dedication of such people
as:
E. Rodney Jones,
Jerry
Bolding,
Al Gee and Johnny Jones,
to mention
a
few, who have, through the years, kept many talented black artists alive. They
have also
laid the groundwork for the future Frankie Crockers.
Unfortunately,
many blacks who are qualified are often not given the opportunities to succeed
(or fail) nevertheless,
qualified blacks (and
this goes for any qualified
individ-
ual) should be
entitled to prove that they can indeed serve the needs of the
community. After
all,
isn’t
it the aware disc jockey who knows the street who
works the record hops and does his thing at the discos—isn’t this the guy or
gal who knows what
is happening. There are many who
really care. Those who
are
for real
really care. Would
it make sense to have Golda Meir running for
Mayor of Cairo?
.
.
. Sparkie Martin (Avco promo) held
a swinging New Years
Eve
party. The
party apartment was
a
total
sea
of grovin’
dancers because
Sparkie kept the music
in the groove. Main
Ingredient dropped
in
after their
Apollo stint. G. Fitz-Bartley and Rod Bristow dropped
in. The affair broke up at
dawn. As usual,
it was a Sparkie (Sparkling Event)
.
.
. The NATRA convention
will be held at the Century Plaza
in Los Angeles the third weekend
in August.
Start
making your
plans
now.
This
convention
should
be
one
of
the
most
significant of
all.
It takes your support. You now have sufficient time to make
plans and
to
eliminate objections
(if you’re from the
East Coast) about the
length of the trip. Details will be forthcoming
.
.
. Comments have come to me
regarding the
Miracles and
their new (one year)
lead
singer, William
Griffin,
sounding too much
like Smokey
R. Actually,
William
Griffin was selected and
practically handpicked by Smokey because the Miracles wanted to
retain their
original sound. William
Griffin
is not Smokey and William you
will discover
is
doing his thing
in the Miracle concept of things.
don drossell
ALL THAT’S JAZZ
ECM/Polydor Announces Six
LP's;
(Chick Corea, Gary Burton , Robin Kenyatta, Keith Jarrett/
Jack De Johnette, Holland & Rypdal)
NEW YORK CITY — The
first
six
albums
to be released under the new
ECM/Polydor
logo
include
award-
winning
performances
by
Chick
Corea, Gary Burton, Robin Kenyatta,
Keith
Jarrett and Jack De
Johnette,
David
Holland,
and
Terje
Ryodal.
Originally produced by Manfred Eich-
er for
the West German ECM
label,
these
Ip’s have already received rave
reviews in the European and Ameri-
can press.
Chick
Corea’s
“Piano
Improvisa-
tions
Volume
One”
(ECM//Polydor
1014)
consists
of
“fragile, mesmer-
ising,
utterly
beautiful”
solo
piano
performances according
to
England’s
Melody
Maker. MM went
on
to
call
Piano
Improvisations
“one
of
the
most sensitive, delicate, inventive solo
piano albums ever made.” Down Beat
gave the album
five
stars,
its highest
rating.
Record
World named
“Piano
Improvisations” “the best jazz record
of 1971” despite the fact that
it was
then unavailable in this country. Even
the grand
piano,
furnished by ECM
for
the
recording,
received
a
rave:
Canada’s
Coda
magazine
said,
“the
quality
of
the
instrument
impresses
with the release of every note, imbues
each
chord with
caloric
richness,
re-
sponds
to the
slightest suggestion
of
movement.”
Vibraphonist Gary Burton has been
a
trend-setter,
a
poll-winner,
and
a
best-selling recording
artist since his
memorable
first
quartet
introduced
guitarist Larry Coryell and triggered
the jazz /rock fusion movement of the
sixties.
Burton’s “The New Quartet”
(ECM/Polydor 1030)
is an astounding
tour-de-force
by
four
incomparable
young
musicians.
Abraham
Laboriel
breaks new
ground
on
the
electric
bass; Melody Maker emphasizes that
“Laboriel
sounds
like
a major
artist
in the making—throughout the album
there’s almost a wall-of-sound rhythm
section
with
astonishing
bass
work
dominating
the pace and, indeed, the
energy
of
the
music.”
Guitarist
Michael
Goodrick
is
subtly
melodic
and
inventive,
and
drummer
Harry
Blazer bridges
the gap between rock
and jazz rhythms with
ease. Original
compositions
by
Chick
Corea,
Keith
Jarrett,
and
Carla
Bley
also
con-
tribute
to the importance
of this
ex-
ceptional
Ip. As Melody Maker
said,
it’s “the best Gary Burton album in a
long while.”
Robin Kenyatta’s “Girl From Mar-
tinique” (ECM/Polydor 1008) features
“a
superb
and
unique
reedman”
(Down
Beat)
performing
a program
of
bright,
lively
originals,
supported
by
a
gifted
Euro-American
rhythm
section. Kenyatta’s recent jazz/reggae
“crossover”
and
his
popular
