---- p26
ash Box/R&B News Report
LeBaron Taylor YP of Special Markets
For Columbia & Custom Label Products
NEW
YORK —
Irwin
Segelstein,
president
of CBS
Records,
has
an-
nounced the appointment
of LeBaron
Taylor
to
the
position
of
vice
pres-
ident of special markets for CBS Rec-
ords.
In his new capacity, Taylor will be
responsible for
all marketing of R&B
product
for Columbia,
Epic
and
the
Columbia
Custom
Labels.
His
func-
tions
will
include the
direct
supervi-
sion
of
the R&B
promotion
depart-
ment and
field
force
as
well
as
the
supervision
of
all advertising,
point-
of-sale,
publicity, and
artist relations
activities in regard to Black product.
Taylor also will be involved
in
sales
activities regarding the R&B market.
He
will
report
directly
to
Bruce
Lundvall, vice president of marketing
for CBS Records.
Taylor brings with him a wealth of
experience, having been involved with
practically every phase
of the music
business
in a career
that spans
over
20
years. Prior to joining CBS, Tay-
lor worked
as
director
of A&R
for
Atlantic Records’ R&B product. While
there,
Taylor was
involved
with
all
aspects of A&R including administra-
tion, creative
direction, recording, en-
gineering and producing, and was re-
sponsible
for
signing
and/or
co-
producing
such
acts
as
Melvin Van
Peebles, Nikki
Giovanni, Betty Swan,

New Technique
To Launch
5 TV Specials
NEW YORK —
Producer
Yuri
Za-
bran
will
launch
a new broadcasting
technique
combining TV
and
stereo
sound
via
five one hour TV
specials.
The new
electronic
process
provides
high quality
2
channel
stereo
to any
local FM station in association with a
live
or
taped network TV
broadcast.
The new
technique
does
away
with
the necessity of individual audio tapes
as
utilized
currently with ABC’s “In
Concert,” and
also precludes the pos-
sibility of the FM sound being out of
sync
with
the
picture.
Zabran
will
shortly
announce
the
content
of the
five
specials
each
to
be
aired
at
the
rate

NAACP Image Awards
Stevie Wonder Cops:
‘Innovator Of ’70’s
HOLLYWOOD —
Stevie
Wonder,
Marvin Gaye, Harold Melvin and the
Blue Notes, War, Helen Reddy, Rob-
erta
Flack,
The
Pointer
Sisters
Gladys Knight and The Pips, The Sta-
ple
Sisters
and Johnny
Taylor were
among those presented with NAACP
Image
Awards
during
a
black-tie
presentation
held
at
the
Hollywood
Palladium
on
Saturday, January
26.
Aretha
Franklin,
Della
Reese,
the
Jackson
Five, the Dramatics Johnny
Nash and
the Cashears provided
en-
tertainment
for
the
seventh
annual
gala event.
Don Cornelius, acting as emcee, in-
troduced awards in
a variety of cate-
gories,
including
Recording,
Televi-
sion,
Motion
Pictures
and
“Special
Awards.”
Stevie Wonder was the recipient, of
three
awards,
two
in
the
recording
category
for
Best Album
and
Best
Producer. He was also presented with
a
Special Award
for “Music Innova-
tor of the
Seventies.” Other Awards
were
given
as
follows:
Recording
ALBUM: “Innervisions,” Stevie Won-
der;
PRODUCER:
Stevie
Wonder,
“Innvervisions”;
MALE
VOCAL
GROUP:
War;
FEMALE
VOCAL
GROUP: Pointer Sisters; COMBINA-
TION VOCAL GROUP:
(Tie) Gladvs
Knight &
Pips,
Staple
Singers; FE-
MALE
VOCALIST:
(Tie)

Arthur
Mc-
Dougall
III
to the

and

International
is

Records
Custom
Label.
McDougal
will

to
Gamble for coordinating all press and
information
services for
all
Philadel-
phia
International
Artists.

will
work closely with the Columbia publi-
city department
in promoting
artists,
and
will
also
work
with
individual
artists
in

of their creative
and
business

McDougal began
his
career
in
the
music business
singing with
a group
called The Larks
in
the
early
fifties.
In 1959 he
first met Kenny Gamble, a
friendship which he has kept through
the
years.
In
1963,
McDougal
pro-
duced
the
hit song “Yes I’m Ready”
for Barbara Mason, and had his own
record
production
company,
Haw-
thorne Publishing
Co., which Gamble
was
a
part
of.
In

began
a
nine-year
association
with
Motown
Records,
starting

as
a
local promotion man
in
Philadelphia
and rising to the position
of director
of

and
special
proj-
ects.

Haywood

in Washington,

in New York City. WOL,

is faced

(it does appear, with the fact that

a
qualified black
(in some ten years),
or any man who

understands what
is
cornin’ down,
a man who
is aware
of the needs
of the
black
audience.
Bobby
Bennett, Chuck Long and
Carroll
Hynson
are
other
(back-to-work) on-the-air personalities who have been serving up the soul-power
at the station
for the Washington area
residents. ...
In the promotion areas
of R & B music,
black women are proving their
mettle. Super gals, such
as,
Rowena
Harris
(national promo
for All-Platinum

her

Ellen Anderson
(Polydor)
who aids Joe Medlin, Nancy Pitts aiding Tom Draper at RCA are also exemplary
of the new trend
in promo. Gretta Hunter (promo with GRC)
is
a
perfect
ex-
ample
of what
it’s
all
about. Many
black women
are doing super job on the
radio
front, such
as, Wanda Ramos serving as Frankie Crocker’s assistant
at
WBLS-FM
in NYC. One thing must be
said about this new trend, and that
is
this—this
is now the time for being—for
real— the
early BS
era
is
over.
It
is an
age
of awareness and
for-real
individuality. The time
is
at hand! The
unreal
is being supplanted by the
real, and this
is especially true when
it comes
to black
radio.
Black radio for a
black-white
ratio
(listening audience).
If any-
one does doubt this,

veterans

Effie Smith
(Stax); and Joe Evans
(president
of

is responsible for putting the Manhat-

into the hit recording groove.

enlighten the most unen-

(36)

in

in a row as Record

of

the NA-

award,

of

mental in signing Gladys Knight and
the Pips. He supervised the recording
careers
of performers on the Buddah
subsidiary

as
Sussex,
Teaneck, Curtom and Hot Wax.
His

sold

self appeared

the TV commercial
promoting
the
L.P. Holmes
also
did
the
“Music
for
Soulful
Lovers”
al-
bum.
Bogart
and
Holmes
will
continue

CARNEGIE
HALL, NYC — When
Charles
Mingus
and
Roland
Kirk
joined forces the jazz lovers came out
in
force.
Such was
the
case
at
this
Saturday night show. Before a sellout
crowd the “New Audiences” presented
the
reunion
of
Charlie
Mingus
and
Old
Friends. And
quite
a reunion
it
was.
Opening the show was the Charles
Mingus Qunitet, consisting of Charles
Mingus on bass, Don Pullen on piano,
George Adams &
Hamiet
Bluitt
on
alto and tenor
sax, and Danny Rich-
mond, one of the best jazz drummers
alive. The Quintet was joined by John
Faddis, a truly surperb trumpet play-
er and
a
friend
of
Charles
Mingus.
Because of the unusually responsive
audience,
the
Quintet performed
for
two hours, spotlighting each musician
several times. The knowledable
audi-
ence seemed to influence the Quintet,
as
they jammed
on such numbers
as
“Peggy
Blue
Skylight,”
“Celia”
and
“Big Alice.”
After a brief intermission the audi-
ence was
anxiously awaiting the
ar-
rival
of
Roland
Kirk,
and
his
per-
formance was no
let-do-wn. The
sec-
ond set saw the Mingus Quintet, along
with
Roland
Kirk,
John
Handy,
Charles
McPherson,
and
John
Fad-
dis work together. What resulted was
an
overwhelming
jam
session.
Four
saxophones
simultaneously
backed
Roland
Kirk
with
power.
Roland
played some leads with two saxes at
once and
jazz was played
as
it was
meant to be played.
In
all, the show
proved
to
be
a
quencher
for a
true
jazz lovers’ thirst.

Forrest Green
BITTER END, NYC — An
interest-
ing
assortment
of
roots,
influences
and techniques
are
incorporated
into
the
fiery
set
of
Forest
Green.
The
opening
night
engagement
of
the
Capitol recording artists proved to be
an enchanting musical sojourn, taking
us
from
rock
to
classical
and
im-
provisational
jazz.
Forest Green has
the
ability to put these rather diver-
gent elements together, and the result
is a
textural meld
that proved
itself
to be both
tight and musically
satis-
fying.
The full instrumentation included a
tenor and
alto
saxophone,
flute, bass
guitar,
lead
guitar,
drums,
bassoon
and two
electric
pianos. At once the
group began
to cook coming up with
intriguing
rhythms,
tight
vocal har-
mony, and instrumentation par excel-
lence.
A sophisticated rock ensemble, their
choice of material was apt because
it
clearly
reflected the
polished musical
diversity the group possesses both as
a
unit
and
as
independent
per-
formers.
“Movin’ To
The
Country”,
a
real
rocking
mover,
began
with
a
flash
beginning that had the group imitat-
ing
a
locomotive
engine.
And
the
cookin’ rhythms picked up speed and
carried
this
superb
rocker
along.
“Scream
Fear,”
an
up-tempo
tune
with
fine piano work
is a song spiced
with most provocative
lyrics and
fine
horn accompaniment. “Mountain” had
a
serenely
tranquil
melody
that
floated forth from the group. A
total
mastery of form and instrumentation,
carried
this
song
very
well.
“Black
Shepard”
clearly
incorporated
classi-
cal elements with an almost Baroque
quality to the flute solos which left us
all very
mellow. “Beggar Man” and
up-tempo
tune
employed
moving
rhythms with
an
excellent
lyric
and
vibrant images. Closing their energet-
ic
set
the
group
performed
“Leave
Your Love”. A complex series of mel-
odies
and
great
instrumental
solo
spots
concluded
the
dynamic
per-
formance of this fine group.

is placed for contrast after the short romantic
spoof
entitled
“Nilsson
Sings Newman"
and
gives
an
insight
into
Paul’s
concept
of
the
pacing and
juxtaposition of
his
material.
Paul
uses no less than 50 musicians and singers to
give
this
LP
the
richness which
is
its
trade-
mark.
COME
LIVE WITH ME—Ray Charles—Cross- 1
over CR9000
Every release of Ray’s
is anxiously expected *
and
this unique
collection
is
certainly not an
exception.
Highlighted
by
the
hit
title
track,
the
LP
is
neatly divided
into
ballads and
up-
tempo
tunes. “Somebody”
looks
like
a
great
potential
single,
capturing the essence of the
artist every
bit as well as
his classic “Hit The
Road
Jack’’
of 1961.
For
diversity, Ray has a
wonderful
version
of the
old
Everly
Brothers’
hit,
“Problems, Problems” adorning side 2
of
this
LP, complimenting
“Louise,” “Everybody
Sing,”
and
“Where Was
He”
perfectly.
His
vocals
are as
spirited as
ever, and the
entire
effort
is one
of
his
best.
LOUD ’N’ PROUD—Nazareth—A&M SP 3609
In
the
great
tradition
of
powerful
British
bands,
Nazareth
has
come
through
in
fine
fashion
on
this
rock
’n’
roll gem
which
will
have
knowledgeable fans
everywhere
up and
boogie-ing around
their
record
players
before
they know what
hit
them. “Go Down
Fight-
ing”
is
typical
of the band’s
straight forward
approach,
and we
all know that the
shortest
distance
between
two
minds
is
a
thumping
rock
beat
with
solid
vocals
behind
it.
“Not
Faking
It,”
“Child
In The
Sun,”
and
a
great
version of Joni Mitchell’s “This Flight Tonight”
are further proof that this group
is on
its way
to the very top.
SKYLARK 2—Skylark—Capitol ST-11256
The quote from
Kahlil
Gibran on the back
cover
appropriately
sums
up
the
group’s
philosophy when
it says
“.
.
.
but who
shall
command
the
skylark
not
to
sing?”, and
this
LP
provides
further
emphasis
that
Skylark’s
intention
is to

air with
beautiful music.
“Love’s A River Flowing”
is one
of the

est and most capably arranged
ballads we’ve
heard
in
quite
a while and displays the
excel-
lent
inner workings
of
the
artists’
minds
as
they make
difficult harmony
parts sound
ef-
fortless.
“If That’s The Way You Want
It” and
“It’s A Wonder”
are
our
favorites from
this
worthwhile
effort.
SWEET FORTUNE’S DARLING—Hotspur—Col-
umbia KC 32541
Exquisite
harmonies
and
powerful,
driving
rhythms
highlight this attractive debut LP for
the
talented
quartet.
“I
Lost
My
Wings
Ir
Memphis”
is a fabulous rocker with
a
steady,
repeating chorus that gives
it enough strength
to be considered as
a
single. Throughout the
collection,
Hotspur
effectively
makes
use
of
percussion,
in
much
the
same
way
as
the
Stones,
using
accents
to

the
feeling
of the song.
“I Wrote This Song,” “The
Best
I
Can
Do,”
“Countryside
Ride,”
“You
Can’t
Lose (What You Never Had),” and “We Need
A
Captain”
are
all
well
worked
pieces
of
music, showing promise
for the band.

ETHNIC STEW—Tribe—ABC ABCX 807
One
of
the
most

to

this

does
so

“Lovin’ On The Outside”

that’s

for this band
in a big way.

Watch for the LP to take

ABKCO 1st Qtr 
Shows Declines 
NEW YORK - ABKCO Industries, 
Inc. has announced results of its op- 
erations, on an unaudited basis, for 
the first quarter ended Dec. 31, 1973 
with revenues of $2,281,287 and a loss 
of $59,830 or 40 per share. This com- 
pares to revenues of $4,356,190 and 
earnings of $364,097 or 250 per share 
for the corresponding period in 1972. 
Wherehouse Earnings Up 
TORRENCE, CAL. - Integrity En- 
tertainment Corp., with headquarters 
in Torrance, Calif., has reported rec- 
ord sales and earnings for both the 
second quarter and the six months 
ended Dec. 31. Second quarter sales of 
$6,978,273 and profits of $178,676 
compared to the year earlier sales of 
$3,480,244 and a profit of $134,428. 
For the six months sales were $10,- 
995,466 (up 88%) and earnings were 
$266,501 (up 151%) compared to the 
same period for last year of sales and 
earnings of $5,838,490 and $106,144, 
respectively. Earnings per share for 
the six months rose 143% from $.07 to 
$.17 (fully diluted). 
Integrity Entertainment Corp. is 
the owner and operator of "The 
Wherehouse," a chain of 41 discount 
record and tape stores operating ex- 
clusively in California. The company 
announced the planned opening of 
five additional stores by June, 1974, 
bringing the total number of new 
stores opened in the 1974 fiscal year 
to 19.

Art Wayne Dies 
HOLLYWOOD - Singer/composer 
Artie Wayne died in Nassau, The 
Bahamas on Thursday (14) at the 
age of 60. Death was attributed to 
a coronary. 
Wayne's most recent composition/ 
production effort of note was his 
`Moses and the Impossible Ten' re- 
leased by BASF Records. 
Wayne had performed as a singer 
with the Freddie Martin Orchestra, 
and later as a Mercury artist with 
such tunes as "Sleepy Baby," "Black 
Lace" and "Mahzel". 
He leaves his wife Vida Haliburton 
Wayne, one son and one daughter. 
RCA To Market 
London `Gypsy 
NEW YORK - RCA Records will 
release the British original cast album 
of the musical, "Gypsy," starring An- 
gela Lansbury coincidental to the be- 
ginning in 
March of an extended 
North American tour by the company. 
Miss Lansbury took the Jule Styne- 
Stephen Sondheim-Arthur 
Laurents 
musical to London last year in a pro- 
duction sponsored by Barry Brown 
and Fritz Holt, and it became a smash 
hit. RCA recorded the original cast 
album for its Red Seal label and the 
album became one of the hit imports 
of the year in the U.S. 
The tour goes from Toronto to Los 
Angeles to Denver, to Oklahoma City 
to Dallas, to Houston to Chicago to 
St. Louis to Detroit and finally ends 
with a limited New York engagement 
opening 
September 
10 
for 
nine 
weeks. 
Also starring with Miss Lansbury 
are Barrie Ingham and Zan Char- 
isse.

Ms Ivil Named 
Atlantic Pub Dir 
NEW YORK-Jerry Greenberg, Ate 
lantic Records senior vice president 
and general manager, has announced, 
that Ann Ivil has been named direc- 
tor of publicity for the firm. Ms. Ivil 
comes to Atlantic's New York head- 
quarters from London, where she has 
been head of creative services for 
Atlantic, as well as publicity director 
of WEA International. 
In her new post she will be in 
charge of Atlantic's publicity opera -4 
tions throughout the country and will 
also liaison with the firm's interna- 
tional publicity activities. She will 
work closely with Bob Rolontz, vice 
president of public relations and ad- 
vertising. 
Ms. Ivil has been with Atlantic 
London office since it was started last 
fall. Before that she was in charge 
of publicity for the entire WEA In- 
ternational operation in London for, 
the previous two years. She had her 
own publicity firm in London for 
many years, which handled Dr. John, 
Frank Zappa, and others.

L.A. Indictment 
(Cont'd from p. 9) 
Records, 20th Century Records, United 
Artists Records and Warner Bros. 
Records. 
Twenty counts of the indictment, 
charging Taxe with mail fraud, said 
he advertised in national magazines 
that he was selling simulated stereo 
tape recordings when the tapes were 
actually duplicates of the original 
sound recordings. 
The indictment further charged that 
Taxe used the mails to transport the 
illegally duplicated sounds 
on the 
tapes to customers in Lakewood, Colo.; 
New Haven, Conn.; Houston, Tex.; 
St. Louis, Mo.; Freeport, Ill.; Colum- 
bia, S.C., and Spartansburg, Penna. 
The defendant was also charged 
with transporting stolen property in 
interstate commerce. The property al- 
leged to have been stolen are the 
sound recordings which were copy' 
righted by the recording companies. 
Maximum penalty for each of the 
copyright violations is one year in 
prison and a $1,000 fine. 
Maximum 
penalty for the mail 
fraud count is a $1,000 fine and five 
years in prison, and the maximum 
penalty for interstate transportation 
of stolen property is ten years in 
prison and a $10,000 fine on each 
count. 
The indictment is a result of an 
investigation 
by 
the 
U.S. Postal 
Service and the FBI.

ABC Set To Enter 
Concert Promo 
Via 12 Hr. Live 
California Jam. 
ABC Entertainment marks its entry 
into the live concert promotion field 
with a day -long rock concert, featur- 
ing all-star acts, to be held April 6 in 
California's Ontario Motor Speed- 
way, it was announced today by Mar- 
tin Starger, President of ABC Enter- 
tainment. 
"California Jam" is scheduled to 
run from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with 
doors opening at 8 a.m. Concert stars 
are Deep Purple, Black Sabbath, Seals 
& Crofts, Black Oak Arkansas, Ea- 
gles, and Earth Wind & Fire -all 
headliners with recordings 
on the 
charts. Another major co-starring act 
will be announced Feb. 21. 
In making the announcement, Mr. 
Starger stated, "With this 12 -hour 
event ABC Entertainment moves into 
the concert promotion field with an 
attraction we feel will merit signifi- 
cant attention in the realm of contem- 
porary music. It also marks the fur- 
ther expansion of ABC Entertainment 
into the non -broadcasting entertain- 
ment arena." 
Bob Shanks, Vice President, Late 
Night Programs for ABC Entertain- 
ment, who has mounted past concerts 
for the ABC Television Network's "In 
Concert" series, will be in charge of 
"California Jam," and the event will 
be coordinated by Pacific Presenta- 
tions of Los Angeles. 
To facilitate the concert, the On- 
tario City Council has lifted its eve- 
ning curfew on that date. In associa- 
tion with Jim Cook, Executive Vice 
President -General Manager of the 
Ontario Motor Speedway, the Ontario 
City Council and the Ontario Police 
Department, measures have been tak- 
en to assure necessary security and 
sanitation services.

CARNEGIE HALL, NYC-Although 
the billing was not nearly as "Super- 
star" oriented as the recent one that 
featured Bob Dylan and The Band, 
this show stood as one of the most 
eagerly anticipated ones in New York 
in some time. Before the evening was 
over, 5,000 completely satisfied pa- 
trons knew it would be some time be- 
fore another show as intensely enter- 
taining would come to pass. 
Linda Ronstadt opened the evening 
and her set was better than ever. 
Opening with her great "Colorado", 
the lady portrayed the ballad more 
stunningly than in any of her other 
previous performances and set the 
stage for an hour plus of mellow bal- 
lads and high spirited country rock- 
ers, each an absolute delight for the 
overflow crowd. 
During the course of her set, ma- 
terial such as "Love Has No Pride", 
"Silver Threads And Golden Needles", 
"Lovesick Blues", "Desperado", "The 
Fast One" and her still stunning 
"Long, Long Time" was portrayed 
perfectly as Linda again proved that 
she is by far the best female vocalist 
alive today. Her encore, a tune she 
claimed to have learned a few nights 
before, "Heart Like A Wheel", was 
a totally mesmerizing experience that 
generated a sincere, rousing standing 
ovation. Again, it's still a mystery as 
to why more folks have not yet picked 
up on her incredible talents. Her two 
current LP's on Asylum ("Don't Cry 
Now") 
and 
Capitol 
("Different 
Drum") are excellent ways to begin 
a Linda Ronstadt love affair. Speak- 
ing for all of New York City, come 
back soon Linda. We adore you! 
Songwirter extraordinaire Jackson 
Browne continued the splendid eve- 
ning's entertainment with a perfectly 
paced set of his classic folk -country - 
rock material. While Jackson alter- 
nated between guitar and piano, his 
four man back up band perfectly 
complemented his material and great- 
ly helped in making the evening as 
magical as it was. 
Jackson's performances of "Rock 
Me On The Water", "Jamaica Say 
You Will", "Take It Easy", "For 
Everyman", "Doctor My Eyes" and 
his current single release, "Ready Or 
Not" were complete delights and had 
the crowd excited every step of the 
way. That's about when the frenzy 
set in. Jackson, with brilliant accom- 
paniment from David Lindley and 
Lowell George (from Little Feat) on 
guitars, as well as the rest of the 
band, started rocking and rolling. 
Carnegie was literally shaking. "Red- 
neck Friend", his recent single hit 
was the motivator and everything was 
letter perfect. With Jackson wailing 
away on vocals and Lowell on guitar 
(electric slide), the performance was 
as electric (if not more so) than any 
of the best of the best rock and roll 
shows to hit New York. 
Linda then re -appeared with Jack -

Joel Grey 
FAIRMONT HOTEL, SAN FRAN- 
CISCO - There were two major mu- 
sic events being chronicled in all of 
the San Francisco papers while this 
reporter was there. One happened to 
be Bob Zimmerman (alias Dylan) and 
the other Joel Katz (alias Grey). 
Since 
Dylan 
tickets 
were 
being 
scalped for cents which made no 
sense, it was off to the Fairmont Ho- 
tel to catch Columbia Recording art- 
ist Joel Grey. This reporter advanced 
to the lengthy line and cooly waited 
for it to diminish so that he could go 
in. Lines? No one waits in lines any- 
more unless you're buying gas, going 
to see "The Exorcist," or happen to 
be seeing Dylan or Grey. When the 
turn to be admitted finally arose, the 
maitre d ushered this journalist to 
his charitable table, only a nose away 
from the entrance doors. However, as 
it turned out, the back seat at the 
cabaret was really the best, for one 
got a marvelous look at the audience, 
their faithful response to Joel, and of 
Joel's uncanny ability to transfix ev- 
ery corner of the showroom. 
Joel opened with "The More I See 
You," which was followed with his 
favorite country and western parody, 
"Romania," at which a table with a 
couple in their twenties and one with 
the teenagers roared with laughter. 
Next the energetic Grey did a George 
Cohan medley. Now it's time for Joel 
to saunter thru still another medley 
of another small giant in the music 
world, Billy Rose (Grey, statistically 
speaking would have towered him by 
three inches). Again the songs were 
performed with such verve and dedi- 
cation that anyone else doing them 
would only come off as a weak imita- 
tion. The grey Rose tribute included 
"Am I Blue," "Paper Moon," "Back in 
your Own Backyard" and a very 
effective, clever routine to "Me and 
My Shadow." For this number Joel 
danced and his shadow box, actually 
an old vaudeville trunk cavorted along 
with him. The trunk appeared floating 
as it synchronized itself to Joel's own 
fancy facile footwork. 
Next Joel segued into a very mov- 
ing interpretation of "Put a Little 
Love in Your Heart," done with a 
concerto sounding backgrouná. Dur- 
ing just a musical interlude of the 
song, Grey went around and tacitly 
touched members of the audience. 
Joel's silence and his careful pacing 
made it all profoundly moving. He 
saved his celebrated role of the mas- 
ter of ceremonies in "Cabaret," for 
last. Then utilizing a few props from 
that trunk he recreated the character 
he created on stage and also got to 
play in the movie. When Joel got the 
Cabaret song "Money," which was 
one of his last songs, it was most 
ironic to watch the waiters scurry 
once more to collect just that. Appar- 
ently this number was the signal 
amongst the waiters to tell them that 
the show had come to its end. There 
was a standing ovation from all gen- 
erations. His encore number 
was 
"Traveling Man." The house lights 
came on and the cabaret was over at 
least until his late show.

Silverhead 
Fresh Start 
WHISKY 
L.A. - You 
can run 
through the whole gamut of cliche 
adjectives: gutsy, flashy, heavy and 
loud; all of them can be neatly and 
accurately applied to the performance 
of MCA's Silverhead. An England - 
based band, they've been through 
these parts several times before but 
have never sounded tighter, looked 
better or generally pulled their act 
off as well as they did recently at the 
Whisky. 
The group is fronted by singer 
Michael Des Barres, an emaciated 
shouter who comports himself with 
all the grace of a spastic Nureyev. 
Their compositions, almost all of 
which are collectively authored by the 
band, are of the hard-core rock vari- 
ety and range in lyrical content from 
the risque to the downright obscene. 
Such picaresque titles as "More Than 
Your Mouth Can Hold" and "Sixteen 
and Savaged" seem destined for a 
special place in the annals of rock 'n 
roll ethos. 
Although their act carries the re- 
quisite 
overtones 
of 
androgenous 
glitter, Silverhead relies more on a 
traditional 
stance 
of 
street -punk 
defiance. 
As vocalist 
Des Barres 
drooled, shouted and strangled his 
microphone, 
lead guitarist 
Robbie 
Blunt produced an endless series of 
provocative riffs and musical doodles, , 
providing a juxtaposition of remark- 
ably similar elements. And some cred 
it, please, for bassist Nigel Harrison,' 
whose competence was above and be-, 
yond the call of duty. As one might 
expect, the material Silverhead per- 
formed can be found, immortalized in 
vinyl, via an MCA LP titled "Sixteen 
and Savaged." 
Although they've been together for 
only eight months, for opening group, - 
Fresh Start its been time well spent. 
Their sound varies from funky r&b to,,, 
some simple and effective pop ar- 
rangements that are occasionally re- 
miniscent of the Doobie Brothers. The 
band consists of Milo Martin on bass, 
Fred Allen 
on drums, singer Bill 
Pratt and guitarist Paul Frank. Re- 
cently signed to ABC -Dunhill, Fresh... 
Start is presently in the studios and if 
their Whisky engagement is any indi- 
cation, they should have a good shot 
at both the r&b and pop markets.

Cheech (i Chong 
Bachman Turner Overdrive 
ACADEMY OF MUSIC, N.Y.C. - In 
an exhilarating display of comic ver- 
satility, Ode recording artists Cheech 
& Chong, made an exciting return to 
the Big Apple, bringing with them 
several of their most memorable char- 
acters. The talented duo made a dozen 
costume changes and featured several 
selections from their current chart 
LP, 
"Los 
Cochinos," 
including 
Cheech's lip -sync version of the sin- 
gle, "Basketball Jones." Prior to the 
duo 
taking 
the stage, 
promoter 
Howard Stein's crew ran a 
five- 
minute animated cartoon based on the 
song, which is about a ghetto kid who 
grows up eating and sleeping basket- 
ball and winds up a star of the game. 
With professional rapidity, Cheech 
& Chong produced "Laid -Back Len- 
ny," everbody's favorite underground, 
west coast FM disk jockey, "Blind 
Lemon Chitlin," "Sister Mary Ele- 
phant," and "Sergeant Studenko," all 
of whom have become well known 
characters through the duo's satiric 
portrayal of .their roles in contem- 
porary society. Tommy Chong and 
Cheech Marin have enjoyed excep- 
tional popularity among a generation 
familiar with marijuana and other 
drugs, and while poking fun at the 
drug sub -culture, made some salient 
points about pushers, police, and drug 
users. 
One skit featured Cheech as a push- 
er and Chong as a supposedly hip 
undercover cop. In his role as the 
law, Tommy garbled such commonly 
used phrases as reefer and upper, 
substituting `roofer' and `speeder' in 
their places, much to the delight of 
the boisterous crowd, who yelled out 
their favorites to the stage as the 
pair went through the fast-moving 
stage act. In the skit, Chong is set to 
arrest Marin when the latter grabs 
his gun, and in a turn of events, 
brings the officer to his knees. It is 
obvious that Cheech & Chong rep- 
resent more than a recording or even 
concert act. Relentlessly poking fun 
at outdated morality and laws, the 
pair has become a symbol of freedom 
for the current generation, a fact 
made plain as day by the packed 
house's demand for a double encore, 
one the artists were happy to satisfy. 
The popular Mercury recording ar- 
tists, 
Bachman -Turner 
Overdrive 
opened the show with a 
raucous 
rock'n'roll set, which included high - 
r, 
lights from their two currently suc- 
cessful chart LP's, both named after - 
the group (numbered I and II). The 
quartet rocked through their previous 
hit, "Hold Back The Water" and 
treated everyone to a stunning ver- , 
sion of their current single, "Let It 
Ride," which is rapidly moving up the 
charts. Tight harmonies and well bal- 
anced (if slightly loud) instrumenta- 
tion keyed the set, which featured two' 
interesting 
change 
of pace jazz - 
flavored tunes that set up the group's', 
encore, "American Woman" (written 
by Randy Bachman) perfectly.

plified 
distortion to 
simulate the

A WORTHY CAUSE-Queen of The Most Holy Rosary, located in Roosevelt 
LI., is operating an integrated school for youngsters through the eighth grade. 
The school is faced with a financial crisis. It is a small private school with 
small resources. But, the school does serve a particular need in its community. 
Donations, which are tax deductible, may be mailed to: QMHR, P. O. Box 344, 
Roosevelt, N.Y. 11575. A receipt will be returned. Additional information may 
be obtained by calling Mrs. Caroly Bantum (516) 378-1482 or Betty Bell (516) 
378-1649. Anything you can do to help these kids in their school will be ap- 
preciated. A concert is going to be held in the school auditorium the week-end 
of March 23 ... Some late NATRA news to pass along ... New Contract net- 
gotiations are about to begin at WVON and WBLS. 
NASHBORO & ABC DUNHILL TERMINATE NEGOTIATIONS: Negotiations be-, 
tween ABC Dunhill & the Nashboro based Nashboro Music complex have been 
terminated. Rumors, of the ABC acquisition of the complex which includes 2 
recording studios, 7 labels, 3 publishing co.'s and Ernies Record Mart, have 
been circulating throughout the industry for several weeks. However, R. E. 
Baulch, Jr. of the Crescent Co., the parent Company of Nashboro, said that 
all negotiations with ABC have been terminated and the complex will continue 
to operate as an independent enterprise.

PASSING REMARKS-First things first, the answer to last weeks photo quiz #1, 
"Rock And Roll: The Way We Were," is The Shangri-Las, those three New York 
City ladies who almost succeeded in taking the early '60's all by themselves. 
Some of their hits? "Remember (Walking In The Sand)," "Leader Of The Pack," 
"Give Him A Great Big Kiss," "He Cried" and "Dressed In Black" are just a few. 
This week's photo may be just a bit tougher. The mystery artist in question is not 
(obviously) Paul McCartney at the keyboard, it's the lady at his right, a '60's 
British songstress, best known for her ballads. Answer to appear here next 
week... 
It's going to be a "live"-ly month of April. Albums recorded in concert are 
expected from Loggins And Messina, New Riders Of The Purple Sage and Liza 
Minnelli (At The Winter Garden, N.Y.C.) ... John McLaughlin former leader of the 
now departed Mahavishnu Orchestra, has left the U.S. to record in London with 
Michael Tilson-Thomas. The pair will collaborate on an album to be recorded with 
the London Symphony Orchestra, due much later this year ... That "California 
Jam" scheduled for April 6 at the Ontario Motor Speedway in Southern California, 
is really getting into high gear, talent wise. The latest acts promised for the event 
are Emerson, Lake and Palmer and Deep Purple. Others previously announced 
include Black Sabbath, Seals & Crofts, Eagles, Black Oak Arkansas and Earth, 
Wind & Fire . .. Air London Studios is very busy these days. Among those folks in 
for sessions of late have been Jethro Tull, Procol Harum and Mott The Hoople. All 
are striving for new album releases sometime during late Spring ... The Rolling 
Stones have, for the moment, scrapped their "live" album in favor of a studio 
album, due mid -April. The "live" collection, says Mick Jagger, will be released 
towards the end of the year ... 
Gary Glitter, British superstar, will be making his first U.S. promotional tour, 
but without performing. That comes later, says Gary and his managers ... New 
LP's on the way from Alvin Lee & Ten Years After, West, Bruce & Laing (their last 
together), Three Dog Night, Cat Stevens ("Buddha and The Chocolate Box") and 
Chicago . 
. 
. Reports have it that Russ Ballard will be leaving Argent after their 
forthcoming U.S. tour 
. 
. 
. The new single from Love Unlimited, Barry White's 
yet -to -be -realized -super -soul -group, "Under The Influence Of Love" (with backing 
from the great Love Unlimited Orchestra) is their best yet. With proper exposure, 
it should be a #1 disk on both pop and soul charts ... The Bee Gees, recently 
here in New York, again wowed the city with a complete set of performances, 
including all of their great hits and a full orchestra to boot. Following one of 
those performances, Maurice Gibb and Dave Mason were spotted together in 
a

Getting back to those Beatles' reunion rumors (which continue to get stronger 
every day), word has it that Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr have already inked 
their pacts for a U.S. tour with John Lennon and George Harrison about to do the 
same. A scalper was recently seen drooling as he passed Madison Square Garden 
all the way from 31st Street to 33rd ... Blue Oyster Cult has finished recording 
their "Secret Treaties" LP. They have abandoned plans to dedicate the disk to 
Helen Reddy . 
. 
. The Climax Blues Band, on their forthcoming LP will have a 
track included entitled "The Nogales Tune" based on a rather wretched true 
experience. Seems when the group was in Nogales, Mexico vacationing, they were 
approached on the street by a group of seedy citizens in shiny suits, all packing 
shotguns who turned out to be Mexican police. For some unexplained reason, the 
band was carted off to one of those legendary Mexican jails where they spent the 
night with murderers, rapists, wife beaters, rats and those New York City 
favorites, roaches. Tony Brinsley the group's road manager was unsuccessful in 
learning what the charges were all about so he did the logical thing-raised all 
the cash he could, paid the locals a ton of green, got his band out of the can and 
got them on the run. Rumors that the band is planning a Mexican tour are 
completely untrue ... "Another Park, Another Sunday" should be the next single 
for the Dobbie Brothers. It's from their great new album, "What Were Once Vices 
Are Now Habits" ... Whats this we hear that a 1960's revival is being readied 
here in New York City with the Lovin' Spoonful and the Young Rascals as 
headliners? ... Also, speaking of revivals, check out the new single on Motown, 
from the Four Seasons, entitled "Hickory." It definitely brings about fond mem- 
ories of the Seasons in their prime, yet captures a certain contemporary feel of 
pop in the '70's . 
. 
. Finally, 
I know I've said it on these pages time and time 
again, but the Linda Ronstadt-Jackson Browne show at Carnegie Hall was by far 
the best concert in the New York City area in years. Thanks again to two great 
performers, two of the best in the whole world today ... 
arty goodman 
HOLLYWOOD-RAY MANZAREK: TRIUMPH OF THE COSMIC DITTY 
The Doors sold a lot of records. Even more than that, they epitomized a whole 
sub -culture, a freak population composed of kids in college, kids on the street 
and kids still too young to have decided just how they were going to kill the next 
few years. It was a spacey sound with an unavoidable, if extremely ambiguous 
message. "We want the world and we want it now." Very sixties stuff. A fiercely 
determined vagueness. But the thing that drove it home, that made the Doors 
one of the first really big acid -rock bands (or whatever you want to call it) was 
that they sounded good on A.M. radio. They were great singles artists. 
In the limelight was a fellow decked out in ominous black leather, a former film 
student whose inclinations towards poetry and exhibitionism led him to sing in a 
rock n roll band. He sang, he shouted, and imperiously, he proclaimed an 
intensely personal vision. From beside him, there oozed the group's instrumental 
trademark, the eerie, medieval wail of a Hammond organ. 
A few years back, the Doors completed their Elektra contract, having delivered 
eight gold albums in just five years, a record matched by only a very few of the 
supergroups. Jim Morrison went off to Paris on a vacation from which he was 
never to return. "We'd been together for almost seven years," former Doors 
keyboardist Ray Manzarek recounted. "And basically, Jim just wanted to disap- 
pear for six months or so." Ray and the other members of the band remained in 
L.A., working out songs and deciding on future plans. 
"We were never very happy with the whole "Lizard King" image," said Ray. 
"That wasn't Jim Morrison to me. Jim Morrison was a poet, first and foremost-a 
poet and a good lead singer, too. The lizard king thing was kind of a drag, but we 
could have lived with it if that was what people wanted to make it into. When he 
died, it came as such a shock that it was impossible to think of breaking up." So 
the Doors remained together for a couple of years and a couple of albums. But 
without Morrison's imposing presence, it was never really the same group. 
What happened to the Doors has happened to countless bands composed of 
several strong personalities. "Everybody started writing songs and each of us had 
enough material for an entire album. When it got around to doing our third LP 
without Jim, 
I had had enough. 
I thought, hell, 
I want to do my songs, my way. 
What 
I hear in my ear is what 
I want to put down on a disc. 
I want to hear it 
played back just the way 
I originally conceived it-that's what its all about for 
me." Ray Manzarek returned to Los Angeles and with former Doors producer 
Bruce Botnick, he began work on his first solo album. 
"After the split, it was as if I had opened the valves somewhere-songs started 
pouring out. 
I had seven years worth of material back there, seven years of 
Ray Manzarek 
bottled up experience that I had never expressed. I would sit down to write lyrics 
and it was as if someone else was writing them. It was sheer inspiration." 
The LP, recorded a few months ago, is a strongly conceptualized work, titled 
"The Golden Scarob." " 
I didn't really intend the album to tell a story," insisted 
Ray, "but I got involved in juggling the songs around, trying to decide in what 
order they should be placed. Then, as I was looking at the lyrics, I said 'Hey, wait 
a minute!' It was starting to take shape as a story." There are eight songs on the 
album, weaving together to recount what Ray describes as a "psychic journey," a 
story of a man searching for some meaning to his existence. "The guy goes 
through a journey through the cosmos, a trip through hell. He explores ancient 
Egypt and at one point worships idols he knows to be false. Finally, at the end of 
the story, he comes to the realization that its not left or right, not north or south. 
There's a level of consciousness above and beyond all choices. In the last song, 
he comes back into contact with a reality that he already understood, but one 
that he's seeing through new eyes, eyes that have been through heaven and 
hell." 
Despite the intensity and importance of the story line, the LP also works as 
eight individual bands of music, a factor that can be partially attributed to the 
musicians Ray gathered for the recording sessions. "I wanted a jazzy feel; for 
guitars, I used Larry Carlton who impressed me with his work on the Crusaders' 
LP. Then there's Jerry Scheff, Elvis Presley's bass player. On drums there's Tony 
Williams, from Lifetime and Miles Davis' group and there's also three other 
percussionists: Miuto, Steve Forman and Milt Holland. I play the keyboards." 
The LP will be released on the Mercury label within the next few weeks. "A lot 
of other record companies didn't accept it," said Ray. "They said 'I don't 
understand it, its too far out, too weird.' It was exactly what happened to me 
seven years ago, when 
I walked the streets with the Doors first album. Mercury 
listened to it and told me they loved it. That was all I needed to hear." 
While soul searching and psychic wayfaring does not necessarily a hit record 
make, Ray has hopes that his album contains enough purely lyrical cuts to 
suffice the A.M. radio needs. "Its weird," he said, "but with the Doors, it was as 
if our worst songs, or our lesser songs anyway, became our greatest hits. Songs 
like "Hello I Love You" or "Love Her Madly" were absolute nothings, ditties. But 
that's what they want for the radio, so 
I guess we'll have to find the ditty on the 
album." 
eliot sekuler

R LI B INGREDIENTS-One of the biggest problems for acts who 
are trying to get their thing together is hooking themselves up with the proper 
management. Management, when involved in the development and training of 
the act, bears the financial load. And, if the act is composed of a large group, 
the money and time involved becomes almost impossible to measure. The 
road to success is filled with heartaches and tears. The dedication and deter- 
mination to come out on top has to override all. It's only when all these facts 
are put into proper perspective, (assuming that the talent is there), can one 
begin to appreciate the sacrifices. It's an exception, rather than the rule, when 
an act does seem to streak to recognition overnite. Usually, it takes years of 
relentless work, in other words, the 'dues' are paid somewhere along the line. 
A case at hand is the group, New Day the vocal team consists of: June Riley, 
Maxine Fitzgerald and Candice Rae (who recently replaced Delores Brooks). 
(Changes do happen). But the consistency of the group has been maintained 
for some five years. This is largely because of the dedicated responsibility of 
The New Day Management, Minnie and Luella McClendon. The group also has 
it's backup band of six pieces. The total is a show in one package. They have 
been working the chitlin circuit and staying in the least expensive hotels. But, 
it is the care and guidance provided by management that holds it together 
and the group is now beginning to emerge onto the broad music scene. The 
New Day was one of the headliners at the United Negro College Fund dinner 
recently held at the NYC Waldorf in the grand ballroom. They supplied dance 
music and a together show. Keyboard artist Jimmy McGriff was the other 
headliner. The packed ballroom was groovin'. NYC Mayor Abe Beame opened 
the event with an address to the audience 
. 
.

with Sparkie Martin presented Blue Magic, March 7-10, at Smalls in Harlem. 
This is an ideal club for acts. The New Day goes into Smalls March 21-24. 
Smalls could indeed again be a hub for black talent because of the lack of 
suitable locations in NYC for the presentation of new or established enter- 
tainment. Check it out ... Alix DeJean, an excellent photographer, works the 
NYC scene. Alix may be reached at (212) 243-6737 . .. Ecstasy, Passion And

R f3 B INGREDIENTS-communicating, in the final analysis, is the 
name of the game. A record promotion man/woman is in truth applying 
communications expertise. When a product is properly promoted (to give it 
all possible exposure) the success of the product is still determined by the 
consumer. Of course, when the promo people are given a record that is right 
from the gitgo (This includes first the material (the song), an artist's honest 
interpretation and the production) then the promo job is somewhat easier. 
It should be increasingly clear to record companys as well as producer or 
artist/producer that it is almost impossible today to sell product that is not for 
real. The fault generally begins in the recording studio. An act may come into 
the studio feeling it can be another Stevie Wonder. When, in truth, the act 
should reveal what it is about. Then, if the talent is really there the stature of 
a Stevie Wonder may be achieved by doing 'your own thing.' Getting back to 
promotion. R & B (referring to it as root music) has grown by leaps and bounds 
in the past couple of years. And, it's only the beginning. Gus Redmond, na- 
tional promotion manager for the General Recording Corp., based in Atlanta, 
has been a standout in establishing the label (Aware) and artists (Ripple) as 
a solid R & B entity, He, along with his team such as Greta Hunter, understand- 
ing what it's all about, can stand proud. Bernie Block has a total understanding 
of his Baltimore/Washington markets. A veteran who stays with the trends 
and now happenings. Bernie is responsible for starting many records that 
have achieved national success. Bernie is now working the new single, "Come 
Down To Earth" by The New Censation on Pride (now distributed by United Art- 
ists). Those into the R & B field are well aware of what Jose Wilson has accom- 
plished at 20th Century Records ... Yours truly (Don Drossell), Curtis Jones 
in record retail (Bklyn) and Marty Mack (RCA) chaired a F.O.R.E. Seminar per- 
taining to the interrelationship between trade charts, radio stations, retailer, 
and, of course, record companies. The well attended session was highly re- 
sponsive and fired out the questions. This is the basic reason for seminars 
(to communicate and exchange views). The seminar was held March 13, and 
it was thoroughly enjoyed by me and 
I hope it was informative for those of 
you in attendance. Aki Aleong (involved with a pigeonnaper demanding ran- 
som) helped to chair the seminar. Aki has made front page in the New York 
Daily News two days running. Some culprits got 28 of Aki's prize pigeons the 
past weekend. The first pigeon returned had a note attached demanding $15. 
A second pigeon released demanded $50. 10 pigeons have been released but 
19 are still missing. Good luck Aki! The record business can often be for the 
pigeons ...

Dirt Band Helps 
Raise $35G For 
Prison Reform 
NEW YORK - The Nitty Gritty Dirt 
Band, a country -rock band, did pro- 
motion for special benefit concert in 
which they performed with John Den- 
ver, Steve Goodman and Oliver at 
Notre Dame University, South Bend, 
Indiana. 
Dirt Band members, John McEuen, 
Jeff Hanna, Jim Ibbotson and Jim 
Fadden, manned the phones to drum 
up press and radio support for and 
coverage of the story of the National 
Coordinating Committee for Justice 
Under Law, an organization formed 
several years ago to formulate new 
approaches to the rehabilitation of 
minor law breakers and offendors. 
Coordinating Committee chairman 
and founder, George Mische, took out 
more than $35,000 for the cause. The 
sellout house was just under 11,000 
persons who paid in a total gross of 
$45,000. Mische, who was convicted in 
the Cantonsville draft records case, 
served 25 months in Federal prison. 
In an interview just after the concert, 
John McEuen, of the Dirt Band, ex- 
plaining that all members of the band 
endorse the program of the organiza- 
tion which seeks another answer than 
incarceration for all but the most 
serious crimes. The approach would 
be to achieve economic and social re- 
habilitation through actual job train- 
ing rather than imprisonment.

Kool & The Gang Gathering Awards 
ALL THAT'S JAZZ 
A KOOL AWARD-In the first "Soul Poll" conducted by Los Angeles radio 
station KGFJ, the listeners voted Kool & The Gang the Top Instrumental 
Group. From every indication, 1974 will bring many more awards to the 
popular band. Their current single, "Jungle Boogie", recently qualified as a 
gold record and their "Wild And Peaceful" album on De -Lite Records is selling 
very well. 
Seen above (left to right): Red Schwartz, West Coast promotion for De -Lite 
Records; Ronald Bell of Kool & The Gang; Ronald Bynum, program director 
of KGFJ; Robert "Kool" Bell and "D.T." Thomas of Kool & The Gang; and 
Fred Fioto, president of De -Lite Records.

completed producing Charles Bevel

Buddy Rich Opens 'Buddy's Place' 
NEW YORK - Buddy Rich, who 
says "I just play my drums," hopes 
that the jazz world will beat a path to 
his own night club door for the first 
time in his career, when he opens 
"Buddy's Place" on Wednesday even- 
ing, April 10th, at 64th Street & Sec- 
ond Avenue 
(above popular steak 
house, Sam's). 
"Buddy's Place" will seat 200 corn- 
fortably. There will be a light menu 
and liquid refreshments. It will be 
reasonably priced and aimed at that 
great cross-section of jazz enthusi- 
asts. Buddy plans to do two shows a 
night (except Sundays) with time out 
for touring. 
NOTE: There will be a gala press 
opening on Tuesday, April 9th from 6 
to 9 PM.

---- p45
cashbox I album reviews 
TRESPASS-Genesis-ABC ABCX-816 
The powerful collective creative energies of 
Genesis are abundantly evident on this ABC 
release of early material recorded before the 
group had 
its current 
large following. The 
unique blend of provocative lyrics, abandoned 
tempo changes, and masterful arrangement is 
obvious even on this LP, one that features 
"Looking For Someone", "The Knife", "Visions 
of Angels", and "Stagnation". With each cut, 
you become more aware of Genesis' progres- 
sive intent and the consummate ability of the 
band to reach individual musical goals within a 
carefully thought out framework. Brilliant gui- 
tar solos and harmonies complimented by a 
variety of accents makes the 
magic work 
here. 
RAGS 
TO RUFUS-Rufus 
Featuring Chaka 
Khan-ABC ABCX 809 
One of the world's funkiest bands explodes 
again on its new ABC album, one that features 
a wide range of material highlighted by "You 
Got The Love", "Walkin' In The Sun", "Ain't 
Nothin But a Maybe", "Swing Down Chariot", 
and the fabulous title track. Throughout the 
entire collection, Chaka Khan's 
lead vocals 
sparkle with fiery effervescence. Dennis Bel - 
field, Andre Fischer, Kevin Murphy, Al Ciner, 
and Ron Stockert provide a great musical and 
vocal backdrop for Chaka's marvelous voice 
and the group puts each song across with the 
poise of the seasoned professionals they are. 
PAST PRESENT AND FUTURE-AI Stewart- 
Janus JLS 3063 
It's always a treat to hear a performer who 
knows his way around the studio and new- 
comer Al Stewart shows a remarkable amount 
of poise and capability on his solo debut LP for 
Janus. Highlighted 
by "Old Admirals" and 
"Warren Harding", the package sparkles with a 
variety of sounds and textures that are ines- 
capably catchy. Al's versatility as a writer, and 
especially as an incisive lyricist, is readily evi- 
dent on "Post World War Two Blues" and 
"Soho (needless to say)". "Nostradamus" and 
"Roads To Moscow" are epic pieces in which 
Stewart uses his fine talent to convey his 
message, one that makes sense and should 
attract the knowledgeable listener. 
THE ROCKY HORROR SHOW-Original London 
Cast-UK UKAL 1006 
Michael White's presentation of The Theatre 
Upstairs' 
production of "The 
Rocky Horror 
Show" is definitely one of the more bizarre 
collections of musical humor we've heard this 
year, but it's also one of the funniest. "Science 
Fiction -Double Theatre", "Damn 
It, Janet", 
"Touch -A -Touch -A -Touch -A -Touch -A -Touch", 
and "Superheroes" are zany sketches featuring 
a variety of characters clowning it up in a way 
very reminiscent of the Firesign Theatre at its 
best. Particularly funny are "Over At The Frank- 
enstein Place", "Time Warp", and "Hot Patootie 
(Bless My Soul)". Crazy and weird, this LP 
might make it big. 
LANE CHANGER-Michael Fennelly-Epic KE 
32703 
Rockin' Mike has himself quite a package of 
dynamite in his debut solor LP, on which he 
has the able assistance of Rod Argent on 
"Touch My Soul", "Won't 
You 
Please 
Do 
That", and "Dark Night". His (Mike's) ability 
to translate images into music word pictures is 
one of the major strengths of this package 
which bubbles with the effusive joy of creative 
consciousness. "Over My Dead Body", "Watch 
Yerself", and "Bad Times" are further insights 
into the artist's capabilities as he weaves a 
musical spell that dominates the effort from 
the outset. 
SITTING ON TOP OF MY WORLD-Rita Jean 
Bodine -20th Century T-431 
Rita's debut solo album on 20th is as good 
a first effort as we've heard from 
a female 
performer this year. 
Gutsy vocals 
key this 
package and Rita's writing is excellent. She's 
particularly effective when she reaches back 
for a note and belts it out holding it long and 
strong as she does so well on "Pacified". Her 
writing talents are further underscored by 
"Wheels", "Knickerbocker Holiday", "Frying 
Pan Song", "I Was Mistaken", and "Do You 
Think of Her". It's very evident from listening 
to her tour de force that this young lady has a 
lot going for her, not least of which is her 
composing potential. 
POP PICKS 
SCRATCHTHECRUSADERS 
NEWCOMER PICKS 
SCRATCH-The Crusaders-Blue Thumb BTS 
6010 
Another outrageously good Crusaders 
LP, 
this time recorded live at the Roxy in L.A. Each 
effort this veteran group undertakes comes out 
with all the earmarks of twenty years of profes- 
sionalism. The title track is in the funky vein 
that the band established a long while back 
and "Hard Times", "So Far Away", "Way Back 
Home", and Eleanor Rigby all bear the unmis- 
takeable Crusader stamp. These gentlemen, 
who have distinguished so many hit LP's by 
playing on them are; Wayne 
Henderson on 
trombone, Wilton Felder on tenor sax, Stix 
Hooper on drums, and the immortal Joe Sam- 
ple on keyboards. 
CRYSTAL SILENCE-Gary Burton, Chick Corea 
-ECM 1024 ST 
Anytime two progressive giants such as Gary 
Burton and Chick Corea get together you know 
you're in for an earful of eyeopening music 
and this LP justifies that assumption 100%. 
"Senor 
Mouse", "Children's Song", 
"What 
Game Shall We Play Today", "I'm Your Pal", 
"Feelings and Things", and the amazing title 
track are adventures 
in rampant emotional 
sensuality, touching 
on a thousand verbally 
inexpressable moods and textures without 
once breaking musical continuity. As usual, 
arrangements and dynamics figure crucially in 
the success of this package. Chick has been 
featured on three LP's in three months and 
when you hear this one you'll know why. 
KANSAS-Kansas-Kirshner KZ 32817 
One of the year's biggest bands may very 
well prove to be Kansas, if we can judge by the 
high velocity musical energy on the sextet's 
debut LP for the new Kirshner label. Power is 
the main ingredient in this package, highlight- 
ed by "Can 
I Tell You", "Bringing It Back", 
"Journey From Mariabronn", "Death of Mother 
Nature Suite", and "Lonely Wind". Stunning 
instrumentation and immaculate lead vocals 
and harmonies make the variety of original 
material a treat to listen to. The Mid -West has 
produced some high quality groups recently, 
but Kansas may top them all-soon. 
FEELING-Mentor Williams-MCA-MCA 404 
Mentor Williams has been around for quite a 
while, and though known primarily as Doby 
Gray's producer/manager, his MCA debut LP 
proves conclusively that he has the knack for 
performance to 
compliment 
his 
business 
acumen. Many of his primary influences are 
visible (and audible) on this collection, high- 
lighted by his collaborations with Troy Seals, 
Ron Davies, and Tom Jans. "Sunday Driver" is 
a 
beautiful little country rocker and "One 
Night Stand" 
is 
an autobiographical ballad 
with some beautiful pedal steel accents. Men- 
tor and Seals produced the LP and the duo's 
touch distinguishes the entire repertoire. 
HOLLYWOOD TOWN-Harriet Schock -20TH 
Century T-437 
When a label not only finds a talented new 
singer/composer but also one with 
a 
birth 
name which lends itself to promotional cam- 
paigns, they've found everything. Schock is 
chock full of single possibilities and tunes 
which will be covered by others. She's the 
counterpart writer to Jimmy Webb and one 
realizes this on "Hold Me," "That's The Way It 
Is With You," the title track, and the strongest 
"You Took The Words 
Out of My Mouth." 
Schock treatment is sure to cure all playlists. 
FOR THE HIGHEST-Aim-Blue Thumb BTS 64 
Soulful spirit and vivacious musical person- 
ality best sum up the first effort by Aim. A 
diverse collection of songs ranging from the 
punchy title track to the jazz laden "You Need 
Me", the album reflects a keen sense of dyna- 
mics to match the captivating original materi- 
al. "Seattle" is a barrel house rocker featuring 
the interesting lead vocals of Mike Overly, a 
very 
capable 
stylist 
whose 
performance 
throughout the LP is highly professional, com- 
plimenting Pat O'Connor's bass work, Warren 
Pemberton on drums, and Loren Newkirk on 
Keyboards. A good, solid first LP.

‘Black American’
From Jewel Label
SHREVEPORT — Stan Lewis,
presi-
dent of Jewel Record Corporation an-
nounced the rush release of a record-
ing by Don Evans entitled “The Black
American”. Lewis stated “The record-
ing
is
a masterpiece
of black
litera-
ture
telling
the
story
of
the
black
man as
it has never been told before.”
The
story
was
written
by
a
Ft.
Worth,
Texas
lady,
Adelle
Jackson
Martin. Her husband,
Otis
J.
Martin,
well known
Ft. Worth
business man
auditioned
several
voices
in
reading
“The
Black
American”.
They
both
agreed
that
the
voice
of Don Evans
was the one that did the work justice.
Otis, who had never been
inside
a
recording
studio
before, recorded
the
basic parts of the selection.
The
recording came
to
Jewel’s
at-
tention through
a
local
gospel group
in
Dallas,
Texas. A member
of
that
group casually mentioned
it to a vice-
president of Jewel. Lewis immediately
sent a representative to Ft. Worth, at
which
time
the
masterpiece was
ac-
quired.
Lewis, who had been produc-
ing many of the Jewel acts, went into
the
studio
again
to
personally
finish
the product.

SPOKANE — Sammy Davis has
ac-

of
Expo
’74 World’s Fair Afro-American Heri-
tage
Day

A

Fair history within the United States,
the introduction of the Afro-American
Pavilion marks the
initial time an ex-
hibition has been created
to trace the
history,
culture
and

to
the
environment
by
Afro-Americans
from the year 1400 through 1974. En-
dorsed by the Governor
of Washing-
ton and

$200,000
for
its
de-
velopment
by
the
State
Legislature,
the Afro-American Pavilion
will seek
to
raise another
$100,000
as a
result
of
the
benefit gala which may
itself
result in
still another “first” in terms
of
the
largest

of
Afro-
American entertainers to ever appear

Michael Kobluk, Director

’74,

that

by Sammy Davis to serve as co-chair-

Day Festival has already been echoed
by

host
of

from

the

ex-
pressed their desires
to participate in
the
benefit
gala. A

of

names appearing on June
14 and
15
will
be

shortly,

to Kobluk.

she

py to announce that our new Mayor,

year
of

for

New-
port Jazz Festival in New York City.
After two years we now know what
we can and cannot do.”

of
America’s

basic

I, has been expanding

its course

secutive classes with

Atkins Donates
Travis Guitar
NASHVILLE — A handmade
guitar
designed
and
played
by
guitarist-
songwriter Merle Travis was donated to
the
Country
Music
Hall
of Fame and
Museum. Chet Atkins, guitarist and RCA
executive,
and
Cecil
Null,
songwriter
and president of Old Masters Records,
donated the instrument on T ravis' behalf.
Atkins noted that "the guitar includes
many features which later became stan-
dard on electric guitars. The strings are
attached
through
the body
from
the
guitar's back and the turning gears are all
on one side of the peghead.
It is obvious
from a glance at the guitar that
it inspired
the Fender line.
"
The
guitar — the
first solid-body
in-
strument
actually used
in
professional
performance — was designed by Merle
Travis
in the
late 1940's, and was hand
built by Paul Bigsby in 1948. Atkins add-
ed that "the guitar
still sounds good.
It
has a pickup designed and hand-wired
by Bigsby, and
it has a particularly
full
and rounded tone even
in the
highest
register of the instrument.
"
Diane Johnson — curator of the Hall of
Fame and Museum — accepted
the
donation
of the
rare
instrument.

Runstein Book
NEW YORK — Robert E. Runstein,
for-
mer chief engineer and technical direc-
tor of Intermedia Sound of Boston, and
currently a&r director of North Country
Productions, Ltd. announced publication
of
his book "Modern
Recording
Techniques" by Howard W. Sams and
Co.. Inc.
He has focused on equipment,
con-
trols, and techniques used in the modern
multitrack studio
with descriptions and
explanations designed for producers and
artists as well as engineers. The text
is
intended
for individual study as well as
tor
use
in
classrooms and
engineer
training programs. Among the topics in-
cluded are the recording
chain, sound
and hearing, microphones, and magnetic
tape recording.
The book is available tor $9.95 at elec-
tronic parts distributors and bookstores
that stock Sams publications, or directly
from the publisher in Indianapolis.

Arnold To Brass Ear
BELLEVUE, VMSH. — The promotion of
David
H.
Arnold
to
vice
president
in
charge of operations
at the Brass
Ear,
Inc. was announced by Robert W. Ebert,
president.
Arnold
joined
the company
in
Aug.,
1971 as a buyer and was later promoted
to field operations manager.
The Brass Ear is a chain of retail stores
selling records, tapes and stereo equip-
ment
with
locations
in
Tacoma,
Bel-
levue. and Spokane Washington, Idaho
Falls, Idaho, Hays, Kansas, North Platte,
,l
Nebraska,
and
Marrysville,
California.
The firm’s Home Office is located here in
Bellevue, Washington.
In
his new
responsibility,
Arnold
is
charged
with
overseeing
the
chains
day-to-day operation
with an emphasis
on purchasing and
advertising. He
will
be representing the firm
at the NARM
convention in Hollywood, Florida.

also gives us an opportunity to present

The high-density 12-inch Disco-Vision
disc
is the audio-visual equivalent of an
LP record.
It revolves at 30 revolutions
per second
and
its
microgrooves
are
scanned by a low-power
laser beam —
rather than a needle — to
relay sound
and pictures from the disc to the screen
of any standard TV set. Disco-Vision will
enable viewers
to see the subjects
of
their choice on home TV screens when
the
system's
relatively
inexpensive
player or player/changer unit is attached
to the VHF input terminals of any stan-
dard television receiver, tuned to a chan-
nel not used for regular programming.

Taylor:
CBS/Records Sales
Up 22% In 1 st Qtr
ATLANTA —
In achieving
it’s best
first
quarter
in
history
the CBS
Records
Group
increased
sales 22%
over
last
year, according to CBS president Arthur
Taylor.
Taylor,
addressing
a
stockholders
meeting
here
last week,
said
that
"Measures taken to halt the deterioration
of
profit margin
have
started
to show
positive results." The recording division,
he
said,
faces “severe
cost
pressures,
particularly
in
the
area
of
recording
talent, and
(vinyl)
is
still
in short supply
(but) long-term contracts are helping to
assure the vinyl supplies we require, and
careful
planning
has helped
to
control
cost increases ..."
CBS
Records
International,
Taylor
said,
continues
to
be
"One
of our
fastest-growing divisions. Though
it ex-
perienced
first
quarter
softness
in
France and Germany, sales were strong
in Latin America, Canada, Australia and,
surprisingly, Great Britain. We cannot be
certain what impact current fluctuations,
inflation and
political
instability around
the world
will have on the
rest of the
year, but the indication
is that the great
popular acceptance
of
our
roster
of
American
and
foreign
artists
should
enable us to perform well
in almost any
climate.”
Taylor also said that the Retail Stores
division,
with
Pacific
Stereo
and
Discount Records
operating
under
a
common management,
saw
'"im-
provement" from Discount, while Pacific
Stereo
"has rebounded
from
slower
sales growth in Feb., and in Mar. ran well
ahead of last year's record pace."

At Warner/Reprise
BURBANK — Michael Olivieri has been
made a general manager
for the War-
ner/Reprise family of labels as of today,
it was announced
in
Burbank by Don
Schmitzerle, executive director of label
management forthe company.
As a general manager, Michael will be
the prime contact within the company for
specific artists and their representatives,
and will be responsible forthe execution
and
inception of
all campaigns and
ef-
forts by the company as a whole. He will
also open up channels of communication
between the
artist,
his
representatives
and the individual areas within Warners.
“Basically," commented
Schmitzerle,
"he'll be the man with the answers.”
Additionally Olivieri will aid and advise
in the acquisition of talent for the War-
ners
label,
and
along
with
general
manager
David
Herscher,
will
report
directly to Schmitzerle.
Before moving to Burbank to assume
his new position, Mike was involved for
the
last four years
in various areas
of
promotion for Warners in his native New
York. Prior to that, he was promotion man
for Empire State Distributors.

6th Solo LP
NEW YORK — "Sweet Exorcist," Curtis
Mayfield's sixth solo album on the Cur-
tom lable,
is being released by The Bud-
dah Group this month. Mayfield who has
three gold albums, “Curtis,” "Super Fly”
and "Back To The World," denied the LP
title is connected with the film.
In talking about the tone of his album,
as well as this song, Curtis added, "There
is also a timely element
in
it, of people
generally
feeling
depressed,
going
through
hard
changes
and down
feelings.” Among
the
songs on
the
album
is
"To Be
Invisible," from Curtis,
"Claudine" soundtrack which deals with
the
crushing
weight
of
the
world
for
many people.
“But instead of giving up to these bad
feelings, what
I am speaking of
is can-
celling them out, getting beyond them,
through
a
‘sweet
exorcism’,”
said
Mayfield.

NEW YORK — “Ray Charles,” children's

to

the
1974

King Award
at

in early July. The

"his
Dream' and become one
of

over Records is “Come Live With Me."

ON STAGE — Loggins and Messina — Columbia
PG 32848
For all Loggins and Messina fans this is an ex-
tra special treat, but even
if you're just into good
music and
technical
perfection,
this
live,
2-
record LP
is right on the money. Totally profes-
sional, the duo and fine band are caught being
themselves
in San
Francisco, New
York, and
Boston (the
first date
in 1972, the
latter two
in
1973). From the outset,
at which
point Kenny
Loggins takes the stage to perform an acoustic
set including “House at Pooh Corner" and “Dan-
ny's Song,"
to the
pair's
great “Angry
Eyes,"
"Vahevala," and
smash,
"Your Mama
Don't
Dance," this LP makes it 100%.

POSITIVE VIBRATIONS -
Ten
Years
After -
Columbia PC 32851
Those rumors that Ten Years After was about
to break up are happily dispelled with release of
this bombastic package of rock
n' roll gems that
have longevity written
all over them. Alvin Lee,
Leo Lyons, Ric Lee, and Chick Churchill have put
together a splendid piece of work, highlighted by
such tunes as "Nowhere To Run,"
“i Wanted To
Boogie," "Stone Me,” “Going Back To Birming-
ham,” and
"You're Driving Me Crazy.” Dynamics
and arrangement are the key elements that make
any music come alive and here the formula
is
perfect. Looks like another ten years of success
for the band.

Grand Funk

Suzi Quatro
MADISON SQUARE GARDEN, NYC — An
incredible rockin' and
rollin' spectacular
happened
to
a
sell
out crowd
for
an
amazing
evening
of
driving
music.
Madison Square Garden housed 20,000
frantic
fans
as
the
frenetic
pulsating
rhythms filled the Garden.
Kicking off the show was Suzi Quatro.
A native of Detroit, Suzi went to England
where she got a band together and has
garnered
three number one
hits over
there. This, her first United States tour,
marks her performance and showman-
ship, full of energy and outrageous elec-
tric bass guitar playing coupled with her
powerful vocals. Highlighting the set was
her present chart single “48 Crash" and
"Can The Can," both
of which can be
found on her Bell LP “Suzi Quatro.”
Capricorn recording artists Wet Willie
played a dynamic set that was flavored
with
that
southern sound made
so
famous
by groups
as
the
Allman
Brothers Band and the Marshall Tucker
Band. Highlighting their set
is their cur-
rent single entitled “Keep On Smilin.”
The absolute devotion and adulation
that Grand Funk fans have for their idols
was something comparable to a Stones
Concert. The fans
literally went wild as
this major musical event unfolded itself.
The band’s heavy-metal steady driving
rock
n
roll
pulsated
in
the
Garden,
driving the
fans
to moans, groans and
auditory and
visual ecstasy. The selec-
tion
of
material,
which
included
their
present #1
chart single “Loco Motion"
from their Capitol “Shinin’ On” LP, was
well paced and very exciting to listen to
and watch.
Visually the band took one
step beyond any group's staging
I have
ever seen by presenting a stage show
which was meticulously worked out and
perfectly
timed.
I
say
took one
step
beyond any show
I have seen
to date
because the visual effects did not merely
augment
the songs
but complimented
them because
it was a show in and of
it-
self.
For example
a 35mm
film
set on
a
large screen backdrop opened the show
with
a stream
of
fireworks.
Flashes
of
Washington
and
Kennedy
flowed
into
the Capitol
building burning down and
then Grand Funk entered to the frenetic
screams of their ardent fans. Songs from
their vast repertoire of Capitol
LP's
in-
cluded
"Foot Stompin’ Music,” “Rock 'N
Roll
Soul,” “Closer To Home," “Heart-
breaker,” “Black Licorice," and "TNUC.”
Their
clothing
was
bright
and
chemically treated
to
react
to
a
black
light and this was interspersed with their
forceful songs and the cinematic visuals.
Interestingly enough
there were
no
glitter freaks
in the audience. Just mid-
dle American
kids out
to have a good
time and
diggin
' on
their
rock
heros.
"We re An American Band," the
title of
Grand Funk’s previous LP,
is indicative
of where the group is at and who they ap-
peal to. They are a heavy rock group who
appeal
to American
kids and seems to
eschew the “drag/gay" touches that so
many groups employ. Where others em-
ploy cheap theatrics to get by with no
talent, Grand Funk uses a carefully put
together
technical
masterpiece
to
highlight
their dynamic
vocals
and
proving beyond
a doubt
that they
are
The American Band!!

Herb

The show

Other songs featured were "Whipped

"Taste Of Honey,"
"Lollipops
and Roses," “Heat Wave" and the com-
plete “This Guy’s In Love With You.”
Highlights
of
the

in-
cluded Bob Findley’s trumpet work, ex-
cellent throughout, and Vince
Charles’
solo on
"Malaguena,"
playing
a
steel
drum that he had made for himself. The
standing
ovation
that
followed
"Zorba
The Greek” was
nothing

tumultuous.
The performance
left the audience
in
anxious
expectation
of Herb

new A&M Records
LP, “You Smile —
The Song Begins."
It will reportedly be
released in the near future.

CARNEGIE HALL, NYC — Jazz extraor-
dinaire was executed with the technical
brilliance of two jazz innovators,
i.e. Her-
bie Hancock and Chick Corea on their
Carnegie Hall concert.
Chick
Corea's
group,
Return
To
Forever
features Corea on
keyboards
Bill Connors on guitar, Stanley Clarke on
bass and Lenny White on drums.
“Theme From The
Mother
Ship,”
featured instrumental techniques parex-
celiance, and there was some excellent
interplay between bass and keyboards
that answered each other with counter
ranges.
The versatile Corea,
building
a mag-
netic rapport with the audience went into
a tour-de-force of a piano solo. Closing
with “Space Circus,” the Polydor group's
intensity was firmly established leaving
the audience wanting more.
Herbie Hancock’s consummate skill on
keyboards provided some of the
finest
jazz
riffs
ever;
accompanied
by
the
talents of Mike Clark on drums, Bill Som-
mers on percussion, Benny Maupin on
sax and bass clarinet and Paul Johnson
on
bass.
The
integration
of
tight
in-
strumentation was a unified together unit
that played some
really fine jazz incor-
porating a moog played by Hancock. The
numbers played included "Funky Lady”
and “Hornets."
The audience was relatively chagrined
because Hancock did not do too many
numbers from his present Columbia LP,
"Headhunters.” However, the music, ex-
cellent
rhythms
and
liquid
jazz
flow
proved to be a very well received set.
m.d.
Buffy St. Marie
BOTTOM LINE, NYC — Buffy St
Marie,
once associated with the folk scene only,
and one of its early superstars, made her
first appearance
in New York since
last
year at Carnegie
Hall and gave an
im-
pressive
demonstration
of
the
old
maxim, you can't judge a book by lookin’
at the cover. Her old image, reinforced
by a fine version of her immortal "Univer-
sal Soldier", nonetheless gave way to a
bright new musical
personality,
spiced
by her seven piece back-up band that in-
cludes her husband, Norbert Putnam on
bass.
Putnam,
a super-producer
in
his
own right, directed the band as Buffy did
a number of tunes from her MCA debut
LP, "Buffy”.
Her music
is emotionally expressive
and when she sang
“I Can’t Take
It No
More”,
the
audience was
obviously
touched. Buffy s stage presence is every
bit as professional as you'd expect and
her buoyancy gave "Sweet Fast Hooker
Blues" a tremendous
lift. She often sup-
ported her whole weight on one leg as
if
to
reach
back
for
that
little
extra
something
that
makes
a
singer come
alive. Both "Generation" and “Sweet Lit-
tle
Vera” came
across
powerfully
as
Buffy radiated smiles at all her musicians
after each song was over.
Currently
in
the midst of an extensive string of
live
dates, Buffy
is sure to bring as much to
any stage as she did to the Bottom Line.
d.b.
Michael Fennelly
Raw Soul
WHISKY LA. — Fennelly is a weird bird
among the rock
n rollers, an essentially
singer/songwriter type who
has an
in-
curable
itch to boogie. His "shiny gen-
tleman” stage costume aside (everybody
has
fantasies;
you
really
can’t
blame
him), you'd expect him to break out in a
James
Taylor song
momentarily.
But
boogie
is what he wants to do, and he
does
it well enough, better
in fact than
most of the hard core kids.
He borrows
a
bit
of Led
Zeppelin's
dynamics
for
intermittent
explorations
into the higher decibels but the effec-
tiveness of his act lies in the originality of
his vocal
style.
Fennelly’s high pitched
warble took us through "Shine A Light”
(his single), "Won’t You Please Do That"
and "Watch Yerself,” most of which were
bone tingling rockers that wiggled the
firmest of bottoms. Considerable oomph,
there.
But
the
clincher,
the more
in-
teresting side of Michael Fennelly was
visible
in
an
emotional
sort
of song
called
"Touch My
Soul,"
with
fine
lyricism and good single potential. Fen-
nelly has a lot more depth than he would
have us
all believe; he records on Epic
and his album is called “Lane Changer.”
Nice Surprise of the Month was Raw
Soul, an unsigned, unsung
better-than-
the-average r&b
act. Their material was
self composed
and
for the
most
part,
very
original sounding
with
great
lead
vocals from a singer who remained, un-
fortunately, anonymous.
Very much
in
their favor was the use of a rock-oriented
lead
guitarist who
provided
really
in-
teresting contrast to the chugga-chugga
rhythm
line. Something
for everybody
there, and enormous potential.
e.s.
30
May 4, 1974

Capitol Skeds
Six Albums
HOLLYWOOD — Six LPs, ranging from
pop to country to soul, including the first
album on
Lambert's &
Potters Haven
label, make up Capitol’s May release, an-
nounced
by Brown
Meggs,
CRI's
executive
vice-president and
chief
operating officer.
“A Piece of Time,”
Lori
Lieberman's
third Capitol
LP, once again unites the
young singer with the songs of Grammy
winners Charles Fox and Norman Gim :
bel.
Glen Campbell, another Grammy win-
ner, returns with “Houston,” a varied col-
lection of ballads and country standards,
named after and including Glen's current
hit single.
Singer Al
Martin's new release
is
"I
Wont
Last A Day’ Without You,” while
legendary fiddler Johnny Gimble debuts
with
his
first solo album, a Merle Hag-
gard-produced country LP appropriately
titled “Fiddlin' Around.”
Another debut album
is Gene Red-
ding's soulful "Blood Brother," on Den-
nis
Lambert's
&
Brian
Potter’s
Haven
label
(distributed
by
Capitol),
and
featuring
“This
Heart,"
Redding's
first
chart single.
From
England comes
"Like An
Old
Fashioned’ Waltz,” Sandy
Denny's
first
American LP on
Island
Records
(also
distributed by Capitol). Ms. Denny, both
as a solo singer and as an integral part of
Fairport
Convention,
has
been
con-
sistently ranked among the finest female
singers
by
England's
most
respected
rock publications.
According to Meggs, Capitol Records
has
already begun
a comprehensive
marketing campaign on
behalf
of
this
release, which
is scheduled to ship May
6th.

Produce For CAM
NEW YORK —
