McCartney Sees No Reunion Of The Beatles
NEW YORK — Paul McCartney's rep has
"categorically denied
and
refuted”
rumors and reports of a reunion for
in-
person appearances of The Beatles.
As far as McCartney is concerned, the
Beatles will not be performing together
at any
time,
nor have
any
offers
by
promoters for any type of performance
been
discussed. McCartney
points out
that
being seen
with
other
Beatles
is
merely social since they are still friendly
and any professional collaboration might
be
assisting
each
other on
recording
tracks.
McCartney
further
states
that
he
is
devoting
all
his talents and attention to
the
reforming
of
his 'Wings
Band
for
recording
and
other
projects
to
take
place later this year or early 1974
Sung Suh to UA
LOS ANGELES— George
Boyle, vice
president and controller of United Artists
Records,
has announced
the
appoint-
ment of Sung Hee Suh to the post of
director of accounting for United Artists
Records. Suh
will also assume respon-
sibility for UA s royalty department.
A
native
of
Korea, Suh
was
most
recently with the accounting firm of Peat,
Marwick, Mitchell and Co. where he was
heavily involved in the entertainment in-
dustry.
It
is McCartney’s contention
that the
proliferation of rumors and stories in the
print and
electronic
media
that
the
Beatles
will
reunite
are
"a
flagrant
misrepresentation and a great disservice
to the public.” McCartney feels that he,
as well as the other former members of
the
group,
are
involved
in
their own
projects which are
ultimately accepted
or rejected by the
public. To
lead
this
same public into believing a reunion
is
imminent, says McCartney,
is damaging
to all of the Beatles as individual artists.
Womack
Injured
LOS ANGELES —
United
Artists
Records artist Bobby’ Womack has can-
celled some of the dates on his current
concert tour because of illness.’ Womack
sustained a slight concussion when he
tripped over an amplifier while recording
in the studio the week before
last, and
thereafter
he complained
of
dizziness
and impaired vision.
Upon advice of his doctor,' Womack en-
tered
Hollywood Community
Hospital
that Friday for neurological tests which
proved
negative.
After being
released
from the hospital on Sunday,’ Womack's
doctor ordered a complete rest for him.
QUITE A CAST — As part of the pre-premiere gathering for the 20th Century Fox film
“Claudine," held at the Park Lane Hotel, Gladys Knight received a commemorative
plaque for her NARM Award as Best Female Soul Artist of the Year. Seen with her
here are (top foto,
left to
right): Art Kass, president of The Buddah Group, Gladys,
Sidney A. Seidenberg, president of SAS,
Inc., management of the group, and Pip
Merald Knight. (Middle) Gladys Knight & The Pips and Curtis Mayfield, performers
and writer-producer respectively of the soundtrack “Claudine,” are seen here at the
gathering. (Left to right) Pips Edward Patten and William Guest, Curtis, Gladys and
Merald Knight. (Bottom) James Earl Jones, "Claudine’s” leading man, arrives at the
DeMille Theatre for the world premiere. Critically acclaimed as having given the per-
formance of his career, Jones is seen here with his wife, Julianne-Marie Jones, and
David Kruger, who appears with him in the film. The "Claudine” soundtrack is on Bud-
dah Records.

Deal With Camillo
NEW YORK — Tony Camillo, producer
for Gladys Knight and the
Pips,
Freda
Payne and other recording
artists,
has
entered into a co-publishing agreement
with
Marks
Music,
Joseph
Auslander,
president, and Dick Stone, professional
manager, have announced.
Camillo, who won
a Grammy Award
this year for Gladys Knight and the Pips'
“Imagination" LP and "Midnight Train to
Georgia”
single,
has won
seven
gold
record and LP awards
in the
last three
years. He
is currently producing Dionne
Warwicke,
Linda
Hopkins,
Richie
Havens,
Barry
Miles, The Chambers
Brothers and Gladys Knight. He
will be
producing Damita Jo
for a
label
in the
near future.
Also
active
with the
Holland-Dozier-
Holland labels, (Hof Wax, Invictus), other
acts under Camillo’s wing
include: The
Isley Brothers, Chairman of the Board,
1 00 Proof and Peaches and Herb.
Negotiations
for
the
co-publishing
agreement with Camillo were instituted
by Dick Stone. Camillo
will maintain an
office for his Venture Productions within
the Marks office complex, and
will con-
tinue to work out of his own studio and
with numerous other projects.

ATV Gains Attache
Music Catalog
. OS ANGELES — ATV Music Group has
made
its
first
major
publishing
j
acquisition through the purchase of the
i
entire catalog of Attache Music, formerly
\ owned
by
Lee
Hazlewood
and
Joe
Nixon.
The Attache Music book mostly com-
prises Country material. Songs featured
in the catalog include Roy Clark's "Right
or Left on Oak Street, "and Dean Martin's
Do You Believe This Town?"
Writers include Charlie Williams, in ad-
dition to Hazlewood and others.
Sam Trust, head of ATV Music
in the
U.S., said of the acquisition: This is part
of ATVs continuing expansion program
since we began operations
last year.
In
the
short time since the
deal was
for-
malized,
we've
had
great
success
in
placing songs from the Attache catalog
and we
ll be announcing further record-
ings within the next 30 days.”
Trust said recordings of Attache songs
to be released within the coming weeks
include
Ferlin Husky on
ABC/Dunhill,
Marty
Mitchell
recording
for
Atlantic,
and Molly Bee, who records for Granite
Records, ATVs West
Coast-based
County label.
"Well
be
giving
the songs
full
ex-
posure here on the West Coast as well as
through our fully-staffed offices in Nash-
ville
and New
York,”
Trust
said.
"It's
been
a
very
successful
West
Coast
catalog and we intend to exploit
it fully in
Nashville and New York.”
ATV Music Group made
its entry into
the American
market
less than
a year
ago, the U S. wing of one of Europe's
largest
and
most
prestigious
music
publishing operations headed by Sir Lew
Grade.
Currently, the ATV Music Group ex-
ploits
a group
of
five
wholly-owned
publishing companies, including Maclen
Music, a catalog
built on Beatles com-
positions.
Chapin Is Keynote
Speaker At AGAC
NEW YORK — The bi-monthly meeting
of the American
Guild
of Authors and
Composers
took
place
April
24th
at
Kings
Court,
located
in
the
Barbazon
Plaza. Ervin Drake, president of AGAC,
summarized the
basic tenets of AGAC
and how
the
organization
works
to
protect the
writer. He then introduced
the guest speaker of the evening, who
was
Elektra
recording
artist
Barry
Chapin.
Also, WHEW DJ Alison Steele
acted in the capacity of moderator, inter-
jecting
and
expanding
on
audience
questions.
Chapin, who was
at one time
a
film
maker between
1965-1971, has always
had an interest in the music industry. He
then wrote his #1
"Taxi" and from there
got
it all together. As he said, "The key is
will
and
determination.
Desire
is
the
most important thing an artist must have.
I've maybe met one out of any 10
tal-
ented artists who had the desire to follow
it through
”
Chapin feels that managers are merely
frustrated performers who never made
it.
Also, commenting
on
the
writer who
wishes to play place his material with an
artist, Chapin said
it was very difficult and
that he at one time had the same idea but
ended up
singing
himself because he
couldn't
find anyone
to
perform
his
material.
Chapin
proved
to
be
an
in-
teresting spokesman
for
a
variety
of
topic
. concerning the industry.
Blue Note “Cooking”
LOS ANGELES — Blue Note Records,
under the direction of George Butler,
is,
in the parlance of the trade,
"cooking."
The United Artists-distributed label, the
oldest
jazz-oriented
label
in
existence
(founded in 1939),
is currently strong on
the pop charts with Donald Byrd’s "Street
Lady” and
Bobbi
Humphrey's
“Blacks
and
Blues;''
the
recent
release
of
Alphonze Mouzon's
“Funky Snakefoot
insures more
soulful sounds from
the
label
that
likes
to
call
its
music
"the
sound of the street,” music which incor-
porates jazz, soul, and rock into a sound
that crosses over in many different direc-
tions.
Butler said that “we are trying to incor-
porate a musical universality in which the
music expressed by various artists on the
label
can
reach
a
wide
spectrum
of
musical tastes.
"
Bobbi Humphrey's “Blacks and Blues"
broke in Baltimore/Washington, Seattle,
New York, Detroit and Chicago, and, with
the
release
of
her
"Chicago,
Damn”
single off the album, her career is in high
gear.
Blue Note's breakthrough began some
14 months ago, when Ed
Levine, then
director of promotion and sales
for the
label, and
his assistant, Jere Hausfater,
began a campaign
to convince people
that the
artists and music on the
label
could become general market records.
Says
Levine:
"Donald
Byrd's
"Black
Byrd” began with jazz play and crossed
over to R & B and pop. We even had
some MOR’son the album.
If the music is
in the grooves, then
it
doesn’t
matter
what the label copy says.
April was Blue Note Month at United
Artists, with the entire organization get-
ting behind a massive Blue Note sales
program. Merchandising aids included a
much-in-demand
poster made
from
a
painting by artist Francisco Toledo. Stut-
ters for retail stores with minis of the top
sellers on Blue Note were also used.
Butler, who
acts
in
creative and
ad-
ministrative capacity, works closely with
Ed Levine, who was upped at the begin-
ning of the year to the post of national
director of promotion
for United Artists
and
with
Hausfater, once
Levine's
as-
sistant, who
is now
in charge
of Blue
Note promotion.

Sets NY Bow;
Schwartz Score

1 4.

("Godspell,"

an

for which

spell" has composed the songs, and Bob
Randall ('6 RMS RIV VU ") has written the
story. The
direction and choreography
are
in
the
sleight-of-hands
of Grover
Dale.
Hennings
feats include The
Floating
Woman, The Mis-Made
Girl, The Neon
Tubes, The Bed
of
Horrors, ESP, The
Zig-Zag Woman,
Metamorphoses
(Beauty
into
Beast,
i.e.
a
Canadian
cougar).
Colecox Formed
HOLLYWOOD —
Producer
Larry Cox
and Songwriter Johnny Cole have
an-
nounced the formation of Colecox Ltd.,
an
independent
production
company,
and the signing of their first artist, Rusty
Lee.
Cox'
credits
include
the
million-
seller
"Precious
and
Few,” which
he
produced with Climax.
Rosen Named To
Warner Publishing
NEW YORK — Ed Silvers, president of
Warner Bros. Music, announced the ap-
pointment
of
Arnold
Rosen
to
the
position
of
manager,
standard
and
educational
division,
effective
im-
mediately. Rosen will be responsible for
publications,
from
concept through
distribution,
for
all WB
material
other
than
contemporary
folios
and
sheet
music. He worked previously with Alfred
Publishing Co. for ten years.
Reviewing the WB catalogue, Rosen
notes, “It's almost a miraculous situation
to have such a wealth of material to draw
from for the educational field. We will be
promoting even more
heavily than we
have
in
the
past.
Our comprehensive
schedule of publications will include not
only the public education market but the
private teaching outlets as well. We will
cover every area of education in depth."
WB
recently closed
its
fiscal
year,
re-
porting
the
largest
gross and
net
in-
comes in its long history.
Frisco NARAS
Chap. Official
HOLLYWOOD — San Francisco officially
became the seventh Record Academy
chapter when the
majority
of
National
Trustees of NARAS voted to accept the
fledging
group. "We
are
really
thrilled
and happy to see the Academy continue
its expansion
into the
well-established
recording field," noted NARAS national
president Bill Lowery. "Now with the ad-
dition of San Francisco,
it
will open up
the Golden Gate of the Record Academy
even farther."
The new group
boasts close
to 100
members, some of whom have transfer-
red
in from
Los
Angeles, where they
were
originally
enrolled.
Leo
Kulka
is
heading
the new
chapter.
All
area
residents wishing to join can contact him
at 6655 Harrison Street, San Francisco
91407.
Other Record Academy chapters are
now
functioning
in
Los
Angeles, New
York,
Chicago,
Nashville,
Atlanta
and
Memphis.
Ellman Joins SSR
NEW YORK — Solter/Sabinson/Roskin
Inc. have announced that Steve Ellman
has joined
its west coast office. Ellman
formerly was
with
the
Jack Wodell
Agency, where he served as national ac-
count supervisor for Warner Bros. Prior
to that he was advertising and publicity
director for The Fanfare Corporation.

Casey Heads V.A.I.
HOLLYWOOD -
Phil
Casey,
formerly
vice president
in charge of concerts at
A.T.I., has resigned
his post to head up
California
operations
for
Minneapolis
based Variety Theatre International.
The
west
coast
operations
will
be
called Variety Artists
International
Ltd.,
and will be located at 91 20 Sunset Blvd.,
Los Angeles, California 90069.
Stanton & Nelson
Forms Century
Cassette Corp.
HOLLYWOOD —
Peter
H.
Stanton,
previously president of Infonics, Inc., has
announced
the
formation
of
Century
Cassette Corporation.
"Century
will
manufacture C-O
(unloaded) cassettes for the professional
duplicator
market,”
Stanton
said.
"We
have no plans to enter the retail market-
place. The Century C-0 is a virgin impact
polystyrene cassette molded on tooling
in comformance to Philips specifications.
It contains lubricated
steel
pins,
Delrin
rollers, hard welded windows, graphite
liners,
annealed
metal
shield,
spring
pressure pad and 26 inch leader.
Joining
Stanton
at
Century
as
marketing vice-president and a director
is Paula Nelson, formerly sales manager
at
Infonics. She stated
that she
is cur-
rently sampling selected duplicators with
C-O's and
is scheduling spring and sum-
mer deliveries.
MFSB 2nd Gold
NEW YORK — Philadelphia International
recording group MFSB has struck gold
for the second time
in two weeks with
their most recent album, “Love
Is The
Message."
Earlier, the
single from the
album, "TSOP"
(The Sound
Of
Philadelphia),
was
certified
gold.
The
album was certified gold by the R.I.A.A.,
signifying sales in excess of one million
dollars.

WEA Gold For Marmaduke
DALLAS — A gold record was awarded
to Sam Marmaduke,
president
of
Western Merchandisers, by Tom Sims,
Warner-Elektra-Atlantic’s
Dallas
branch
manager.
Western
Merchandisers was
named WEA
Dallas'
"Customer
of the
Year" in 1973 based upon “sales volume,
low
returns and
prompt
bill
payment."
Western has rack operations
in
Dallas,
Houston, and Oklahoma City. The award
was presented
during
a
party
held
by
WEA for Western's executive staff at the
Amarillo Club.

Ember To Glow in U.S. 
HOLLYWOOD - "I'm determined to 
establish artists for longevity," averred 
Jeffrey Kruger, president of Ember 
Records, after a luncheon launching his 
new artist Denny Doherty's initial Em- 
ber/Paramount single "You'll Never 
Know," held here last week. Kruger's aim 
for "longevity," is a bit of a double enten- 
dre since the tune itself which Doherty 
has recorded was written in 1943. This 
Bregman/Voceo. & Conn (20th Century 
Music) published song won the Oscar 
that year for the film "Hello, Frisco, 
Hello." In a way Kruger's own Ember 
label is saying "Hello, U.S., Hello," via 
his new distribution deal with Famous 
Music and by establishing west coast of- 
fices headed by John Madara, who was 
just appointed Ember vp in charge of 
creative development. Madara produced 
the new Doherty single and will be 
producing several of the new artists sig- 
ned to Ember/Paramount, among whom 
include Mother Trucker (an all girl's 
group from England), Susan Maughn (a 
Melody Maker poll winner set to open 
the Persian Room next month), and Rick 
Sandler (a songwriter/composer who 
Krueger likened to Elton John). Kruger 
and Tony Martell, president of Famous 
Music are also very excited about the 
forthcoming LP release of Desmond 
Dekker's "Greatest Hits," (which in- 
cludes his "Israelites," hit). Krueger also 
disclosed that Dekker is currently in 
England recording some new material 
for Ember/Paramount. Also operating 
out of Ember's Los Angeles office is Rick 
Palladino, the label's new director of 
national promotion.

Wyman Set For 
TV's `Speak Easy' 
HOLLYWOOD - On May 25, eighteen 
minutes of film from the Rolling Stones' 
latest movie, "Ladies And Gentlemen, 
The Rolling Stones,"will be shown for 
the first time on TV on "Speak Easy," 
new rock/talk series hosted by Chip 
Monck. Featured guest on the show is 
Bill Wyman, bass player for the group. 
Film shown features Mick Jagger and 
The Stones performing "Midnight Ram- 
bler" and "You Can't Always Get What 
You Want." "After working for the Rolling 
Stones on their last three tours, it was 
such a marvelous pleasure to have them 
work for me on my show," affirms Chip. 
Also featured on the May 25 "Speak 
Easy" is Dr. John. This marks the artist's 
second appearance on the show. Discus- 
sion with Dr. John centered around the 
New Orleans sound of his new album, 
"Desitively Bonnaroo," which contains 
tunes all self -penned. 
Paula Batson 
To Press Dept. 
At RCA On Coast 
NEW YORK - The appointment of Paula 
Hyun Batson as administrator of press 
and information on the west coast for 
RCA Records has been announced by 
Grelun Landon, manager of press and in- 
formation, west coast. 
Ms. Batson most recently worked as 
public relations rep for artists Waylon 
Jennings and Willie Nelson. She was as- 
sociated formerly with the publicity 
department of Ode Records, working 
with their artist roster. As a freelance 
writer her work has appeared in the L.A. 
Free Press and other publications. 
Ms. Batson, a graduate of Sarah 
Lawrence College, first gained ex- 
perience in the music business as as- 
sistant to New York attorney, Johanan 
Vigoda. After her graduation, she was ac- 
cepted at Hastings Law School, 
however, she found that her commit- 
ment and interest in the record business 
won out over a law career.

New L.A. Governors 
To NARAS Named 
LOS ANGELES - The Los Angeles 
Chapter of the Record Academy 
(NARAS) reports that voting members 
have elected 21 new governors to serve 
2 year terms on the chapter's Board Of 
Governors. Those elected and the mem- 
bership categories they represent are: 
Vocalists/singers: Ray Charles, Sally 
Stevens; leaders/conductors: Don Ellis, 
Peter Matz; producers: Kelly Gordon, 
Bones Howe; songwriters/composers: 
Mel Larson, Jerry Marcellino; engineers: 
Bruce Botnick, Ben Jordan; instrumen- 
talists: Jay Cooper, Vince DeRosa; ar- 
rangers: Dave Dexter; spoken word: Milt 
Larsen, Ruth White; and classical: Peter 
Christ, Don Christleib, and Mario Guar- 
neri. 
The governors -elect will attend their 
first Board meeting Tues., June 4, when 
they will join incumbent governors who 
have another year in office. At that time, 
new chapter officers for the coming year 
will be elected. 
Blaskey To Haven 
HOLLYWOOD - Lindy Blaskey has 
joined Lambert and Potter's Haven 
Records as general professional 
manager of the company's publishing 
divisions, announced Eddie Lambert, 
Haven's general manager. "We feel that 
acquisition of Lindy Blaskey," com- 
mented Brian Potter, "marks a step for- 
ward for our company, in becoming a 
viable and competitive publisher." 
Blaskey's responsibilities, according 
to Lambert, will encompass ad- 
ministration of Haven's two publishing 
divisions, Touch of Gold Music Inc. 
(BMI) and Natural Songs Inc. (ASCAP), 
as well as One Of A Kind Music, affiliated 
with ABC Dunhill Music. 
Prior to joining Haven, Blaskey was 
professional manager of the Music 
Publishing Division of ABC.

Hit Via Eng.

Miracle."

Joseph Forms 
Jasmine Music 
HOLLYWOOD - Rick Joseph, executive 
head of Dawnbreaker Music (BMI) an- 
nounced formation of Jasmine Music 
(ACAP) to meet expanding needs of the 
publishing company. The first two 
writers Jasmine has signed are Kay 
Dunham and Walter Heath. Dunham has 
placed songs with such artists as Eddie 
Kendricks, Three Dog Night, Harry 
Belafonte, Thelma Houston and Hoyt 
Axton. His latest material can be heard in 
the movie, "The Last Detail," which used 
two of his songs. Walter Heath has recor- 
ded for A&M records under the name 
Lawrence Heath, and is currently 
opening the show for Seals & Crofts on 
their national tour. 
Also signed with the newly formed 
Jasmine is Jack Goga, former staff writer 
for Jobete Music and producer at 
Motown Records. He was co-author of 
the Temptations gold record, "You", as 
well as having penned songs for Martha 
and the Vandellas. Pictured here (I. to r.) 
are Rick Joseph, head of Dawnbreaker; 
Walter Heath (seated) and Kay Dunham.

HOLLYWOOD - United Artists Records, 
a subsidiary of Trans America Cor- 
poration (NYSE), has announced un- 
precedented sales of $33,640,000 since 
1971 of records featuring the seven 
member rock group, War. 
According to Michael Stewart, United 
Artists Records president, no large 
progressive Black ensemble in history 
has ever achieved sales of a similar 
nature. 
"The total has been attained with five 
albums and five single records," Stewart 
said. "Three of the albums have ex- 
ceeded platinum status (more than $2 
million in sales) and a fourth, the current 
"War Live," is approaching the coveted 
horizon," he added. 
War is composed of Charles Miller, 
saxophone; Howard Scott, guitar; Lonnie 
Jordan, organ; B. B. Dickerson, bass; 
Harold Brown, drums; Dee Allen, conga 
drums; and Lee Oskar, harmonica. 
The group is managed by Steve Gold 
of Far Out Management and produced 
by Jerry Goldstein of Far Out Produc- 
tions.

RCA Appoints Harris 
NEW YORK - Ray Harris has been ap- 
pointed manager, merchandising rhythm 
and blues, RCA Records. The announ- 
cement was made by Jack Maher, direc- 
tor, product merchandising, to whom 
Harris will report. 
Harris joins RCA Records from adver- 
tising Contractors, Inc., where he was an 
account executive servicing such 
organizations as Carson Chemical Co., 
Monarch Wine Co. and the Wella Corp. 
primarily in the radio and TV areas. His 
specific account responsibilities in- 
cluded the coordination of media plans 
and subsequent radio and/or TV buys. 
A native New Yorker, Ray Harris is cur- 
rently attending Bernard Baruch 
Evening College, where he is majoring in 
advertising. 
Platters Set 
For MGM Grand 
NEW YORK - Las Vegas fans of The 
Platters will be pleased to learn that 
MGM Grand Hotel buyer Bernie 
Rothkopf has just signed The Platters for 
three forthcoming appearances in the 
Lion's Den - the first four weeks to 
begin July 10, 1974. 
Buck Ram, musical director and foun- 
der of The Platters, has just signed con- 
tracts with Phonogram International of 
Holland to produce three LP's and 
several singles, which will be released as 
quickly as possible once he delivers 
them to Phonogram. Ben Bunders, Inter- 
national A&R Manager of Phonogram, is 
planning on being here from Holland for 
The Platters' opening and bringing 
representatives from their United States 
staff. 
Since The Platters have been breaking 
attendance records at all their appearan- 
ces, Jean Bennett, manager of the 
group, who resides in Las Vegas, stated, 
"You haven't seen anything yet! The 
Platters' act today is so polished and 
professional, and they complement each 
other so completely now, that it's really a 
refreshing act. They delight every 
audience with the many reminiscent 
sounds of their golden hits and at the 
same time add their own contemporary 
youthful presentations of today. The 
Brown Brandy combo that accompanies 
The Platters is composed of such 
dedicated musicians, under the direction 
of Henry Lee, that they've also become a 
valuable and integral part of the act as a 
whole. We'll have no qualms about our 
opening night, even at the impressive 
and beautiful MGM Grand Hotel." 
"In an era of instant trends and over- 
worked nostalgia, there are certain 
musical "institutions" that appreciative 
audiences can look to for longevity, 
professionalism, and, simply, classic in- 
terpretations of great songs," said Buck 
Ram. 
Despite stars who flash on the horizon 
never to be heard from again, The Plat- 
ters - founded by Buck Ram in 1954 - 
will celebrate their twentieth year in the 
music business with their July 10 -August 
6 engagement in the Lion's Den in the 
lavish new MGM Grand Hotel in Las 
Vegas, to be followed by a posh date in 
New York in the early fall. 
The Platters have proved that there 
has always been and continues to be an 
audience for their classic interpretations 
of the Buck Ram -written hits "Twilight 
Time," "The Great Pretender," "Only 
You," or the Buck Ram -arranged "My 
Prayer" and "Smoke Gets In Your Eyes." 
Over the last 20 years, Buck Ram has 
been responsible for 16 gold records for

Earth, Wind & Fire 
Hit Gold Status 
NEW YORK - Columbia Recording 
group Earth, Wind & Fire has garnered 
its second gold record with their latest 
album, "Open Our Eyes." The disc was 
certified Gold by the RIAA, signifying 
sales in excess of one million dollars. 
For Earth, Wind & Fire, an eight -man 
group from Chicago, this is their second 
gold album. Their second Columbia 
album, "Head To The Sky," went gold 
last year. The two previous Earth, Wind & 
Fire LP's were produced for Columbia by 
Joe Wissert and "Open Our Eyes" was 
produced by Wissert and group leader 
Maurice White. "Open Our Eyes" 
reached gold status less than three mon- 
ths after its release in February, 1974. 
McCann Store Promo 
PHILA. - Les McCann, Atlantic Records 
recording artist and one of the top names 
in jazz, made a highly successful per- 
sonal appearance recently at Franklin 
Music's center -city Philadelphia store. 
McCann, who was appearing at one of 
the city's clubs at the time, spent two 
hours meeting the public and signing 
autographs at Franklin's newest store of 
the five -store Delaware Valley rec- 
ord/audio chian. 
The appearance was the most recent 
in a series of in-store promotions and 
visits by famous recording personalities 
that has helped lend support to 
Franklin's major"Music Man" advertising 
effort, a campaign which has sought to 
establish Franklin's personnel as people 
who "know something about the music 
they sell." 
McCann's appearance was supported 
by newspaper ads and in-store signing. 
Commenting on the purpose and suc- 
cess of the appearance, Edward H. 
Rosen, president of Franklin's parent 
company, Raymond Rosen and Com- 
pany, said, "Philadelphia is really 
becoming the music capital of the coun- 
try. And we felt we should help add to 
the aesthetic momentum, rather than 
just capitalizing on the retail benefits. By 
doing more and more of this type of 
thing, we're giving the people a chance 
to meet, in person, the kind of major 
talent our city's attracting." 
The Platters alone. The LP "Encore of 
Golden Hits," which included 10 Buck 
Ram, songs sold a million and in 1967 
The Platters added another million seller 
with their "More Encores of Golden 
Hits," with six Ram originals in the 
album. In total, Ram is a prolific com- 
poser, having written over 500 songs.

NARAS Trustees Meet: 
Lowery Re-elected President; 
Academy Sets Varied New Projects 
MEMPHIS - Atlanta's Bill Lowery was 
chapters on reactions to both this year's 
re-elected national president of NARAS, 
presentations. 
the record academy, and Lou Busch was 
re-elected national secretary/treasurer 
during the three-day meeting on the 
weekend of May 19 of the National 
Trustees of NARAS. Also elected were 
New York's Brooks Arthur as 1st national 
vice-president and Lincoln Mayorga (Los 
Angeles), Murray Allen (Chicago), Jim 
Fogelsong (Nashville), Knox Phillips 
(Memphis), and Ed Wetteland (San Fran- 
cisco) as additional vice presidents. 
Procedure Changes 
The actions taken included several in- 
novations in the annual Grammy Awards 
voting procedures. Companies will hen- 
ceforth be able to submit entries twice, 
instead of just once a year, while as- 
sociate members will be extended the 
privilege of also recommending product 
for voting members' consideration. A 
new category, "Producer of the Year," 
with nominations to come from commit- 
tees of producers in each of the chap- 
ters, was also approved, as was the 
future availability of special certificates 
for all back-up musicians and singers on 
Grammy -winning recordings. 
In a move to encourage greater 
cultural and educational activities within 
the chapters, the trustees agreed upon a 
new revenue -sharing procedure, with 
the national office supplying additional 
funds directly to the local units. The 
trustees also entered into a lively discus- 
sion with Pierre Cossette, packager of 
the Academy's two revenue -producing 
national telecasts, the Grammy Awards 
shows and the Grammy Salutes series, 
and presented reports from the various 
Love -Rosen: 
`Contact' Hits 
The Promo Mark 
NEW YORK - Radio contact by Love - 
Rosen Productions - an indie national 
promo firm formed eight months ago by 
Noel Love and Howard Rosen - may 
sometimes involve "insanity in stereo" 
by telephone, but the firm has been as- 
sociated with a lot of successes. 
The firm is basically a two -man 
operation, wherein Love and Rosen, 
working out of 575 Lexington Ave. in 
New York, do all telephone contact with 
radio by themselves and spend 
Thursdays and Fridays ("slow days for 
the industry") doing extensive mailings 
of records to radio. 
According to Love, who has held key 
promo slots with such labels as Polydor, 
DJM, Bell and Famous Music, he and 
Rosen reach on a weekly basis the top 
200 secondary and primary stations 
through their own Watts lines. Included 
in their service to accounts are mailings 
of disks to retailers in areas where they 
have gotten airplay and a general check 
of inventory of the disks they're working 
on. 
'Starting' Disks 
"Basically," says Love, "we're out to start 
records while our label clients are 
working on hits. When the record has 
reached a certain plateau, the label will 
tell us to stop working on the record and 
go on to a new release. We'll work no 
more than eight records a month." 
Rosen feels that he and Love - who of- 
ten work the phones together to a single 
(continued on page 26) 
NY Grammy TV'er 
The rotation for future Grammy 
Awards shows was also agreed upon, 
with New York (as had previously been 
announced) picked for the 1975 site, 
with Chicago, Atlanta, Memphis, Nash- 
ville, Los Angeles and San Francisco to 
follow in that order. 
The Trustees also approved additional 
topics as follow-ups to this year's 
"Grammy Salutes Oscar" show, namely 
Rock, Rhythm and Blues, Country, Jazz, 
Broadway, Big Bands, Television, The 
Bi -Centennial and A History of Re- 
corded Music. 
Future plans for the NARAS Hall of 
Fame also received the Trustees' atten- 
tion. After Nashville, with Mayor Brierly 
putting in a surprise appearance, had 
presented a slide -tape show, narrated by 
Johnny Cash, and Memphis had pointed 
out the advantages of locating in its en- 
virons, the Trustees voted to appoint a 
site selection committee of members 
from each of the seven chapters. It also 
approved consideration of an offer from 
Universal City to house the Hall on a 
temporary basis until a permanent site 
has been recommended by the commit- 
tee and approved by the Trustees.

Rice, Webber 
Adds 5 Years 
Thru Stigwood 
NEW YORK - Tim Rice and Andrew 
Lloyd Webber, the lyricist and composer 
of "Jesus Christ Superstar" and "Joseph 
and His Amazing Technicolour Dream - 
coat," have extended their management 
contract with the Robert Stigwood 
Organization for a further five years, ef- 
fective immediately. Rice and Webber 
have extended their contracts together 
with David Land, managing director of 
Superstar Ventures Limited. 
The Stigwood Organization has 
represented Rice and Webber for the 
past three years. 
The original recording of "Jesus Christ 
Superstar" on MCA Records is quoted in 
the Guinness Book of Records as being 
the most popular LP in history, with 
worldwide sales exceeding five million 
double -LP copies, equivalent to 10 mil- 
lion single LP's. The LP of the film ver- 
sion of "Superstar" has sold more than 
600,000 double copies, world wide. 
There have been 14 different produc- 
tions of the original stage musical, in 
eight different languages. The show 
played on Broadway for more than two 
years and has broken box-office records 
from Iceland to Japan. 
The film version of "Superstar" was 
the 7th largest grosser of 1973. 
New Projects 
Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber 
are currently working on the film scôre of 
"The Odessa File," currently filming in 
Germany, and a stage musical based on 
the life of Eva Peron. Webber is working 
with other collaborators on a stage 
musical based on Jeeves, the classic 
character created by P. G. Wodehouse. 
In addition, Rice and Webber are 
developing several new projects for 
stage, film, television and recordings. 
Nader Teaming w/UA Theatres 
NEW YORK - Salah M. Hassanein, exec 
vice president of the United Artists 
Theatre Circuit, Inc., and Richard Nader, 
president of The Richard Nader 
Organization, Inc., have announced a 
joint venture for the production of five 
major concerts between May 31 and July 
6 in New York and Atlantic City under the 
UA Happy Associates banner. 
The agreement marks UA's first ven- 
ture into the promotion and presentation 
of live concerts thru UA's Special Events 
Division. The UA -Nader association will 
debut with the 6th New York Latin Music 
Festival on May 31 and Volume 16 of 
Nader's "Original Rock & Roll Revival 
Show" on June 7, both to be presented 
at Madison Square Garden's Main 
Arena. 
Three major events are scheduled for 
the Convention Hall in Atlantic City on 
the world-famous resort city's 
traditionally biggest weekend - July 4 
to 6. The Fourth of July concert will 
headline the Gramy-winning Gladys 
Knight & The Pips. Nader's Original Rock 
& Roll Revival Show, hosted by national 
TV personality Dick Clark, will be pre- 
sented on July 5. Negotiations are cur- 
rently being conducted for the July 6th 
concert. 
Headlining in Volume 16 of the Rock & 
Roll Revival Spectacular at Madison 
Square Garden on June 7 are Little 
Richard, Bo Diddley, The Chantels, 
Johnny Maestro of the Crests with the 
Brooklyn Bridge, The Channels, The 
Coasters, Danny & The Juniors, Gary U. 
S. Bonds and special guest star Chubby 
Checker. The 6th New York Latin Music 
Festival will feature Sophy, Johnny Ven- 
tura, Pellin Rodriguez. Tommy Oliven- 
cia, Los Satelites, Kako and special guest 
star Cal Tjader and his Quintet. 
Island Forms 
Firm In U.S. 
KINGSTON, JAMAICA - Chris Black- 
well, founder of Island Records, has an- 
nounced that the label has formed a 
company in the United States to be 
known as Island Records, Inc. 
Coincidental to the announcement is the 
appointment of Charlie Nuccio as 
president. Nuccio was previously direc- 
tor of Apple Records in the United 
States. Blackwell, however, will be 
primarily responsible for talent 
acquisition. Headquarters of Island 
Records, Inc. will be at 7720 Sunset 
Boulevard, Los Angeles. California 
90046. Telephone number of the new 
company is (213) 874-7760. 
BLACKWELL 
Crossover Moves 
NEW YORK - Larry Newton, president 
of Crossover Records, has announced 
the company's relocation to new offices 
at 120 East 56th St., effective May 27. 
Crossover Records' new telephone 
number is: (212) 759-7841 (2, 3). Ray 
Charles heads the list of artists signed to 
Crossover. 
Other Plans 
A full range of contemporary, progres- 
sive, ethnic and youth -oriented enter- 
tainment will be staged in select subur- 
ban and metropolitan theatres. Plans are 
now underway to present live, in -theatre 
concerts in key locations on a regular 
basis in at least 14 cities by the fall. This 
concept was originally tested with a 
presentation of Nader's Rock & Roll 
Revival starring Lloyd Price, The 
Coasters, The Five Satins, The Orlons 
and Freddy Cannon at the UA -owned 
State Theatre in Easton, Pa. on May 17. 
Sly's 11th MSG 
Stand A Record 
NEW YORK -- Sly Stone becomes the 
first performer to headline Madison 
Square Garden for a record breaking 
11th time when he tops the bill in New 
York's mecca on Wednesday, June 5. 
Capping the evening will be his on- 
stage marriage to California model Kathi 
Silva in an all gold wedding before more 
than 20,000 well-wishing fans. 
Last seen in New York onstage with 
Stevie Wonder at the Garden in a sur- 
prise guest appearance, Stone will be 
joined by Eddie Kendricks. The concert 
has been planned to coincide with the 
completion of Sly's new Epic LP, "Small 
Talk." 
Currently in New York to firm up wed- 
ding arrangements, Sly will also co -host 
the Mike Douglas Show to be taped this 
week (28-31) in Philadelphia. 
Stuart Sees 
Top Year For 
Curtom Records 
CHICAGO - Curtom Records of 
Chicago, starting its sixth year this 
season, will probably have its biggest 
year ever. according to manager Mary 
Stuart. 
Curtis Mayfield. he pointed out, has a 
big hit in the movie soundtrack 
"Claudine," and also will be starring in 
the motion picture "Mimi." His "Sweet 
Exorcist" album has hit the charts in a big 
way, and all previous Mayfield product is 
doing well. 
Curtom, which in the past has broken 
such artists as Donny Hathaway, the 5 
Stair Steps. Major Lance and Gene 
Chandler, currently boasts the only 24 - 
track studio in Chicago, Stuart noted. 
"This looks like our biggest year ever," 
he pointed out. "It looks as though the 
Natural Four will break through this year, 
and the Impressions are already 
breaking big. As far as Curtis is con- 
cerned - well, this should be the best 
year." 
The Natural Four are hitting on both 
the r&b and pop charts with their two 
singles, "Love That Really Counts" and 
"Can This Be Real?". They've appeared 
on numerous major TV music shows, and 
have a chart album in "The Natural 
Four."

1 Mil. In Sales 
NEW YORK - RCA Records sold a total

William DeVaughn, John Denver, Hues 
Corporation and Elvis Presley.

CBS Publishes 
Book On Progress 
Against Pirates 
NEW YORK - CBS Records has written 
and published a booklet, Progress 
Against Piracy, which has been 
distributed throughout the music in- 
dustry. It is estimated that there are over 
4,000 copies of the booklet currently in 
circulation. 
The booklet, which was compiled 
through the efforts of the CBS law de- 
partment, describes the progress that 
has been made in legislation, civil 
litigation and criminal litigation to protect 
recording artists and record companies 
against record and tape piracy. The 
booklet cites the steady progress that 
has been made in the courts against 
unauthorized duplication of sound re- 
cordings. It has been estimated that tape 
pirates alone have been selling more 
than $200 million of pirated tapes each 
year. 
CBS Records has distributed the 
booklet not only to its own employees, 
but to customers, state legislators and 
retailers as well. Copies were given out 
at the NARM convention and at a recent 
Eastern Regional Conference of Attor- 
neys General in Newport, R. 
I. By 
making people more knowledgeable on 
the subject of record and tape piracy, 
CBS Records feels it's making another 
important contribution towards gaining 
more effective anti -piracy legislation, 
both on the state and federal levels.

HOLLYWOOD - Lee Magid, president

for release this month are two Ip's, "Boss

Band and "Blues Man," premiering Rod 
Piazza as a featured performer on har- 
monica.

CBS Records Names 
2 To WC Pub. Dept 
NEW YORK - Bob Altshuler, vice 
president information services, CBS 
Records Group, has announced two 
shifts in the CBS Records west coast 
publicity office: Pat Siciliano has been 
promoted to the newly created position 
of west coast manager press and infor- 
mation, Epic and Columbia Custom 
Labels and Charley Copien has been ap- 
pointed to Siciliano's former position as 
general publicist Columbia Records, 
west coast. Both appointments were 
made by Judy Paynter, assistant director 
press & information, west coast. 
These two appointments come as an 
expansion of the responsibilities of the 
west coast publicity office. 
In his new capacity, Pat Siciliano will 
be responsible for maintaining press 
relations on behalf of Epic and Columbia 
Custom labels with various publications, 
both consumer and trade, throughout 
the western region. He will also perform 
other publicity functions, including in- 
volvement with the Epic and Columbia 
Custom artists based on the west coast. 
Siciliano joined CBS Records in 1972 
as general publicist in CBS Records' 
west coast office, a position he has held 
until his new promotion. Prior to joining 
CBS Records, he worked for A&M 
Records in their publicity department. 
Charley Copien joins CBS Records af- 
ter having worked at ABC/Dunhill 
Records as a publicist. Before that, he 
was a writer for Cash Box in Los Angeles. 
In his new capacity at CBS Records, 
Copien will assist Judy Paynter in the 
direction of all press and information ser- 
vices for the west coast area.

Wartoke Makes 
2 WC Appointments 
LOS ANGELES - The Wartoke Concern 
has announced the opening of a West 
Coast office here staffed by Barbara 
DeWitt and Mary Greifinger, who join 
Pat Costello, Jane Friedman and Rod 
Jacobson as full partners in the publicity 
and public relations company. Assisting 
DeWitt and Greifinger in the Los 
Angeles office will be Janet Ferguson. 
Ms. DeWitt, whose career in the music 
business spans 10 years, began doing 
publicity for New York's Bitter End, 
before joining United Artists in 
promotion in New York. She later 
headed up UA publicity in London for 
three years before opening her own 
publicity company there, Three's Com- 
pany, which specialized in arrranging 
tours and tour publicity for American 
acts touring Europe. She then returned 
to the U.S. to do worldwide publicity for 
Frank Zappa's film "200 Motels", and 
later rejoined UA publicity where she 
remained in various capacities until 
joining Wartoke. 
Greifinger, a veteran of eight years in 
the music business, also comes from 
United Artists, where he was in UA's 
publicity department. Before moving to 
the West Coast, he spent four years as 
director of publicity and artist relations in 
UA's East Coast office. Greifinger began 
his career as a freelance writer and 
published his own magazine, Teen's Top 
Ten before joining United Artists five 
years ago. The Wartoke Concern is cur- 
rently celebrating it's fifth anniversary.

RAY CHARLES - ARTIST AND MAN: TOTAL CREATIVITY 
Everything must start with the individual," said Ray Charles. The interview took 
place in his suite in the stately Waldorf Astoria. Ray was headlining in the famed Em- 
pire Room at the Hotel; but he was totally relaxed and ready to talk when 
I sat down 
with him shortly after the noon hour. He was sitting at a card table with a deck in his 
hands. My thoughts, for a moment, ran wildly as 
I tried to key into some relevant facts 
about the professional life of the man whose career has spanned some thirty years. 
But 
I had no need to fear. In a second he was discussing his total love for music. And, 
music is his life. 
"There is always something to guide you in your life," he said, and "life does offer 
two choices which will either come up as a minus or as a plus. 
I must be good to 
myself - 
I study myself to maintain an aware -positive outlook. How can one be aware 
of what life is all about if the individual is not 'aware' and being 'for -real'. This 
awareness, of course, does develop to the point where it is possible to determine the 
realness. Growth and maturity after all, are the true measures of 'the man'." 
Ray says that he sees a lot of Stevie Wonder in himself. What Stevie is all about, Ray 
recalls, is not unlike what his young years were. Ray, born in Albany, Ga., said that his 
parents took him to Florida when he was about 6 -months old. Also, at the age of five, 
Ray was totally aware of tonal sound. And, the keyboard served as the front for a 
creative flow that has not stopped. Ray attended the St. Augustine School For The 
Blind. According to Henry Stone (Tone Distributing), Ray cut some material for a label 
of Henry's called 'Rockin' Records'. Ray was also with the 'Swingtime' label, and 
releases included "Kiss Me Baby," "I'm Going Down To The River And Kill Myself. 
Then, with one of his first releases on Atlantic, "It Should Have Been Me," it laun- 
ched him with the label and a string of hits. In '57, "Swanee River Rock" firmly set the 
tone for his creative writing ability. His association with Atlantic remained thru 1960, 
during which time he had some releases on Impulse. Then began his long association 
with ABC. "Sticks And Stones" and "Georgia On My Mind" were top charters. In '61, 
"Hit The Road Jack" was a number one seller. He repeated with a number one seller 
in '62 with "I Can't Stop Loving You." His influence on the total musical scene is im- 
possible to measure. He said, "I Can't Get Away From My Roots", and, after all an ar- 
tist does "become disillusioned if nobody is paying attention to what you are doing". 
But, it must be noted that countless millions pay attention to Ray Charles. Whether 
one grooves to his records or catches him in -concert, the beauty and excitement is 
never lacking. He simply turns one on with his whole heart and soul. "Music is meant 
to be inspirational and alive. 
I always try to relate to a 'true feeling', something in 
which people relate too." 
He is truly a man who continually strives to improve and progress. He has done it all 
- concerts, TV, Sound Tracks such as, "In The Heat Of The Night" which was a top 
seller in '67, and he has given his all. Good gracious Lord, the man can sing the blues. 
He can make one cry and that is good for the soul. "Your Cheating Heart" a '62 marker 
along with "Born to Lose" plus many others. "That Lucky Old Sun" came along in '63. 
The ABC hits came rolling right along until 1970. 
Ray Charles is now on the Crossover label. His current release, "Louise" typifies 
the total stature of this musical giant. Ray said, "The only difference between those 
early recording days and the recordings of today, is that the day of the $200. sessions 
are over. Blacks are now on a more equitable footing when it comes to recording. "Ar- 
tists and producers doing record sessions today, including black talents, have at their 
disposal the finest in studio technology and equipment. And, tomorrow we can ex- 
pect more.- Undoubtedly, we can and will be able to share with Ray Charles more of 
what he is about. For he is, above all, a creative musical giant.

WET WILLIE - CHARACTER SMILIN' THROUGH 
In a dimly lit corner of a notorious singles bar, a curiously loud conversation took 
place between Capricorn vice-president and national publicity director Mike Hyland, 
Jimmy Hall and Rick Hirsch, lead singer and lead guitarist respectively of the now 
renowned Wet Willie Band, and yours truly. The discussion, while centered upon the 
group's new Capricorn LP, "Keep On Smilin'," also touched upon the massive Grand 
Funk tour which afforded the band an opportunity to play before thousands of fans 
every night, a far cry from the Southern gin mills and go-go bars where the fellows got 
their start. 
"It certainly was different in those days," recalled Hall, his eyes fixed upon the Vic- 
torian decor of the restaurant. "We'd have to play five and sometimes six sets a night, 
so we had no choice but to get it together." Hirsch looked up from his steak and 
potatoes nodding assent, saying, "We used to work hard all the time, but now we're 
getting a chance to play for a wider audience and their reaction is one of the things 
that keeps us going." 
Of course the fact that the group has established itself through countless appearan- 
ces across the country and the success of three previous LP's ("Wet Willie," "Wet Wil- 
lie II," and "Drippin' Wet,") has to be considered sufficient motivation to keep them on 
their toes. One of the most significant turn of events for Wet Willie took place in 
January, 1974 when the group was introduced to Atlantic Records producer Tom 
Dowd, an old friend of Capricorn president Phil Walden. Dowd sat down with the band 
and listened to them play the material that ultimately wound up on the "Keep On 
Smilin' " LP and made the decision to produce the group. He recalls his first impres- 
sion of Wet Willie as that of an extremely motivated and dedicated band with a unique 
quality - character. 
The final pieces began to fall into place after the band played a sold -out New Year's 
Eve concert at New Orleans' celebrated Warehouse in which they used the services 
of the Williettes who are now a permanent part of the group. Dowd stated up front that 
"Keep On Smilin' " would not be "a typical Wet Willie album." Though the accent has 
shifted somewhat away from the "Shout Bamalama" sound that so many of the 
group's early followers became so partial towards, the songs have matured musically 
to the extent that the group has reached the charts with the powerful title track single 
off the LP, something they would have hitherto considered somewhat unlikely. 
"Tom Dowd helped us refine our sound and polish it up for the record," stated Hall, 
"but he never asked us to play anything we didn't feel comfortable with. The energy 
7- 
d t 
1tä 
á 
and feeling is still there and that's something that'll never go away. Hirsch added, "In 
terms of technique Tom helped us shape our ideas without taking them over." Ob- 
viously the finished product speaks for itself and the sales figures point to the recep- 
tion both single and LP are getting in all major markets in the country, but another sig- 
nificant fact is the support that Capricorn is throwing into the success of the album. 
According to Walden, the label is launching the biggest merchandising and sales 
campaign in its history for the LP, one that will include displays and a host of 
promotional items. The confidence Walden, Frank Fenter, Hyland, and all the 
Capricorn people are showing in the group and its new product is merely an exten- 
sion of the confidence and poise they assume each time they take the stage to per- 
form or go into the studio to cut a tune. 
The band, consisting of Hall on lead vocals, sax, and harp, Hirsch on lead guitar, 
Jack Hall on bass, John Anthony on keyboards, Lewis Ross on drums and Donna Hall 
and Ella Avery (the Williettes) on backing vocals, should be sufficiently pleased with 
all the activity they've stirred up to last them for quite some time, but laziness is not 
among their qualities. "We're a hard workin' band," stated Jimmy Hall, as if he needed 
to remind anyone of the fact, "and we don't intend to stop doin' what's been success- 
ful for us so far. Now is no time to rest on our past achievements." 
With an attitude like that, Wet Willie has tossed its hat into the toughest arena in all 
of show business - the pop music field. But there are no trembling hearts or in- 
decisive heads among the group or at Capricorn. The fruits of hard labor which the 
band is finally getting a chance to savor, will only serve to spur them on to greater 
achievements in the future. Hirsch noted that the band, despite a heavy touring 
schedule, is determined to put in an appearance at the Capricorn annual bar -b -que to 
be held this August in Macon spotlighting Capricorn month, not only to party, but to 
thank all the fine people who work behind the scenes in valuable capacities. 
With a solid track record already to its credit and praise flowing in from everywhere 
as a result of the gigantic cross-country tour, the best seems still to lie ahead for Wet 
Willie. Certainly Tom Dowd's production assistance as well as Phil Walden's guidance 
and encouragement have been a big part of the story, but let's never forget the guts 
and intelligence it takes for any band to emerge from the local bar level to superstar 
status. If any band deserves the good fortune that ultimately is the reward for hard 
work and persistence, Wet Willie does. Keep on smilin'. 
david budge.

EAST COASTINGS - Off and running, the answer to last week's "Rock and Roll: The 
Way We Were" photoquiz #12, was The Serendipity Singers, whose name was almost 
enough to make p.d.'s from coast to coast sit up and take notice whenever the folk ar- 
tists released a new disk. They were giants in that early and mid -Sixties folk 
revolution. This week's mystery artists, #13 in this series, were super British hit - 
makers during that British Invasion period, but had little success here in America. 
This five -man band's hits in Great Britain were many and their name should be 
familiar to any British rock fan of the period. Answer here next week. 
Talk about rock and roll getting tougher, Yes had an experience recently they may 
care to forget. The concert was held at the Palais des Sports in Paris, but was held up 
because the group's equipment arrived late from America. When said equipment did 
arrive, it was immediately noticed that two of Rick Wakeman's Moog synthesizers 
were smashed by the airline, unintentionally, of course. Then, 700 ticket forgeries 
were discovered at the door. The unruly mob waiting outside was repelled by firemen 
sporting hoses ... The annual Schaeffer Music Festival begins in New York City's 
Central Park (Wollman Memorial Ice Skating Rink) on June 12. All tickets, priced at 
$2.50 and $1.50, still remain as the best pop music bargain in the world. Some of the 
acts to be appearing this Summer in the Big Apple include; the original Righteous 
Brothers (billed with the original Sam and Dave); Melanie; the James Gang (with 
Maggie Bell and Steeleye Span also on the bill); John Sebastian; Todd Rundgren's 
Utopia; John McLaughlin's Mahavishnu Orchestra; King Crimson (billed with Golden 
Earring); ZZ Top with Brownsville Station; Robert Klein (with Melissa Manchester and 
Jim Dawson; the anxiously awaited new trio of Richie Furay, John David Söuther and 
Chris Hillman (billed with the incredible Leo Kottke); America; Jesse Colin Young, 
Linda Ronstadt, Martin Mull (all on the same bill); Harry Chapin; Poco; Dave Mason; 
Boz Scaggs, Anne Murray & Brewer and Shipley (on the same bill); Uriah Heep and 
Manfred Mann together; the Earl Scruggs Revue (billed with the Charlie Daniels Band 
and David Bromberg); the Marshall Tucker Band; Don McLean; Billy Cobham, billed 
with Deodato; Peter Frampton and Montrose; the Pointer Sisters; Foghat; Lynyrd 
Skynyrd; and Savoy Brown. An excellent line-up of talent. It all promises to be a 
super -Summer in New York (that is, of course, if the weather ever gets itself 
together).

COMMENT ... With Summer just about here, it's time I mentioned the aspect of rock 
and roll and it's almost medicinal value on the big city populous. Here in New York, 
Summer has always meant an amazing number of pop concerts, therefore a place for 
the young to congregate when the streets (and tempers sometimes) get hot. The 
Schaeffer Festival is probably the best case in point, due, not only to the low price, 
and pleasant concert (outdoor) atmosphere, but to the low price that has the young 
wallet in mind. The out -of -school youngster not only gets the best possible entertain- 
ment, but can afford it and has a good time in the process. Summer in the city is 
tough, but it's getting easier thanks to promoters with the consumer in mind. 
arty good man 
POINTS WEST - Early summer activity is gurgling all around us these days with a 
flurry of movement stepped up in local recording studios, concert promotion offices 
et al. Those reported to be waxing at A&M studios currently include Billy 
Preston, Joan Baez, Jack Jones, Joni Mitchell and Cheech and Chong. The latter duo 
has been cropping up in such distant locales as Zagreb, Yugoslavia (well-known 
center of the Serbo-Croatian recording industry) where their "Basketball Jones" film 
short will be presented by Ode Visuals at the Second Annual World Animated Film 
Festival. Meanwhile, back at the Ranch (Caribou) Jim Guercio and Chicago are 
working on "Chicago VIII" and preparations are being made for the onslaught of 3 
Dog Night and, later on in August, Elton John. At Village Recorders, it was Les 
McCann (with Joel Dorn producing) John Lee Hooker (Ed Michel) and Gene Harris, 
with Keg Johnson producing for United Artists. Clover had the Section working on 
their next LP, Paul Rothchild finishing up Cottonwood South's album for Columbia 
and Linda Ronstadt will be arriving there soon to do her next with Peter Asher. 
Mason's at Cherokee Studios, finishing an LP and shopping for a label, which just 
might turn out to be either RCA or MGM. John Haeny has been set to produce John 
Klemmer's next for Impulse. He's currently engineering for Tom Jones and the 
afore -mentioned Cottonwood South. Expect new LPs, fairly soon, from Steve Miller, 
who's booked some time at Kaye -Smith up in Seattle, Seals and Crofts, and Coven; 
the latter group is finishing up at the Producer's Workshop. 
An organization called the Wings Fun Club has emerged in London, a belated 
attempt at reviving Beatlemania. That Bill Wyman billboard on Sunset Blvd. almost 
didn't make it. Apparently, some stuffy billboard operators (with no allusion intended 
to another publication) demanded that the top be chopped off of one of the bananas. 
Aesthetics, fortunately, prevailed. 
Led Zeppelin is supposedly interested in doing a bunch of festivals this summer, 
with Hawaii and Ontario, Calif. mentioned as prime targets. The group will also 
partake in an English fest that will also feature Van Morrison, The Doobie Brothers, 
the Allman Brothers, Mahavishnu and Tim Buckley. 
David Cassidy, currently on the loose, will reportedly be emerging with a new 
affiliation within the next week or so. Cheyenne, a new Bell Records act has arranged 
a new production deal with Norman Malkin. 
Congratulations to Frank and Gail Zappa on the recent birth of their son, Ahmet 
Rodin Zappa. Frank is reportedly looking for a girl "with a strong voice and acting 
ability" to play the role of the Queen of Cosmic Greed in an upcoming film project. 
The girl must also be "adaptable to the Mothers' act" and we wish her lots of luck.

Regarding the news story about The Platters, which ran in the May 25 issue of CB 
R&B News Report, picking up some history of the Buck Ram Associated Platters from 
1954, Ralph Bass informed this office that the story begins in 1953. Ralph says that 
he founded The Platters in 1953 by placing Toni Williams with a local Los Angeles 
group called The Platters. Ralph also says that he cut several sessions with them 
before Buck Ram came into the picture. "I recorded them for a label called Federal a 
subsidiary of King Records. In fact, "Only You their first hit was recorded for me as 
their producer before they re-recorded it for Mercury," said Ralph. Sorry for the goof. 
Just trying to set some platters ... Be on the loockout for a new Donnie Elbert album 
coming from Trip Records ..

From Pittsburgh 
PITTSBURGH - A new soul label 
known as SOULVATION ARMY 
RECORDS has been formed in Pitt- 
sburgh as a division of Western World 
Music, located in suburban Carnegie, 
Pennsylvania. 
Bill Lawrence who also owns and 
operates Pittsburgh's largest one -stop 
heads the Western World complex which 
houses a complete sixteen track studio, 
custom pressing plant and the label's of- 
fices in a brand new luxury building. 
Reporting directly to Lawrence will be 
director of Sales and Promotion, Alan 
Leeds. Leeds is best known for his leng- 
thy relationship with James Brown 
Productions where he served as 
publicity director and later as booking 
manager for the James Brown roadshow. 
Leeds' experience also includes stints 
with Kool and the Gang, Starday-King 
Records, Gene Redd Productions and as 
a deejay for WANT Radio in Richmond, 
Virginia. 
Leeds is quick to admit that a strange 
story surrounds the debut release on 
SOULVATION ARMY, "Yesterday Stan- 
ding By" by These Gents. 
"Initially the record came to us as an 
outside master and we released it on the 
parent label, Western World. Response 
in many key markets was strong but we 
felt the production quality could be im- 
proved. We decided to re -cut it in our 
own studios. We have no reservations 
anymore and indications are already that 
we have a hit!" 
Leeds has set out on a lengthy 
promotional tour which will include the 
Carolinas, New York, Philadelphia, 
Boston & the Midwest. 
Rustic Records 
First LP Release 
HOLLYWOOD - Neil Ames, general 
manager of Rustic Records has announ- 
ced the release of the label's first LP 
product. The LP, titled "The Check- 
mates, Bobby Stevens, Sonny Charles 
and Sweet Louie have had releases on a 
variety of major labels, including the 
top -ten hit, "Black Pearl," on A&M 
Records. Recently, they decided to 
pursue their careers in the form of an in- 
dependent label. "This is show 
business," Stevens emphasized, "not 
merely show. For too long, artists, and 
especially black artists, have received 
the lop -sided end of record deals. Rustic 
Records hopes to help change that 
situation."

LOS ANGELES - Hillery Johnson, 
director of R&B Products for Playboy 
Records has announced the signing of

Master" for the U.S.

label in the U.K., has been getting exten- 
sive discotheque play in New York, 
where copies of the import were being 
sold for as high as five dollars a copy.

of Hillery Johnson, who immediately 
recognized the potential of the single as 
well as the artist.

ned almost every aspect of the music 
business. He was musical director for 
five years at Brunswick Records and 
helped establish name acts such as the 
Chi -Lites, Barbara Acklin, Lost 
Generation, Jackie Wilson, and Tyrone 
Davis. As a producer, his credits include 
several national chart hits, and he has 
produced such acts as Tyrone Davis, Lit- 
tle Richard, Laine Kazan, King Curtis, 
and the Beautiful Zion Choir. 
Tyree Glenn 
Is Dead 
At Sixty -One 
NEW YORK - Tyree Glenn, who played 
the trombone and vibraphone during the 
big band era died Saturday (18) in 
Englewood (N.J.) Hospital. He was 61 
years of age and lived at 308 West 
Englewood Avenue in Englewood. 
Glenn joined Louis Armstrong's All - 
Stars in 1964 and stayed until Arm- 
strong's death in 1971. Armstrong and 
Glenn would switch parts when Arm- 
strong was not capable of hitting the high 
register. Glenn organized á sextet which 
played at the Royal Box in the 
Americana Hotel. 
He picked up the vibraphone while 
with Lionel Hampton, and played five 
years with the Ethel Waters group. In 
1949 he was asked to join the Duke El- 
lington group. He also was a member of a 
quintet that was part of Jack Sterling's 
early morning WCBS program. 
Survivors include his widow, Gloria, 
and two sons, Tyree Jr. and Roger. The 
funeral was on Thursday (23) in the Cen- 
tral Presbyterian Church, 593 Park 
Avenue.

Barskin, Jossey 
Form Music Firm 
For Country Acts 
HOLLYWOOD - Doovid Barskin, former 
director of business affairs at Capitol 
Records in Hollywood, and John Jossey, 
former vice president 
in charge of 
distribution at Capitol, 
have formed 
Music Support Inc., a multi -music com- 
pany with various divisions, specializing 
in country music. 
Music Support Inc., the parent firm, 
represents Buck Owens 
Enterprises, 
and 
is 
coordinating, 
with 
Capitol 
Records, in the marketing and promotion 
of such artists as Buck Owens, Susan 
Raye, Buddy Allan, Freddy Hart, Tony 
Booth and Lawanda Lindsey. 
"We have gone into the country end of 
the music industry," explained Barskin, 
"because I see it still growing, and with a 
tremendous future." 
Barskin and Jossey have also set up 
Naptown 
Records 
as 
a record and 
distribution company, which is handling 
Cliffie Stone's Granite label, plus Sonny 
Burke's Daybreak Records. Both are 
well known in the country music field. 
An ASCAP and BMI company has 
been set up as the company's music 
publishing wing. Music Support Inc. is 
located 
at 6255 Sunset Blvd., 
Los 
Angeles, Calif. 90028. Phone number is 
(213) 461-4215. 
Jennings To Appear 
At N.Y.'s Bottom Line 
NEW YORK - Recently in New York, 
Waylon Jenning's purpose was twofold 
for visiting the "Big Apple." He filmed a 
television interview at RCA studios for 
UPI Services. And he negotiated a five 
day stint at New York's newest club The 
Bottom Line. This appearance will be 
another major step foward for the in- 
tegaration of country music into the New 
York metropolitan area. His gig starts on 
July 30th. 
Having had the good fortune to chat 
with Jennings at the RCA studios here in 
Manhattan, 
I found him to be affable and 
ready to discuss country music in 
general and his career in particular. Jen- 
nings stated," It's now becoming hip to 
be country." And one need only look 
around this area and see what a tremen- 
dous influx of country music there has 
been. Jennings has been categorized as 
a singer of "country soul." Though 
categorizations of this type are arbitrary 
at best, it means that he incorporates a 
little more r&b and rock into his country 
sounds and comes up with a brand of 
music that puts him in the same class as 
Willie Nelson. As a matter of fact he and 
Nelson are good friends and have been 
for quite a while. 
"People are reaching for something to 
be real," he says. And this is why he does 
not alter his set for a specific region. The 
same set he would play in Ft. Worth 
Texas would be played in Los Angeles 
and New York. As a matter of fact he has 
played the Troubadour in Los Angeles 
and this new wave of pop clubs is self ad- 
mittedly a new facet of Jennings' career. 
"I'm into playing showcase places," he 
says and he added "I never change. If 
they (the audience), are going to like us 
they are going to like us for what we do." 
And this firm conviction of musical in- 
tegrity remains the steadfast tenet which 
Jennings gears his music to. 
Jennings is working on a very special 
LP which will be a tribute to the late 
Buddy Holly. He is working with the 
Crickets, Holly's old back-up band and 
the sessions are being co -produced by 
Duane Eddy and Jennings. It is an LP 
that we look to with great enthusiasm. m.d.

EAST COASTINGS - Off and running, the answer to last week's "Rock and Roll: The 
Way We Were" photoquiz #14, was Jackie DeShannon, whose hits during the Super 
Sixties were numerous. They included "What The World Needs Now Is Love," "The 
Weight," "When You Walk In The Room" and others. She's still recording, on the 
Atlantic label now, and her new single, released last week, is "Jimmie Just Sing Me 
One More Song," a disk that should become a smash if given the proper label and 
radio support. Check it out. This week's photo #15 in this series, is a duo who scored 
once on a major scale and faded after that disk ran its successful course. This one is 
tough. Answer here next week... 
Rick Springfield, teen idol, while preparing to debut his new Rick Springfield Band 
at Max's Kansas City, was the victim of a freak accident that landed the Australian rock 
and roller in the hospital and almost caused postponement of his premiere New York 
City performance. During a dress rehearsal, a rented amplifier attached to Rick's 
guitar proved to have a faulty ground. Grabbing hold of the microphone in front of 
him with both hands, Springfield received a massive electrical shock which sent him 
flying onto the stage floor. On the way down, he struck his head on an electric piano, 
opening a gash. He was rushed to St. Vincent's Hospital in the Village where he was 
stitched up and released. Believe it or not, he went on that night ... Laura Nyro 
emerged from her very private life recently to attend a LaBelle concert in Philly. The 
show fell on the same day as Patti LaBelle's birthday so, after the show, Laura and the 
group returned to Patti's house for a birthday party and a sing -along of all the material 
they did together on the "Gonna Take A Miracle" LP, released a couple of seasons 
back ... The Manhattans are back in the studio recording their next LP (Sigma Sound 
in Philly ... Don Nix has announced that he is marrying Claudia Lennear ... An- 
nouncements have been coming fast and furious from the Yes group. First, Rick 
Wakeman has announced he will be leaving to further pursue his solo career. Secon- 
dly, Steve Howe has announced he will be cutting his debut solo LP sometime this 
summer. Aside from his usual guitar, Howe stated that he will also be playing bass 
and drums for the album. No way of knowing at this point whether he plans to split the 
group or not ... 
Two dates have been added to the Eric Clapton tour. They are July 10 at the 
Providence Civic Center and July 21 at the Cow Palace, San Francisco ... Spooky 
Tooth is near completion of their latest LP with Eddie Kramer and Gary Wright 
Rock And Roll:

producing ... According to lead vocalist Peter Gabriel, Genesis will not return to the 
U.S. to tour until late Fall. The group is currently working on their new LP in England . 
.. Chicago has gone to producer Jim Guercio's Nederland, Colo. ranch to begin work

Brothers recording artists, The Good Rats, a local band here in New York with a large 
following, are in the process of recording their debut LP for the label. Stephan Galfas 
is producing. The LP is scheduled for release sometime late this summer ... Elliott 
Randall has officially joined Sha Na Na as lead guitarist on a permanent basis. He 
replaces Chris Donald who passed away following an appearance while the group 
was on tour... 
Add this week's rocking and rolling birthdays: Paul McCartney (June 18), Richard 
Perry (also June 18); Elaine "Spanky" McFarlane (Spanky and Our Gang) and Al 
Wilson (both June 19); Brian Wilson (Beach Boys) (June 20); Ray Davies (Kinks), Nils 
Lofgren, Brenda Holloway, O. C. Smith and Joey Mullen (of Badfinger) (all June 21); 
Alan Osmond, Peter Asher and Howard Kaylan (Flo & Eddie) (all June 22). Happy 
birthday to all ... 
Linda Ronstadt's newest single from her still incredible "Don't Cry Now" LP should 
be a two sided winner. "Colorado" is officially listed as the A side with "Desperado" on 
the flip. Both are incredible ballads, two of the best the lovely lady has ever turned 
out. Given the chance, Linda is the one lady in the business who can kill us all softly 
with her songs. Hopefully, the audiences around America (and the world) will take the 
time to listen ... The summer concert scene here in the Apple seems to be getting 
brighter every week. This week, the schedule of shows for the Asbury Park (N.J.) 
Casino Arena was announced. They include: King Crimson & Golden Earring (June 
28); Blue Oyster Cult and Aerosmith (July 5); America (July 16); The Marshall Tucker 
Band (July 20); Climax Blues Band (August 10); Joe Walsh and Barnstorm (August 
17); New Riders Of The Purple Sage (August 24); and Loggins and Messina (August 
24). As other dates are announced, they will be printed in this column. At least we'll 
have rock and roll here this Summer if nothing else... 
COMMENT - This week's comment again revolves around people, specifically those 
in the music industry. It's simple and goes ... Misery may love company, but don't in- 
volve those who don't want it, or need it. You all know who you are out there, too. 
arty goodman 
in new york 
POINTS WEST - What began as an unusual booking last week metamorphosed into 
what might have been the first great 60's folke-nostalgia review. The Nitty Gritty Dirt 
Band had been set to play the Troubadour beginning Thursday, leaving an empty 
spot for Tuesday and Wednesday nights. Phil Ochs was asked to fill in but he refused 
to do so unless the club's owner, Doug Weston also took to the stage. Doug, the club's 
founder, had never before appeared there in all the years of the club's operation but, 
in an apparent fit of bravado, agreed to Phil's suggestion. Soon after the set's begin- 
ning, after Phil had sung his "Bells" song and Doug Weston had read "The Love Song 
of J. Alfred Prufrock," members of the audience began filing on stage to sing, rap and 
swill Doug's wine. ("Dilute it with water!" he yelled to a waitress.) 
Appearances were eventually made by ex-Monkee Peter Tork, who flailed a banjo 
(which he used to do regularly at a New York joint called the Four Winds, back in 
pre -Kirshner days), Dorsey Burnett and son, David Blue (who tried but just couldn't 
ruin his "Grand Hotel" song), Bob Lind (who sounded pretty good and ingratiated 
himself to the audience by not singing "Bright Elusive Butterfly of Love"). Dave Dil- 
lard, and producer Peter Asher (ex -Peter and Gordon) who teamed with Chad Stuart 
(ex -Chad and Jeremy) for a medley of their combined repertoires. David Clayton - 
Thomas also did a song and to and behold, Jerry Moss was eventually summoned to 
the stage where he found himself explaining why A&M hasn't released Phil's live LP 
("Gunfight in Carnegie Hall") in this country; the album is on the racks in Canada. A 
second set, later that evening, had Jackson Browne and Loudon Wainwright on the 
stage. Hell of a night. 
GENERAL STUFF - Unconfirmed rumors are running rampant through the street 
concerning the upcoming move of a New York -based Columbia exec to a top position 
at United Artists. We should find out soon. Richard Perry has been floating about 
town, to and from a series of meetings at United Artists, Warner Brothers, Capitol and 
possibly others. Something's going on. Pam Grier and Bobby Womack have been 
conferring on a film project lately which turns out to be a movie about Sam Cooke. 
War guitarist Howard Scott recently injured himself doing something or other; he was 
hospitalized briefly but is now back in action. Congratulations to Synthia James of 
Shelter Records on a sexy photo spread in Players magazine. 
Don Hartman of the Edgar Winter Group flew into town recently to pick up a new 
"guitar suit," designed for him by Bill Witten. A weird contraption, the suit features a 
built-in chordless guitar with volume controls located on the sleeve. No word on what 
was happening at ABC -Dunhill last week but police, who were scurrying about and 
later, guarding the building, have long departed. Epic is planning a major promotional 
event for the first week in July. They'll fly 7 of their acts through the northwest 
(Spokane, Seattle and Portland) for what they're calling "An Epic Event." Major 
changes have been taking place at David Bowie's Mainman Productions. Cherry 
Vanilla has already left the firm to start a new radio -video production company and we 
hear that Lee Childers and Pat Wadsley have also left ... Apologies to Andy Meyer for 
misspelling his name. 
Bernie Taupin, whose book of poems will soon be published, is or was in town 
looking for an illustrator. And last month's rumor that had Elton John planning a split 
from MCA has now been supplanted by claims that he will soon sign a new contract 
with the company. (Mike Maitland was recently in England for negotiations). Aren't 
rumors fun? 
Phil Ochs, Brewer and Shipley. Loudon Wainwright. Dan Hartman 
A recent ad in Daily Variety was addressed to Island president Charley Nuccio. 
"This town isn't big enough for the two of us," it said and was signed by Bob Levinson. 
No explanation was given for the ominous -sounding message. 
EXHIBIT "A" - Popular legal hassles making the news this week include a Frank 
Zappa-A.T.I. litigation that reached our ears in the form of a hefty 34 page brief. And 
Reb Foster is after Three Dog Night for a whopping 2-1/4 million, sought in a breach of 
contract suit stemming from the recently completed Caribou -3 Dog production deal. 
We haven't read the brief yet, but it promises to be equally exciting. Aren't law suits 
fun? 
SIGNINGS - Blue Thumb has an LP from a fella named Ken Burgan called "The 
Big Bow -Wow Strain." Ken, who was introduced to the label via Dan Hicks, produced 
the record himself. Neil Merryweather completed negotiations with Phonogram and 
his "Space Rangers" LP will be reaching us in July via the Mercury label. He'll be 
touring with Bachman -Turner Overdrive for a spell, possibly with collaborator Tim 
McGovern. Capitol has signed Mike Lookinland, an actor who is featured on the 
"Brady Bunch" series; they'll release his first single soon. And Epic's new act is called 
Masters Of The Airways; they're produced by Michael Sunday and Norm Curbon. 
RECORDING GRUNDGE - Let's see, we had Roger McGuinn at the Record Plant, 
being produced by Bill Halverson who was also busy working with Steve Stills. Al 
Kooper was there as well, laboring on an unidentified project. Clover was the site of 
some new Temptations sessions, engineered by Robert Appere and produced by 
Steve Cropper (!). Gotta hear that. The Crusaders are at Heiders working on their 5th 
LP for Blue Thumb. They'll be embarking soon on that European -African tour. Brewer 
and Shipley were at it again, and this time the guest musicians included members of 
the Eagles. Capitol is preparing to release some old Sid Barrett product (ex -Pink 
Floyd) that was previously unavailable in this country. The New Riders of The Purple 
Sage, complete with Skip Baffin, will be going into the studios sometime this summer. 
B. J. and David Foster brought their Skylark group into Clover and A&M studios were 
playing host to Tango. 
THIS BUSINESS OF PARTY -GOING - On the slow side here last week, but back 
east, The Who were supposedly getting together a bash at a local roller rink. For en- 
tertainment, the band hired two roller derby teams to mix it up on the floor. Top that 
one, Siciliano.
