New Guess Who 
GRT Sets 
To Be Held Up 
Oct. Release 
HOLLYWOOD - Burton Cummings, 
lead singer of The Guess Who, and new 
guitarist Dom Troiano, have co -written 
the next album for the RCA group, called 
"Flavors." A release date has been set 
for early January, according to manager 
Don Hunter. 
There is a good chance the label will 
not distribute the record for some time, 
since The Guess Who's "Road Food" LP 
is doing well in sales and on the charts, 
while their single "Clap For The Wolf - 
man" is currently a hit. 
Speaking about his newest writing 
partner, Cummings said: "Things are a 
lot better than they've been for years." 
As for "Flavors," Cummings thought 
there might even be a country hit off the 
album. 
"I used to know what hit singles were, 
and 
I don't really any more," the lead 
singer admitted. "I never expected 'Star 
Baby' or 'Wolfman' to be hits. They were 
flukes. But we've got pretty good com- 
mercial roots - 
I grew up on AM radio, 
and it comes round to that again, sooner 
or later. So here we go again."

NARAS Readies 
Lecture Bureau 
NEW YORK - A new Recording 
Academy Lecture Bureau has been for- 
med by NARAS. It will be administered 
by the American Program Bureau of 
Boston. 
Bob Walker, president of the American 
Program Bureau, is presently coor- 
dinating plans for a series of seminars 
and lectures at colleges and universities 
across the country. Recording Academy 
members from all sectors of the industry 
will be invited to participate in either 
one- or two-day group seminars or in- 
dividual lecture appearances before 
campus audiences. 
Emphasis in both lectures and 
seminars will be placed on educational 
information, with special attention given 
to the professional opportunities open to 
college students who wish to pursue a 
career in the music industry. 
Edvard Moritz Dies 
NEW YORK - Edvard Moritz, composer 
and symphonic conductor in both the 
United States and Europe, died in New 
York City on Sept. 30. Mr. Moritz, who 
was born in Hamburg, Germany on June 
23, 1891 was 83. 
A member of the American Society of 
Composers, Authors and Publishers 
since 1939, he wrote many orchestral 
works. His compositions included four 
symphonies, two piano concertos, and 
many works for chamber groups. He is 
survived by his widow, Johanna.

Friedman Joins 
ABC E/Coast PR 
LOS ANGELES - Christie Barter, direc- 
tor of communications at ABC Records, 
has announced the appointment of Larry 
Friedman to the position of publicity 
coordinator in the company's east coast 
office. Friedman comes to ABC from the 
New York office of Solters & Roskin, 
where he had been assistant to the head 
of the music department since 1971. 
In his new position, Friedman is 
charged with coordinating publicity ef- 
forts on behalf of ABC artists on tour as 
well as for those artists who come to New 
York. He will report to Howard Bloom, 
ABC's east coast manager of public and 
artist relations.

THE IMPULSE YEARS - Elvin Jones - 
Producers for Re -Issue: Ed Michel, Steve Backer 
- ABC/Impulse ASH -9283-2 
The amazing drumming talents of Elvin Jones 
come to life on this dynamic two record set which 
features the master percussionist playing with 
such greats as John Coltrane, Sonny Rollins, Mc- 
Coy Tyner, Richard Davis and Rashied Ali. Of the 
better selections on this great record set, we 
favor "Pursuance From A Love Supreme," 
"Shiny Stockings," "Aborigine Dance In 
Scotland," "Concluding Selection of Serenity" 
and "Vigil." Throughout both records Elvin main- 
tains as many as four different levels 
simultaneously and displays the master's touch. 
ELLINGTONIA, VOLUME TWO - Duke Ellington 
- Producers For Re -Issue: Ed Michel, Steve 
Backer - ABC/Impulse ASH -9285-2 
Featuring an enormous quantity of quality 
musicians, all of whom were close to the Duke, 
this retrospective two record LP serves as a 
beautiful reminder of the genius that was Duke 
Ellington. McCoy Tyner, Kenny Burrell, Charles 
Mingus and Grady Tate are but four of the more 
than two dozen musicians who are a part of this 
musical treasury which includes such selections 
as "Black And Tan Fantasy," "Do Nothing 'Til 
You Hear From Me," "East St. Louis Toodleoo" 
and "Action In Alexandria." A superlative collec- 
tion well worth listening to. 
BROTHER, THE GREAT SPIRIT MADE US ALL - 
Dave Brubeck: Two Generations of Brubeck - 
Producer: Michael Cuscuna - Atlantic SD 1660 
Dave Brubeck and his family have merged 
again in another delightful LP, one that definitely 
dispels the old myth that there is a universal 
generation gap. Darius Brubeck and his ensem- 
ble as well as Chris and Dan Brubeck join their 
talented father in a tour de force that reinforces 
the concept that the family that plays together 
stays together. Particularly enjoyable cuts here 
include "Mr. Broadway," "The Duke," "Temp- 
tation Boogie," "Christopher Columbus," "It's A 
Raggy Waltz" and "Sky Scape." A fun and ex- 
citing LP. 
FIRST LIGHT - The Family of Mann - Atlantic 
SD 1658 
Herbie Mann's impeccable musical reputation 
is further enhanced on this new Atlantic LP 
which features super 'family' members Pat Rebil- 
lot, David Newman, Tony Levin, Armen 
Halburian, Steve Gadd and Sam Brown. The 
relationship that develops musically between 
Herbie and these talented journeymen comes 
across strongly in bold, powerful strokes, 
especially on cuts such as "Toot Stick," "Sunrise 
Highs," "Lullaby For Mary Elizabeth," "Music Is 
A Game We Play" and "Thank You Mr. Rushing." 
A thoroughly enjoyable LP. 
UPON THIS ROCK - Joe Farrell - Producer: 
Creed Taylor - CTI 6042 S1 
Joe Farrell's mastery of tenor and soprano sax 
as well as flute has never been more evident 
than on his new CTI LP, one that features the 
talented jazz artist accompanied by Joe Beck on 
guitar, Steve Gadd ("I Won't Be Back") and Jim 
Madison on drums, Herb Bushier on bass, Her- 
bie Hancock (piano on "I Won't Be Back") and 
Don Alias (also on "I Won't Be Back"). "I Won't 
Be Back," an epic piece of some ten minutes, is 
one of the most compelling pieces of music 
we've ever heard -and the interplay between Far- 
rell and Hancock is breathtaking. 
THE FINAL SWING - Trapeze featuring Glenn 
Hughes - Producer: John Lodge - Threshold 
THS 11 
Glenn Hughes may have broken the group up 
with his decision in 1973 to join Deep Purple as 
its bassist, but the memories of Trapeze in some 
of its finer moments are captured here in a 
powerful retrospective set that features the band 
in those moments of blazing fury when they were 
masters of all they surveyed. Dave Holland on 
drums and Mel Galley on lead guitar com- 
plement Hughes' work on these tunes, notably 
"Send Me No More Letters," "Medusa," "Coast 
To Coast" and "Dats It."

cash box,' news 
Capitol Makes 
Shifts In PR Dept. 
HOLLYWOOD - Dan Davis, director, 
creative service and press, Capitol 
Records has announced a realignment 
of the Capitol Records' press depart- 
ment. 
Remaining in her post as national 
publicity manager is Patti Wright whose 
duties include the coordination of 
national press activities in relation to 
Capitol artists. Ms. Wright will provide 
national tour support for the company's 
major acts. in addition to providing 
publicity material for national trade and 
consumer publications. She will report 
directly to Davis. 
Effective immediately, Michael Leh- 
man has been named western publicity 
manager. Lehman was formerly an as- 
sistant to the vice president of the enter- 
tainment division of Rogers & Cowan, in 
addition to his freelance work for 
periodicals. His duties include working 
closely with Capitol sales and promotion 
in order to coordinate all efforts on 
behalf of Capitol artists appearing in the 
western half of the United States. He will 
also be responsible for generating album 
and concert reviews, and maintaining 
liaisons with the trade magazines and 
west coast consumer publications. Leh- 
man replaces J.R. Young who has been 
appointed manager, press and editorial 
services. Both will report directly to Ms. 
Wright, and all will work out of the 
Capitol Tower in Hollywood. 
Lehman's counterpart in the New York 
offices of Capitol is Soozin Kazick, 
eastern publicity manager. She has been 
with Capitol Records two years after ser- 
ving as the director of publicity for Bud- 
dah Records and then as the director of 
publicity and promotion for Grossman/ - 
Glotzer, a managerial firm based in New 
York. Kazick's duties will be the same as 
Lehman's except her operations will be 
east coast oriented. 
Kathy Wagner, national publicity coor- 
dinator, remains at her post in the Hol- 
lywood offices, and her duties include 
the production of publicity material, in- 
cluding bios, photos, and clippings of 
Capitol artists. She also maintains 
Capitol's mailing list to the press 
throughout the entire country. She has 
been with Capitol Records for five years. 
Says Davis: "We are delighted with the 
latest changes within the department, 
and we feel that this new fully experi- 
enced staff will be able to coordinate not 
only with the trade and consumer press, 
but also with the various related depart- 
ments within the Capitol Tower itself. No 
longer will the press department be 
separate from the other departments, 
but will integrate its activities closely 
with sales, merchandising, promotion, 
and the art departments.

Jay Warner Joins 
Wes Farrell Org. 
NEW YORK - Jay Warner. a multi- 
faceted music industry figure who has 
been involved in composing, production 
and management, has been promoted to 
the position of East Coast Director of 
Professional Activities for the Wes Far- 
rell Organization's publishing com- 
panies. 
Since his arrival at the company, War- 
ner's accomplishments have included 
originating and compiling the publishing 
industry's first musical quiz promotion, 
"Musi -Quiz", placement of songs with a 
number of acts, including Dawn, Johnny 
Winter, The Shirelles, and the First 
Class. 
Prior to joining the Farrell 
Organization in 1973, Warner served as 
assistant to the president of S.A.S., Inc., 
management company for B.B. King and 
Gladys Knight and the Pips. From 
1970-72 he served as General Manager 
of Record on Film Inc. and its affiliates, 
Exhibit Records and Hello Music 
Publishing. A record producer and song- 
writer, he has also written commercial 
and motion picture theme music.

GRC Appoints 
Mazur Director 
Creative Services 
HOLLYWOOD - General Recording 
Corporation announced the appointment 
of Ruby Mazur to the position of director 
of creative services for GRC, Aware and 
Hotlanta labels. Mazur was named to the 
creative post by GRC president Michael 
Thevis and GRDC president Buz 
Wilburn. 
In joining the GRC record complex 
headquartered in Atlanta, Mazur brings 
an experienced background in both 
executive and creative capacities, en- 
compassing over eight years in the 
music industry. His previous affiliations 
include positions with ABC/Dunhill as 
executive art director; Paramount 
Records as art director, and, most re- 
cently, creative director of Ivy Hill 
Packaging. 
During his tenure in the industry, he 
has designed and overseen the com- 
pletion of many national campaigns in- 
cluding such top selling artists as the 
Rolling Stones, Jim Croce, Rufus, Dusty 
Springfield. the James Gang, B. B. King, 
Dave Mason, Billy Joel, Elton John, 
James Brown, the Four Tops, etc. 
Mazur is credited with designing the 
Rolling Stones (single sleeve) "mouth 
and tongue" logo, recognized worldwide 
as the rock group's trademark. 
His background also includes a year's 
work in England where he designed 
album covers, posters and media adver- 
tising campaigns for various labels in- 
cluding Columbia, Warner Brothers, 
Polydor and M.C.A. 
In 1971 his album cover concept for 
the group, Crowfoot, brought a 
nomination for the Grammy Award com- 
petition. Two years later he received the 
Society of Illustrators Award for his Cur- 
tis Mayfield cover design. 
In his new post as creative services 
director for GRC Records, Mazur will be 
completely responsible for all album 
cover designs, marketing aids, adver- 
tising, press and photographic services. 
Mazur

cash box/album reviews 
MOTHER LODE - Loggins & Messina - 
Producer: Jim Messina - Columbia PC 331X75 
In typically excellent fashion, Loggins & Mes- 
sina and friends (you really can't dismiss their ex- 
cellent band) have come up with an exotic and 
enticing new Columbia LP, one that holds as 
much chart potential as their live two record set, 
"On Stage" did when it was released. The 
changes they have brought about in pop music 
have been gradual but steady and this LP 
reflects a greater sophistication and musical 
maturity without losing the effervescence that 
has distinguished their past efforts. We dig "Be 
Free," "Fever Dream," and "Move On" best, but 
each will have his own favorite. 
GOT TO FIND A WAY - Curtis Mayfield - 
Producer: Curtis Mayfield - Curtom CRS 8604 
Curtis multi -faceted career continues strongly 
on his new LP comprised of six new originals that 
span a variety of emotional textures and moods. 
Love Me (Right In The Pocket)" is a fantastic 
track featuring the patented Mayfield syn- 
copated bass line and straightforward romantic 
lyrics that are effectively catchy. The LP flows in 
the manner of a 'concept' package yet each tune 
is a separate entity that sparkles with precision 
arrangement and tasteful orchestrated. We also 
like "Mother's Son" and "A Prayer." 
CHER'S GREATEST HITS - Cher - Producer: 
Snuff Garrett - MCA -2127 
The lady that created such a lasting mystique 
with her songs about "Dark Lady," "Gypsies, 
Tramps & Thieves" and "Half -Breed" now puts 
everything into focus with her greatest hits LP, a 
collection that really demonstrates how much 
Cher has meant to the industy and the millions of 
fans that have followed her from 1965 to the 
present. Other smash cuts sure to jog the 
memory pleasantly are "I Saw A Man And He 
Danced With His Wife," "The Way Of Love" and 
"Melody." Another hit LP for Cher. 
ARTISTRY - Deodato - Producer: Eumir 
Deodato - MCA -457 
Highlighted by his sensational "Super Strut," 
Deodato's latest finds the keyboard whiz doing 
once again what he has done consistently in the 
past - make magic music. His arrangements are 
the fibers that hold this tapestry together as they 
have in the past and, as usual, each has been 
woven carefully. Deodato's ear for riffs and 
melody lines keeps him on the charts consis- 
tently and when you listen to this LP, you'll 
discover more of his 'artistry.' We particularly like 
"St. Louis Blues" and "Jivin'." 
WALKER'S COLLECTIBLES - Jerry Jeff Walker 
- Producer: Michael Brovsky - MCA -450 
Thank God for Jerry Jeff Walker. His inimitable 
wit and musical mellow profiles are always a 
delight to listen to and his latest on MCA is no ex- 
ception. Highlighted by the tracks "Salvation 
Army Band," "She Left Me Holdin' " and "Rock 
Me, Roll Me," Jerry Jeff's record is a rare treat in 
that it always holds the promise of the unex- 
pected. His lyrics never cease to amaze in their 
incisive way and the music he writes to go with 
them is natural and easy. 
TERRY SYLVESTER - Terry Sylvester - 
Producer: Ron Richards - Epic KE 33076 
Terry Sylvester may be well known for his high 
harmonies with the Hollies for the past six years, 
but once folks start picking up on his first solo LP 
they're going to be very impressed with both his 
vocal range and song writing ability. In fact, Terry 
wrote everything on the album except the single, 
For The Peace Of All Mankind," an Albert Ham- 
mond composition. The successor to Graham 
Nash in the Hollies, Sylvester proves himself to 
be a very capable solo artist, though by no means 
does he plan on leaving the group that made him 
a star. We like "End Of The Line" and "Pick Up 
The Pieces Again."

I FEEL A SONG - Gladys Knight & The Pips - 
Producer: Tony Camillo - Buddah BDS 5612 
The sensational Grammy winners have come 
through again, this time with a beautiful new 
Buddah LP filled with a great combination of 
soulful ballads and struttin' up -tempo numbers. 
The impeccable harmonies of the Pips carry 
Gladys' lead vocals like a strong breeze carries 
an eagle and the precision arrangement and 
production of Tony Camillo adds even more 
luster to the package. Particularly fine are the hit 
single title track as well as "Better You Go Your 
Way" and "The Need To Be." Fine material writ- 
ten mostly by Jim Weatherly and Bill Withers. 
HOMELESS BROTHER - Don McLean - 
Producer: Joel Dorn - United Artists UA -LA 
315-G 
Once again the insight and foresight of 
talented Don McLean leap into the spotlight via 
his brand new UA LP, one produced by Joel 
Dorn and one that features the artist doing what 
he's always done so well - painting vivid 
emotional pictures in lyrics and music. Par- 
ticularly impressive tracks on this superbly ar- 
ranged and orchestrated album are "Great Big 
Man," "Did You Know," "Wonderful Baby," "The 
Legend Of Andrew McGrew" and, of course, the 
stunning title track. Hard to pick a favorite here, 
especially if you like most, are a Don McLean 
fan. 
WHITE GOLD - The Love Unlimited Orchestra - 
Producer: Barry White - 20th Century T-458 
Conducted by "The Maestro," Barry White 
whose own "Can't Get Enough Of Your Love, 
Babe" LP is currently holding down the #1 spot 
in this week's Cash Box album chart, the new 
Love Unlimited Orchestra prackage is a sheer 
delight. The record is as mellow as a lazy 
evening in July with the sun setting on the 
horizon and is keyed by "Barry's Love (Part 1)," 
"Always Thinking Of You," "You Make Me Feel 
Like This (When You Touch Me)" and "Only You 
Can Make Me Blue." Looks like a sure chart 
smash for Barry's outfit. 
HEAVY - The Stylistics - Producers: Hugo & 
Luigi - Avco AV -69004 
Once again this great soul/pop group has 
come through with a fine LP loaded with those 
sweet ballads and assertive uptempo numbers 
that have distinguished them so notably in the 
past. Russ Thompkins, Jr., Airrion Love, James 
Smith, Herb Murrell and James Dunn blend their 
vocal talents exquisitely here, especially on cuts 
such as "The Miracle," "What's Happenin' Baby," 
"She Did A Number On Me," "From The Moun- 
tain" and "Don't Put It Down Til You Been 
There." Without doubt, this LP has all the neces- 
sary ingredients for success. 
I'VE GOT THE MUSIC IN ME - Kiki Dee - 
Producer: Gus Dudgeon - Rocket/MCA 
MCA -458 
Touring with Elton John, Kiki has gotten 
tremendous exposure already for some of the 
material contained on her new LP. The rest of 
the record will make everyone who hasn't seen 
her perform perk up their ears with interest. The 
title track is a knock out, an uptempo rocker that 
is worlds apart from her first Rocket LP and the 
remainder of the tunes are similar in their bright 
clarity and catchy inventiveness. Gus Dudgeon, 
Elton's producer has done wonders for Kiki and it 
shows. We also dig "Step By Step" and "You 
Need Help." 
BOOGIE BANDS & ONE NIGHT STANDS - Kathy 
Dalton - Producer: Greg Dempsey - DiscReet 
DS 2208 
The amazing one returns, this time with a sure 
fire hit in the exciting title track to complement 
the other fine tunes that were released earlier in 
a different package. Kathy's range and delivery 
are remarkable and her style is infectiously 
catchy. Some of her strong points are found in 
"At The Tropicana," "Gypsy Dancer," "Cannibal 
Forest" and "Midnight Creeper," but listen to 
each cut to get the full impact of Kathy's talent. 
Her stage presence is great so compare it to her 
music and you'll dig the real Kathy Dalton.

Loyola U. Sets 
Radio Confab 
CHICAGO - Loyola University will hold 
its Fifth Annual College Radio Con- 
ference, Nov. 1-3, at the Lewis Towers 
Campus, 820 NORTH Michigan Avenue, 
Chicago, III. 
The Conference, which annually at- 
tracts hundreds of student represen- 
tatives, trade journal editors and mem- 
bers of the recording industry from 
throughout the U.S., is planned and 
organized by Loyola's radio stations, 
WLT and WLUC. 
Sessions will cover a broad range of 
topics including a discussion of the basic 
structure and philosophy of the National 
Academy of Recording Arts and Sci- 
ences conducted by Henry Romersa, 
national NARAS coordinator and 
women's roles in commercial radio, con- 
ducted by Chicago female air per- 
sonalities. 
Technical sessions and programs 
dealing with music, general station 
management, programming, public serv- 
ice, the needs and problems of com- 
muter colleges and universities, produc- 
tion, advertising and sales, and an 
exhibition and demonstration of late 
model studio equipment will complete 
the conference format. 
Coordinators for the conference in- 
clude students John Dundee of WLT and 
Bill Paige of WLUC, and faculty member 
Dr. Sammy Danna. 
Additional info may be obtained by 
contacting either John Dundee at (312) 
670-3129 or Bill Paige at (312) 338- 
WLUC. 
WPLJ Adds 
Berger As 
Program Dir 
NEW YORK - Larry Berger has been 
named program director for WPLJ Radio, 
announced Willard Lochridge, vice 
president and general manager of the 
ABC owned FM station in New York. 
Berger has been program director of 
WRIF, the ABC owned FM station in 
Detroit. An 85% increase in total 
audience was realized at WRIF during 
Berger's past sixteen months as program 
director. 
His programming experience includes 
director of programming for WALL radio, 
Orange County, New York from Sept. 
1968 through Mar. 1973. He was music 
director for WWRL radio, New York from 
1966 through 1968 and prior to this was 
traffic manager and air personality for 
WCTC radio in New Brunswick, New Jer- 
sey. 
DayVideo Formed 
By Seals & Crofts 
SAN FERNANDO - Seals & Crofts 
Productions in Los Angeles have formed 
a new company, DayVideo with Marcia 
Day, president of Dawnbreaker 
Publishing. Dawnbreaker holds ex- 
clusive copyright to all Seals & Crofts 
music. Don Dexter, a graduate student of 
film and television from the University of 
Kansas, has been named executive 
director for DayVideo. 
According to Dexter, DayVideo is 
presently distributing on a national basis, 
video tape copies of the Seals & Crofts 
television special "Live In Chicago," to 
colleges, universities, and cable - 
television systems. Dexter also stated 
that in Jan. of 1975, DayVideo will begin 
production of film and video tape 
programs for commercial distribution. 
In addition to Seals & Crofts, some of 
the artists to be featured are singers 
Walter Heath, England Dan & John Ford 
Colley, and Danny & Joyce Deardorf. 
DayVideo also plans to produce docu- 
mentary and educational films. 
The film and video facilities are 
located in San Fernando, California, in a 
large studio and office building recently 
purchased by Dawnbreaker Music. This 
facility will also house Dawnbreaker's 
24 -track recording studio, sound & light 
company, publishing house, and Day Ar- 
tists Management Company.

Classical 
TV Series

months. These programs are being made

concerts will present Arthur Rubinstein,

Bach. Tchaikovsky and Mozart.

Concertgebouw Orchestra, with Bernard 
Haitink conducting, will be broadcast at 
9:00 p.m. Maestro Rubinstein plays the 
Brahms Piano Concerto No. 
1 
and 
Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 3. 
Great Performances, produced in 
Europe by Unitel and in America by 
Unitel and Amberson Productions, is 
presented by WNET/13 and distributed 
by PBS, the Public Broadcasting Ser- 
vice, through a grant from Exxon Cor- 
poration.

Pointer's Headline 
PBS `Sound Stage' 
LOS ANGELES - The Pointer Sisters 
one -hour PBS television special will air 
Dec. 10 over 220 stations, as part of the 
"Sound Stage" series. Show is entitled 
"Yes We Can Can," from a Pointer hit 
single. 
Program will be televised at 10 p.m. on 
the West Coast, 9 p.m. Central time. 
Ken Ehrlich is executive producer, and 
Dave Erdman directed. Erdman and 
Elliot Wald are also associate producers. 
Special was filmed in part at the 
Pointer's parent's home in Oakland. and 
at their old school yard. Following, 
taping sessions were held at WGTW in 
Chicago, over a three-day period. 
The four sisters are seen and heard 
doing at least 10 songs, and put on their 
own fashion show, with numerous 
costume changes. 
"Sound Stage" usually presents one 
act or performer, but on an occasion 
televises a "concept" show. 
Although the Pointers have made 
numerous television appearances in the 
past year. this is their first headlining 
special.

spots, point -of -purchase merchandisers 
and posters. Walker commented, "I was 
very impressed with the way our 
distributors reacted, especially to the 
merchandising tools we're providing 
them. It was really exciting to see them 
open up and contribute ideas, rather 
than just sitting back like in a typical 
sales meeting. The give-and-take was 
terrific!" 
The wheels have been set into motion 
to mass -market and merchandise all 
these albums in an effort to bring them to 
the attention of the buying public. Farrell 
and Walker and their local distributors 
are currently visiting key retail accounts 
throughout the country and will be doing 
so for the next three weeks. "Co- 
operation from the retail level has been 
extremely encouraging," reported Far- 
rell. 
Al Peckover 
Dies At 48 
NEW YORK - Albert Peckover, vice 
president of Midland International 
Records, died suddenly of a heart attack 
Fri., Oct. 18 at thé age of 48. 
A veteran music man with a 
background in finance, administration 
and dealing with foreign based music 
publishing firms, Peckover had been af- 
filiated with Big 7 Music and was general 
manager of M.R.C. Music prior to joining 
Bob Reno, president of Midland, at the 
label's inception 
He leaves his wife Dorothy and two 
daughters Celia and Karen. The family is 
receiving people at 574 Winchester 
Avenue, Union, New Jersey. 
Lanzetta continued from 10 
"Full utilization" is the catch phrase for 
Lipman's approach. In a recent television 
spot campaign for Jim Stafford's album, 
Lipman and Lanzetta personally con- 
tacted each participating store prior to 
airing the spots. "Dealer awareness is 
always crucial to the success of any cam- 
paign," says Lipman. "I wanted to make 
inventory checks with each store in each 
chain before we ran the spots. While 
I 
was at it 
I made sure in-store display 
material was up and that individual store 
management knew exactly where, when 
and how often Stafford spots would run 
in their market." After the campaign Lip- 
man and Lanzetta called back each store 
for a first-hand response. In Stafford's 
case the response was very favorable. 
Lipman is also finding ways to make 
"full utilization" work in radio and print 
campaigns. "There is an album on Bang 
Records by Paul Davis, called "Ride 'Em 
Cowboy." We decided to start with a full 
page ad in National Lampoon. To get the 
most out of this ad we dealer -tagged it 
region by region and worked out a 
program of in-store play and point of pur- 
chase material with each store when we 
placed the ad. When the ad ran, we 
called back each store to coordinate the 
program and then called back once more 
for store reports." 
For a Mac Davis campaign, Lipman 
decided that the best way to capitalize on 
Davis' summer television exposure was 
to feature the new album, but to include 
catalog wherever possible. The results 
brought Mac's current album to gold 
status and caused a tremendous surge in 
his catalog at the same time. 
A particularly gratifying experience for 
Macey Lipman Marketing is the Randy 
Edelman "Prime Cuts" album on 20th 
Century Records. "So far, we have been 
very successful and we've only done a 
small amount of trade magazine adver- 
tising to call this album to people's atten- 
tion." The bulk of the campaign has been 
direct contact on the dealer and radio 
levels. Posters designed like those seen 
in butcher shops were sent out as 
teasers by Lipman to 500 key dealers 
across the country. A few days later, this 
mailing was followed -up by the album 
and a few days after that 500 prime cut 
steaks were packed and shipped directly 
from Chicago. Winners of the market by 
market Randy Edelman "best window" 
contests were treated to steak dinners 
for two. 
Lipman believes that unusual 
promotions like this one can be effective 
in calling dealer attention to a particular 
project. "They're not right for everyone, 
but when they are right they can be very 
useful." 
The appointment of Tony Lanzetta will 
give Macey Lipman, "more time to deal 
directly and on a creative level with large 
accounts and racks ... to set up chain - 
wide promotions."

Exec Backgrounds 
Randazzo comes to RCA after a 
decade of success as an artist, writer and 
producer. He's also starred in five full- 
length rock 'n roll films. 
Holden will act in liaison capacity, with 
new artists and outside producers as well 
as with artists already on the label. He 
will also figure heavily in the auditioning 
and signing of new talent in the contem- 
porary music area, with whom he'll work 
closely in -studio and out. 
With RCA since 1964, Lipskin has 
produced Lighthouse, Papa John 
Creach, Vintage product, and, most 
recently, "The Gil Evans Orchestra Plays 
the Music of Jimi Hendrix." He has also 
performed as a pianist, having cut his 
own LP, "California Here 
I Come," on 
Flying Dutchman. 
Somerfeld's producing credits include 
David Warner's "Whizz Kid" album debut, 
Nina Simone's current LP, "It Is 
Finished" and Don Imus' "One Sacred 
Chicken To Go." He was assistant 
producer on Lou Reed's "Rock And Roll 
Animal" and has worked closely in all 
A&R matters with Reed, Brian Auger, 
Mick Ronson and Sweet Pete. Berniker 
said he will also function as a coordinator 
in administrative activity.

for newly signed artist McDuff. He's 
previously produced Emperor, Buster

Thomas' hit, "Painted Ladies."

Los Indios Tabarjaras, and Hugo Mon- 
tenegro, all of whom he produced. 
Steeleye Span 
To Begin Tour 
NEW YORK - English folksinging group 
Steeleye Span who just returned from a 
world concert tour will embark on an ex- 
tensive British tour through November 
and December. 
Highlights of the tour include dates in 
Oxford, Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool, 
Glasgow, and London where they will be 
doing two concerts at the Rainbow 
Theater, Nov. 28-29. 
Anderson continued from 7 
Lynn Anderson has cut more than a 
dozen albums since joining Columbia in 
1970, her most recent being "Smile For 
Me" and her forthcoming LP, "What A 
Man My Man Is," due in Nov. All of her 
disks are produced by song- 
writer/producer Glenn Sutton, who is 
her husband. 
Conniff has cut 35 albums since 
becoming a Columbia artist in 1956. Ten 
of these albums have been certified gold 
by the RIAA. His most recent set is "The 
Happy Sound of Ray Conniff," produced 
by Jack Gold. 
Ivil Named To New 
Post At Atlantic 
HOLLYWOOD - Ahmet Ertegun, 
president of Atlantic Records, an- 
nounced today that Anni Ivil has been 
appointed to the newly -created post of 
director of international public relations 
at Atlantic. She will be in charge of 
special projects for key acts involving ar- 
tist development, artist relations, and 
publicity both here and abroad. Anni Ivil 
was formerly the head of Publicity at 
Atlantic, as well as publicity director for 
WEA International and head of creative 
services for Atlantic in London. 
AFE's Nov. 
Disks Set 
NEW YORK - Following on the heels of 
their first Two for One Series set, 
Audiofidelity Enterprises is now 
releasing three additional sets in this 
$7.98 list series: "From Rome And Paris 
With Love," Joe Basile; "Giant Wurlitzer 
Pipe Organ," Leon Berry, and "Circus 
Calliope." 
In the regular $6.98 list series, the new 
records will include four releases with an 
international flavor: "Argentine Hits," 
Dino Hernando & Orchestra; "Mexico 
Sings & Dances," Orquesta De Rafael 
Hernandez Canchola & Sus Voces; 
"Heart Of Mexico," Sonora de Lalo 
Acosta Y Sus Voces, and the long 
awaited new release in the Belly Dance 
series: "Belly Dance Music - An 
Evening With Uncle Tanous." 
One entry in the rock field is a new 
album by a new group: "Iko Iko," The 
Scorpio Brothers, and Sunny Gale will 
break with "Sunny Sings Dixieland." 
Further expansions of European jazz 
are also scheduled for release at this 
time on the Enja label: "With Silence," 
Karl Berger, "African Space Program," 
Dollar Brand, and "Live At The Vangard," 
Elvin Jones.

POINTS WEST — Well, we saw Elvis emerge in the fabulous 50s, watched with dismay
and then awe as the Beatles led the vanguard of the new rock of the 60s, and now, as
1974 draws to to close we will all soon be witness to the latest dance craze to sweep
America and perhaps herald the
arrival of the next BIG
star, Tom Seufert. Who?
Seufert
is not to be trifled with my friend, nor his new Epic single “Casablanca Belly
Roll." Complete with a snake charmer, shiek and belly dancer (who unfortunately
wasn't
either
Little Egypt
or
Fatima), Tommy and
producer Dave Kirshenbaum
displayed the new product at our popular Sunset Blvd. offices before an astounded
staff. What shook everybody up so much was the impact the disk had —
I mean, Manu
Dibango, look out! We've got a record here.
It’s got Hollywood in a frenzy and when
that happens, can Ames, Iowa be far behind.
“The Phantom of the Paradise,” after a long series of legal delays, finally debuted in
Hollywood (Oct. 31). With music by the film’s star, Paul Williams, the comedic horror
flick runs the gamut of tongue
in cheek industry one liners while providing an up-
tempo story line of music and mayhem. Jeffrey Commanor and Keith Allison play
cameo roles, while William Finley plays the elusive Phantom
.
.
. Lee Radziwill was
spotted
at the Marvin Gaye concert at Radio City Music Hall
in the Big Apple (NY)
boogieing like mad with Robert Stigwood and Andy Warhol — soul is where you find
it
.
.
. Andy Kim is in L.A. working on the follow up single to his recent #1 smash, “Rock
Me Gently.”
Iron Butterfly will soar into Paramount studios to cut their first LP with MCA starting
this week with all new material. The eyes and ears of the world will be tuned in for the
results of those sessions to see
if the magic of “Inna Gadda Da Vida”
is
still there.
Check us in January for the results
.
.
. David Gates, former lead singer of Bread will
be Al Schlessinger’s special guest Nov. 3 at the Sherwood Oaks Experimental Col-
lege.
Apparently the
series of
lectures
is going
quite
well and generating con-
siderable interest. Where was
it when
I was slaving away in History 235 at Syracuse?
Enjoyed a fascinating talk with veteran studio engineer Lee Kiefer, particularly his
anecdotes about the various hits he’s tracked. Recently, while taking a break around
5:00 o’clock in the a.m. at a record plant session, Lee and the “artist" shared a couple
of drinks to relax, then said artist solo'd into the studio, sat behind the keyboards and
in one take knocked out a thing called “Nothing From Nothing Leaves Nothing.” Billy
Preston, natch, and Lee says
it was a bit of magic. “We never intended really doing
anything, just kind of filling up time when Billy did his thing.
First take, too, and his
foot tappin’ against the piano gave us the guide for the background laid down later on.
Tom Seufert (behind Fatima) Bellies Up
You can hearthat foot tapping on the record,” Lee says, “if you listen closely.”
Of the more than 1000 LPs I've reviewed this year (so far) for Cash Box, perhaps
the most exciting and rewarding one has been “The Gregg Allman Tour” featuring
Boyer & Talton along with a 24 piece orchestra backing Gregg.
I’ve mentioned the
cuts
I dig in the album review section, but
I feel compelled to praise Gregg for going
out on his own not only to tour, but to make (with the invaluable assistance of Johnny
Sandlin) such a fine record.
In my estimation
it rivals “Live Rhymin' ” for “in studio"
quality which
is remarkable considering the much funkier music that’s dealt with on
this two record set. Most bands and probably individuals would have folded up after
sustaining losses like Gregg did with the death of his brother Duane and bassist Berry
Oakley, but Gregg Allman’s a proud man and should be singled out for extraordinary
merit and praise for carrying a tremendous load on his shoulders and doing
it with
such soul and dignity. Sure, the Stones are greatest, but Gregg, my hat’s off to you
and I’m sure all the folks at Capricorn and in Macon are every bit as proud as
I am of
this superb new LP.

it is still
up in the
air, but
it sounds like a great team
.

.

all that’sjazz
Clear Skies Ahead For Weather Report
picksoftheweek
The music of Weather Report, like its meteorological namesake,
is a uniquely sub-,
tie combination
of
different sounds, moods, and
emotional
attitudes. The com-
positions utilize elements from different musical mediums. The notes, like clouds in a
storm, contest and confirm each other.
In isolation, each note, each measure, and
each composition, in fact, appears remotely detached as
if suspended in mid-air. Yet,
the sensitive organization of the musicians, based as
it
is upon an uncanny under-
standing of each player's proficiency and emotional affectibility, energizes the music
and gives the pieces their meaning. Each note, each composition, however, like the
daily passage of climatic elements, can only be understood after the sun has set and
the end has been revealed.
Joe Zawinul
is one of the energetic leaders of the group. Yet, as Zawinul said, the
title
of “leader”
is
a misnomer. “The
total sound
is the product
of
five unique
musicians. Each of us is very sensitive to the other's feelings. We all take a humble at-
titude towards the other musicians. Our creative philosophies fit together very well.
All the musicians are great improvisors and a creator
is always looking
for fellow
creators, rather than followers. Everyone has an equal voice and the same impor-
tance."
The present members of the group — Zawinul, Wayne Shorter, Dorn Urn Romao,
Darryl Brown and Alphonso Johnson — put together three improvisational lines to
produce the total sound. Supporting the melodic excursions
is a strong and vibrant
wall of rhythm. Zawinul said that “rhythm is life, there’s nothing without rhythm. Only
through
it can you communicate
life. Dorn on percussion and Darryl on drums bring
the music closest to the people. Their backing exudes warmth and yields a strong rap-
port with the audience.”
Zawinul on keyboards and Shorter on tenor and soprano sax are the primary
soloists. Yet Al Johnson on bass provides a smooth harmonic undercurrent that ac-
cents the lead lines and that can also articulate the difficult melodies without a hitch.
The total sound is electic, borrowing elements from rock, “cool” jazz, and the genius
that is Ornette Coleman. Each musician is recognized as a distinct musical individual,
who may take the music in the direction he feels
it is best defined. "We always solo,
but we never solo,” Zawinul said. “Whatever you play, even
if
it
is accompanied,
is
JAZZ: IT’S THE ESSENCE THAT COUNTS
always a solo. Though everyone is playing away from each other and everything is ap-
proached
soloistically,
it
is never completely individualistic, because the solos
fit
together. One could play background, but it isn’t really just background, dig?”
The band was formed in the late ’60’s. Zawinul and Shorter were both in Washing-
ton during the early part of the decade, Zawinul playing with Cannonball Adderly and
Shorter with Art Blakey. Zawinul
related that “Wayne
is such a great writer and
musician. We used to play and talk music all night long.” When Shorter joined Miles
Davis' band, the two separated. However, their musical ideas were developing
in
similar directions: a relaxed, free-form
style of improvisation based upon strong
melodies. They both played with Miles on “In A Silent Way,” “Bitches Brew,” and
“Nefertiti." Zawinul, in fact, wrote many of the key pieces for the group, including “In
A Silent Way,” which was, in many ways, the precursor of the present jazz-rock fusion.
"After Wayne left Miles and
I went back to Cannonball,
it was kind of natural that we’d
eventually get together. We hooked up with Miroslav Vitous, who had similar ideas.
He, too,
is a great improvisor. We added Airto on percussion and Alphonso Mouzon
on drums. No one dominated the other, we just had a good deal of reciprocity.
"
In 1971, the first album, “Weather Report,” was released to unanimous critical ac-
claim. Since that time, the group has released three additional albums on Columbia
(they are presently in the studio cutting their fifth album). Except for Darryl Brown,
the present personnel is featured on the latest record, “Mysterious Traveller.”
It may
seem ironic that the early albums have begun to sell only as a result of “Traveller’s”
commercial success. However, Zawinul reflected, “It takes time, because our music
can only be understood retrospectively, like history. Even when we compose, there is
a lapse of time between the actual writing and the time you can understand
it. Each
part only makes sense in light of the whole. The albums will do better as the people
begin to appreciate them. The last album has the most strength, bottom, and,
I think,
the most emotional sensitivity. The music is more secure and less fragile. People can
really get off on it.”
A band as philosophically and musically unified as Weather Report can remain
coherent even as the
relaxed,
free-form
improvisation suggests an absence
of
musical structure. The emotional respect each musician has for the others sensitizes
the music and gives Weather Report its unique power. Zawinul smiled and said, “Our
music is always fresh, we feel like we haven’t even started. When we get started on
the material we now have, when we can really get it down, it’s going to be some trip!”
Steven marks
THE BADDEST HUBBARD - Freddie Hubbard -
CTI 6047 S
An anthology of Hubbard’s work at CTI. The
first chorus
in
"First Lights" shows Hubbard
at
his best as his melodic variation on the theme
creates a suggestive textual blend with Ron Car-
ter's bass. Echoes of Miles dance on the album's
most interesting piece, “Red Clay,” as Hubbard
plays notes devoid of ornamentation in a relaxed
style that still manages a few rhythmic surprises.
The accents
in
it are often shifted to the even
beats. Of interest, also,
is his dialogue with Her-
bie Hancock on piano. The all-star personnel in-
cludes
Keith
Jarrett
(piano),
Billy Cobham
(drums), and George Benson (guitar).
IN MEMORIAM - The Modern Jazz Quartet - Lit-
tle David 0698
The
final
album
by
the
“third
stream”
in-
novators who have been together for 23 years.
"In Memoriam’s Second Movement,”
is a tribute
to some of the world's greatest musicians,
in-
cluding Schoenberg, Dolphy, Parker and Lester
Young. The MJQ explores the motif announced
by the orchestra in the third chorus. The perfor-
mance is based on Parker’s innovative use of ac-
cents and unstated notes that the listener yearns
to
fill in. The third
riff of “Jazz Ostinado” is an in-
teresting rewrite of a piece originally penned for
Eric Dolphy.
Milt Jackson on vibraphone sug-
gests
here
the
melodic
textures
of
Ornette
Coleman.
NO ANSWER — Michael Mantler — Watt/2
Michael
Mantler
has
set Samuel
Beckett’s
“How
It
Is” to music. The album captures the
confusion that is the meaning through repetitive
piano phrases accented by discordant blasts that
signify
Beckett’s two
voices. The trumpet on
Side A, "Part
3,"
is a
brilliant example of the
voice that speaks yet receives no answer. The
two sides are variations on a similar theme. The
second
is somewhat more
lyrical than the
first.
Carla Bley is on piano, clavinet, and organs. Don
Cherry plays trumpet and Jack Bruce voices the
Beckett narration and plays the bass.
FEEL - George Duke - BASF M C 25355
George Duke’s second solo album for BASF.
A member of the Mother’s of Invention, Duke’s
music
reflects many
of
the
group’s
charac-
teristics: short phrases of percussion-like notes
and simultaneous voicings of the melody line by
differently pitched
instruments. Duke most
ef-
fectively utilizes the
latter technique
in “Funny
Funk" by overlapping statements by
his piano
and
synthesizer.
"The Once
Over”
is
an
in-
teresting
implementation
of
electronics.
The
percussion
instruments take the
lead and
are
backed
by
Duke's
electric
piano. Ndugu and
Airto are on percussion, an unnamed Mother Ob-
dewl’X on
guitar, John Heard on bass and Flora
Pu rim vocals.
JUST ONE OF THOSE THINGS - Stephane Grap-
pelli — Black Lion 211
Grappelli, here heard live at the Montreux Jazz
Festival
of
1973,
re-interprets many
old
up-
tempo standards and ballads. He adds certain
lit-
tle twists which keep them
interesting. The
in-
troduction and the
first chorus on "More” are
subtle
shifts
in harmony and
rhythm. On Cole
Porter’s “Just One of Those Things," the unex-
pected is struck as the piano chorus jumps out of
the medium fast tempo into a more ballad-like 4.
“Honeysuckle
Rose's" combines
stop-chords
with
Grappelli’s
linesflying
over
the accom-
paniment. Grappelli
is on violin, Marc Hemmler
piano.
Jack Sewing
bass, and
Daniel
Humair
drums.

talent on stage 
Roy Clark 
Diana Trask 
FRONTIER, LAS VEGAS - Powerful - 
good entertainment was served up by 
ABC/Dot stars Roy Clark and Diana 
Trask at their recent opening here at the 
Frontier. Roy enthralled the packed 
house with his vocal hits ("Yesterday," 
"When 
I Was Young," et al) but in a 
departure for him, concentrated 
basically on his guitar instrumentals, or 
better said, his "incredible" guitar in- 
strumentals. 
Clark's one of the cleanest and 
quickest pickers on earth and nothing's 
beneath his dexterity, whether it be 
"Orange Blossom Special" "Alabama 
Jubilee" (the opener) or "Malaguena" 
(the clincher). 
A picker's delight was Roy, joined with 
Buck Trent, for a rip through "Dueling 
Banjos." (Buck himself provided a few 
solos on his own which place him among 
the current banjo greats.) 
Diana Trask's performance almost 
drained the audience. She's an outstand- 
ing artist whose vocal power and lyrical 
interpretation continue to surprise. 
While every vocal was outstanding, 
those we'd place on the top shelf include 
"Country Bumpkin," "Behind Closed 
Doors," "Satin Sheets" (which she re- 
styles as "Cotton Sheets") and "Stand By 
Your Man." 
Roy and Diana were backed up the en- 
tire performance by a talented young 
vocal group called the Surrlows, who not 
only helped their friends but helped 
themselves and the audience to three 
tunes on their own. Fine work. 
e.a. 
Frank Zappa and The 
Mothers of Invention 
FELT FORUM, NEW YORK -A famous 
novelist once called his works "serious 
jests." There is no better description of 
the music of Frank Zappa and The 
Mothers of Invention. In many respects, 
Zappa is the most humorous musician 
playing today. He sings about penguins, 
making love to gorillas, and dental floss. 
More importantly, Zappa's knowledge of 
music allows him to perform blues pat- 
terns composed of an odd number of 
bars, when the' normal progression is 
even numbered. So too, he reminds one 
of Peter Schikele, for the chromatic 
scales he plays seem never ending. Only 
the limits of the instruments range ap- 
pear to stop him. 
On the other hand, there are few rock 
guitarists who can even approximate his 
musical abilities. Zappa is one of the 
finest guitar executors and his 
knowledge spans the mediums of jazz, 
rock, and blues. When Zappa joins his 
keyboard specialist George Duke in a 
duo, the resulting sound is both well per- 
formed and intellectually stimulating. 
Even heard in conjunction with Zappa's 
zany lyrics, the music primarily drawn 
from DiscReet's "Apostrophe" and 
"Roxy and Elsewhere," stands forth as a 
testimony to his genius. 
Zappa is acutely aware that most 
musicians take themselves too seriously. 
The Mothers, on the other hand, played 
charade games with the music and 
decorated the stage with strange odds 
and ends, such as a ring buoy, a rubber 
chicken, and a skeleton wearing head- 
phones. His audiences, too, seemed to 
enjoy wearing bizarre costumes. Many 
showed up in Frank Zappa plastic faces, 
glitter make-up a la Kiss, and assorted 
girl scout uniforms and long dresses 
(sometimes on the men). The Mothers 
responded to the atmosphere with a 
jocular attitude. One must wonder 
whether or not the audience under- 
stands Zappa's music and whether or not 
Zappa is laughing with them or at them. 
s.m. 
Loggins & Messina 
Danny O'Keefe 
AVERY FISHER HALL, NYC - As with 
all truly creative musicians Kenny Log- 
gins and Jim Messina have undergone 
changes in their musical structure and 
come up with a more complex main- 
stream of musical expression. Messina 
has taken to the mandolin and come up 
with some very adroit riffs which charac- 
terize most of the new L&M Columbia LP 
entitled "Mother Lode." Their musical 
evolution has taken them past such dit- 
ties as "Danny's Song." "Love Song," or 
"House At Pooh Corner" which when 
performed in an acoustic set came off 
rather weak and lacked the vitality of 
their highly moving electric set. They 
seemed to be straining on the acoustic 
set and felt a great deal more comfor- 
table on the electric set with the rest of 
their accompanying musicians. 
The set was short but well paced and 
the strength came from their newest 
material including "Be Free," "Brighter 
Days" and "Changes." Some of Mes- 
sina's mandolin playing sounds almost 
like a native Greek dance with a tremen- 
dously infectious quality about it. The 
singing was very tight and the accom- 
panying horns and various rhythm in- 
struments filled the sound out. 
A medley of "My Music," "Mama, Don't 
Dance" and "Angry Eyes" brought in- 
stant audience response and the encore 
of "Vahevala," was very well received. 
Atlantic recording artist Danny 
O'Keefe opened the show with an 
acoustic set of minor chord dissonance 
that seemed a suitable backing to his 
somewhat plaintive singing style. The 
highpoint of the set was "Everybody's 
Leavin' Town" which is his best known 
number. 
m.d. 
Paul Anka 
ARIE CROWN THEATER/CHICAGO - 
Paul Anka put on a great show at Arie 
Crown Theater, playing to a packed 
house of very enthusiastic people who 
responded, with obvious affection and 
vigor, to his every move on stage - his 
songs, his quips, his gestures; even the 
discarding of a faulty microphone 
couldn't break the spell and, needless to 
say, this unfortunate occurrence, han- 
dled so adeptly by the star, in no way 
hampered the performance. Here is a 
super entertainer and a professional in 
the truest sense of the term, who can 
cope with just about any situation, in- 
cluding the young lady who seemed to 
appear out of nowhere to present him 
with flowers, and the line of kiss -hungry 
females who besieged the stage at the 
opening set! 
Anka's repertoire centered on his own 
very familiar compositions both from the 
past and present, including a nostalgia 
medley ("Diana," "Puppy Love," "Put 
Your Head On My Shoulder," et al.), the 
classic "My Way" and his current mil- 
lion -seller "Having My Baby"; as well as 
the works of others (i.e. Jim Croce's "Bad 
Bad LeRoy Brown," Neil Diamond's "I 
Am, 
I Said," Elton John's "The Bitch Is 
Back") - all superbly done; and he 
added new dimensions to many of the 
compositions written for and popularized 
by other artists. 
Odia Coates, whom Anka introduced 
about a year or so ago, joined him in a 
very exciting version of "Jubilation," one 
of the stand -out offerings of the evening. 
Her solo reading of "My Imagination" 
was just great! 
Other embellishments on this very en- 
tertaining bill were conductor John Har- 
ris and Anka's newest discoveries, the 
vocal trio Rhodes Chalmers and Rhodes. 
c.c. 
Willie Nelson 
Roy Wylie Hubbard 
TROUBADOUR, L.A. - Willie Nelson 
took his place on stage at the 
Troubadour recently and proved in no 
time at all why he is a mainstay in con- 
temporary country circles with a set that 
polished many facets of his long and il- 
lustrious career. A guitar picker of the 
first magnitude he literally has worn his 
guitar out, coaxing fluid, plaintive lines 
from his old, trusty Martin. 
His band was given ample room to 
show their wares too as Willie led them 
through tunes from his Atlantic albums, 
"Phases and Stages" and his recently 
released "Shotgun Willie." With a 
smooth, controlled and comforting 
singing style, Willie was a true master on 
stage and the audience appreciated 
every minute of it. 
Nelson's power comes particularly 
from his thoughtful reading of country 
lyrics. The songs dealt with familiar 
country themes - love, heartbreak, 
hardtimes, broken relationships, per- 
sonal happiness - but they were made 
unique, and completely Willie Nelson's 
in his personal, one-to-one delivery. 
"Whiskey River," from the new LP, 
opened the show and may prove to be 
one of Nelson's most popular songs. It is 
a perfect drinking lament which found 
more than a few sympathizers in the 
Troubadour crowd and it allowed the 
band to augment Nelson's voice with 
boozily brilliant harmonies. A superlative 
blues medley - "Funny How Time Slips 
Away," "Crazy" and the autobiographical 
"Night Life" - took a tired and battered 
form and made it seem brand new with 
riffs that somehow bridged the years be- 
tween the dirty thirties and contem- 
porary times. 
Other favorites were "Stages and 
Phases," "Bloody Mary Morning" and 
"Stay All Night, Stay A Little Longer." 
Even the instrumentals, a fast break- 
down and a convincing piano boogey, 
proved Nelson's musical taste and 
precision and complemented his song - 
poems beautifully. 
Opening the show for Nelson was Roy 
Wylie Hubbard, a cosmic cowboy bal- 
ladeer who mixed moody, thoughtful 
country laments with lighthearted, frolic- 
some satire. Laid back but certainly not 
limp, Hubbard and his Cowboy Twinkles, 
deserve to be heard a by a wider 
audience. 
j.b. 
Claire Hamill 
BOTTOM LINE, NY - Claire Hamill is a 
young singer with a bubbly personality 
and an engaging voice. She also hap- 
pens to be the first act signed to Ray 
Davies' Kong record label (distributed by 
ABC), so her recent appearances here 
elicited more than just the usual amount 
of curiosity. 
Claire came bounding out on stage 
bolstered by a five piece rock band and 
mixed her material well, going back to 
her first album for a sultry "Baseball 
Blues," dipping into her current album 
for the cabaret styled "Stage Door John - 
nies" and "Oh Daddy," and surprising the 
audience with her interpretations of 
"Tracks Of My Tears" and Davies' 
"Everybody's In Showbiz." 
If fault is to be found in Claire's presen- 
tation, it is due to her band, who after 
only one week have yet to establish a 
rapport. Nevertheless, Claire is finally 
beginning to realize her potential, and 
gracefully overcame this handicap 
through the strength of her original 
material and the rousing nostalgic 
showcloser, "We Gotta Get Out Of This 
Place." 
b.t. 
Henry Mancini 
Anthony Newley 
URIS THEATRE, NY - Pop music 
MOR -style got a big boost in a week in 
which New York was deluged with rock 
talent at the opening on Thurs., Oct. 31 
of Henry Mancini & Anthony Newley at 
the Uris Theatre. 
While Mancini offers the instrumental 
end of the twin -bill and Newley the vocal 
thrust, each has a very special talent in 
common: both are collaborators on some 
of the most successful non -rock songs of 
recent years. These songs (in the case of 
Mancini many of those TV-cinema 
themes) form the bulk of the repertoire 
presented by both. 
The show gets underway with a New 
York medley featuring both Mancini (on 
keyboard) and Newley. It's spirited stuff, 
with the tiresome comic exceptions of 
some put-downs of New York in a let's - 
do -a -New York -stand phone conver- 
sation between the two. As Mancini later 
stated, "any town that could give me 
such great musicians can't be bad." Time 
and time again, the orchestra, with some 
superb solo work, proves this point. 
Mancini's segment opens with a 
muscular "Tommy" Overture, continuing 
on the well-known Mancini melodies and 
a perfectly swell "That's Entertainment" 
medley, from the film scored by Mancini. 
The second half is Newley's turn. 
Newley, a very theatrical, animated per- 
former, often sounds like a self -parody of 
Anthony Newley. He sometimes seems 
eager to finish -up quickly on his Newley- 
Bricusse hit segment, pausing only to of- 
fer some unfamiliar material, one of 
which includes a song he's written for 
the film, "Love Has The Longest Memory 
Of All." The audience liked his "Middle 
Age Rock & Roll Star," introduced by 
Newley as his concession to rock, as ad- 
vised by his manager. Mancini (on flute) 
and Newley also team -up in a fine, sen- 
sitive rendition of Newley-Bricusse's 
"Feeling Good." Newley, by the way, is a 
rarity among English singers: he retains 
his English accent in song. 
i.1. 
Dave Mason 
RADIO CITY MUSIC HALL, NYC - 
Dave Mason has finally settled down with 
a permanent quartet for touring and 
recording devoid of "superstar" per- 
sonalities and the results are an impec- 
cably cohesive blend of music which 
surely ranks with the best Mason has 
produced. 
This was further emphasized with the 
opening segment of the show which saw 
Mason's backing band, the Melons, 
alone in the spotlight led by guitarist Jim 
Kreiger. Along with drummer Rick 
Jaeger, bassist Bob Glauu, and Mike Fin- 
nigan on keyboards, the group exhibited 
fine instrumental prowess during their 
short set which was highlighted by 
Kreiger's "It Can't Make Any Difference 
To Me" from Mason's new Columbia 
album. 
Mason calmly walked out on stage 
cradling an acoustic guitar and im- 
mediately reduced the dimensions of the 
vast hall with a smooth, intimate set of 
acoustic material which included "Can't 
Stop Worrying, Can't Stop Loving," "Just 
A Song," and the delicate "Every 
Woman." He demonstrates a tasteful 
synthesis of harmony and melody which 
carried over to some of the more 
energized electric numbers following in 
the next portion of the show. Of these, 
"All Along The Watchtower," "You Can't 
Take It With You When You Go," and "It's 
Like You Never Left" saw Mason in top 
form, singing in a rich, pliable voice 
while weaving a tapestry of sound from 
his Firebird guitar with an elegantly 
economic touch that earned him three 
encores before the SRO audience could 
be persuaded to leave.

Monument's Major Shifts, 
Expansion Of Exec Duties 
NASHVILLE - Expansion and realign- 
ment of the entire executive staff of 
Monument Records has been revealed 
by Rick Blackburn, vice president and 
general manager. The new exec team 
was introduced during a special 
Monument Afternoon presentation held 
at the Exit/In during Country Music 
Week. 
Monument staff members assuming 
new duties and responsibilities are Tex 
Davis, manager of artist relations and 
country promo manager; John Dorris, 
vice president of finance; and Steve 
Singleton, operations manager. Joining 
the label are Frank DiLeo, director of 
national promo; Ken Kim, advertising 
and merchandising manager; and Janis 
Wainer, publicity manager. 
The entire staff is headquartered in 
Monument's Hendersonville offices and, 
with the exception of Dorris, who reports 
to label president Fred Foster, all will 
report directly to Blackburn. The staff 
reorganization was planned by Black- 
burn, recently named by Foster to ad- 
ministrate Monument and to co-ordinate 
all activities with Columbia/Epic, which 
distributes the label. 
As part of their duties, the new 
Monument department heads will be 
working closely with their counterparts 
within the CBS organization. All promo, 
merchandising, publicity and advertising 
activities will be carried out jointly. 
Several major programs in these areas 
will be announced shortly. In addition to 
working with Monument, Ken Kim will 
continue to operate his design and 
photography studio on a limited basis. 
"The growth potential of Monument 
Records is tremendous." said Blackburn. 
"Fred Foster's ability to discover and 
develop top talent is unmatched. Now, 
we've organized a highly qualified ad- 
ministrative staff so that all of our current 
artists, and those we sign in the future, 
will receive the best support possible." 
He termed the moves a "new era for 
Monument." 
Exec Backgrounds 
Tex Davis adds artist relations to his 
duties as national country promo 
manager, which he's handled since he 
joined Monument in 1968. An extensive 
career in broadcasting, as a radio per- 
sonality and sports director at such 
stations as WCMS, WLOW, WBLJ and 
Davis, Dorris 
KWWL, and as a promoter of country 
music shows, led Davis to his sole record 
company job with Monument. 
John Dorris has been handling finan- 
ces at Monument since he joined them 
as treasurer in March of 1971. Prior to 
that, he was treasurer for Gregg In- 
dustries for two years, a controller of LIN 
Broadcasting for a year and a CPA for 
Price Waterhouse & Co., Certified Public 
Singleton, D. Leo 
Accountants, for three years. He has a 
B/S in accounting from Tennessee Tech 
University. 
Steve Singleton's previous ex- 
perience includes stints as a recording 
engineer at the Jack Clement Recording 
Kim, Ms. Wainer 
Studio, a&r director for the Shelby 
Singleton Corp. and professional 
manager for Raleigh Music.

Ruppert Named 
Buddah's Nat'l 
Promo Director 
NEW YORK - Lewis Merenstein, vice 
president and general manager of The 
Buddah Group, has announced that Fred 
Ruppert has been named national 
promotion director for the company. 
Ruppert will be directing all phases of 
promotion, both AM and FM, with the ex- 
ception of r&b. Art Kass, Buddah's 
president, said, "I know 
I speak for the 
rest of the company in extending the 
warmest welcome to Fred, for as Buddah 
expands the scope of its operations, his 
abilities are as timely as they are first- 
rate." 
A native of New Jersey, Ruppert en- 
tered the music industry in Florida, fol- 
lowing the completion of college at the 
University of Miami. His first job was as a 
buyer in the audio department of Jordan 
Marsh Department Stores. Subse- 
quently he joined RCA's Florida 
promotion staff, and, after breaking three 
records in a year, he was moved to New 
York City. In New York he worked with 
RCA for eight months, the last three as 
associate national promotion director. 
1969-70 saw him with Bell Records, 
first as national album promotion direc- 
tor and then as east coast promotion 
director, in which capacity he handled 
albums, singles, distributor relations, and 
sales. In 1971 he joined Elektra, first as 
assistant to, and then becoming, national 
promotion director. 
During the fall of 1972, he worked with 
Jonathan King, setting up King's U.K. 
Records office in the United States, 
before taking a six months vacation from 
the music industry. 
Famous Music lured him back to the 
industry, and he served, again, first as as- 
sistant and then as Famous' national 
promotion director for 18 months, until 
the company closed down on July 31. 
Prior to joining The Buddah Group, 
Ruppert worked as regional east coast 
promotion director for Shelter Records. 
RSO To Stage 
Musical Based 
On Wodehouse 
LONDON - Andrew Lloyd Webber and 
Alan Ayckbourn, a new song writing part- 
nership, have completed their Jeeves 
musical. They recently arrived back here 
from the U.S., where they visited P.G. 
Wodehouse, now 93, to let him hear the 
final version of the musical, based on the 
famous character Wodehouse created. 
"He made several helpful comments," 
said Webber, "and it's all systems go now 
that we're back in London." 
With the final polishing on the score, 
book and lyrics completed, The Robert 
Stigwood Organization is readying the 
production for a Spring opening in the 
provinces before it comes to London. 
The musical is based largely on "The 
Code of the Woosters," and as yet is 
without a firm title. 
Buddah Inks 
Melba Moore 
NEW YORK -Art Kass, president of The 
Buddah Group, reports that Melba 
Moore has signed an exclusive record- 
ing contract with the company. 
Stated Kass, "Since her success in the 
Broadway Production of 'Hair,' Melba 
has distinguished herself as one of the 
finest performing artists of today, 
whether on records, on the stage, on 
television, or as a nightclub performer. 
Her signing with The Buddah Group is 
something that gives me great personal 
pleasure, and 
I look forward to many, 
many years of success for her as a re- 
cording star." 
A native of New York City, Ms. Moore 
rose to national recognition in late 1968, 
for her starring role in the Broadway 
production of "Hair." Subsequently, she 
starred in the show "Purlie" and won a 
Tony Award for her work. She has per- 
formed in Las Vegas and in major night 
clubs around the country. She was also 
the host of her own television special, 
broadcast by CBS. Considering herself a 
singer first, and an actress second, Ms. 
Moore will shortly go into the studio to 
record her debut album on the Buddah 
label. Also under consideration at this 
time are several offers for starring roles 
in major motion pictures. She has 
previously recorded for Mercury 
Records.

Boudreau Joins Island 
HOLLYWOOD 
Charley Nuccio, 
president of Island Records, Inc., has an- 
nounced the appointment of Steve 
Boudreau to the staff of the recently -es- 
tablished independent label. 
Boudreau will headquarter at Island's 
Los Angeles offices, assisting in all 
aspects of local sales, promotion and 
merchandising. 
He joins Island following four years 
with the Wherehouse record stores. 
Most recently, he was supervisor and 
buyer for the northern California division 
of the Wherehouse, where he was di- 
rectly involved in import buying. 
Griewank Named 
To CBS Marketing 
NEW YORK - Joan Griewank has been 
appointed to the position of marketing 
planning of Columbia Records, an- 
nounced Jack Craigo, vice president of 
marketing of CBS Records. 
In her new capacity, Ms. Griewank will 
be responsible for activities relating to 
the development of overall marketing 
plans and programs for Columbia 
Records product. Her responsibilities 
will include the Market Research func- 
tion and special projects that involve 
coordination between marketing plan- 
ning or market research and the finance, 
long range planning and operations 
departments. She will report directly to 
Craigo.

Sherman To 
Casablanca Post 
HOLLYWOOD - Dick Sherman, with 
Bell Records the past two years, has 
been named national director of 
marketing and sales for Casablanca 
Records in Hollywood, it has been an- 
nounced by Neil Bogart, president of the 
independent label. 
"His past experience with major com- 
panies will be invaluable to us," Bogart 
stated. "His sales and marketing 
background for independents and major 
corporations sets his understanding of 
that end of the business far above the 
normal sales managers." 
Sherman has been executive director 
of west coast operations with Bell, han- 
dling a&r plus marketing. Prior to that, he 
had headed west coast marketing for 
Motown's MoWest and Natural Resour- 
ces labels and was Warner Brothers 
Records national sales manager from 
1967 to 1971. 
His background also includes five 
years with Mercury in national sales, as 
product manager for Limelight label and 
for pre-recorded tape. 
Sherman, a former pro basketball 
player, has a track record of 20 years in 
the record industry. He holds a BS in 
economics and an LLB in law.

Capitol Secretary

EMI, Inc. 
Tillinghast joined Capitol in April of 
1963 as an attorney in the law depart-

positions of increased responsibility in

Carbone Named 
ABC Product Mgr. 
LOS ANGELES - John Rosica, vice 
president of marketing at ABC Records, 
has announced the appointment of Joe 
Carbone to the new position of product 
manager for the label. Carbone, who has 
worked for ABC in various capacities for 
the past nine years, was most recently in 
charge of special projects at the com- 
pany. 
As product manager, Carbone has 
been charged initially with supervising 
all facets of ABC's Oct. release. Sub- 
sequently, his duties will focus on acting 
as a liaison between ABC and its artists 
and their managers, planning and coor- 
dinating advertising, merchandising and 
promotional campaigns for all new 
product. He will report directly to Rosica. 
Commenting on the appointment, 
Rosica said, "Carbone's background and 
experience in the sales area will be in- 
valuable to him in his new position. And 
having been much involved in our new 
distribution system he can readily relate 
to the needs and wants of our 
distributors as well as to those of our 
sales department.'

Atlantic Pacts 
With Nemperor 
NEW YORK - Ahmet Ertegun, chairman 
of the board and chief executive officer 
of Atlantic Records, has concluded a 
worldwide distribution agreement with a 
new custom label, Nemperor Records. 
Nat Weiss, president and founder of 
Nemperor, was the American partner of 
the late Brian Epstein, and as such, 
represented the affairs of the Beatles in 
the U.S. He has also worked as a lawyer 
and advisor for James Taylor, Peter 
Asher, Cat Stevens, John McLaughlin, 
and Chick Corea. Regarding initial Nem- 
peror projects, Weiss has made it known 
that the first record scheduled for 
release this month will be a rock album 
performed by Jan Hammer and Jerry 
Goodman titled "Like Children." Both of 
the artists are former soloists with the 
Mahavishnu Orchestra. 
Among the releases to follow, will be 
an album by Stanley Clarke, the well- 
known bassist who plays with Chick 
Corea's group, Return To Forever. This 
album includes performances by Tony 
Williams (drums), Airto (percussion), Jan 
Hammer (keyboards), and Bill Connors 
(guitar). 
Weiss, in establishing the label, has in- 
dicated that Nemperor will not be con- 
fined to any one category of music, but 
will cover all areas of jazz, folk/rock, and 
rock. 
The Nemperor offices will be at 75 
Rockefeller Plaza. 
CBS Merch Posts 
Dempsey VP, DeVito 
Oberman Fill Slots 
NEW YORK - CBS Records has made 
three promotions in its merchandising 
division, according to Jack Craigo, vp of 
marketing. 
Don Dempsey has been named vp of 
merchandising at CBS Records; Don 
DeVito has been appointed director of 
national merchandising at Columbia 
Records, while Ron Oberman has been 
named director of west coast merchan- 
dising at Columbia. DeVito will report 
directly to Dempsey, while Oberman 
reports to DeVito. 
As vp of merchandising, Dempsey, 
who reports to Craigo, will be respon- 
sible for the creation of merchandising 
programs for all Columbia artists and for 
overseeing the creation and implemen- 
tation of all national and retail adver- 
tising, sales promotion and graphic 
design for the label. He will maintain 
liaison with a&r for assigned artists and 
with the marketing dept. for the ad- 
ministration of support programs for 
CBS Records product. He will also have 
ultimate responsibility for merchandising 
activities with the artist development, ar- 
tist relations, product management and 
college departments. 
DeVito and Oberman, on a national 
and regional basis, respectively, will 
have creative responsiblities for mer- 
chandising programs in retail adver- 
tising, sales promotion and graphic 
design. 
Dempsey has been assoicated with 
CBS since 1964, most recently as 
regional director of the southeast region. 
DeVito joined CBS in 1967, and most 
recently served as director of product 
management at Columbia Records. 
Oberman joined CBS in 1972 as as- 
sistant director of press and information 
services, and most recently served as 
director of the dept.
