Hal Leonard To Pub 
Woody Herman Charts 
For School Ensembles 
NEW YORK - Jazzman Woody Herman 
and Hall Leonard Publishing, producers 
and distributors of educational musical 
products, recently co -announced the in- 
troduction of a new music series for high 
school and college jazz ensembles. To 
introduce the series, the publishing firm 
currently packages the appropriate 
Woody Herman Fantasy album with the 
new arrangements, which now include 
"Corazon," "Blues For Poland," "Alone 
Again (Naturally)," and "The First Thing I 
Woody Herman and his Young Thun- 
dering Herd have appeared at the Mon- 
treux Festival last summer. The results 
were recorded on the Fantasy album 
"The Herd At Montreux." In the last few 
months, the band has toured with Frank 
Sinatra and has performed in concert 
with the Houston Symphony. 
The Herd is presently visiting schools 
for jazz seminars and concerts. They use 
an approach to teaching that typifies the 
changes occurring in school music to- 
day. The jazz ensemble has been placed 
in a new position of importance 
alongside the marching band, sym- 
phonic band and orchestra. Each solo 
part in the published score is an exact 
transcription of the performers im- 
provisation. The soloist's name is noted 
on the part. 
The Woody Herman Series arrange- 
ments are now available through area 
music dealers throughout the U.S. and 
Canada. 
picksof the week 
IN CONCERT - Freddie Hubbard/Stanley Tur- 
rentine - CTI 6044 
One of the finest CTI releases to date. The 
"session men" include Herbie Hancock, Jack 
DeJohnette, Ron Carter and Eric Gale. The LP is 
composed of two extensive tracks. entitled 
"Poyo" and "Gibralter." Hubbard's articulation on 
the latter 32 -bars of his 64 -bar chorus of "Poyo" 
is clear and precise. It blends into Turrentine's 
solo. which is characterized by rhythmically 
spiced scales. Hancock's solo is quite 
percussive. as one would expect. His chordal 
dialogue with Eric Gale is the most interesting 
harmonic moment on the track. The album truly 
abounds with feeling. 
LIVE AT THE VILLAGE VANGUARD - Elvin 
Jones - Enja 2036 
One member of John Coltrane's old band who 
has not been unfairly typecast as "a Trane 
sideman" is Elvin Jones. On this live album. 
Jones is joined by George Colman on tenor. 
Wilbur Little on bass and Marvin Peterson on 
trumpet. Jones (with Sunny Murray) developed a 
polyrhythmic style which has rarely been 
equaled. His solo on "By George" is an 
avalanche of notes which are expertly articulated 
in spite of (or because of) the rapid tempo. Note 
the spaces in Coleman's sax solo on "Laura." He 
interestingly uses the rests to change the line's 
rhythmic quality. 
STANLEY CLARKE - Stanley Clarke - Nem- 
peror NE 431 
Stanley Clarke's first album as a leader. The 
talented bassist is best known for his work with 
Return To Forever, though he has also gigged 
with Horace Silver and Art Blakey. and has re- 
corded with Pharoah Sanders and Stanley 
Cowell. The rhythmic "Vulcan Princess" is driven 
by Clarke and Tony Williams on drums. Watch 
the movement from minor to major keys and 
back again. Williams, in many ways, is the pro- 
totypical jazz-rock drummer. Check the free 
rhythms on "Lopsy Lu." For Williams, the gaps 
between the notes are as important as the notes 
themselves 
DOM UM ROMAO - Dom Um Romao - Muse 
5013 
This is Dom Um Romao's first album as a 
leader. Though best known as the percussionist 
of Weather Report. he has also played with Brasil 
'66. The music is "samba de rica." sambas of the 
street. It is characterized by its percussive feel 
and textures. However. it doesn't exhibit the 
weak syncopation and lack of drive characteristic 
of old bossa nova tracks. In many ways. "Braun- 
Blek-Blu" is the album's motif. A solo track, the 
piece is marked by an extraordinary scat and 
closes with a rhythmic flourish. Among the musi- 
cians are Stanley Clarke. Eric Gravatt and Joe 
Beck. 
TRANSITION - Buddy Rich and Lionel Hampton 
- Groove Merchant GM 3302 
A combination of two moods and styles. as the 
jacket proclaims. the record is "a passage from 
one state, stage or subject to another." The first 
side is composed of standards like "Avalon" and 
"Ham Hock Blues." Zoot Sims' crystal clear 
chorus on "Avalon" is backed by George 
Duvivier on bass and Teddy Wilson on piano. 
Check out Hampton's first two multi-malleted 
12 -bar choruses on "Blues." The second side. 
tracked by somewhat abstract sounding tunes 
like "E.G." and "Fum," attempts to integrate rock 
patterns by adding rhythmic guitar and sax lines. 
Note Sal N istico and Jack Wilkens' solos. 
AT BASIN STREET - Clifford Brown and Max 
Roach - Trip TLP 5511 
Trip Records has begun to reissue the old 
Emarcy catalogue of jazz records. Now. many im- 
portant tracks will again be available to the public 
and many historical gaps will be filled. This 
record is a stylist's delight. Brownie was one of 
the few trumpeters who developed a viable post - 
bop style. His strong tone and sensitive 
harmonic experiments are most clearly stated in 
"What Is This Thing Called Love?" Roach. too, 
helped to make the drum a meaningful solo in- 
strument: a creative force which could do more 
than keep time. Note also the performance of an 
unknown saxophonist named Sonny Rollins.

HOLLYWOOD -CASH BOX'S GREATEST HITS: THE EDITORS DISCUSS THEIR '74 FAVES 
JACK BRESCHARD 
TIM HOGAN 
The best music in 1974 came from the 
many seasoned veterans who used their 
years of popular success as a base from 
which to explore new modes of ex- 
pression in popular song. Mature. 
sensitive artists like Joni Mitchell, Randy 
Newman, Paul Simon and Jackson 
Browne painstakingly polished their craft 
while trying to reflect on life around and 
within them. There was spectacle to 
spare too without the obvious banality of 
glitter and pseudo -theatrics in the return 
of Bob Dylan and George Harrison to the 
concert stage. There was even one over- 
night sensation (years in the making) in 
the meteoric career of Johnny Bristol 
who wrote and produced hits of the 
highest caliber for himself and his many 
friends. 
But of all the acts who produced 
brilliant music in 1974 Loggins and 
Messina stand out as the artists most 
likely to continue growing throughout 
the coming year to take an even more 
commanding place in the music scene in 
1975. 
Changes For L&M 
Loggins & Messina 
The academy is no longer in peril as 
the flow of continental flavored rock and 
jazz floats across the oceans toward 
these sometimes distant shores. The 
tastes of the public are maturing at a fan- 
tastic rate, forcing artists to continually 
search their musical souls for innovative 
performances, both on record and in 
concert. The horizons of rock and roll are 
forever expanding and it looks like the 
next big thing is right around the corner. 
There have been upheavals and overnite 
sensations, millions made and millions 
lost. There's been great news and sad 
stories. But most of all, there's been 
another year gone by that makes living in 
the ear a grand pleasure. To all those in- 
volved in the fun of it all, 1974 has got to 
register as a year to tell the 
grandchildren of. And to all my out -of - 
work friends, the most sincere bushel of 
good luck. 
It's Only Rock 'N Roll 
But I Like it

BEST NEW GROUP - Though Paul 
Kantner and Grace Slick after their years 
of success with the Jefferson Airplane 
can hardly be called new artists, their 
new band called Jefferson Starship 
featuring David Freiberg, Papa John 
Creach, John Barbata, Craig Chaquico 
and Pete Sears showed more life and 
zest than anything else around. With 
Marty Balin, '75 should be remarkable.

BEST NEW MALE ARTIST - After serv-

Orchestra, Billy Cobham stepped out on- 
to his own and produced spectacular 
sounds. In concert he displayed a 
formidable command of all styles of 
drumming and led an impressive group

Jefferson Starship 
BEST NEW FEMALE ARTIST - The 
popular acceptance of Kiki Dee was long 
overdue and much appreciated. Touring 
with Elton John he introduced Kiki to 
thousands and thousands of new ears 
and helped break her loose. Minnie 
Riperton's time is yet to come, but she 
too made an impressive bid for the 
spotlight. 
Billy Cobham 
BEST OF THE NEW SOUNDS 
BEST NEW GROUP - Not exactly new to 
the scene. Genesis have made their pre- 
sence felt this year by way of four albums 
of new and old material. Led by rock 
dramatist Peter Gabriel, Genesis have 
moved far into the forefront of perform- 
ing acts by backing their intriguing stage 
show with powerhouse musicality, laying 
out a magnetic force field of deluxe en- 
tertainment. 
Eno 
BEST NEW FEMALE ARTIST - Flora 
Purim's lilting Brazilian flavored vocal 
stylings have delighted jazz fans through 
two solo albums released on Milestone 
this year. Surfacing on an imported re- 
lease of Chick Corea's original Return To 
Forever, Flora has proved herself a solo 
artist to watch and listen to. with baited 
anticipation of her next recorded move. 
Genesis 
BEST NEW MALE ARTIST - Why 
"Baby's On Fire" was never relesaed as a 
single Stateside, I'll never know. But it 
could have been Eno's big move to 
public attention. Springing out of the 
foxy Music fold in 1974, Eno, in his own 
esoteric way, redefines music, while ex- 
hibiting one of the most unique voices to 
hit rock in years. Let's hear more!

all that's jazz 
RETROSPECT - JAZZ '74 
Perhaps the most obvious deficiency in jazz music in the '70's is the absence of a 
responsible musical leadership. It is a truly curious want, because the '60's was a 
veritable cornucopia of dynamic, articulate individuals. Men like John Coletrane, 
Omette Coleman, and Archie Shepp tellingly revitalized the post -bop stagnation. 
Many of the creative possibilities suggested by their free -blowing, anti -structural 
sound, in fact, still remain unexplored. Most importantly, they developed a style and a 
quality of performance which has become an almost indispensable part of an artist's 
repertoire. 
The past year has seen the proliferation of groups and the elaboration of different 
musical moods and textures. So, too, jazz seems to be gaining the respect it deserves 
as America's only original musical artform. Yet, in spite of the, commercial popularity 
of musicians like Chick Corea, Billy Cobham, and Herbie Hancock, the '70's still lack 
the leadership and charisma of men like Coltrane and Coleman. It is Keith Jarrett's 
dedication to music as Music, and his personal selflessness which mark him as a 
performer worthy of emulation. For this reason, I have selected him as "Jazzman of 
the Year." 
Keith Jarrett 
Flora Purim 
TOP MALE PERFORMER - Keith Jarrett is an outspoken, iconoclast who has 
criticized some of the more questionable devices his contemporaries have used to 
achieve commercial success. So, too. he has tried to terminate the period of stagna- 
tion which many musicians have fallen into persuasively demanding a new musical 
evolution. His own recent solo performances are technical and emotional 
masterpieces which create a link between the audience and the artist, which form a 
spiritual chain uniting listener and performer. It will only be a matter of time before 
Jarrett receives the attention and critical acclaim that he deserves. 
TOP FEMALE PERFORMER - Flora Purim's vocal style will be as influential in the 
'70's as Billie Holliday's was in the late '40's and early '50's. Ms. Purim handles her 
melodic lines in a unique manner. Her voice breaks up the structure of a chord into its 
intervallic parts. Her combination of note groups and repeated modulations cannot 
be described - they must be heard. Her vocal effects, to put it mildly, are ex- 
traordinary 
Weather Report 
Bill Waltrous 
TOP ENSEMBLE - Weather Report is, perhaps, the most philosophically and 
musically unified jazz-rock combo. And yet, the band never locks itself into one kind 
of sonority. The members are constantly reaching out for new styles to play and new 
musical moods to latch onto. Weather Report's albums must be heard together, for it 
is the total sound which gives the band its unique power. 
TOP BIG BAND - Bill Watrous has payed his dues with' many important jazz big 
bands, such as the Quincy Jones group and Woody Herman's Herd. He has also 
performed with "The Dick Cavett Show" band and jazz-rock's Ten -Wheel Drive and 
Eclipse. All these influences come to bear in "Manhattan Wildlife Refuge." The 
group's first album on Columbia is a gem. In many ways, MWR will be the big band of 
the future.

Vee Jay Sponsors LA Jazz Concerts 
HOLLYWOOD - The week of December 
10 was proclaimed as "Jazz Week" by 
Mayor Tom Bradley, and Vee Jay In- 
ternational Records complied with the 
Mayor's proclamation by staging a free 
jazz concert Wed. Dec. 12, which was 
held at LaBoe's On The Strip (formerly 
Ciro's). 
Assisted by Chuck Niles of KBCA/FM 
Radio Station, Pat Britt vice president of 
Vee Jay International Records as- 
sembled a group of available jazz musi- 
cians on short notice, and the results 
brought back shades of "Jazz At The 
Philharmonic." to a very receptive au- 
dience that filled three fourths of the 
large room. 
The concert was played in three sets. 
with the first set featuring Gary Barone, 
trumpet; Mayo Tiana, trombone. Kent 
Glenn, piano; Mark Proctor, bass; Harold 
Jones, drums; and Pat Britt on alto; this 
set unveiled several original composi- 
tions an 
ig ig e. a musica n. u - . 
the Mayor in the form of a swinging tune 
entitled "Mayor Bradley's Blues." 
Vocalist Bill Henderson joined the 
group in the second half of their set, and 
brought the house down with his vocal 
renditions of "That Ole' Black Magic," 
"Funny Valentine," and a crowd pulsat- 
ing version of "Goin' To Chicago Blues." 
The following guest sets included Wild 
Bill Moore, tenor; Hart Smith, trombone; 
John Gross, tenor; Foster Johnson, 
piano; and Alex Rodriguez, trumpet; wit- 
nessed by Jerome Richardson, Harry 
"Sweets" Edison, and Al Viola in the au- 
dience. 
picks of the week 
REBIRTH - Earl and Carl Grubbs - Muse 5047 
The Grubbs Brothers, known professionally to 
Philly jazz fans as the Visitors, have put together 
their second album as leaders. Cousins (by mar- 
riage) of John Coltrane, the brothers have 
benefited from the sax master's tutelage in music 
theory. They have, additionally, gigged with 
Pharoah Sanders and Leon Thomas. The two 
saxophonists have put together a superb rhythm 
section composed of Buster Williams on bass. 
Albert Heath on drums and Sonny Morgan on 
percussion. "Glad To Be Sad" revolves around 
the interaction of the two sax lines above Kenny 
Barron's piano. Carl reminds one here of Dolphy. 
HOMAGE TO ELLINGTON IN CONCERT - Gun- 
ther Schuller - Golden Crest - CRS -31041 
This collection of some of Ellington's greatest 
hits was. recorded live early this year before the 
Duke's death. The pieces are performed by the 
New England Conservatory Jazz Repertory 
Orchestra. As Schuller writes, the album is "a 
sort of musical verite": the tunes are played ex- 
actly as Ellington's orchestra recorded them in 
the studio. Bruce Henderson performs Harry 
Carney's solo on "Jack The Bear" and his re- 
construction of Carney's tone and phrasing is so 
perfect that it is quite frightening. The sides help 
demonstrate the historical importance of Ell- 
ington's music. 
DIMENSIONS - Maynard Ferguson - Trip - 
TLP-5507 
Another of Trip's re-releases of the old Emarcy 
catalogue. The tracks were recorded in 1954 and 
1955 and show Ferguson's work with two dif- 
ferent ensembles. The cuts are composed of in- 
terestingly mixed periods of improvisation and 
orchestration. In fact, on tunes like "Breakfast 
Dance" a traditional 12 -bar blues, it is the fully 
orchestrated sections that command the major 
interest. The musicians and each solo with an 
ensemble figure, giving the piece a feeling of 
continuity. It gives the group a big band feel 
without mitigating the freecinm of the small 
group. 
THE CUTTING EDGE - Sonny Rollins - 
Milestone - M-9059 
This album was recorded live at the 1974 Mon- 
treux Jazz Festival. It is one of the best of the 
several albums recorded at the historic date 
Rollins is joined by several outstanding sideman 
including Stanley Cowell on piano, Masuo on 
guitar, Mtume on percussion, and Bob Cranshaw 
on electric bass. There is an air of excitement 
running through most of the charts. In fact, the 
somewhat staid European audience called the 
band back for three encores. On the title track, 
Rollins reflects his experiences with Brownie 
through a repeated series of forcefully articulat- 
ed notes which shatter the calm of the backing. 
NEWLY DISCOVERED PERFORMANCES - 
Lester Young - ESP disk -3017 
ESP has collected some previously un- 
released "Prez" live broadcasts from the Royal 
Roost in Nov. and Dec. of 1948. Symphony Sid, 
of course, is the master of ceremonies. Young is 
joined on most of the tracks by Ted Kelley on 
trombone, Freddie Jefferson on piano. Roy 
Haynes on the drums, Jessie Drakes on trumpet, 
and Ted Briscoe on bass. The first side naturally 
opens with "Lester Leaps In." This rendition may 
be one of the finest Prez performed. "How High 
The Moon?" a massive jam session featuring 
Ella Fitzgerald, codas with a nice version of 
ology." 
LET IT HAPPEN - Jazz Piano Quartet - RCA 
CPL -1-0680 
The Jazz Piano Quartet is composed of Marian 
McPartland, Dick Hyman, Roland Hanna, and 
Hank Jones. The obvious pleasure in listening to 
an album of this kind is to compare the different 
phrasings and styles of the four pianists and to 
see how the changes in choruses underlie shifts 
in moods. The album includes Herbie Hancock's 
"Maiden Voyage" and "I mproviso" a composition 
based upon a fragment by Satie. The four piano 
lines on the latter pieces is a musical journey 
through the history of French School and such 
representative artists as Ravel, Debussy, and 
Scriabin. 
Lester Young
